en: I bow to that Lord, the enemy of Kaiṭabha, in whom neither karma nor its fruition exist, from whom all afflictions have ceased, and who is not subject to the limitations of anyone; whom the Goddess of Time, though she measures all things in the world, cannot perceive as limited by time.

Salutations to that Guru, the teacher even of teachers, who is all-knowing and possesses the power of all sovereign manifestations; whose actions and their fruits are free from defects; and who is the cause of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe.

[1.21] Now begins the *Vivaraṇa* on the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* of the *Pātañjala-yoga-śāstra*, starting with the words "atha" (now) and so forth. In this regard, since a connection and purpose that have not been stated do not suffice to motivate a person toward engagement or desistance, the connection and purpose intended by the author of the Sūtras—which serve as the cause for such engagement—are first made manifest.

[2,1] Regarding that, first the purpose: it has been explained by way of demonstrating the fourfold arrangement (*caturvyūha*) in the science of medicine (*cikitsāśāstra*). That is to say: the science of medicine consists of four arrangements—disease, the cause of disease, health, and the remedy. Furthermore, by way of injunctions, prohibitions, and restrictive rules, it is dedicated to the exposition of the subject matter of these four arrangements.

Likewise here too, beginning with the aphorism, "To the discerning person, all is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the fluctuations of the guṇas" (YS 2.15), the fourfold structure of the treatise is demonstrated. Namely: the cycle of existence, which abounds in suffering, is to be abandoned; its cause is the conjunction of the seer and the seen, which is rooted in ignorance; and the means of abandonment is unflinching discriminative discernment.

When discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) has arisen, there is the cessation of ignorance; upon its cessation, there is the absolute end of the conjunction between the seer and the seen, which is liberation (*hāna*). That itself is isolation (*kaivalya*). Because this [purpose] is motivated by isolation, which stands in the place of health, that isolation alone is its purpose.

[2.10] But surely, that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) and its cause (*taddhetu*) need not be introduced, because they serve no purpose; for the scripture is motivated by abandonment (*hāna*), and thus only discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), which is the means to that [abandonment], should be taught. For one whose foot is pierced by a thorn does not inquire about the pain and its cause, but rather seeks only the removal of the thorn. This is not so; for the means to abandonment depends upon that which is to be abandoned and its cause.

As long as it is not explained that this wheel of saṃsāra must be abandoned by this means, and that its cause is the conjunction of the seer and the seen, which has ignorance as its source, so long can discriminative discernment—which is the antidote to ignorance—not be explained. For we observe that a sick person seeks medicine only when they desire the abandonment of what is to be abandoned along with its cause; indeed, a medical treatise is never taught without taking into account both the disease and the cause of the disease.

[2.18] Furthermore, the relationship (*sambandha*) is such that the fruit to be accomplished (*sādhya*) for discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is indeed liberation (*hāna*), and the means (*sādhana*) for liberation is precisely discriminative discernment; thus, there is a mutual restriction between the goal and the means, and no other relationship. For example, the fruit of medicine is health alone, and the means for health is medicine alone; this is a mutual restriction, and that [restriction] is derived from the treatise (*śāstra*). Therefore, the instruction on yoga (*yogānuśāsana*) possesses both a relationship and a purpose.

[2,23] But surely, if cessation (*hāna*) is the goal and discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is its means, then it should have been stated there as "Now, the instruction on discriminative discernment" (*atha vivekakhyātyanuśāsanam*). For what purpose was it formulated as the aphorism "Now, the instruction on yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*)?

[2,26] Since yoga is the means (*upāya*) for that [attainment], the means itself must be explained. For when the goal (*upeya*) is demonstrated, the goal remains expectant of the means; thus, the means, along with its constituent parts and branches, must be explained once again. And when that has been stated, everything indeed has been stated.

[3.1] How is it that this constitutes the means (*upāya*)? Because the author of the Sūtras says: "From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). And also: "In the clarity of the state beyond discursive thought (*nirvicāra-vaiśāradya*), there is internal serenity; therein, wisdom (*prajñā*) is truth-bearing (*ṛtaṃbhara*). Likewise, the Commentator also says: "But that which, in a one-pointed mind, illuminates the real object. And the comprehension of the real object is indeed discriminative discernment.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the instruction on Yoga as the means was formulated as the very first Sūtra.

[3.6] But surely, discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) results from the practice of the limbs of yoga; therefore, one might object that it should have begun with "Now follows the instruction on the limbs of yoga. This is not so, because the work begins with the result: since the result of practicing the limbs of yoga is indeed yoga itself, it is appropriate to begin with that.

[3,9] If it were thus approached by means of abandonment—no, because that [abandonment] is not the goal to be attained; for that [abandonment] is indeed merely the goal itself. Yoga, however, is both the goal and the means of its own constituent parts, as well as the means for the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) and the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā*; thus it is more highly esteemed, because it consists of both the fruit and its means (or because it is the cause of the fruit and its means).

[3,12] And because it is for the purpose of explaining the meaning of the subsequent sūtras. For when it has been stated, "Now follows the instruction on the limbs of yoga," it would not be appropriate to immediately state, "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. In that case, the sūtra concerning the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), and so forth, would have had to be recited first.

If it is argued that this very [sūtra] should be recited [at the beginning], we say no; for the purpose of this sūtra, "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind," is to demonstrate the relationship between yoga—which is the means (*upāya*) for attaining the goal (*upeya*), namely discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) which serves as the means for abandonment—and the fruit, which is abandonment itself.

[3,18] But how is this for the purpose of demonstrating the connection, given that this is a statement of the characteristics of seedless samādhi? True, it is so; nevertheless, it is precisely by illuminating the connection between abandonment and its means that the sūtra attains the status of being a definition of seedless samādhi.

[3.21] For abandonment is not something distinct from the concentration characterized by cessation. Rather, there is this much distinction: in the concentration characterized by cessation, there is no further activity [of the mind], whereas in abandonment, there is absolute cessation. However, during the state of concentration, there is indeed no difference regarding abandonment. And so it has been said: "Then the seer abides in its own nature."

"And the power of consciousness established in its own nature is isolation (kaivalya). Thus, it states that isolation is indeed being established in one's own nature. Consequently, through seedless samādhi, isolation itself is directly realized for the sake of strengthening the conviction regarding the meaning of the scriptures.

Therefore, as for what some say—that "seeded samādhi" (sabīja-samādhi) is the means to liberation—that is not so. Rather, discriminative discernment (khyāti) alone is the means, by way of the cessation of ignorance (avidyā). For bondage has ignorance as its cause.

Thus, although the instruction on yoga (yogānuśāsana) was formulated as a sūtra, since yoga exists for the sake of discernment, it also demonstrates the connection to the abandonment of discernment through that very door. Consequently, it is rightly said that the sūtra "the instruction on yoga" should be formulated for the purpose of connecting with the subsequent sūtras.

[4,6] Although there is indeed instruction regarding the means for those seeking a result who desire that very means in the present, nevertheless that [instruction] is not the purpose; since everyone engages in action with a view toward the result, that [result] alone is the purpose.

[4.8] Regarding the phrase *yogānuśāsanam*: just as a student (*śiṣya*) is instructed by means of rules concerning specific activities and abstentions, so too, because it shares the commonality of being merely a rule regarding the specific goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and their constituent parts (*aṅga*), it is called "the instruction on yoga" (*yogānuśāsana*), like the instruction given to a pupil. Instruction (*anuśāsti*) is "instruction" (*anuśāsana*). That by which yoga is instructed, or that in which yoga is instructed, is the treatise (*śāstra*) known as the *Yogānuśāsana*.

[4,12] Now, the word *atha* (now/then) has the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*). Introduction means commencement or preface; its meaning is that which is to be expressed, because it is authoritative according to the traditional codes of the learned (*śiṣṭasmṛti*). But surely the learned remember the word *atha* as having the sense of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*)? And so it is said: "The sense of 'the treatment of what follows immediately after' is observed. No, for it does not have that meaning in every instance, since it serves here as an introduction and because immediacy is already understood. Just as when the word "son" is uttered, the "father" is understood, yet [the word "son"] does not [primarily mean father].
The meaning of the word "son" is the father; likewise here too, the very commencement is what is denoted, while immediate succession is merely implied.

For this very reason, it is said: "The purpose of the *prakriyā* is seen for that which follows immediately after the *vṛtti*. If it were intended to mean mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*), then one would have said: "In the sense of immediate succession after the *vṛtti*, there is the *prakriyā*. Furthermore, the term "of that which follows immediately" (*anantarasya*) is a designation specifically for that which occurs immediately thereafter.

Moreover, tradition (smṛti) states as follows: "Some indeclinables (avyaya) have the meaning of a case-ending (vibhaktyartha) as their primary sense, while others have action (kriyā) as their primary sense. For example, 'uccaiḥ' (high), 'nīcaiḥ' (low), and so forth, have the meaning of a case-ending as their primary sense; 'hiruk', 'pṛthak', and so forth, have action as their primary sense. And apart from these, no meaning of indeclinables exists. In that regard, if the word *atha* has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the non-hearing of a case-ending—or rather, the hearing of a case-ending—is improper, because its primary sense is that of a substantive (*sattva*).

But if [the suffix] has the sense of the action of beginning, then it is not unreasonable that the meaning of the case-ending is not heard, because its primary function is to denote a non-substance (asattva).

Therefore, it is logical that the word *atha* has the sense of an introduction (*prastāva*). Thus, it is correct to say that *atha* signifies the commencement of a topic (*adhikāra*). The word *iti* is for the purpose of illuminating the essential nature [of the meaning], as in the expression, "He said, 'A cow'. Although the meaning of the word *atha* is well-known, it is stated here with respect to the subject matter being introduced in order to focus the student's mind. For this principle is established in the Śruti: "I shall explain to you; but while I am explaining, you must meditate upon it."

[5,5] But what is this yoga whose instruction has been introduced? He says: "Yoga is concentration" (*samādhi*). By using the term "concentration," the root *yuji* in the sense of "joining" (*yoge*) is set aside, and the root *yuja* in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhau*) is adopted. Yoga is the act of concentrating. Now, one might object: since the Sūtra is explained by the statement "Yoga is concentration" up to that point, the Bhāṣya beginning with "And that [concentration] is universal" (*sa ca sārvabhaumaḥ*) appears to be disconnected. This is not a fault.

When "concentration" (samādhi) is mentioned here, since it depends on that which is being concentrated and because there are many things that can be concentrated—such as whether it is the self, the body, or the sense organs—there is a manifold disagreement among various theorists. Furthermore, since concentration requires its own qualification, when the question follows—"To what does this belong? What is its qualification?"—this is said: "And that is a quality of the mind (citta) belonging to all stages. It is a quality of the mind and not of the self or other such entities. Moreover, that very mind is itself concentrated, because it does not depend on anything else for its concentration.

[5.14] What, then, are these stages (*bhūmi*)? To this he says: "The distracted (*kṣipta*), the dull (*mūḍha*), and so forth, are the stages. The term *kṣipta* is a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) used in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*), as in the expression "the granary has burst of its own accord. It is "distracted" by being attached to undesirable objects; "dull" means lacking discrimination (*nirviveka*); "distracted" (*vikṣipta*) means scattered among various [objects]; this too is in the reflexive sense, for it is incapable of discrimination precisely because of its state of distraction. "One-pointed" (*ekāgra*) is a flow of similar cognitions (*tulyapratyayapravāha*). "Restrained" (*niruddha*) is the mind that is empty of cognitions.

[5,19] But surely, when the *dharmas* (mental states) belonging to the stages (*bhūmis*) are intended to be discussed, for what purpose is the *dharmin* (the subject possessing those states) mentioned by means of the words "What is the distraction? and so forth? This is not a fault, because it is precisely the *dharma* that is taught by means of the *dharmin*. This is because *dharmas* have the *dharmin* as their objective domain. For example, when asked, "What is the mark (*liṅga*) of 'cowness' (*gotva*)?", one teaches the *dharma* itself by means of the *dharmin*: "It has horns, a hump, and a tail with a tuft at the end. Therefore, the meaning is that distraction and the other states are the *dharmas*—the mental states—of the mind (*citta*).

[5.23] But if the stages (*bhūmi*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are both of the nature of mind (*cittadharmatva*), how is it that absorption is distinguished by the stages as its "support" (*ādhāra*) in the expression "universal to all stages" (*sārvabhauma*)? Because absorption is common to all, whereas the stages are specific. Just as one says "it remains in the scattered state," "it remains in the dull state," "the distracted," or "the one-pointed"—in these states such as the scattered and so forth, "remaining" (*sthiti*) persists as the common factor. And "remaining" is absorption. Therefore, it exists in all stages in its general form.

"It exists as the primary [element]" means that in the term *sarvabhūmipṛthivī*, the suffix *-an* has the sense of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). Because it belongs to the *anuśatikādi* group, there is vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) in both members of the compound.

[5.29] Others, however, call the external and internal objects of restraint "stages" (*bhūmi*). For them, there is an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "when the mind is distracted. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with their own words: how can something be called "distracted" (*kṣipta*) because it is scattered therein, or "deluded" (*mūḍha*) because it is bewildered therein? And when this is the case, there is no status as an object of restraint; for restraint occurs only in the state of one-pointedness (*ekāgra*), since distraction and the like are impossible therein.

[6,3] Furthermore: because objects such as the "distracted" state (*kṣipta*) lack permanence (*dhrauvya*) and other such qualities, there can be no application of the *niṣṭhā* suffix (the past passive participle) to denote a locus. Moreover, when the mind is suppressed (*niruddha*), even *saṃyama* is absent therein because it is devoid of mental modification (*vṛtti*); thus, there is an absence of an object for *saṃyama*. For the mind is not suppressed while remaining fixed upon a specific object; rather, at that time, it ceases precisely because it is the subject (*viṣayin*). Furthermore, the enumeration [of five states] is untenable, for the distracted and other states are not only five; they are infinite.

[6,8] But surely some desire yoga to be otherwise; for they say: "Pleasure and pain arise from the contact of the sense-faculties, the mind, and the objects; when the mind is established in the self, there is no commencement of those [contacts], and thus there is an absence of pleasure and pain for the embodied one. Yoga is that conjunction which depends upon the restraint of the vital breath and the mind. The word "that" (tat) refers back to what has been mentioned: that which is the cause of pleasure and pain—the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the objects—its non-commencement is its non-arising.

How does that come about? When the mind is situated within the self and not situated in the senses; for one who possesses a body, yet whose body has not disintegrated. Then, because of the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect; thus, in the absence of sensory contact, there is also the absence of pleasure and pain. In that state, that conjunction of the all-pervading self with the mind—which depends upon the restraint of the vital breaths and the mind—is a specific type of conjunction called *yoga*.

[6,16] To this it is replied: the statement "when the mind is situated in the self" is untenable, because the mind is always situated in the self. If it is argued that "situated in the self" refers to the non-commencement of contact with the sense organs and so forth, then since that non-commencement is already established by that very fact, the phrase "when the mind is situated in the self" would be redundant.

[6,19] Furthermore, even for one who is liberated, yoga would result because the mind remains situated within the self and there is an absence of contact with the sense organs. For since that [self] is omnipresent and the mind is eternal, the mind is indeed always situated within the self.

[6,21] Furthermore—since the self has no spatial location, it is illogical to say that [contact] resides in the self. Nor can a conjunction with a metaphorical location of the self be the cause of a conjunction in the ultimate sense, because that which is metaphorical is false.

[6.23] Furthermore, since the absence of contact between the mind and its object is already established, the mention of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) would be redundant. If it is argued that because there is no such contact in the absence of the sense-faculties, the [cognition] does not arise—and thus a prohibition [of contact] is not appropriate when there is no attainment (*prāpti*)—this is not so. By stating that there is no contact between the mind and its object without the sense-faculties, one who prohibits contact is, by implication, demonstrating that the attainment of the object occurs through the medium of the sense-faculties.

Furthermore, since the attainment of pleasure and pain by all living beings is well-established through the contact of the sense organs, the mind, and their objects, and since the connection of the self [to these] is eternal, it would follow that liberation (*yoga*) is simply the absence of pleasure and pain; thus, the remainder of the *sūtra* would be purposeless.

[7,5] Now, it might be argued that since pleasure and pain do not exist without the contact of the sense organs, the mind, and their objects, it would follow as a consequence that even a liberated person (mukta) possesses the state of a yogin, because pleasure and pain are absent for him as well. To preclude this, the remainder of the sūtra is taken up. But that is not correct; for there is no attainment of pleasure and pain by the liberated, and a negation is logically appropriate only with respect to what has been previously attained. Therefore, it is proper to reject the remainder of the sūtra, on the grounds that yoga is precisely the absence of pleasure and pain regarding those very things whose attainment of pleasure and pain one possesses.

[7,9] Furthermore, even if the assumption of a body were accepted, it would be impossible to effect its cessation for one who is liberated, because there would be no purpose for it. If yoga consists in the absence of pleasure and pain, then even an existing body would be useless since it performs no function; for if there is no dependence on a function, there would indeed be no distinction at all between the liberated and the unliberated.

[7,12] Furthermore, the claim that [the restraint of breath and mind] depends upon the restraint of breath and mind is also untenable. Since the sustaining effort is inherent in the self, even if the mind possesses activity, one is unable to effect the restraint of the mind and breath without the mind being conjoined with the sense organ. Moreover, it is illogical to say that when the mind is conjoined with a sense organ, there is no initiation [of that activity]. Furthermore, because the mind is either engaged in or withdrawn from the restraint of breath, its non-initiation [of such activity] is impossible.

[7.16] Furthermore, there can be no restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) without the contact of the sense organs and the vital air. Nor can there be *yoga* when the vital breath is unrestrained, because the restraint of the vital breath is the cause for the connection with mental activity by means of the effort that sustains the self within. Now, it might be argued that *yoga* is *samādhi*. But that is not so; because the self is devoid of action, it is eternally in a state of *samādhi*, and this very state is called *sthiti* (stability). Therefore, it is correctly stated: "And that is a universal property of the mind."

[7.21] If this is so, and if *samādhi* is *yoga*, then since that is a mental state (*cittadharma*) common to all stages, it would be accomplished without effort by all people, because it is present even in states such as the "distracted" (*kṣipta*). And that being the case, just as the practice of breath-control (*śvāsapraśvāsa*) and so forth would be useless because they are accomplished without effort, so too the instruction on *yoga* would be useless.

To this he says: "In that regard, when the mind is distracted (*vikṣipta*), concentration (*samādhi*)—being subordinate to distraction—does not belong to the category of yoga. This is because that which follows the states of being distracted and so forth is not intended to be part of the category of yoga. Indeed, a concentration associated with distraction and the like is incapable of illuminating the nature of reality, because distraction and the like predominate therein. For, by the very negation of distraction—according to the maxim of defeating the champion wrestler—the states of being distracted (*kṣipta*) and stupefied (*mūḍha*) are also negated.

And the primacy of concentration (*samādhi*) over distraction (*vikṣepa*) is due to its suitability for the primary purpose; for a mind situated in distraction can be directed toward a desired object because it is free from partiality. Indeed, a mind that is distracted by attachment to objects or deluded by separation from a desired object cannot be led elsewhere.

[8,8] Regarding the term "the side of yoga" (*yogapakṣa*): although it possesses the nature of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is called a "side" because it does not perform its full function. This is just as, for one who is walking, the state of standing exists at every step, yet it is not called "standing" because it does not perform the function of standing. Its being subordinate to distraction is intended with reference to a single manifestation of concentration existing amidst distraction. However, the term "universal" (*sārvabhauma*) indicates its predominance due to its occurrence generally across all stages (*bhūmi*).

[8.12] If being subordinate (*upasarjanībhāva*) were the cause for the non-occurrence of the side of meditative concentration (*samādhipakṣa*), then here too, in one-pointedness (*ekāgra*), there would be subordination to one-pointedness; and consequently, there would be a non-occurrence of the side of yoga. To this he says: "But that which is one-pointed... There is no subordination to the stage (*bhūmi*) within one-pointedness. Why? Because of the lack of strength in afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma. Indeed, when afflictions and karma lack strength, there is no arising of distractions (*vikṣepa*) and the like.
[8,16] That concentration which exists on the stage of one-pointedness is the true object in its actual nature.

It illuminates and causes comprehension. The inclusion of the word "real" (*bhūta*) indicates that knowledge of an unreal object is merely tainted by the scent of being contrary to reality. It destroys and exhausts the afflictions (*kleśa*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, which consist of five branches. It loosens and relaxes the bonds of karma—the very actions mixed with merit and demerit that serve as the cause for birth and so forth—and brings about their cessation, making it manifest. This is designated as "cognitive" (*samprajñāta*) by the teachers.

"And that [samādhi] is accompanied by vitarka and accompanied by vicāra," and so forth, is the commentary. Since it would have been appropriate to state the definition of *samprajñāta* first because of its priority, it is said, "We shall explain *samprajñāta* later," on the grounds that it is more fitting to state the definition of *asamprajñāta* here because of its greater importance.

[8.24] For this reason as well, the definition of *asamprajñāta* must be stated right here, in order to demonstrate that even independent of *samprajñāta*, *asamprajñāta* is accomplished through the practice of supreme (*prakṛṣṭa*) dispassion and the cognitive state of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*).

If the definition of *samprajñāta* were stated here and the definition of *asamprajñāta* were stated later, there might be the suspicion that one is qualified for *asamprajñāta-samādhi* only by means of depending upon *samprajñāta*. Therefore, he says: "We shall explain it further below. ||1||

"But when all fluctuations have ceased, it is *asaṃprajñāta*. The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of restriction. This sūtra was composed with the desire to state the definition of that very kind of *samādhi*, which is exclusively *asaṃprajñāta*; thus it should be stated: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind."

[9,12] But surely this Sūtra was intended to state its definition; and that being the case, it should have been stated as "yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*cittavṛttinirodhaḥ*), for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not appropriate—since the object of definition cannot itself be the definition—or rather, it should have been stated as "having the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind as its definition. This is not a fault, because the definition is superimposed upon the object of definition. Just as in the expression "This lump is Devadatta," the definition is superimposed (or projected) upon the object of definition.

[9.17] But surely, when all mental modifications (*vṛtti*) have ceased, that is the "seedless" (*asamprajñāta*) state, and its definition is such; therefore, it should be stated that "yoga is the cessation of all mental modifications. Yet this has not been stated. Consequently, the definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpin*). The reason for not including the word "all" is now stated: if the inclusion of "all" were made, then the status of "cognitive" (*samprajñāta*) yoga—which is caused by the cessation of only a portion [of modifications]—would be excluded. To prevent that from happening, the word "all" is not included.

[9.21] "Let it be, then, that this is the general definition of both *samprajñāta* and *asamprajñāta* samādhis, since no specific distinction is mentioned. This is not a fault; for when "yoga" was already the subject under discussion, the term "yoga" is mentioned again. Indeed, if no specific distinction were intended to be expressed, the repetition of the term "yoga" would be purposeless.

[9,24] But surely, since yoga is subordinate in the *anuśāsana*, if the term "yoga" were not included here, the statement "cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" would merely have the sense of an instruction (*anuśāsana*) and not that of a *sūtra*. This is not so, because it is the instruction on yoga (*yogānuśāsana*) that has been introduced, not an instruction on non-yoga. For if one were to state the definition of something other than that, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and there would be a lack of consistency with the subject matter (*padārthāsaṅgati*). Indeed, the subject matter does not cohere if "cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" is taken as the instruction on yoga.

[9.29] Even so, since the term "yoga" is employed, why is this the definition of *asaṃprajñāta* alone and not the definition of *saṃprajñāta*, given that the employment of the term "yoga" is common to both?

[10.3] It is said: because of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). That which deviates is not its definition; for cessation (*nirodha*) exists even in *asaṃprajñāta*, and thus it deviates from *saṃprajñāta*. Indeed, "horns" is not a defining mark (*liṅga*) of a cow, because it deviates from buffaloes and the like.

[10,8] But does not even *asaṃprajñāta* (the unconscious) deviate from this definition, since *saṃprajñāta* (the conscious) is also characterized by the cessation of the functions that are to be abandoned? True, it is so; however, *asaṃprajñāta* cannot be defined by anything other than cessation, because there is nothing else that serves as its defining characteristic. For *saṃprajñāta*, on the other hand, is defined by its own specific characteristics such as *vitarka* (gross thought) and so forth.

Just as when "characterized by touch" is said, it is air alone that is defined by its possession of touch due to its uniqueness; yet the possession of touch certainly exists in fire and other elements as well.

[10.12] This being the case, the mention of "yoga" is merely a restatement. For this very reason, the word "all" (*sarva*) was not included in the aphorism. Since the definition of the "seedless" (*asaṃprajñāta*) state is already established by the mention of "cessation" (*nirodha*), if the word "all" were used, it would exclude the status of "yoga" from the "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) state. Therefore, this is the definition of the seedless state alone. Accordingly, the author of the Commentary concludes: "Because nothing is cognized therein, it is 'non-cognitive'; that yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind."

[10.18] With the desire to explain the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*) and their cessation, the commentary begins with the words "The mind, indeed... Now, what is the nature of that mind whose fluctuations are to be restrained—that is, what constitutes *yoga*? To this he says: "The mind, because its nature consists of manifestation, activity, and stability, is composed of the three *guṇas*. In this context, the statement "the mind is composed of the three *guṇas*" is the thesis (*vyākhyā*), while "because its nature consists of manifestation, activity, and stability" is the reason (*hetu*). Manifestation (*prakhyā*) means the act of manifesting or illuminating; for that is the property of the *sattva* *guṇa*.

Activity, setting in motion, and functional operation—these are indeed the attributes of *rajas*. Stability, persistence, and obstruction—these are the attributes of *tamas*. Since the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* possess these characteristics, and the mind possesses the nature of luminosity and so forth, it follows that the mind must be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the three *guṇas*.

Anticipating the objection that the cause for its manifestation and so forth is unestablished, he says: "For the nature of manifestation is the *cittasattva*. The word "for" (*hi*) is intended to indicate what is well-known. For it is well known in both the world and the scriptures that the mind (*citta*) is the illuminator of all things. The mind itself is the *sattva*; thus it is called *cittasattva*, because it is a transformation of the quality of *sattva*, which predominates therein.

Alternatively, he says that the mind (*citta*), which exists as many through association with and dissociation from other things and is mere manifestation (*khyātimātra*), can be clearly demonstrated by the statement: "The essence of the mind is its luminous nature (*prakhyāsvarūpa*)."

[11,11] Now the modifications (*vṛtti*) are explained. Regarding their multiplicity and their opposition—which is caused by the alternating emergence and subsidence of *rajas* and *tamas*—he says: "When it is conjoined with *rajas* and *tamas*, that is, when it is conjoined with these two predominant qualities, then it becomes fond of sovereignty and objects of sense."
The meaning is that there are mental modifications consisting of attachment, passion, and being joined with passion for power and sense objects.

[11,15] That same mind, whose nature is luminosity, when permeated by tamas which has become predominant over rajas, then afflicted fluctuations (vṛtti) arise, having as their objects the fourfold group beginning with demerit (adharma).

[11.17] That very [cognition] is "one whose obscuration of delusion has been destroyed. Because of the destruction of darkness (*tamaḥ*), its darkness has become subsided, like the orb of the sun shining everywhere once the clouds have departed. When it is permeated by even a mere trace of passion (*rajas*), that is to say, by a slight residue of passion, then it has attained the [fourfold] qualities (*dharmādi*). The unafflicted mental modes (*vṛtti*) having the fourfold qualities as their object come into being.

When that very [mind], freed from the stain of even a particle of *rajas*, is established in its own nature and abides solely in its own form of luminosity (*prakhyā*), then there occurs the mere discernment (*anyathākhyāti*) of the difference between *sattva* and the *puruṣa*. *Sattva* is the mind (*citta*); the *puruṣa* is the enjoyer. Their "difference" (*anyatā*) is their distinctness; the "discernment" (*khyāti*) of them is the realization thereof. The use of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of showing the absence of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. It becomes accompanied by the meditation called the Cloud of Virtue (*dharmamegha-dhyāna*); the "Cloud of Virtue" is a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

[11.24] By the power of that very discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), having set aside *rajas* and *tamas*, the yogis who meditate call "discernment" (*prasaṃkhyāna*) that state of abiding through the pure nature of consciousness (*khyāti*), which consists solely in the vision of the true nature of the *puruṣa*.

[11.26] When the nature of its functioning has thus been explained, he says "the power of consciousness" (*citiśakti*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate its cessation. The power of consciousness is consciousness itself as power. Just as powers such as "to cook" and the like are dependent upon a possessor of power and are produced in relation to an object to be reached, they are not powers in themselves; consciousness, however, is itself the power and does not depend on anything else. Therefore, it is eternally established. The grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the word *citi*—which denotes pure consciousness—with the word *śakti* is for the purpose of demonstrating that consciousness, in its unmodified form, possesses the capacity to be an object of experience.

[12.7] Since this is so, it is therefore unchanging (*apariṇāminī*). Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the manifestation of another attribute through the concealment of a previous attribute while the underlying substrate (*dharmī*) remains constant. It is called "unchanging" because its nature is not such that it can be transformed. For this very reason, it is non-transmigrating (*apratisaṅkramā*), since it is only changing things, such as the mind (*citta*), that are observed to transmigrate toward objects and the like.

[12,13] For this very reason, its object is shown; that is, the object is shown by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) to it. By that same [organ], it is pure. For this very reason, it is infinite in terms of space and time. Each preceding [attribute] should be understood as the cause for each succeeding one. The mind and the senses serve as the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).

"Sattvaguṇātmikā" means that its very essence (ātman) or nature (svarūpa)—its manifestation—is the quality of *sattva* itself; the meaning is that its nature is the manifestation of the quality of *sattva*. Alternatively, it is called "sattvaguṇātmikā" because its function is not distinct from the function of the quality of *sattva*.

[12,18] Or rather, if *khyāti* (manifestation) is connected with *sattva*, then manifestation consists of the quality of *sattva*. Therefore, discriminative manifestation (*vivekakhyāti*) is the opposite and distinct from the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) as previously defined; it possesses transformation and other such qualities.

[12.20] Since the Puruṣa is superior and devoid of qualities such as transformation (*pariṇāma*), while the other is inferior and possessed of qualities such as transformation, one becomes detached from—that is, dispassionate toward—that manifestation (*khyāti*) upon seeing the defects inherent in its own nature, and thereby restrains even that manifestation from oneself.

That state is the state of cessation, accompanied by residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), where only the impressions remain. When the fluctuations have ceased, only the impressions produced by those fluctuations persist. The concentration (*samādhi*) that exists in this stage of cessation is "seedless" (*nirbīja*). It is called seedless because the seed—namely, all seeds such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth—has departed from it and been utterly destroyed therein. Therefore, he concludes that this aphorism is intended solely to define the characteristic of *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. (1.2)

[12,25] It has been stated that "yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. In this regard, the existence of the *puruṣa* is understood precisely through its nature as the cognizer (*boddhṛ*). Furthermore, when the fluctuations—which serve as objects—cease, someone might suspect that the *puruṣa*, the cognizer who is the subject, also ceases. If that were the case, one would consider even discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*)—the means for attaining its isolation (*kaivalya*)—to be useless, and one would conclude that the instruction on yoga, whose purpose is that [isolation], is likewise fruitless. Therefore, regarding the *puruṣa*:

Desiring to demonstrate non-cessation through the cessation of mental fluctuations, and directly showing the fruit of discriminative discernment (*khyāti*), he says: "When the mind is in that state," and so forth.

"In that state"—that is, in the state of cessation (*nirodha*). "Due to the absence of its own object": its own object is the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*); because of the absence of that [modification], [the Self remains]. The Puruṣa is the knower of the intellect (*buddhi*), for he knows the intellect as it has transformed into the form of modifications; thus he is the knower of the intellect. Indeed, this very act of knowing is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Puruṣa; there is no other knower, nor any other act of knowing. For if the knower were distinct from the act of knowing, he would possess the nature of change (*vikriyātmakatā*).

Furthermore, there would be no manifestation of objects, and thus it would follow that the person (puruṣa) must depend upon other instruments. Therefore, both the state of being an illuminator and the act of illumination are metaphorical, based on the similarity [of the self] to the modifications of the intellect (buddhi). As he will say later: "The seer is pure seeing. Therefore, he says: the person whose very nature is the illumination of the intellect is the "intellect-illumination-self" (buddhibodhātmā) puruṣa. What is his essential nature? Is it a perishable nature, or is it a nature of existence? And if it is a nature of existence, what is its essence, or how does its existence come to be?

Then there is the seer’s abiding in his own nature. When the fluctuations have been restrained, he is established in his own nature; at that time, the power of consciousness (citiśakti) is established in its own nature—this is the meaning. As in the state of liberation (kaivalya). He will later state this with such words as, "But its existence then is not self-manifested, because it is an object of perception. Since its existence is thus established, the phrase "established in its own nature" is stated in order to remove the doubt that might arise from drawing [the conclusion] from that [preceding argument].

The sūtra has been explained as if it were already established; in this regard, the following point arises: elsewhere there is no establishment in its own nature (*svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā*). For otherwise, the qualification "then" (*tadā*) would be meaningless. If there were no establishment in its own nature elsewhere, then because of the connection with another state and because of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), a fault would result. Desiring to avoid that, he says: "But when the mind is in a state of emergence (*vyutthāna-citta*), they exist even so. By this, he shows that there is establishment in its own nature even elsewhere.
By the phrase "not thus," he demonstrates the purposefulness of the qualification "then. ||3||

[14,10] But the other [the opponent], even so, being perplexed by the thought that if "establishment in its own nature" (*svarūpapratiṣṭhatva*) is asserted by this [sūtra], and yet "not so," then the negation of establishment in its own nature would contradict both the state of being thus and the state of not being thus for a single entity, asks: "How then? The other says: "In the other case, there is conformity with the modification (*vṛttisārūpyam*). Why, again, is there conformity with the modification? Because its object has been presented [to the mind].

Although there is no difference in both cases regarding the fact that [the mind] is established in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is a distinction made by whether it conforms to or does not conform to the mental modifications (*vṛtti-sārūpya*); thus, there is no contradiction between its being such and its not being such.

[14,15] But surely, when there is a correspondence with the mental modification (*vṛtti-sārūpya*), because it enters into different states, defects such as being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) would indeed follow? No; for this has been refuted by the fact that [the Self] has objects shown to it. For that [transformation] is superimposed upon the Self by the mental modification, not inherent in itself, just like the coloring of a crystal or similar object by a proximate substrate (*upadhāna*). This refers to the state of "emergence" (*vyutthāna*).

Apart from cessation (nirodha), whatever modifications of the mind there are—such as the afflicted and so forth—the Puruṣa’s own nature is a modification indistinguishable from and similar to them; for there is no modification of the Puruṣa apart from the modifications of the mind, nor apart from its own nature, and because it would be impossible for it to undergo transformation if its objects were always already known.

[14,21] And thus, the Sūtra of the former teacher states: "The vision of both Intellect (*buddhi*) and Spirit (*puruṣa*) is one and the same. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Vision is nothing but manifestation (*khyāti*). The modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) itself is vision. It is called "manifestation" (*khyāti*) because it is manifested by the Spirit; and it is called "manifestation" because through it the essential natures of both Intellect and Spirit are manifested. That very [modification], by assuming the form of the object—since the form of the object is grasped by it—functions as an instrument (*karaṇa*); and by its own nature as manifestation, it is also the object (*karman*) that is grasped.
Likewise, "vision" (*darśana*) is that by which one sees; and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is that by which one knows—thus all such terms are to be understood.

As for the claim that since the mind possesses both the nature of manifestation and agency, it is known as "that which is known" and "that which knows"—lest there follow the absurdity of postulating another cognition (jñāna)—we shall provide the refutation of that very point under the verse: "It does not manifest itself, because it is an object of perception."

[15,4] But surely, if all this is merely the unfolding of the mind, and the soul remains indifferent, how can it be the enjoyer? It is not so, because of the diversity of causal factors (*kāraka*). Some causal factors are active, while others attain the status of agent through mere presence, even without activity.

[15,7] Just as a person who is actively engaged in the acts of placing [fuel] on the fire and so forth is called the "agent" when one says "he cooks," whereas a pot is said to "cook" even though it is not actively engaged in the acts of containing or supporting [the food], so too, the space situated within the pot provides room; we do not perceive any activity on its part.

And just as a king is the agent merely by his presence, so too all causal factors (kārakas) are to be considered agents within their own respective operations. Furthermore, the sun, while illuminating, does not depend on another instrument nor does it exert effort; for illumination does not produce something that was previously non-existent, unlike the act of going or similar actions.

For its very existence consists in its nature as luminosity; nevertheless, because objects such as jars are manifested in the form of light by the mere act of seeing, it is said that "it illuminates. Similarly here too, since the mental modifications being perceived by the Puruṣa—who is pure consciousness—are pervaded by the conscious self through the mere act of seeing, the meaning is shown that "the Puruṣa is the seer," and thus [the Sūtra] states: "The mind is like a magnet."

[15,16] Even for one for whom cognition arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, it is said that the self is "the knower" by virtue of pervading the object of knowledge through cognition, not because it is actively engaged in action. Since cognition, being a quality (*guṇa*), is devoid of activity (*niṣkriyatva*), it reveals the object only for the sake of the self. Furthermore, since no action is admitted, expressions such as "he knows" are not tenable; for it is said that "he knows" when he pervades the object of knowledge by means of cognition.

[15.20] Furthermore, another point: when a novel cognition (*apūrvajñāna*) arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind, why would it be that this cognition belongs to the self and not to the mind? What could be the reason for the claim that "the self alone knows, not the mind"? If it were argued that it is because the self is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), this is not so, because it is unproven (*asiddha*).

Just as it remains to be proven that cognition belongs to the self, so too it remains to be proven that the self alone is the inherent cause and not the mind; for, while the mind is not of the nature of the self, it is admitted that [cognition] is produced by the conjunction of both.

Furthermore, it might be argued that because the self, which possesses the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by cognition, is observed to perform the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) through memory as a single agent, [the self exists]. But this too is something yet to be proven; for in that case as well, one must prove that cognition, latent impressions, memory, and synthesis belong to the self alone and not to the mind (*manas*). If it is argued that this is because desire and so forth share the same locus as their result, we say no, for the same logic applies there as well. Since they are produced from contact, it is difficult to prove that the self’s results—desire and so forth—belong to the self and not to the mind.

Furthermore, since this cognition itself is admitted to be an object of knowledge, there follows the consequence of an infinite regress. For it is not possible for one cognition to be known by another cognition acting as its instrument; for that too would require another, and that yet another, which leads to an undesirable infinite regress.

[16,6] Now, if—in order to avoid the consequence of infinite regress—one goes so far as to say that some cognition, whether it be the first or another, is not apprehended by another cognition but is apprehended by itself alone, then it follows that, just like cognition, the object too would be apprehended by itself.

[16,8] Now, if it is argued that—just like a lamp—it illuminates itself and illuminates others because its nature is luminosity, whereas the object is not of a luminous nature, and thus there is no fault; even so, it would follow that objects whose very nature is light could not be apprehended by consciousness.

[16,11] Now, if it is argued that cognition apprehends itself through its two natures—namely, its inherence in the self (*ātmasamavetatva*) and its manifestation (*prakāśa*)—whereas external objects, having properties contrary to those of cognition, do not incur this fault; that too is not correct. For if both inherence in the self and the nature of manifestation were the causes for the self-apprehension of cognition, it would follow that everyone would be omniscient.

[16,14] Now, if even the state of having the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāratva*) is the cause, and if that [state] does not constitute the causality of one cognition for another because it has a different form—just as it is so, for cognition as well, since it has a different form from the apprehended object, one distinct cognition would have to be the cause; and in that case, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would indeed be difficult to avoid.

[16,17] Furthermore, there exists no example whatsoever to establish that something can be both the grasped and the grasper by itself; for even a lamp is grasped by the eyes and other senses. Moreover, cognition does not possess two parts, because it is partless.
Even if it did have two parts, since both would consist of the nature of illumination, they could not stand in a relationship of mutual grasper and grasped, just as in the case of two lamps.

[16.21] Furthermore, if one accepts that cognition possesses the nature of both the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), then the existence of a self (*ātman*) is likewise impossible to establish. Therefore, the qualities of being non-self (*anātmadharman*) are established for the recollection of the form of an object, the synthesis of cognitions, effort, desire, and so forth, because they are apprehended objects, just like visible form (*rūpa*) and other such things. Moreover, because they exist for the sake of another and because they depend upon a composite aggregate, they are like the examples of visible form and the rest. Likewise, their status as non-self is proven by such reasons as having a substratum (*āśrayavat*), being impermanent (*anityatva*), and being preceded by effort (*prayatnapūrvakatva*).

[16,25] Like a magnet-stone. It is precisely like a magnet-stone; just as a magnet-stone assists iron in its own pervasion merely by being present, so too the mind assists the Self, whose nature is consciousness, in its own pervasion by way of being an object of perception.

[17,9] It has been stated that, like a dancer, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) displays objects; in that regard, by what is the mind’s role as the exhibitor and the Spirit’s (puruṣa) role as the observer established? By their relationship as property and owner. But how is there such a relationship of property and owner? Because it is the very nature of things. If one asks how so, it has been said that the mind is like a magnet.

Now, what is the cause for the Puruṣa’s awareness of the fluctuations of the mind? It is said: because the mind assists [the Puruṣa] merely by its proximity as an object of perception, therefore this cause for the Puruṣa’s awareness of the mental fluctuations is that beginningless connection which exists between them. 4.

[17,15] Furthermore, those fluctuations must be restrained, even though they are manifold, because it was stated that through these fluctuations of the mind during emergence (*vyutthāna*), the Person (*puruṣa*) assumes a semblance of them. Why, then, must they be restrained? He says: because the fluctuations are either afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*).

[17,18] But surely, since they are manifold, they cannot be ceased? To this he says: "fivefold. Although the afflicted and unafflicted fluctuations are infinite, nevertheless they are fivefold—that is, of five types—and consist of exactly five families. And therefore:

Since cessation is established precisely through the practice of detachment (*vairāgya*) which serves as the antidote to the fivefold fluctuations, there is no contingency of impossibility regarding cessation despite the multiplicity of those fluctuations, because the means for cessation applies to each individual fluctuation. They are caused by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and have the afflictions as their motive; for the mind, impelled by the five afflictions beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), repeatedly makes itself known through its fluctuations.

Regarding the accumulation (*ācaya*) and gathering (*pracaya*) of karma: actions—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or mixed—are called by the term "karmic latency" (*karmāśaya*) because they persist until they yield their fruit. Their "gathering" (*pracaya*) is their integration through the relationship of mutual subordination and predominance. It is upon this cause—the gathering of karmic latencies—that [the afflictions] become the field for ignorance and the rest; the meaning is that they have an afflicted basis (*kliṣṭāśraya*). For it is only when those [afflictions] exist that the karmic latency becomes oriented toward its maturation (*vipāka*).

[17,27] They have discernment as their object and discernment as their locus. The "authority" (*adhikāra*) of the qualities (*guṇas*), such as *sattva* and the rest, is the activity of their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Those [other states] are opposed to that. Precisely because they have discernment as their object, they are "unafflicted," since they are the cause of liberation.

[18,11] Now, if unafflicted mental states (*akliṣṭa-vṛtti*) arise in the midst of an afflicted series (*kliṣṭa-paṅkti*), are they themselves afflicted—like a drop of water cast into a jar of milk? Likewise, if afflicted states fall into the flow of an unafflicted series, are they themselves unafflicted? What follows from this? If unafflicted states occurring within an afflicted series were to become afflicted, then memory (*smṛti*), which conforms to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of those mental states, would result in corresponding behavior; yet that behavior is not established when there is a deviation from their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Therefore it is said: even during interruptions by afflicted states, the non-afflicted [states] remain indeed non-afflicted; and even during interruptions by non-afflicted states, the afflicted [states] remain indeed afflicted. Because this is so, conditioned factors of such a nature are produced solely by the mental fluctuations.

[18,18] Even though afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth also initiate formative forces (*saṃskāra*), nevertheless, because they too are formative forces by way of their activity (*vṛtti*), the meaning of the particle "only" (*eva*) is that [the mind is conditioned] by activities alone. Likewise, activities are produced by formative forces in accordance with themselves; thus, the wheel of activity and formative force revolves incessantly and without interruption. Such is the mind, possessing the nature of causes, effects, activities, and formative forces. Its scope has come to an end, its functioning caused by ignorance has ceased, because it remains in a state of mere causality, as if it were the self.

By means of a mere manifestation resembling a person, it persists for some time through the continuation of the remaining impressions of what has been commenced; or it goes to dissolution at the exhaustion of those impressions. (5)
[18,25] What, then, are those fivefold functions, both afflicted and non-afflicted? He says:
they are valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory.
[18.27] There are only these many modes of activity. Among them, perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The mental modification known as valid cognition is divided into exactly three types. Among these, regarding the mental modification of the mind known as valid cognition:

The first division is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, its definition alone is stated here, because the other two divisions are preceded by it. [It occurs] "through the channel of the sense organs" (*indriya-pranāḍikayā*). By "sense organ" (*indriya*) is meant the pentad beginning with hearing; the organs of action are not included, because they are not causes of mental modification (*cittavṛtti*). For their purpose is action. Therefore, although the word *indriya* has a general meaning, since it is intended to explain mental modification, it refers specifically to the objects of hearing and so forth, and because hearing and the others serve as the means for that modification.

The sense organ itself is the conduit, the gateway for the mind as it undergoes transformation into the form of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) bearing the aspects of sound and so forth. Therefore, the mind, transforming through that gateway of the sense organ into the form of external objects consisting of both general and particular characteristics, becomes colored by them. Because of that coloring of the mind, its modification—which, like a seal and its impression, primarily determines the particular even while being colored by an object consisting of both general and particular characteristics—is precisely the means of valid cognition known as perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[19,13] Now, regarding the capacity of the ears and other sense organs, as well as of the mind, to manifest the general and particular characteristics of their respective objects, what causes the predominance of the ascertainment of particulars? [19,15] It is said: because the rejection, acquisition, and so forth, are contingent upon particulars, there is a predominance of the ascertainment of particulars; thus he says "[predominance]. It is not that the general characteristic is not ascertained at all; rather, it is indeed apprehended, but only as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*).

Just as in the expression "blue form" (*nīlaṃ rūpam*), although the emphasis is on the determination of "blue," one determines that "form alone is blue," making the latter subordinate; likewise for the words "suffering," "pleasure," or "delusion. Thus, it is logically established that there is a mode of operation (*vṛtti*) in which the emphasis is on the determination of the specific attribute.

[19,20] Furthermore, because the perception of a universal is the cause of doubt and error: for when a universal is perceived, doubt arises regarding the particular one desired to be known; or else, from the recollection of the perceived universal, error occurs. However, for one who has already ascertained the particular, neither doubt nor error can persist; thus, it is said that the primary function [of perception] is the determination of the particular.

[19,24] Even where it is intended to determine only the universal, such as "cow" or "horse," there too, since the determination of one occurs through the exclusion of the other, it is primarily the determination of the particular. For every entity whatsoever is both a universal and a particular in relation to another entity.

Furthermore, for one who holds that the universal (*sāmānya*) is merely a superimposition upon a non-existent thing—like water in a saline wasteland (*ūṣara*) and is not an object of the senses—for such a person, the superimposition of a specific universal is untenable. For a superimposition cannot occur with respect to a primary entity (*mukhya*) that has never been perceived before, because recollection would be impossible. One who has never seen actual water can never superimpose it upon a saline wasteland. Moreover, if one were to superimpose even without remembering, then one might as well superimpose "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) and so forth upon the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of color.

Now, if it is argued that the superimposition of "sound-ness" and so forth upon the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of form is contradictory because they belong to the objects of different sense faculties, we say no; for this would be the case only if they were non-entities (*avastu*), since there is no distinction [between them as non-entities]. Furthermore, if a distinction is admitted, it follows that they must be real entities (*vastu*), just like the specific individuality of sound is distinct from the specific individuality of form.

Furthermore, if one does not accept perception as qualified by differences of place and time, there would be the total collapse of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). For there could be no occurrence of memory such as: "In this location and at this time, I saw this object with such-and-such qualifications due to this very cause. Nor is memory possible regarding qualifiers that were not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), just as it is not possible for memory regarding the qualified object itself. Moreover, no one is seen engaging in worldly transaction by means of something that is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and beyond the sphere of worldly transaction.
Therefore, it is only logical to follow the perception as it is established in common worldly experience.

[20,11] But surely, the vision born of the non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) of yogins must be admitted as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), since it does not possess the aforementioned characteristics; likewise, consciousness such as pleasure or passion must either be admitted as a distinct means of valid cognition or be called perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it does not presuppose the channel of the sense organs. It is replied: this is not so, because it has already been refuted that perception (as a means of valid cognition) depends upon the cognition of a person (*puruṣapratyaya*). For there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) that is devoid of cognition.

It is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Perception belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) endowed with its objective content precisely because it is the cause for the arising of consciousness (*caitanya*). Thus it has been said: "The result is the awareness of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), which is non-different from that [modification] and pertains to the Person (*puruṣa*). This being the case, the status of perception is established for the cognition of pleasure, passion, and so forth—whether afflicted or unafflicted—since they culminate in a result consisting of the cognition of the Person, which is non-different from them.

The mention of the channel of the sense organs (*indriya-pranāḍikā*) is merely a restatement of the arising of worldly perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*). Otherwise, the knowledge of the Yogin and the Lord (*īśvara*), which is independent of the sense organs, would not be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For indeed, when there is an absence of obstructions such as the afflictions (*kleśa*), there occurs a simultaneous apprehension of subtle, concealed, and other objects by means of the mental substance (*citta-sattva*) which has all things as its object. Thus it is said: "The knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) is saving (*tāraka*), has all things as its object, has all aspects as its object, and is non-sequential.
Therefore, it is not determined that [knowledge] arises solely through the channel of the sense organs.
[21,6] "Due to the coloring by external objects" is stated for the purpose of removing error; "by means of primarily ascertaining the specific [nature]" is for the purpose of removing doubt.

In this regard, for some, the result (*phala*) is that very same [cognition which is the] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For others, however, the result is something other than the means of valid cognition, namely another manifestation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavyaktyantara*). For example, the cognitions of rejection, acquisition, and indifference are the results of the means of valid cognition that is the cognition of a jar. Because the cognitions of acquisition and so forth have as their objects the qualities, defects, or the absence of both—which are distinct from the jar itself—there is an absolute difference between these cognitions of acquisition and so forth and the cognition of the jar which constitutes the means of valid cognition; and thus, [the result] has a different object.
The fruit [of the means of knowledge] is another individual instance of the object of that [means of knowledge].

[21,13] For it is not logical that the cutting of a *khadira* tree should have either the taking up of the *khadira* wood or its abandonment as its result; for taking up and abandoning have as their results separation and connection respectively. Furthermore, a result cannot be the result of another result, because it is already mediated by the result consisting in the state of being split.

Furthermore, if the fruit were itself the fruit, there would be the absurd consequence that it is independent of action. For action is undertaken for the sake of the fruit; if that fruit were established even without action, and even apart from the fruit [itself], then one would not perform the activity whose accomplishment depends upon manifold exertions. Moreover, the search for the means [of attainment] would be untenable, because of the absence of action.

Nor is the action itself the fruit, because it would follow that the action would never cease; for actions do indeed terminate in a fruit. Furthermore, if the action were the fruit, it would follow that there would be no desire for a fruit, since that [action] is of the nature of suffering.

Therefore, the result is neither the very nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself, nor another means of valid cognition distinct from it; thus he says, "the result is non-different from that," and so forth. "Non-different from that" means not different from that activity called the means of valid cognition, being equal to it by virtue of having its form (*tadākāratva*).

"Human" means "this is the cognition of a person. For it is the person who possesses the form of the mental modification (*vṛtti*). Therefore, the result is not eternal, nor is it something unproduced by action, nor is it merely the essential nature of a substance. What then? It is a specific state of the substance itself, produced by action, occurring at the time of the completion of the action; for the result arises upon the cessation of the action. Indeed, the cessation of the action is logically possible only when the result is accomplished. If such a thing were the primary result, then there would be a substance [as the result] of an action remote from the principal action, or an action [as the result] of a substance.
The metaphorical designation of "fruit" will not be contradictory, because by way of their mutual presentation, they cause the primary fruit to be directed toward itself.

[22,14] But is it not the case that for you as well, the result is merely metaphorical (*upacita*), since you admit that the result belongs to the intellect (*buddhi*) which is indistinguishable from its function, and because the Person (*puruṣa*) is pure, [the cognition] is unreal by virtue of taking on that form? For the appearance of lac-dye on a crystal gem is not real.

[22,17] Certainly; nevertheless, this very [liberation] is the primary fruit, because it is directly perceived. For no other primary fruit is observed, since the entire collection of actions and their factors exists for the sake of this fruit. Indeed, all that culminates in this. And so it has been demonstrated.

[22.20] But surely it is only that which is illusory (*mithyā*)—namely, the form of the mental modification (*vṛttyākāra*)—that constitutes the primary fruit; and thus, desire for it would be impossible. Certainly, experience (*bhoga*) is indeed illusory when it follows after a mental modification. Thus he says: "Experience is the non-distinction of the cognition between the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely unmixed. The Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) also states: "When their own essential natures are perceived, how could there be experience? For this very reason, cessation through absolute means is logically established by means of right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

For those for whom the fruit is not false, there is an absence of liberation because of the lack of a cause for dispassion and the impossibility of seeking right vision. Furthermore, liberation is not something to be accomplished through ritual action, as that would entail the consequence of it being impermanent.

[23,4] Now, if it is argued that the state of being the cognizer of cognition does not belong to the *puruṣa* and that its existence is unestablished, he says: "We shall demonstrate later that the *puruṣa* is the experiencer of cognition."

[23,6] Furthermore, even those who maintain that the contact between the sense-organ and its object is perception do not hold a correct position, because contact is the fruit of an action. For them, contact is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and that is held by them to be produced by action. Since that which arises from something is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that thing, and that which arises is its fruit (*phala*).

[23,9] If it is argued that the contact (*sannikarṣa*) is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the cognition as its result, that is not so; for it is improper to introduce a causal instrument (*kāraka-pramāṇa*) in the context of discussing an informative instrument (*jñāpaka-pramāṇa*). For contact is the producer of cognition, not its informant. Indeed, perception and the other [means of knowledge] are for the sake of the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*), not for the cause of the production of cognition. To discuss that [contact] would be irrelevant to the present topic.

[23,13] Now, it might be argued that since cognition is also an object of knowledge (*prameya*), it too is known when it arises; therefore, the sense-contact (*sannikarṣa*) which is its cause of production possesses the status of a cognizer (*jñāpaka*). But that is not so, because cognition would have to be known by cognition itself, as they [the Naiyāyikas] accept that to be the case. Furthermore, sense-contact is not cognition, because it is accepted as being the producer of cognition.

[23,16] Now, if it is argued that the contact (*sannikarṣa*) between cognition and its object is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is the instrumental cause, then what is the objection to [considering] the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the will of God (*īśvara-icchā*), or even the blinking of an eye as means of valid knowledge, since these too are instrumental causes? Furthermore, if cognition were itself an object of cognition, and if one does not accept that the self (*ātman*) has the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), it would be impossible to avoid an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

[23,19] If it is argued that the knowability of cognition consists solely in its inherence in the self (*ātman*), and no other cognition is required such that an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would occur, then another definition of perception must be stated for this case as well; for the inherence of cognition in the self does not have the nature of sense-object contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) and so forth. Furthermore, since contact has the production of cognition as its result, when there is an interval in the production of that [cognition], there is no immediate succession (*ānantarya*) for that cognition.

Therefore, even by virtue of immediate succession, cognition does not possess the quality of being a proximate result. Thus, it has been stated that it is likewise untenable for cognitions such as those of avoidance and so forth to be results of the cognition of form and other objects.

[23,25] And because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). For instance, when a single cognition of the same object, such as a woman's body, has arisen in many people, one person has the thought of grasping (*upādāna*), another has the thought of rejecting (*heya*), and for another there is the absence of both; in that case, the thoughts of rejection and grasping deviate. Since it is the very same cognition in one instance that deviates into both [thoughts] for the indifferent observer, that which deviates from something cannot be its result.

Furthermore, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is indeed non-existence (*abhāva*), because it consists merely in the absence of both rejection (*hāna*) and acceptance (*upādāna*). And non-existence cannot be the result of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an object. Moreover, the cognitions of acceptance and rejection arise from attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*); since these are absent, there is an absence of the effect when there is an absence of the cause. Thus, even when a cognition through a means of valid cognition exists, the absence of the cognitions of rejection and acceptance is itself equanimity. Therefore, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is not the case that [the result of a pramāṇa] consists in the cognitions of rejection and so forth.

Furthermore, if passion, hatred, and their absence were also the fruits of cognitions such as grasping (*upādāna*), it would follow that they too possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, if they are understood as human mental states (*cittavṛtti*), nothing is contradicted.

[24,7] But is it not the case that the cognizability of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) is unestablished? For an instrument cannot itself be its own object; a sickle, for instance, is not what is cut. This is not a fault, because action and its causal factors possess distinct natures. With respect to the accomplishment of an action, the causal factors operate collectively by standing in a mutual relationship of subject and object. However, since action is the cause of the result merely by its existence, the status of being an "instrument" is figuratively attributed to it, but not in the same way as other causal factors. For that which is currently acting may cause another to act; thus, action would be subordinate to the causal factor. A completed state is not taught for the sake of that which is yet to be accomplished.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If an action were itself an instrument, then for its cessation, another action would have to occur. For without another action, its status as the cause of an instrument is not tenable. And that other action which is the cause would itself be the instrument for yet another action; that too for another, and so on ad infinitum. Consequently, because the continuum of actions would never cease, the fruit would never be produced.

In that case, if the final action were the cause of the fruit even without another [intervening] action, what objection could there be to the first [action] being likewise? However, since it is the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) that manifests [the result], it is experienced; thus there is no fault.

[24,18] Furthermore, it is observed that the very nature of manifestors, such as lamps and the like, consists in their being perceived through their own form, which constitutes their instrumentality; so too it is with the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*). If it is argued that there is a deviation because the eyes and other organs, though they are manifestors, are not themselves apprehended, how can this be so when there is no confusion with things of the same class (i.e., those that are conscious)?

[24,21] For those who hold that the sense organs are composed of material elements (*bhautika*), because the eye is of the nature of light (*taijasa*), there is a lack of distinction regarding what is being perceived due to its intermingling with external light of a similar kind. Just as, when the radiance of many lamps is intermingled, one cannot distinguish which belongs to which, so it is also in the case of the ear and the other senses.

Even for those who hold that [the senses] are non-material, their status as belonging to the same genus is due to their being manifestors; yet there is no perception [of the self] because they are manifestors [of objects], not of the self.
