That is not so, because [the self] cannot be discerned by virtue of its dependence on the apprehension of consciousness, and because it is not obstructed. Furthermore, even though the self is omnipresent, it is established that the fruit [of action] is indeed experienced, since it is not separated from the mind due to the self's subtlety and transparency.

Furthermore, for those for whom the activity of the mind is not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend its result. And if the result were apprehended, it would follow by implication (*arthāpatti*) that knowledge itself is unestablished. Yet the result is not apprehended, because the operation of a means of valid cognition is not admitted. If that operation were admitted, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*): whatever means of valid cognition is admitted for the apprehension of a result, that too would have another result, and that means of valid cognition yet another, such that one would never come to rest anywhere.

[25.8] Now, if there is no operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) upon it, then, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition, the non-existence of the result follows. For we accept that whatever those means of valid cognition—which apprehend existing things—do not operate upon, that thing does not exist.

[25,11] If it is argued that even though it is not perceived, that very same cognition is also the result, we say no, because it would violate the properties of the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*). For a manifestor is never seen to manifest its object while itself being unperceived; indeed, even atop a mountain peak, a torch does not transcend its own inherent nature.

[25,14] Now, if it is argued that even while manifesting [the self], it is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to the result [of that manifestation], then our desired point is established; for it is logically possible to apprehend passion and so forth as qualifiers of the activity (vṛtti). If [it is argued that] "I am impassioned" or "I am hateful" are qualifiers of the notion of "I" (ahaṃ-pratyaya), then the apprehension of passion and so forth as qualifiers of the activity is indeed established, because they are apprehended precisely by virtue of being conditioned by the state of that activity. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that, like color-form (rūpa) and other objects, they would depend on another means of valid cognition;
and from that, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would follow.
Therefore, the lack of understanding regarding the result of valid cognition among those who consider themselves wise is merely a matter of conceit; it should be disregarded.

[25.21] Now, inference is stated: "that which follows the inferable among those of a similar class. "Of the inferable" means of that which is qualified by the property one wishes to know. It is "following" among those of a similar class by virtue of possessing that property, merely through its existence; it is "excluded from those of a different class," meaning it is absent from those possessing contrary properties. Regarding "the connection": what is the connection, or between which two?
For a connection cannot attain the status of being a connection without depending on the two related members, such that it is spoken of as "that which" is well-known.

[25,26] But surely, since inference is the subject under discussion, the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) is already well-known, because it is not non-indicative. It is not the mere relationship that is the indicator. It is said: the relationship of the mark itself consists in its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anuvṛtti*). What, then, is this? It is the mark itself. For there is nothing other than the mark that is both inclusive and exclusive; and that [mark] is the indicator.

Now, is it not the case that even the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not a means of cognition (*gamaka*) independent of its connection with the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)? And if it were a means of cognition independent of its connection with the *liṅgin*, then—by way of the sequence of the occurrence of the [mark] on the ground and so forth—it would follow that something could be a means of cognition only after first implying both [the *liṅga* and the *liṅgin*]. Therefore, the relationship between the *liṅga* and the *liṅgin* must be stated.

[26,7] Because it has already been stated. This is because it has already been stated by the words "that which occurs in things of the same class as the object of inference" and so forth. For that which is not connected with the probandum (*liṅgin*) does not occur in things of a similar class, nor does it exclude things of a different class. Therefore, the phrase "that which" merely restates a well-known connection.

[26,10] Its object is thus the object of the related term as determined by positive and negative concomitance. Inference (*anumāna*) is a cognitive operation whose primary function is the ascertainment of a universal, specifically the ascertainment of the universal of the logical mark (*liṅga*).

[26,12] For example: "The moon and stars possess motion because they reach other locations, like Caitra. Although that [property] is manifested by the mere statement of its definition, it is even more clearly so through the demonstration of examples and counter-examples; thus, the presentation of examples is undertaken. In this regard, in the statement "the moon and stars possess motion," the possession of motion by the moon and stars is the object of inference (*anumeya*).

That [property] which is the reaching of another location, occurring among those of the same genus such as Caitra and others who possess motion, and excluded from those of a different genus who lack motion such as the Vindhya mountains, is non-deviant; for it is eternally connected with that which possesses motion.

Granted that for non-contradictory things—such as reaching another location and so forth, which possess a permanent connection—the relationship of the signified and the signifier may exist; but how can the relationship of the signified and the signifier exist for those such as the victim and the executioner, in the absence of any connection? This is what is being asked.

[26,21] Even in that case, there is no fault because of the eternal connection. For here too, a connection characterized by "reaching" (prāpti) is not intended; otherwise, it would result in the fallacy of inferring [the imperceptible] through what is observed in common (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). Indeed, in the case of the moon, stars, and so forth, a connection characterized by reaching another location is not perceived by direct perception. If something that is not perceived could be an indicator, then everything would be an indicator of everything. For nothing is unconnected with anything else, since space and other such entities exist everywhere.

Therefore, in the domain of inference, the relation (*sambandha*) is precisely the cause for the arising of the cognition that apprehends and that which is apprehended. And thus, even in the case of the bound and the slayer, when the absence of one is observed, the presence of the other is understood; this is indeed inference. This is also the case for one who understands the presence of something elsewhere from its non-perception in a suitable location—just as the absence of the victim is inferred by seeing the slayer, or as Caitra’s being outside is inferred upon seeing the living Caitra’s absence from his house.

[27,1] But surely these two are presumptive implications based on non-existence (*abhāvārthāpatti*), not inferences; for they do not conform to the definition [of inference], unlike [the cognition of] a cow and so forth.

[27.2] It is not as has been stated, because the relationship between the victim (*badhya*) and the slayer (*ghātaka*) is characterized by contradiction (*virodha*), since it is established by their definitions. Wherever there is the state of being a slayer, there is necessarily the absence of the victim; this is the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). For the absence of the slayer does not deviate from the absence of the victim, nor does the presence of the victim deviate from the absence of the slayer, just as the presence of smoke does not deviate from the presence of fire.

[27,6] But how, again, is it understood that the cognition of the absence of the victim in the locus of the killer arises solely from the perception of the killer’s existence, and not rather because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend an existent thing have no operation upon the victim, just as the killer has none?

It is said: when the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is occupied with the absence of the killer, there arises the cognition of the absence of the victim; when the means of valid cognition is occupied with smoke, there arises the cognition of the absence of a particular victim; and just as when the means of valid cognition is occupied with a particular kind of smoke, there is the cognition of a particular fire.

[27,12] However, for one who maintains that non-existence is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the absence of a means of valid cognition is indistinguishable in all cases, it is untenable that the perception of the absence of one contradictory would follow the perception of a specific contradictory, just as the perception of a specific probandum (*liṅgin*) follows a specific mark (*liṅga*). For there is no distinction whatsoever in the absence of the operation of the means of valid cognition that apprehends an existent, such that a cognition of a particularity would follow that particularity.

[27,16] Now, if it is argued that this is because there is an absence of any valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for apprehending a real entity in a specific instance, that is not so; for it is impossible for a non-existent thing to depend on the concomitance of memory, desire, and so forth. Indeed, nothing non-existent—such as a hare’s horn—is ever observed to produce an effect by depending on auxiliary factors. If it is argued that such a case is indeed observed here, we say no; for where there is a point of dispute, there can be no supporting example. If it is argued that the case is equal, we say no; for in the case of a jar and the like, which are existent, dependence [on causes] is observed.

Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that which is devoid of activity is not a real entity (*vastu*). Indeed, nothing in the world is observed to initiate an effect while its activity has been eliminated. Therefore, the cognition of the non-existence of an object of knowledge (*prameya-abhāva-buddhi*), being produced by a means of valid cognition whose nature is activity, has the non-existent as its object, just like the cognition of a jar or similar things. This is because it is a real entity and because it serves as the cause for engagement or withdrawal from action. The counter-example (*vipakṣa*) consists of such things as a rabbit’s horn.
Thus, the cognition of non-existence is not produced by the absence of a means of valid cognition, as is seen from the previously stated reason and example.

[27.25] The perception of the slayer is the mark (liṅga) for the cognition of the absence of the victim, because it is a conditioned state, like the cognition of smoke which is the cause for the cognition of fire and so forth, and because it removes doubt; or else, the cognition of the absence of the victim is produced by a mark, because it has the nature of a certainty, like the cognition of fire.

[28,1] Here, it is said that there is no inference in the case of "there is no jar here," because the relationship between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) has not been apprehended. For, unlike the search for a mark such as smoke when there is a cognition of fire and so forth, there is no search for a mark in this case of "there is no jar here," since the cognition arises even before any search for a mark.

This is not a fault, because here it is the very form of the cognition "here" that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*). For when the cognition of the logical mark has already arisen for the first time, there is no further search for a logical mark. The cognition colored by the form "here" is itself the logical mark, just like the cognition of a killer is the logical mark for the cognition of the absence of the object killed—namely, the jar and so forth—which is distinct from that coloring factor. And in this case as well, the relation is precisely that characterized by contradiction.

Furthermore, where the coloring factors (*uparañjaka*) are not contradictory, the cognition of existence is established; by this very principle, the inferential nature of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is explained through the relation of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). In that case as well, for a living Devadatta, his absence from the house implies his presence outside; when he is present in the house, he is not present outside—thus, inference is made by means of one of the two. The example is the state of being absent inside while being directly perceived as present outside.
For the reason for the apprehension of non-existence has been stated as the distinction between a functioning coloring factor and a non-coloring factor.

[28,13] Even in the case of fire and the like, the apprehension of the capacity for wealth and so forth is indeed inference. This is because the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the capacity and the accomplishment of the effect has been observed in oneself with respect to eating and other such acts. For, in the case of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), there is indeed the apprehension of capacity—which is an attribute of the self—just as there is of the self itself, in the form: "I am capable of performing this action" or "I am incapable. Since the effects such as burning are themselves brought about by capacity, the establishment of this is through inference.

[28,17] But surely some maintain that non-existence (abhāva) is perceptible. For instance, when an object is being perceived by means of a lamp or similar illuminator, that which is not apprehended in the composite whole is said to "not exist"; thus, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that clarifies what exists also reveals what does not exist. And so they illustrate this: having been told, "Bring the unmarked cloth," one enters the storehouse and, amidst the presence of both marked and unmarked cloths, by the very act of taking the marked cloth—

Perception leads to the apprehension of the cloth as qualified by the absence marked [by it]; therefore, non-existence itself is indeed perceptual, since no other means of characterization is possible.

[28.23] That is not so, because it would entail the falsity of the determination of the object by means of the form of the cognition. For when a cognition has a certain form, the nature of that [object] being directly perceived is admitted as being determined by that form. Just as in the case of "the blue thing is yellow," even here the cognition of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is false.

It follows [this conclusion]. For example, when one says "there is no jar here," there is a cognition of a relation between this location and the absence of the jar, even though no such relation exists. Indeed, there is no relation—whether characterized as "attainment" (*prāpti*) or designated as "inherence" (*samavāya*)—between the absence of the jar and this location, unlike the case of "Devadatta is here.

Therefore, since the cognition of the absence [of a jar] would be false, the cognition of the relation between the qualifier and the qualified, such as "the object is blue," would also necessarily be false, because it too is a cognition of a relation.

Just as there is a cognition of a relation even when there is no actual relation between the absence of a jar here and this place, so too, even with respect to a non-blue object, there would result the cognition of a relation to blueness despite the fact that no relation to blueness actually exists; and the same would apply to the relata themselves. If, on the other hand, the relation were actually present, it would contradict the dual location (dviṣṭhatā) of a relation, because you admit that an absence is not a real entity.

Furthermore, even if one were to maintain that there are one hundred and sixty types of genitive meanings (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), such that the genitive meaning is intended to be "relation" (*sambandha*), then it would not be tenable to claim that relation is of only two kinds—namely, that called inherence (*samavāya*) and that called conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
[29,9] Now, even if it were said that the one hundred and sixty meanings fall within both extremes, they do not exist in non-existence, because neither of the two would be possible.

Furthermore, in this case, since the sky—which serves as the locus for the statement "there is no flower in the sky"—is itself imperceptible, it follows that the absence of the sky-flower must also be imperceptible.

If you argue that it is indeed imperceptible, then it would follow that the absence of a jar in this spot of ground is likewise imperceptible, just like the absence of the sky-flower. A distinction must be stated.

[29,14] Now, as for the argument that "because space is imperceptible," that is not correct; for since one perceives the existence of a falling flower in the sky, the imperceptibility of space is not a valid reason. Just as the imperceptibility of space is not a reason when there is the actual presence of a falling flower, so too it would not be a reason even when perceiving something that contradicts its existence. If you say, "precisely because space is imperceptible," then anything whatsoever—even something unrelated—such as the imperceptibility of what is obstructed, would also become a reason.

If it is argued that the non-existence of sky-flowers is perceptible, then the uselessness of the contact between the sense-organ and its object would follow in all cases; and this being so, since everything would be perceived without such contact, it would follow that everyone is omniscient.

[29,20] Now, if it is argued that the object of inference (*anumeya*) is located there, then—just as with the absence of sky-flowers—the absence of a jar here is established as being purely inferential (*anumānika*), since there is no distinction between them. This being the case, even for those who maintain that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the absence of fire and so forth in water that is obstructed or distant is itself an object of inference due to its similarity to other absences, it is logical to conclude that the absence of a jar here must likewise be apprehended by inference on account of that same general principle.

[29.24] "The Vindhyas" and "non-motion due to non-arrival" constitute another formal argument (*prayoga*). "The Vindhyas are without motion" is the proposition (*pratijñā*). "Due to non-arrival" is the reason (*hetu*). The phrase "like Caitra" applies to both cases, like the "eye of a crow. There is a connection through similarity (*sādharmya*) with the statement "the moon and stars possess motion," and a connection through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the statement "and the Vindhyas, because of non-arrival. This being the case, there is no fault arising from the failure to demonstrate positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Alternatively, it has been proposed that in this application there is no fault because the contrapositive is observed; and since the definition is to be understood in relation to a specific instance of the defined, there is no defect.

[30.9] An authoritative person (*āpta*) is one who is motivated by the desire to benefit others, is free from defects, and has perceived or inferred the object. By him—whether the object has been perceived or inferred—the meaning is conveyed through words for the sake of transferring his own cognition and transmitting his own realization to another specific listener; this is called "verbal" (*śabda*) because it is a sentence, since from it there is the comprehension of a specific object. Therefore, the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) which has the sentence-meaning as its object, arising from that sentence taught by him, is primarily characterized by the determination of a universal (*sāmānya*), just like inference.

[30,14] Thus, the scripture (*āgama*) of the hearer is preceded by the apprehension of properties such as being trustworthy (*āptatva*), but that is not so for the speaker. For the speaker possesses knowledge of the object that is either perceptual or inferential; his cognition is either based on the senses or based on a mark (*liṅga*). However, the certain cognition of the hearer alone—which is preceded by hearing and is distinct from both inferential and perceptual cognition—is scripture (*āgama*). It is not perception, because its object is not an object of the senses; nor is it inference, because it is independent of the relationship between a mark and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) as previously described.

For in the case of words such as "heaven," "unseen potency" (*apūrva*), or "deity," a cognition associated with an object does not arise preceded by the apprehension of a relationship between a mark (*liṅga*) and the thing marked (*liṅgin*); rather, in all such cases, the result is simply the understanding of the speaker's intention (*vṛttibodha*).

[30,20] Regarding that scripture whose proponent, by uttering words as the cause for the arising of the function called "scripture," has demonstrated the fruit through the presentation of its application—just as before—even when there is only a single application, because what is intended is merely the absence of the probandum and the probans, it is not said [to be fallacious] on account of observing a contrary negative concomitance (viparītavyatireka).

[30,23] Scripture itself is distinguished by being spoken by one whose meaning is not to be trusted. How is it that this speaker’s meaning is not to be trusted? To this he says: "The object has neither been seen nor inferred by that speaker"—referring to the Buddha, the Arhat, and others, because they propound what is well-known among the learned and the world in a contrary manner. For one whose internal organ is not afflicted by defects such as passion does not describe what is well-established otherwise. Such scripture "floats," that is, it becomes a mere semblance.

[30,27] Even though the demonstration of fallacious objects of perception and inference was not explicitly formulated by its own specific terminology, nevertheless, by the very presentation of the fallacies of scripture (*āgamābhāsa*), it should be understood that in the preceding cases as well, the fallacies of perception, inference, and so forth—by virtue of being the opposite of the characteristics as previously stated—are expressed by implication (*arthāt*).

But in the case of the original speaker—the first speaker, the Lord—that scripture which originates from him would be free from error, because of the absence of any cause for error, just like a speaker who speaks in accordance with reality.

Comparison (*upamāna*) is preceded by verbal testimony; because it falls within the scope of that [testimony], it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example, when one has ascertained similarity from a statement delivered by a forest-dweller, such as "The *gavaya* is like a cow," then even upon seeing a *gavaya* in the forest, there is merely the recollection of the similarity previously established by the heard statement—nothing more. Indeed, the similarity was already understood from the statement itself.

Nor is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) merely through the comprehension of the relationship between a name and the named, because that relationship is also understood from that very sentence itself. For indeed, by the mere word "cow," even one who has not previously learned the name "gavaya" and sees a gavaya in the forest does not achieve the realization of the relationship between the name and the named, thinking "this is a gavaya."

Therefore, just as "like a cow," the word *gavaya* must also be expected in that sentence. And this being the case, everything is understood from what was previously heard alone. Now, if it should be argued that "this is like a cow" is not the object of the previous cognition, even that appears to be like the behavior of a cornered, tormented dog by those who, while failing to see the refutation of their own objection, remain stuck in their position.

For in that case, there would result a multiplicity of types of analogy based on differences such as proximity or remoteness in space and time. If it is argued that "let it be so," we reply that this has already been established previously: the object must be conveyed by the preceding cognition precisely as it is, with all its specific qualities internalized. Indeed, when the word "cow" is uttered, there is no failure of comprehension of the referent from the word "cow" merely because of the absence of specific details regarding place, time, and so forth.

[31,17] Furthermore, the apprehension of the relationship between a name and the named object is not analogy (*upamāna*), because that by which something is compared is analogy, and that is a cognition of similarity. Indeed, nothing is compared through the apprehension of the relationship between a name and the named object, because that occurs at a later time. For it is only after the similarity has been ascertained that the notion "this is a *gavaya*" subsequently arises.

[31,21] If that were so, there might be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) not preceded by verbal testimony, such as the cognition of a villager that "the cow is similar to this" arising from the sight of a *gavaya*.

That too is not the case, because of the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*). For the operation of a means of valid cognition—which is intended to apprehend what exists—occurs only when an object of cognition exists. Indeed, there is no single entity called "similarity" that exists in reality as something both distinct and continuous between the cow and the *gavaya*.

[31,25] But surely there is indeed the cognition of similarity; it ought not to be without an objective basis (*nirālambana*). True, that is so; however, the investigation concerns precisely that: is this [cognition] like the cognition of a forest or a herd of deer, or is it like the cognition of a jar and so forth? What follows from this? If it were like the cognition of a forest, then just as trees themselves—possessing a specific arrangement—are the cause of the cognition of a "forest" despite the forest not existing apart from them, in exactly the same way, the parts of the cow and the gavaya themselves, depending upon the perception of both and upon memory, would be the cause of the cognition of "similarity" which does not exist apart from their own selves.
It follows that [the object] is a non-entity, since it is merely the cause for cognition.
Alternatively, if it were like the cognition of a jar or similar objects, then it would possess both substantiality and the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In this regard, the nature of the object (*vastu*) is investigated as follows: Is there a single similarity (*sādṛśya*) that persists between the cow and the gavaya, distinct from the universals of "cowness" (*gotva*) and "gavayaness" (*gavayatva*)? Or are those two very [universals] themselves, distinguished from one another? Or rather, are there two similarities, distinct from those two, residing in the substrates—the cow and the gavaya—either independent of each other or dependent? Is it simply the individual (*vyakti*) itself, qualified by either of the two universals? Or is it the universal itself, qualified by either of the two individuals, or qualified by both individuals? Or is it the relation between these?

Regarding the phrase "according to the application of conceptual construction," many other conceptual constructions should also be brought forth, such as [the relation of] each being a qualifier distinguished from the other, and so on. In that regard, if there were a single similarity residing in both [the object and the standard], then there would be no status of being the object of comparison (*upameyatva*) because of their identity, just as in the case of "a cow is like a cow."

[32,10] Now, if one individual is compared with another by means of that [universal], this too is not possible because it resides only within itself, as in the case of "a cow" [being compared] by means of "cowness. Or, if one individual possessing that [universal] is compared with another individual, this also is not so; for cowness is not the cause for the status of being the object of comparison between a spotted and a hornless cow. If it is argued that similarity, in dependence upon other properties, is the cause of that cognition [of similarity], then similarity is lost; let that [other property] itself be the cause of that cognition—what is the use of your imagined, wretched "similarity"?

Furthermore, regarding that property which is being depended upon, there would arise conceptual alternatives such as: "Is it one, like similarity, existing in both [the similar and the dissimilar], or is it distinct? As before, these are impossible. Now, if it is said that the similarity is distinct, that is not so, precisely because of its distinctness; for it does not occur that "a cow is like a horse. Just as [similarity] is untenable due to its being a single entity, so too is it untenable when depended upon by many. By this, the previously conceptualized relations between genus and individual, and so forth, are refuted.

[32,19] Now, if it is argued that the postulation of similarity is necessitated by the impossibility of the arising of such a cognition otherwise, then why is substantiality not likewise postulated, given that the experience of the cognitions of "forest," "cleft," "east," "south," "north," and so forth, would otherwise be impossible? You might think: "In this case, the trees and so forth themselves are the causes for the arising of those respective cognitions. If that were so, then the cognition "the cow is similar to the gavaya" would be a false perception, just like the cognition of a "forest."

Now, as for those [features] that are excluded, what is the sense of the analogy here, such as "like a cow, like a horse"? Even if both those parts possess the nature of being both excluded and inclusive and are the causes of the cognition of that [object], nevertheless, it follows that [the object] must be like the cognition of a forest.

Therefore, since it cannot withstand thorough investigation, those very same parts, being perceived in both cases, are the cause of the cognition of similarity—just as trees are the cause of the cognition of a forest. Thus, it is established that there is no such separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called analogy (upamāna).

Nor can the postulation of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be based on the duality of the objects to be known. Why? Because the apprehension of an object occurs by virtue of the means of valid cognition; it is not the case that the means of valid cognition are postulated by virtue of the object. Furthermore, if the means of valid cognition were postulated by virtue of the object, then for those who do not know everything—that is, for non-omniscient beings—the cognition that "heaven results from the worship of a shrine" would have to be false, because the causality of the shrine-worship with respect to heaven is not within the scope of perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*). Alternatively, one would have to postulate another means of valid cognition for that purpose.
[33,7] Now, if it is argued that this cognition is the fruit of inference, then it would follow that the fruit exists apart from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And in that case, there would be no liberation, because the cognition whose object is the meaning of the sentence regarding the three instruments and so forth would likewise [be a fruit apart from its cause].

Nor is the intention here to define the characteristics of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the work is devoted to demonstrating the means for the cessation of the functioning of well-known means of valid cognition and so forth. For this very reason, the author of the aphorisms (*sūtrakāra*) did not compose any such aphorisms. However, the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) has relied upon a mere restatement of what is already well known; therefore, I have said something following that [commentary]. (6–7)
[33,13] Having explained the function termed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he now says, "Error is false knowledge," wishing to provide a detailed exposition of the function called error (*viparyaya*).

[33,15] But surely, since cessation (*nirodha*) is the subject under discussion, and since that consists of abandonment (*hāna*), and since abandonment depends upon that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), and since that which is to be abandoned has its root in ignorance (*avidyā*), and since ignorance is a misconception (*viparyaya*), it is precisely this misconception that ought to be ceased primarily, because that from which it arises is what is to be abandoned. For when the cause is ceased, the effect is ceased as a matter of course. Therefore, misconception should be explained first, on the grounds of its primacy and its status as the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[33,19] It is true that error has primacy because it is that which must be suppressed; nevertheless, since a person’s engagement toward suppression depends upon the knowledge of qualities and defects, it is indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that constitutes the knowledge of qualities and defects. For the defectiveness of error is not apprehended by what is not a means of valid cognition, nor are its suppression, its results, or the means for achieving them known [by such means]. Therefore, [the sequence follows] precisely from the operation of valid cognition.

Priority is appropriate [for the first two]. Furthermore, since virtue and defect are known through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the statement of error (*viparyaya*) follows immediately after that. However, with respect to other modes of functioning (*vṛtti*), error has priority; for since the other modes are rooted in that [error], the cessation of the others is logically possible only preceded by its cessation.

[33,25] "Error is false cognition" is a statement of synonyms. "Not established in that form" is the definition. Its "form" (*tad-rūpa*) is the appearance of the consciousness; and its "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the objective support (*ālambana*) of that consciousness. Error is a cognition consisting of a mere generality regarding something whose specific qualities have not been grasped, which is accompanied by the recollection of another object previously perceived, and which arises in the form of a determination (*niścaya*).

For doubt arises for both parties when one who has grasped a commonality thus desires to know the specific distinction; therefore, it is included within memory itself. As in the case: "Is this a post, or..."

Doubt arises for one who remembers a specific feature previously perceived as "man," but error does not arise in that same way; for [error] is determined by the mere remembrance of one [of the two alternatives]. For example, when a post stands before one, through the perception of its mere common features such as circumference and height, there arises in one who has previously experienced both a man and a post the certain cognition: "This is indeed a man."

[34,12] Although that [cognition] has as its primary object the generality (*sāmānya*) of the thing perceived through the path of the senses, nevertheless, because it is established upon a thing that is not actually present but is being remembered, it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For it terminates in memory, since it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge due to having as its object something that is not the actual reality (*abhūtārtha*). (Thus, for this reason...)

[The opponent argues: "Because it is established [as a distinct cognition]. For at that time, the object being remembered is non-existent. If this were so, it would follow that it is merely memory; [we reply] no, because it is distinguished. Memory arises elsewhere by taking a perceived object as its cause, having as its domain an object previously experienced. It is not the reverse. Even though the finality of the recollection lies in a thing that possesses only a present general form accompanied by specificities of place, time, and so forth, a mistaken cognition (*viparyaya*) arises in the form of a specific [identification], such as "this is that."
Therefore, since it possesses neither the characteristic of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor that of memory (*smṛti*), it constitutes a distinct mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*).

[34,20] Therein, he presents an example to demonstrate how that which is being cognized is sublated by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely: "the perception of two moons. Just as the perception of two moons—whose object is a non-existent thing because it is produced by a visual faculty impaired by cataracts, jaundice, or other defects—is sublated by the perception of a single moon, which has an existent object and a real thing as its referent, and is supported by the knowledge of the logical possibility of the absence of a second moon and by memory; so too is the case here.

[34.24] But surely, since *dvicandram* is a *dvigu* compound—like *dvipūlī* or *pañcapūlī*—and because of the rule "the *dvigu* is singular," and because that condition applies here, and because of the rule "a *dvigu* whose final member ends in *a* is desired in the feminine," the suffix *ī* would follow from the word *dvicandra* (as it ends in *a*)? This is not a fault, because of the prohibition regarding words beginning with *pātra*. And in that context, the word "etc. (*ādi*)...

Because it expresses a variety (*prakāra*), and because a variety follows the usage of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), [the term] "two moons" (*dvicandra*) should also be understood as referring to vessels and the like. It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that perception in which there are two moons. Furthermore, since the word "one moon" (*ekacandra*) is not a *dvigu* compound, there is no possibility of such an objection. And that...

Ignorance has five branches; that ignorance, which functions as a misconception, has five parts. What, then, are those parts? He says: "ignorance, egoism," and so forth. For this very reason, the afflictions beginning with ignorance, distinguished by their own specific names—such as *tamas* and so on—which are well-known in other treatises, will be discussed in the second chapter (*pāda*) in connection with the impurities of the mind (*vitti*). (1.8)

[35,16] Now he shows conceptual construction (*vikalpa*): "Conceptual construction is that which follows upon the cognition of a word and is devoid of an objective reality. The "cognition of a word" (*śabdajñāna*) is the knowledge of words according to the fixed rule of the signified and the signifier; it is the knowledge of correct and incorrect words. That which has the habit of following such a cognition is "that which follows upon the cognition of a word" (*śabdajñānānupātī*). "Devoid of an objective reality" (*vastuśūnya*) means: it is empty of the actual referent corresponding to the signified object of whichever word its cognition follows. For conceptualization is indeed a mental construction that occurs apart from the actual state of things.

[35.21] For since that [conceptualization] follows upon the cognition of words, it would follow that it is included within scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, he says: "It does not ascend to the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is not included within the means of valid cognition because it is devoid of a real object (*vastu-śūnyatvāt*). For scripture, even though it follows upon the cognition of words, is not devoid of a real object; for scripture is a mental state whose object is the referent of a word, whereas conceptualization (*vikalpa*), being devoid of a real object, is not a means of valid cognition.

[35,25] Furthermore, the conceptual construction (vikalpa) of both the speaker and the listener is the same; for when a word is uttered, the cognition of both arises as nothing other than a conceptual construction. This is not the case with scripture (āgama). For scripture belongs only to the listener, whereas the speaker has already perceived or inferred its meaning.

Furthermore, for one who has attained the state free from discursive thought (*nirvitarka*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) ceases, but not the scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, [the scripture] is eternal, yet it does not function as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

[36,6] If this is so, then because it is empty of a real entity (*vastu*), it follows that it falls within the category of error (*viparyaya*); therefore, he says: "it does not ascend to error. Why? Because it does not follow from verbal cognition (*śabda-jñāna*). For even when it is empty of a real entity, error does not depend upon verbal cognition; since it has been stated: "Error is false cognition (*mithyā-jñāna*) which is not established in the nature of that [object]. Furthermore, because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is subordinate to the cognition that is to be determined by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For conceptual construction is not sublated by contradiction in the same way that the misconceptions of all [ordinary beings] are, precisely because it possesses the status of being a subordinate factor within the cognition of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[36,12] Therefore, by means of the apprehension of the emptiness of the object and the apprehension of the conformity to verbal cognition—which are mutually related—it is shown that there is a distinct, separate mode of operation called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is not even slightly tainted by the nature of either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or its opposite (*viparyaya*). Just as it is from the mere application of that scent that conceptual construction immediately follows, it does not possess the nature of memory (*smṛti*), because memory has as its sole domain that which has been previously experienced.

[36,16] Now, if it is argued that such a mental state is not well-known—that is, that no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) whatsoever serves as the cause for a mental state—it is said in reply: "Even when devoid of a real entity (vastu), linguistic usage is observed to be based solely on the power of verbal cognition. The inclusion of the word "solely" (mātra) is intended to demonstrate the absence of any cause other than verbal cognition. If one asks where this is observed, it is said: "For example, 'consciousness (caitanya) is the essential nature (svarūpa) of the person (puruṣa')."

Since it has been stated that the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is unchanging, the *puruṣa* is indeed consciousness itself, and that alone is its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Consequently, because there is no distinction [between them], the designation based on distinction—namely, "the consciousness of the *puruṣa*"—would not be possible. And thus, relying on this very point, the author of the *Vārttika*, who is learned in grammar, has said: "But [the usage] is established through the treatment as if possessing a designation. In the same way here as well, just as in the case where a distinction exists one says "Caitra’s cow," so too one says "the consciousness of the *puruṣa*."

For there is no person (puruṣa) as a distinct entity from consciousness (citi), such that it could serve as a ground for designation in the way that Caitra is designated as distinct from a cow; nor, conversely, is consciousness designated as distinct from the person. Nevertheless, with respect to the relation of difference (vyatireka-sambandha), there occurs the linguistic usage: "Consciousness is the essential nature (svarūpa) of the person."

[37,7] "One whose substantial properties are negated" (*pratiṣiddhavastudharma*): the property of a substance is a "substantial property" (*vastudharma*). One for whom the substantial property has been negated is "one whose substantial properties are negated. According to the rule *dharmād anic kevalāt*, the suffix *anic* at the end of the compound is to be considered optional. By the word "substance" (*vastu*), the qualities such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth are meant; their properties are negated in this one.

For the properties such as existence (sattva) and so forth, though negated, do not become related to this person simply by virtue of being negated, such that they could be designated as "belonging to this person. Rather, the meaning there is merely their non-existence. Nevertheless, just as there is a cognition when one designates "these variegated cows belong to him," so too is there a cognition when one designates "the properties of things have been negated for him."

[37,16] "Action has departed from this"—here too, departure is a form of going away (*apāya*). And going away is preceded by a prior connection, as in the case of action having departed from Caitra. However, since action is impossible in the case of the *puruṣa*, such a departure from the *puruṣa* is not possible. Nevertheless, the designation "the *puruṣa* is devoid of action" does function [as a valid expression].

[37,19] Likewise, "the person (puruṣa) has the property of non-arising. This means that the property of arising does not exist in him, just as before. Here, the commentator himself explains the meaning: "Only the absence of the property of arising is understood here. Examples such as "without qualities," "untainted," and "partless" are also [to be understood] in this way. The presentation of these numerous examples concerning the self is for the purpose of determining the true nature of the self.

[37.23] The citation of the example well-known in the world, "the arrow stands," is for the purpose of removing the suspicion that it is not established. "Stands" (*tiṣṭhati*) means the cessation of motion, which is the absence of motion. Now, the connection with the three times does not belong to a non-existence, nor to a substance such as an arrow that is independent of action. Nor is there a relation of the real entity, the arrow, with the non-existence consisting of the cessation of motion. Thus, there are three examples: "the arrow stands," "it will stand," and "it has stood."

[38,12] “The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the cessation of motion. Now, if the cessation of motion itself is the meaning of the verbal root, how can there be a locus (*ādhāra*) expressed by “in the cessation of motion”? For this very reason, this is another example; because when there is no distinction, the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) cannot exist. And yet, in the designation “the meaning of the verbal root is in the cessation of motion,” there arises a cognition produced by the power of the words which takes hold of the relationship between locus and located. Therefore, one should see that many examples of this kind are objects of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). 1.9.

[38,17] Now he explains the mental modification called sleep: "Sleep is the mental modification whose object is the notion of non-existence. Since it arises by suppressing the three previously mentioned modifications which have waking objects, the modification called sleep is explained immediately after them.

"Non-existence" (abhāva) refers to the absence of objects perceived during the waking state, but it is not absolute non-existence, because a mental modification (pratyaya) cannot arise with respect to that. A "modification consisting of the cognition of non-existence" (abhāvapratyaya) is a cognition whose object is non-existence; the mental state (vṛtti) which has that as its support is "the modification having the cognition of non-existence as its support. That is sleep, the state of deep slumber (suṣupti).

[38,23] But is it not the case that even the state of dreaming is simply sleep? This is not a fault, because the author of the Sūtras has taught them as distinct by stating, "or the objective support for the cognition of dream-sleep"; thus, in this context, "sleep" is intended specifically as the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

[38,25] Furthermore, it is deep sleep alone that has non-existence as its objective support (*abhāvapratyayālambana*). For dream does not have non-existence as its objective support, because it is a memory (*smṛti*); and memory has as its object that which has been previously experienced. Thus, the author of the Bhāṣya shows its nature as memory by stating that in a dream, "those things to be remembered are already imagined."

Furthermore, since a dream is a mental state (*cittavṛtti*) and is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*), no doubt [regarding its existence] can even arise. Thus, having raised the doubt that it is a mental state, he says: "But that [is known] through recollection upon waking," and so forth. Therefore, sleep is a particular cognition (*pratyayaviśeṣa*); for in the absence of a particular cognition, a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) would not be possible. And this reflective awareness exists for one who has awakened, such as "I slept happily," and so on. What is called "reflective awareness" is the thought, "I experienced something."

The observation of conditions would not occur in the absence of experience; nor would memories having those as their objects be possible. If sleep were not a condition, the mind would make wisdom lucid. [In the state of sleep: the agency of the mind is true, yet it is motionless and inactive. [The word *guru* is reduplicated] according to the rule for words expressing a quality in the sense of "of such a kind" (*prakāre guṇavacanasya*), meaning "of a very heavy kind. It is sluggish, as if stolen by a wrestler, as if carried away; these effects of the experience of conditions would not exist.

Certain memories, certain actions, and certain reflective recognitions—this triad, as presented by the author of the Bhāṣya, is logically possible only on the basis of being specific types of cognition (pratyaya).

Furthermore, in cases such as being in a private chamber, for those who have not perceived any external cause, the reflective awareness—"I slept for a long time" or "I was tossed about"—would otherwise be inexplicable, given that there is no distinction [in the conditions].

[39,16] But is it not the case that there are no memories here, because they are qualified by the thought "I experienced these memories"? For one who has arisen from deep sleep does not remember such a distinction. To this it is replied: In this world, even a child who has had no experience in this life regarding the connection with breast-milk is seen to have a desire for it immediately after birth. And this is not innate, because we observe that non-children act preceded by memory. It is the same here as well.

Therefore, it is established that sleep is a specific cognition, because the effects—such as heaviness of the limbs—experienced by one who has awakened from deep sleep are preceded by a cognition; for they are effects regarding the heaviness of the limbs and so forth, which are preceded by the experience of pain and the like, just like the heaviness of the limbs resulting from the experience of well-known pain. (1.10)

[39,23] Now he explains *smṛti* (memory): "Memory is the non-losing of an experienced object. Memory is placed at the end because it is the effect of all the mental modifications, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It is an "experienced object" (*anubhūtaviṣaya*) because it is both experienced and an object. That very thing which was experienced—manifesting like the waves of the great ocean of bliss—is the object; it is not the case that whatever is an object is necessarily what was experienced. Furthermore, since memory itself is not sound and so forth, it would follow that a memory whose object is another memory would not be a memory.
And it is maintained that memory, even when its object is [already] remembered, is self-cognizable; for memory is the non-forgetting, the non-removal, the non-obscuration of an experienced object.
Even in the case of indirect perception, memory is the appearance of an experienced object as if it were being seen, depending on causes such as similarity.

In this regard, since there is no distinction between the appearance of the object's form in the cognition and in the memory, one might ask: what constitutes the difference between the two? Desiring to demonstrate that distinction, he says: "Does the mind remember the cognition? and so forth.

[40,9] Even though there is a distinction between them by virtue of being objects that have been experienced and are currently being experienced, nevertheless, he clarifies the error caused by their similarity in order to demonstrate their relationship as cause and effect. And this very point is the reason why the Nihilists (vaināśika) maintain that external objects are untenable, because it is the mind that is the cause of cognition. In both cases, the genitive case is used for the object of the verb "to remember" (*smarati*). Thus, "the mind remembers."

This refutes the agency of a person (puruṣa) for the purpose of demonstrating that memory and cognition have a single agent. For neither the agency of cognition nor the agency of memory belongs to the person. This is because cognitions are objects of perception; and we shall explain that things which are objects of perception, like jars and so forth, must be perceived by something distinct from themselves.

What follows from this? If one remembers the object, then since the cognition also has the object as its domain, memory would not be distinct from the cognition. If, on the other hand, one remembers the cognition itself, then it is incorrect to say that "memory is the non-loss of the experienced object. For in that case, it should rather be said that "it is the non-loss of the experience. To this he replies: "colored by the object" (*grāhyoparakta*). The "object" (*grāhya*) is the objective support (*ālambana*); it is "colored" (*uparakta*) by that, like a crystal colored by lac-dye and the like.

It manifests in the form of both the grasped and the grasping; for it arises as the manifestation of both the grasped—such as a jar—with its broad base and other features, and by way of its own nature as a manifesting form. Thus, it is a manifestation of both.

And that condition (pratyaya), having arisen and then ceased, deposits a latent impression (saṃskāra) in its own substrate, which is the possessor of the condition. And that latent impression, because it conforms to its cause, is indeed of the nature of falling into both [categories]. Regarding the phrase "the collyrium that manifests itself": the action (karma) belonging to the condition that possesses the latent impression—which has become the cause and has already yielded its fruit—is the "manifestor" (svavyañjaka); that is, another action of a similar kind which is now oriented toward yielding its own fruit.

And so he will say: "Therefore, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are concordant with the maturation (*vipāka*) of that [karma]. Thus, either the karma brought forward, or similarity, focused attention (*praṇidhāna*), and so forth, is manifested by its own manifestor; hence it is said to have "its own manifestor as its applicator" (*svavyañjakāñjana*). It produces a memory consisting of the grasping of the object of perception. Otherwise, the maturation of the karma that manifests it would be impossible.

In this context, cognition preceded by the mode of grasping is "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), which means appropriation (*svīkaraṇa*). This very appropriation occurs first and initially for the cognition as it arises; it does not depend upon a specific object, because it precedes the grasping of what is desirable or undesirable, like the mass of light emerging from a lamp when a jar has been broken.

[41,13] Memory is preceded by the form of the object grasped (*grāhyākāra*), because it depends upon what has been experienced. If memory were preceded by the act of grasping (*grahaṇa*)—just like a present cognition—it would not depend upon what was experienced; yet it does depend upon it. Therefore, its prior element is the object to be grasped (*grāhya-viṣaya*), not the act of grasping. Nevertheless, it possesses the nature of both, because memory and its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) are of a single nature. Nor is it possible for it to exist by the rejection of either one. Thus, it is logically established that memory is "the non-forgetting of an experienced object."

Since both memory and cognition have the same object, and since the status of being a "grasping" (grahaṇatva) is possible in all cases, the aforementioned fault is not seen in either of the two positions.

And that [recollection] is of two kinds. How so? There is that in which what was cultivated is to be recollected (*bhāvitasmartavyā*), because it has been repeatedly cultivated (*asakṛdbhāvitatvāt*). Just as oil and the like, when repeatedly cultivated by means of another substance, do not require a further effort such as a formal resolve (*praṇidhāna*) once they have been cultivated; because it has been repeatedly cultivated, it does not depend on a subsequent effort such as a resolve. That in which what was cultivated is to be recollected without depending on a subsequent effort such as a resolve is "that in which what was cultivated is to be recollected" (*bhāvitasmartavyā*) in the state of sleep. However, at the time of waking, it does depend on a subsequent effort such as a resolve; thus, it is the opposite of that.

[41,24] And all these modifications arise from the experience of the fivefold group beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). All these are essentially composed of pleasure and so forth (*sukhādi*, or *sattvādi*). And *saṃsāra* has that as its essence. Furthermore, pleasure, pain, and delusion have been explained by the author of the Sūtras among the afflictions (*kleśa*). For he will say: "To the discriminating, everything is pain. And it is the abandonment of that which is intended here. Therefore, because they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, the modifications must be restrained.
Moreover, upon their restraint, there occurs either cognitive (*samprajñāta*) or non-cognitive (*asamprajñāta*) meditative absorption (*samādhi*). ||1.11||
[42,16] Now, what is the means for their cessation?

[42,17] He teaches the means: "Their cessation occurs through practice and dispassion. Practice and dispassion will have their characteristics explained later. Through these two, there is the cessation of the fluctuations (*vṛtti*) whose characteristics have been described, because of their mutual opposition. Cessation is tranquility. This commentary, beginning with "the river of the mind," is intended to demonstrate the distinction between the objects of practice and dispassion.

By means of the mind, those wandering in *saṃsāra* are constantly led around among sense-objects, like rivers that have their source in *saṃsāra* and their terminus in the ocean—that is, they end in the ocean. "To be made barren" means to be obstructed. "To be opened" means to be set in motion; it is called "opened" (*uddhāṭyate*) because the act of opening (*uddhāṭa*) is performed. Otherwise, because [the root] belongs to the *mit* class, as in "ghaṭādayo mitaḥ," the rule "shortening occurs for *mit* roots" (*mitāṃ hrasvaḥ*) would apply.

Thus, the meaning is that [this applies] to both systems (*tantra*). (1.12) In this regard, intending to explain the nature of practice (*abhyāsa*), he says: "Practice is the effort toward stability therein. "Therein" means in that cessation (*nirodha*); and that [word] is in the locative case of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). That effort which is the cause of the mind's stability—which is itself the fruit of effort—having cessation as its cause, that is practice. And thus it has been said: "For one who is free from fluctuations, whose mind is like a pool of water with its mud and ripples stilled, there is practice characterized by a tranquil flow and a serene form."
Transformation is the state of the mind whose fluctuations have been suppressed; effort is vigor, which is enthusiasm.

Synonyms: Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the performance of the means of yoga, such as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), with the desire to achieve stability. (1.13) But how does that become stable? To this he says: "Practiced for a long time and without interruption. Practice does not become firmly established if it is devoid of a long duration or devoid of continuity; therefore, both are indeed qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). However, in the phrase "practiced through refinement" (*saṃskārāsevita*), it is practice itself that is being qualified.
The explanation of "firm ground" is "by the latent impression of emergence. It means that one is not suddenly or abruptly overcome by the latent impression born of emergence. (1.14)

In order to demonstrate dispassion (*vairāgya*), he says: "Dispassion is the perception of mastery in one who is free from thirst for both seen and heard objects. The word "objects" (*viṣaya*) is to be connected with each term, as is the phrase "free from thirst" (*vitṛṣṇasya*); thus, it refers to one who is free from thirst for seen objects and free from thirst for heard objects.

And that object has been seen therein. What, then, is it? It consists of women, food, drink, and power; this is said with reference to specific instances. Although objects such as sound and so forth are infinite, these are mentioned by way of their predominance because passion for them is exceedingly intense. For here, passion is most powerful and must be restrained with great effort. Such is the case with the objects of the revealed tradition (*ānuśravika*). "Revealed" (*ānuśravika*) means derived from scripture (*āgamika*), and it is to be experienced here through the attainment of heaven and other such realms.
It is the object of experience for those who have merged into primordial nature (prakṛtilaya), and it is to be experienced upon not attaining liberation (vaidehī).

[44,14] But is it not the case that freedom from thirst (*vaitṛṣṇya*) itself is dispassion (*vairāgya*), since it will be stated later that "passion (*rāga*) is thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), greed (*gardha*)"? No, because what is intended here is a specific state [of that process]. Thus, there are four specific designations: the designation of striving (*yatamāna-saṃjñā*), the designation of transcending (*vyatikrānta-saṃjñā*), the designation of one-facultiedness (*ekendriya-saṃjñā*), and the designation of mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*). Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the general designation for these four.

This being the case, what is meant by the phrase "one who is free from craving for objects seen or heard" is as follows: for one who has not yet reached the three previous stages, that which is the fourth stage is intended here as *vairāgya* (detachment). Therefore, in this context, a detachment other than mere freedom from craving (*vaitṛṣṇya*) is intended. And so he demonstrates this: [it belongs] to one who perceives the defects in sense-objects, because perceiving defects is the cause for turning away from sense-objects.

For that perception of qualities is the cause of passion; yet, by the power of higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and the power of practicing the perception of their defects, it becomes effortless in nature and free from the agitation of sense objects. Even when there is contact with both divine and non-divine objects, the mind—being devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted and liberated from attachment—abides like a crystal freed from coloration, being released from passion for sense objects.

The notion of mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*): in this state, all secondary objects (*gauṇāḥ padārthāḥ*) are perceived as being capable of being mastered; furthermore, in that state, the senses are perceived as having been mastered, or mastery itself is perceived in this state. (1.15)

[44,26] And that is of two kinds: higher (*para*) and lower (*apara*), distinguished by their objects and causes. The lower has been explained; now the higher is being stated: "The higher is dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward the *guṇas* resulting from the discernment of the *puruṣa*. The word "that" refers back to dispassion. It is called "higher" because it occurs at a later stage than the previously mentioned [lower] dispassion. Alternatively, it is "higher" or "superior" because its objects and causes are superior, or because it is more closely proximate to *kaivalya*.

[45,12] What is its cause? He says: "from the cause that is the discernment of the Puruṣa. What is its object? He says: "dispassion toward the guṇas," meaning dispassion toward the guṇas such as sattva and the others. "One who perceives the defects in objects seen or heard"—this reference to objects is for the purpose of distinguishing between the causes of the previously mentioned dispassion and the present one. "From the cause that is the practice of the vision of the Puruṣa. "His intellect is nourished by the discernment resulting from its purification. The word "that" (tat) refers back to the vision of the Puruṣa.

Its purity is "tacchuddhiḥ," which means the state of having the impurities of the afflictions washed away. Alternatively, its purity is "tacchuddhiḥ," meaning the purity of that person. The vision of that [purity] as its object is now being distinguished. By that distinction, the intellect of this yogin becomes further refined.

"From the *guṇas*" is the presentation of the objects [of detachment]. However, whereas the former [type of detachment] is dispassionate even toward perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and traditionally heard (*ānuśravika*) objects, this [latter type] is dispassionate specifically toward the *guṇas* which are their cause. Those existing as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth have the nature of the manifest (*vyakta*); those abiding in the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) have the nature of the unmanifest (*avyakta*). One who is dispassionate toward these—that is the two-fold detachment.

And here, that which was previously mentioned as the subsequent [result]—namely, the perception of the Puruṣa characterized by the objects of the guṇas—is merely the clarity of that knowledge; it amounts to the ultimate discernment of the perception of the Puruṣa itself.

For one who perceives the Puruṣa becomes a mind devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted. Thus it is said: "Even when there is no interest in discriminative discernment (prasamkhyāna), because of the complete manifestation of discriminative knowledge (vivekakhyāti), there is the Cloud of Dharma (dharmamegha) samādhi."
Upon the arising of which—namely, upon the arising of that dispassion—one possesses arisen discriminative knowledge.

[The yogin] has direct perception of the present. He thinks thus: "That which was to be attained has been attained," and so forth; for liberation follows as an invariable consequence of this state, since beyond that there is no further need for means. Since dispassion (*vairāgya*) consists merely in the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*), and because knowledge and dispassion are not distinct from one another, it is established that their opposites—attachment (*rāga*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*)—are likewise not different in essence from each other. This being the case, attachment is merely another state of ignorance itself, and thus it is logically consistent that ignorance has five aspects (*pañcaparvāvidyā*).

[46,7] But would this not contradict the eightfold nature of the intellect (*buddhi*)? For its sixfold nature is accepted on the basis of the distinctions between the various states of meditation (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, even though dispassion (*vairāgya*) is a form of knowledge (*jñāna*), it is accepted as being more serene; likewise, passion (*rāga*) is merely a specific variation of another state of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

[46,10] But if this is so, then because knowledge and ignorance possess many distinct states, would they not again fail to constitute eight qualities? This is not a fault, because of the restriction based on being a fruit and being its opposite. There is a restriction of distinction for the four states of knowledge by virtue of their being fruits; likewise, there is a restriction of the fourfold set beginning with *adharma* by virtue of being the opposites of the four states of ignorance. Thus, the status of the eight qualities is established; for only the opposites of *dharma* and the rest are restricted as "qualities," and not all the various types of ignorance. (1.16)

It was stated previously that "concentration accompanied by discernment (samprajñāta-samādhi) is followed by applied thought (vitarka) and the rest," and we shall explain this further below. That [discernment], having reached its proper occasion, is now defined. It has been explained that detachment (vairāgya) is of two kinds, superior and inferior, for one whose mental fluctuations have been stilled by means of the two methods. By implication, the twofold nature of practice (abhyāsa) is also determined. How so? He will state in the very aphorism that the practice of the concentration without discernment (asamprajñāta-samādhi) is preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation (virāma-pratyaya).
Therefore, it is determined that the object with a support is the practice of a previous [experience]; and he will state, for the purpose of negating that, "the practice of a single principle."

The author of the Bhāṣya also said: "By dispassion (*vairāgya*), the stream of sense-objects is blocked; by the practice of the vision of discernment (*viveka-darśana*), the stream of the auspicious is opened. He did not state that the nature of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) itself is discarded in *samprajñāta-samādhi*. For its arising from the cessation of modifications depends upon the subsequent occurrence of the stopping of engagement with undesirable objects; indeed, it is still accompanied by specific objects of those modifications.

And likewise, it is explained in the second sūtra that cessation is not the characteristic of cognitive concentration (*samprajñāta*). Therefore, one might ask: how can it be said that the mind whose fluctuations have been suppressed by the two previously mentioned means—practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*)—is characterized as cognitive? To this, [the sūtra says]: "Cognitive [concentration] is so called because it follows after the forms of reasoning (*vitarka*), reflection (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*). The word "follows after" (*anugama*) is to be connected with each term individually.

"Because it follows upon applied thought (*vitarka*), because it follows upon sustained thought (*vicāra*), because it follows upon joy (*ānanda*), and because it follows upon the form of the sense of 'I' (*asmitā*). The word "form" (*rūpa*) has the sense of "mere" (*mātra*), for the purpose of indicating the exclusion of the three preceding factors, namely applied thought and the others.

[47,11] *Vitarka* is a gross application of the mind toward an object. It is a gross state of mingling; it is that engagement with the object (*ālambana-vyatikara*) of the mind as it first transforms according to the form of the object. *Vicāra* is a subtle application of the mind; the connection is that it is a subtle [application]. *Ānanda* is joy; *vicāra* is a subtler application of the mind, the third [limb]. Its specific characteristic is the state of being accompanied by joy (*sānandatā*). *Asmitā* is consciousness whose nature is uniform; for one who has attained absorption (*samāpanna*) in the ego-sense (*asmitā*), which is its own primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is the state of being merely the cognition of "I-am-ness," which is the state of having a uniform nature.
And so he will cite [the scripture]: "He follows after that subtle Self, thinking 'I am'; thus much does he perceive."

[47,18] But surely, egoism (*asmitā*) will be enumerated among the afflictions (*kleśa*), for it has been said: "Egoism is the apparent identity of the power of the seer and the power of seeing. How then can samādhi be accompanied by an affliction in the form of egoism? True; however, because egoism manifests the form of its own preeminent cause and because its nature consists in the withdrawal from all other objects, there is no fault even if it takes the form of samādhi. Or rather, even though the object in the form of egoism is non-existent (*avidyamāna*), the cognition of the yogi is not itself ignorance (*avidyā*). Indeed, when one desires to know another's mind, that other's mind is not itself ignorance. Certainly not.
Grasping at another's mind as a condition, one becomes possessed of ignorance oneself through the fault of taking as an object the form of another's ignorance-conditioned state.

Furthermore, whatever is an affliction (*kleśa*) is necessarily characterized by cognitive distortion (*viparyaya*), such as "I am going" or "I am emaciated. In the case of the mind of a yogin, however, *rajas* and *tamas* have become subordinate; thus, it is not so.

[48,11] In this regard, each preceding [stage] is accompanied by its own respective subsequent qualities, while each succeeding one is devoid of the qualities of its predecessors. Since this conscious concentration (*samprajñāta-samādhi*) is indeed accompanied by these fourfold qualities, it is defined by them; thus, the aphorism is for the purpose of defining its characteristics. Even in the world, whatever is followed by its own unique properties is defined by those characteristics, just as a cow is defined by the dewlap and so forth.

Lest anyone should suspect that these concentrations lack an object because they grasp at mere "I-am-ness" (*asmitāmātra*), he says: "All these have an object. Furthermore, the view held by some—that "I-am-ness" is non-conceptuality—is incorrect; for the word *asmitā* is well-established as referring to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Thus it is said: "The state of being 'I am' is *asmitā*" (YS 1.17).

Now, regarding that state of asamprajñāta-yoga whose definition has been established as "the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind," by what means is it approached? What is its instrument? By what method is it attained? This is the sense of the question. Furthermore, what is its nature (svabhāva)? What is its essential form (svarūpa)? In what state does it exist? To demonstrate its connection with its specific nature and its instruments, [the author] says: "Preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation, it is otherwise characterized by residual latent impressions (saṃskāra)."

By the phrase "preceded by the practice of the means of cessation," he explains the connection with the means of attainment (*sādhana*). The term "consisting of residual impressions" (*saṃskāraśeṣa*), however, is an explanation of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). The word "other" (*anya*) means that this seedless (*nirbīja*) non-cognitive (*asamprajñāta*) state is distinct from the previously described cognitive (*samprajñāta*) state.

The word "other" (*anya*) is connected with both [preceding terms]: that which is preceded by the practice of the thought of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya-abhyāsa-pūrva*), and that which consists of residual impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*). To the question "What is this that is distinguished from both?", he says: "the other."

Abstention (*viramaṇa*) is *virama*. That which is both an end (*virāma*) and a causal condition (*pratyaya*) is the "condition of cessation" (*virāmapratyaya*). Because its nature is that of cessation, that very condition is called "cessation. For one who is withdrawing from all objects, at the moment of withdrawal, prior to attaining the state of being a condition, there exists the nature of a condition. This is just as a blazing fire, whose fuel is being consumed and which is gradually subsiding, possesses the nature of a flame prior to reaching the state of embers.

Therefore, the cognition whose nature is cessation is "the cognition of cessation" (*virāma-pratyaya*). That which has this as its prior and primary practice is "preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation" (*virāma-pratyayābhyāsa-pūrva*). That of which the residual element is only the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is "residual of latent impressions" (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*). When the cognition has ceased, only the latent impression of that cognition remains. The meaning is that the mind, having ceased from cognitions of objects, is indeed residual of latent impressions alone. Supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*) is the means for that samādhi; "supreme" means higher than that [previous stage].

[49,16] But should it not be stated as "and supreme detachment," since the cessation of mental fluctuations is intended to be achieved through both practice and detachment? This is not a fault. Since the practice of the cognition of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*) is already included in the Sūtra, its practice need not be suspected [of being omitted]. Detachment, however, is not explicitly mentioned and might therefore be suspected [of being omitted]. Therefore, in order to explain that very [detachment], the word "and" (*ca*) has been read [in the commentary] to indicate that liberation is not [attained] without it.

[49,19] If this is so, why was the term "detachment" (*vairāgya*) not included in the Sūtra itself, since it was already recited previously? If you ask for what purpose it was recited there, it is because of the context of detachment (*vairāgyaprasaṅga*). Since the subsequent detachment is simply a specific form of the preceding detachment, it was stated subsequently by way of that context.

Since the former type of detachment has already been applied to the domain of *samprajñāta* [samādhi], and since it serves as a means for the latter [asamprajñāta] without distinction yet pertains to a different object, its connection is established solely through seedless [nirbīja] [samādhi]; therefore, the term "detachment" (*vairāgya*) was not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra. However, the author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates that it is obtained by implication.
