[49,24] It has been established that "its cessation is achieved through practice and dispassion. For practice possesses an object, and because it is contrary to objectless concentration (*samādhi*), it is not fit to be its means of accomplishment. Therefore, even the thought-moment of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*), though devoid of an objective referent, is made into an object because it conforms to objectless concentration. Consequently, by means of the practice of that [cessation] and the method of dispassion, the mind becomes objectless, as if it had reached non-existence. This very state is seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*), whose nature consists of residual impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*); it is called "cognition-less" (*asaṃprajñāta*). ||1.18||

[50,11] This indeed is of two kinds: that seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*) is conditioned by means (*upāya-pratyaya*) and conditioned by existence (*bhava-pratyaya*). It is "conditioned by means" because it is attained through means; this belongs to the yogins. Although the bodiless ones (*videha*) are also indeed yogins, nevertheless, those who practice the application of the means of yoga such as the restraints (*yama*) and so forth are intended here. For them, concentration is obtainable through means such as faith (*śraddhā*), energy (*vīrya*), and the rest.

[50,15] However, for those who have dissolved into the *prakṛti* of the Videhas, this [state] is obtainable through birth alone. For they possess only a very slight residue of obstruction; yet that residue of obstruction is not sufficient to obstruct the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of those who, having attained it once, will take birth only one more time. That [residue] serves merely as the cause for the acquisition of birth. Since the state of being dissolved in *prakṛti* like the Videhas results from the practice of knowledge, dispassion, and so forth, the sūtra implies the meaning: "that [state] is the result of such practice. For such is the greatness of the power of that practice for those of this kind.

That is to say, even when the desired fruit is not attained due to deficiencies such as a lack of capacity, one nevertheless attains the highly venerable state of dissolution into the nature of Videha.

[50.21] There are gods named Videhas who are bound to bodies consisting of the eightfold city. Through a mind that consists of nothing but the experience of their own residual impressions (*saṃskāra*)—impressions produced by the practice of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and which have as its sole remainder those impressions—they experience isolation (*kaivalya*) here through the experience of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*). Thus, through the complete enjoyment of the quality of *sattva*, they exhaust the maturation of such similar residual impressions.

[50,24] Those who have merged into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) while still possessing a task to perform are not yet finished with their duty. For as long as the discernment between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the Spirit (*puruṣa*) has not been accomplished, the mind remains with its task incomplete;

when it has merged into that primordial nature, they experience a state like liberation (*kaivalya*). As before, as long as they do not return again due to the force of their remaining task or the force of what must still be done by knowledge (*vidyā*), so long do they experience that which is like liberation. 1.19.

[51,14] For those yogins for whom the means (upāya) is the causal condition, their concentration (samādhi) is preceded by faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Faith is the clarity and serenity of the mind, like water when it comes into contact with the *kataka* fruit, occurring upon attaining liberation and upon hearing of its means. For it protects and guards the yogi from unwholesome things, just as a virtuous mother protects her child.

For one who seeks discernment and seeks right vision, vigor—meaning enthusiasm—is born toward the practice of the means of yoga. For one in whom vigor has arisen, a firmer mindfulness regarding the objects of knowledge derived from scripture and so forth presents itself. The phrase "one who seeks discernment" is to be supplied everywhere [in the following].

When the foundations of mindfulness are firm, the mind is concentrated without distraction. For one whose mind is concentrated, wisdom—the clarity of the intellect—is the capacity to illuminate all objects. It is by means of this that one distinguishes and knows the objects of the self and so forth exactly as they are.

Through the practice of that, this is what is meant: through the practice of the means for the cessation of the perception of a self; and through detachment from its object—that is, from the object known as detachment—from a higher form of detachment. This is the *asamprajñāta* (seedless) samādhi. (1.20)

Those [practitioners] who employ means such as faith and so forth also become non-conducive [to the goal]. This is shown as follows: "namely, the mild means, the middling means, and the intense means. Each of these is further divided into three types; therein, "mild means" refers to a slow commencement regarding the practice of the means, "middling commencement" refers to a moderate commencement, and "intense commencement" refers to one characterized by intense and extreme spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). The same applies to the others. There is nothing hidden here.
[52,18] In that regard, for those with superior means and intense spiritual urgency, the attainment of meditative concentration and the fruit of meditative concentration are near at hand. 1.21.

Since even those [preparations] are distinguished by the sequence of their methods—whether mild, moderate, or intense—there is a further distinction in the refinement resulting from the performance of the practice. Due to that distinction, the attainment of the subsequent meditative concentration (samādhi) becomes even more imminent.

This is the purpose of this Sūtra: so that yogins, with respect to the practice of the means for yoga, may become possessed of increased enthusiasm. It is just as in the world, where this result accrues to those who run toward a boundary with great speed; or else, by demonstrating how even yogins whose efforts are very slow may attain their desired fruit, they will proceed with undaunted minds. Otherwise, being struck with fear produced by excessive exertion, they would despond. (1.22)

Is he [the yogin] brought closer to this [samādhi] by this alone, or is there some other means for its attainment? He says that there is another means: "or from devotion to Īśvara. He will explain the meaning of the word *īśvara* later.
Here he explains *praṇidhāna* [devotion] as being "inclined" due to a particular kind of *bhakti*. [This results in] grace (*anugraha*).

Having been brought into a state of direct presence, he favors that yogin—who is endowed with an excellence of devotion—merely by his contemplation; for, due to being the Supreme Lord, he possesses the power of true resolve and thus acts without effort. Furthermore, through his favor, the attainment of samādhi becomes even more immediate, and this is the fruit. ||1.23||
[53,18] Now, in the Sāṃkhya treatise, it is asked: "Who is this Īśvara who is distinct from both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*?"

Because there is no consensus [on this matter], and since the existence of God must necessarily be established through reasoning, someone who has not yet understood the specific nature of God asks about it. To that end, he first makes a formal declaration: "God is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and their latent impressions. Regarding "afflictions": ignorance and the others are called afflictions because they cause suffering. Actions are the virtuous and non-virtuous deeds performed preceded by those [afflictions]. The term *kuśalākuśalāni* is a single remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*) for both "virtuous" and "non-virtuous"; it means simply "virtuous and non-virtuous."

The fruit of that [karma] is its maturation (*vipāka*), characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience. These very things—afflictions and so forth—are called "residues" (*āśaya*) because they lie dormant (*śerate*) within *nirvāṇa*. Alternatively, the "residues of afflictions, karma, and maturation" are the accumulations (*rāśi*) of afflictions and the rest.

[53,26] Since they arise from the activity of the mind, these [qualities] are attributed to the Puruṣa when they reside in the mind. Why? Because he is the enjoyer of their fruit. Just as victory and defeat, though occurring in battles, are attributed to the king because the fruit thereof belongs to the king.

For that which is said to be "unaffected by this experience" does not intend to specify a particular time; rather, it serves as an illustration. It means that one is not being affected, will not be affected, nor has one ever been affected—meaning one is disconnected from the latencies of afflictions, karma, and their maturation.

Establishing the purity of the meaning of the Sūtra, he says: "In that case, has he attained isolation (*kaivalya*)? Since it is possible for the non-contact with afflictions and so forth to be merely occasional, there are many who have attained isolation; are they therefore also Lords (*īśvara*)? Because contact is also possible, they are not exclusively untouched by afflictions and so forth. For both contact and non-contact exist for them. It is only the one touched by lordship (*īśvaratva*) who is [the Lord]. Indeed, a word-meaning that is not determined cannot be accepted as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, he is said to be one who is exclusively untouched.

For they, having abandoned the three types of bonds—the natural (*prākṛta*), the incidental (*vaikṛta*), and the personal (*dākṣiṇa*)—through right vision, have attained isolation (*kaivalya*). But for the Lord, that connection with those [bonds], namely the connection with afflictions and so forth, has not occurred, just as it is known from the case of one who is liberated that liberation occurs only after having been previously bound; for liberation is preceded by bondage. Nor will it occur in the future, as in the case of one merged in primordial nature (*prakṛtilīna*); for in his case, since he has not begun a cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), a subsequent limit of bondage is not possible.

For one whose mind has not dissolved into its primordial nature (*aprakṛtilīnacitta*) and who is engaged in the cycle of existence (*pravṛttasaṃsāra*), both the prior and subsequent limits of bondage are possible because of the presence of objective conditions (*sādhikāratvāt*). Since all of this has not been considered here, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that time is not intended to be expressed [in the definition of the Lord]. He, however, is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord (*sadā eva īśvaraḥ*).

[54,25] Since it has been stated therein that "the Lord (īśvara) is a particular kind of person (puruṣaviśeṣa)," and because the quality of non-mastery belongs to the ordinary person while the quality of mastery belongs to the mind, and because unsurpassed mastery depends upon a connection with an eminent mind, the author restates what has already been established for the sake of the subsequent argument: "The eternal excellence of the Lord arises from his assuming a preeminent *sattva*. This "excellence" (*utkarṣa*) consists in the perfection of the power of eternal, unsurpassed, and omniscient sovereignty.

[55,4] Therein, for the sake of purifying the proposition, he begins with a question: "Is he possessed of a cause (*sanimitta*) or rather without a cause (*nirnimitta*)? The word *nimitta* is a synonym for "cause" (*kāraṇa*). Thus, the question becomes: "Is he possessed of a cause or without a cause? What follows from this? If, first of all, he is possessed of a cause, then it is illogical to say that Īśvara exists eternally, because [whatever has a cause] is impermanent. If, on the other hand, he is without a cause, then since excellence (*utkarṣa*) is something produced as an effect, it would follow that [Īśvara] is non-existent;
for in the world, no effect is ever seen to be without a cause.

To this it is replied: [the cognition] is not without cause, because it has scripture as its cause. Scripture is knowledge. Because scripture is the cause, knowledge—which has sattva as its object—is eternal, and its locus consists of substances, intrinsic natures, means and ends, the concealed, and the remote.

If this is so, since knowledge must be preceded by attainment from another source, it follows that there can be no excellence prior [to that attainment]; therefore, he asks: "What, then, is the cause of the scripture? If knowledge were intrinsic, like the cognition of one who is intoxicated or insane, it would not be a cause for excellence; however, if it is held that knowledge has a cause, then there can be no excellence prior to that cause.

[55,15] It is not, first of all, signless (*nirnimitta*), because it has the signs of superior beings (*prakṛṣṭasattvanimitta*)—that is to say, it has superior beings as its basis. For this very reason, there is an absence of defects regarding the knowledge of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvajñāna*).

Furthermore, even though it consists of innate knowledge (*svābhāvikajñāna*), it does not possess the quality of being a cause for decline, as is the case with the cognitions of those such as myself; this is because it has as its substratum sentient beings who are eternally free from afflictions and the like. In this regard, just as there is an beginningless connection between the series of knowledge, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and memory through their mutual relationship as cause and effect—like that of a seed and a sprout—exactly so is there an endless connection between the scripture (*śāstra*) and excellence (*prakarṣa*) in the mind of Īśvara, which exists in the form of an eternally proceeding series.
Among these, excellence is indeed the effect of knowledge, yet knowledge is also the cause of that excellence.

[55,22] According to the explanation of others, the word *nimitta* denotes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Its treatise (*śāstra*) is the *nimitta*, that is, the means of valid cognition, for by it the excellence of that [treatise] is measured. Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition for the treatise? It has as its means of valid cognition the Lord’s stainless being (*sattva*). For the authority of a treatise arises from its being composed by a pure being, just as in the case of Manu and others. And thus says the Śruti: "Whatever Manu declared was medicine," and as it is said in the world: "That which has been spoken by the teacher."

Between these two—the excellence of the scripture and the excellence of the teacher—there exists a beginningless and endless relationship characterized by the status of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and the object of knowledge (prameya).
[56,9] But surely, if God does not exist, how can the excellence of the mind be established by means of a treatise that exists [within him]?

This is not a fault. Because it originates from Him, the treatise exists within Him; and precisely because it exists there, the treatise also originates from Him, solely due to His omniscience. Even in the world, whatever originates from something exists within it, just as cloth and the like exist in their threads and so forth. That it originates from Him is understood through both inference and scripture.
Excellence has the scripture as its authority, while the scripture has the Lord as its authority; thus, because their bases are distinct, there is no circularity between the scripture and excellence.

[56,14] But surely, since the authority of the Lord (*īśvara*) would derive from the scripture and the authority of the scripture would derive from the authority of the Lord, a circular dependency (*anyonyāśrayatva*) is asserted; [we reply: there is no such fault, because the authority of the Lord is established through inference (*anumāna*).

[56,16] This arises from this. Why? Because that which has as its substratum the Lord and the pre-eminent *sattva*, and which consists of the unsurpassed excellence of knowledge in the form of cause and effect, is eternal by virtue of being a continuous stream; therefore, it follows that "He is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord. (To this, he says: "And that sovereignty of His is free from equality and superiority"—this is the result of the proof to be stated hereafter, or the summarized meaning of this aphorism.

[56.20] He explains the state of being liberated from excellence: "It cannot be excelled by another form of sovereignty. Why? Whatever other sovereignty you consider to be that which excels it, that very thing is what I have designated as "sovereignty. The point is that wherever sovereignty exists as something excelled by another sovereignty, that alone is the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, there is no sovereignty equal to it, because it is impossible for there to be a pre-eminence of identical attributes.

For it is not possible for two kings to exist in a single kingdom, nor for one king to possess two kingdoms; by establishing it thus, the equality of those two would follow as a consequence, since it is not the case that one of them exists in the other.

The exercise of one's own power (*prākāmya*) is possible only when it does not obstruct another; however, when two things directed toward the same object occur simultaneously, there can be no exercise of power by one due to that very power, because the object of equal intensity is contradictory. That which possesses equal intensity is precisely what is obstructed by that [other]. Moreover, this obstruction is not merely verbal; rather, the excellence of form and the excellence of manifestation of the one are contradicted by those of the other.
We shall explain later, however, that generalities (*sāmānyāni*) do coexist with excellences.
Therefore, he whose sovereignty is free from both equality and superiority is the Lord (īśvara).
Thus, it is established that the Lord is a particular Spirit (puruṣaviśeṣa) distinct from both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the ordinary spirits (puruṣa). ||1.24||

In establishing the existence of Īśvara as it has been asserted, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is presented; therein lies the unsurpassed seed of omniscience. In that regard, it must exist in an unsurpassed degree within that Īśvara whose characteristics have been asserted. What is this? It is that which is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*).

The knowledge of perception and inference has as its objects the past, the future, the present, the combination of the past and so forth, and that which transcends the senses. It is called "transcending the senses" because it is possible for it to apprehend the past and the future, both of which transcend the senses.

And that apprehension of supersensuous objects is threefold: having subtle objects, having concealed objects, and having remote objects—whether small or great. As this is well known, it increases by way of excellence and is the seed of omniscience, just as the cognition of smoke is the seed of the cognition of fire. How so? Where it reaches the ultimate limit of excellence. Since cognition has a cognizer as its substratum, "where" refers to the cognizer; that is, in whichever cognizer [this cognition reaches its limit], he is established as omniscient.

[57,24] Likewise, that power (*śakti*) which, increasing through excellence, reaches its ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhā*), is the "Omnipotent" (*sarvaśakti*). By this, there is established his agency in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world. Similarly, that in whom sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), also increasing, reaches its ultimate limit, is the "Supreme Lord" (*parama-īśvara*). Consequently, there is established the absence of defects such as incapacity and the like, which are the opposites of these qualities.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even ignorance—which increases, is established by its own nature, and reaches its ultimate limit—is established in that Lord; but this is not so, because of the contradiction with knowledge. For there can be no conjunction of the two opposites, knowledge and ignorance, in a single locus. Indeed, when knowledge is at its height, ignorance cannot possibly exist therein.

For wherever light increases, there darkness is indeed removed. If it is argued that the reverse is also possible, that is not so; because when light exists, darkness is not perceived. Indeed, existing darkness is dispelled by light, but existing light is never overcome by darkness.

[58,7] Even the non-appearance of the sun during the rainy season due to the obstruction by clouds is merely the intervention of a visible object; it is not that the light itself is obstructed, as in the case of darkness. Therefore, where there is no increase of knowledge, there is the presence of ignorance, just as darkness exists in a mirror. This is because its material cause consists of the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are eternally and utterly obscured by *sattva*.

Furthermore, since ignorance has a non-entity as its object, its increase is not possible; whereas for knowledge, because it has an entity that is an object of knowledge, its growth is logically established. For if ignorance were to have an entity as its object, it would necessarily attain the status of being knowledge.

Furthermore, as for the claim that there is an intensification of ignorance within stable entities, that is not an intensification. For it is spoken of only in relation to the absolute absence of knowledge. If there were indeed an intensification of ignorance, then a single instance of knowledge would not be able to sublate a thousand instances of ignorance; rather, each individual instance of ignorance would have to be sublated by multiple instances of knowledge arising in succession. Therefore, in its own nature, there is no such thing as an intensification of ignorance that is eternal.

For that which possesses degrees of excellence is seen to reach a culminating point, just as the dimensions of fruits and the like reach their limit in space; likewise, the seed of omniscience also deserves to attain the highest pinnacle.
[58,18] The entire collection of objects, both collective and individual, is directly perceived by a single person, because it is knowable, like a jar and so forth.
Because it is a human goal by virtue of being an object of knowledge, just like a jar or similar things.
And the earth possesses the property of origination, because it has parts, like a jar and so forth.

[58.21] The world is produced by a single [intelligent agent] who knows the division between living beings and the means for their accomplishment, because it possesses specific arrangements of places and so forth to be enjoyed by them, like a palace or similar structure.
[58,23] The earth, though produced as a single entity, is experienced by many living beings, because it is an object of enjoyment for many living beings, just like rice, barley, and so forth.
The earth, created by a single being seeking various purposes, is just like houses and other such things.

The collection of mountains, rivers, and oceans, which serves as the support for all living beings, is produced by a single wholesome [karma], just like the consciousness capable of inhabiting and utilizing them;
this is established by both the primary reason and the illustrative example.

The sun is produced by a single agent who possesses the knowledge of the capacities for illumination and so forth belonging to many living beings, because it consists of light, like a lamp and other such objects.

The movement of the sun and other celestial bodies at fixed times, such as rising and setting, is impelled by a single agent who possesses knowledge of its purpose, because it occurs at specific times, just like agriculture and similar activities.

The activity of the sun, planets, moon, constellations, and so forth, is directed by a single intelligent Lord, because, while being of the nature of suffering, their activity occurs at fixed times, just like the activity of religious duties, disciples, servants, and the like.

The waxing and waning of the moon are set in motion by a single agent who possesses knowledge of time, such as the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth, because they serve to demarcate time, just like the *ghaṭikā*, days, and other units of time.
The moon is produced by one who possesses knowledge of the divisions of time, because it is subject to increase and decrease, just like the ghaṭikā and other such measures.

[59,11] The world has a single intelligent master, because it consists of many mandalas presided over by numerous leaders of living beings who are mutually opposed, just like a single kingdom of such a nature.

[59,13] All this—perception in its state of the operation of means and ends—is for the sake of a single purpose, because it possesses a certain internal consistency in terms of opposition and favor, like the state of a battle; and because it is a composite, like the case of a potter and so forth. That is the very proposition.
And everything would be perceived simultaneously if the one were not manifold, because of the mutual connection, like multiple objects whose connections are already established.

[59,18] When that which is to be accomplished by means such as the *agnihotra* is perceived by someone, it possesses the nature of both the probandum and the probans, just like the act of eating and the resulting satisfaction.

[59,29] All powers are perceptible to someone, because they are real entities, like a jar or other such things. In the absence of any intervening obstruction, the entire range of real entities would be perceptible to someone without interruption, due to their connection with qualities such as sound; just as for one eating a very long piece of fried cake, the sounds and other qualities [of the whole] are perceived.

[59,23] Nothing whatsoever is perceived as a whole through direct perception by any single person acting independently, because it is intended as an object of knowledge, like the subject matter of a drama.

[59,25] Without obstruction, everything that is perceptible to anyone is [a collection] when there is multiplicity of beings, because of their mutual connection, like dancers and others connected in a performance.

He is free from cyclic existence and is omniscient because of the absence of ignorance, like a liberated soul; the Lord (Īśvara) is free from afflictions and the like because his knowledge is unimpeded, like a perfected yogi.

By this, it is established that [the mind of the Supreme Lord] possesses knowledge of all objects independent of the collection of sense organs such as the eyes, due to its being free from the ignorance that constitutes the obstruction of afflictions and so forth. This is because the mind of the Supreme Lord—which is capable of grasping all objects, is all-pervading, and is simultaneously connected with all objects—is thus present. Such being the case, the absence of the apprehension of all things would logically follow from the absence of its cause.

Nor is there any obstruction by material objects for the mind, even though it is connected to all objects, just as in the case of space. Because objects do not persist [in the mind], the occurrence of their appearance and disappearance, as well as memory and volition, is established; for the mind acquires its functional state by assuming the forms of the objects, like the light of the sun.

For the sentient being whose mind is bound by the obscurations of afflictions and so forth does not possess such [purity], because of its association with non-dharma and the like. Even though the sentient being is omnipresent and possesses all objects, it is logical that it must depend upon the doors of the sense faculties and so forth, because its own path of activity has been obstructed by the impediments of non-dharma and the like. This is just as a lamp enclosed within an inner chamber or similar obstruction illuminates the outside through the openings of those obstructions;
yet that same lamp, once the chamber-obstruction has been shattered, illuminates everything on all sides without depending on any particular opening.

In the very same way, because the existence of God is free from the connection with the obscurations of the afflictions and so forth, and because there is no cause for the obstruction of specific objects, there is the simultaneous apprehension of all objects without exception; and consequently, there is an absence of defects such as jumping over one's own self or failing to jump over it.
Because everything is an object of experience, the entire world has a single Lord;
for it consists of various specific entities such as protectors, places, and so forth, just as a well-known kingdom under a single monarch likewise possesses such diverse elements.

[60,19] Likewise, because it possesses many auxiliary factors that serve as causes for its fixed duration, because it consists of many regions characterized by numerous difficult terrains that are mutually suppressive, and because it possesses various distinct bodies with an indestructible structure, it is clearly like a single kingdom of such a kind.

The observances of the castes, stages of life, and so forth, have been taught by one who possesses specific knowledge of the relationship between various agents, enjoyers, actions, means, and results; for they are practiced by those seeking fruits and fearing transgression, just like the practice of medicinal elixirs and rejuvenatives.

[60,25] Likewise, those instructions are for the sake of others because they are instructions; because they are to be accepted by the wise and the faithful; and because, in the absence of such instruction, their meaning would remain incomprehensible to human beings, just like the instructions regarding medicine and the like.

[60,27] The body and the sense-faculties, which one who knows all their purposes understands to be produced by a single causal agent, exist because they serve as the means for establishing restricted functions, just like palaces, houses, wooden machines, and so forth.
And because it possesses an arrangement with a fixed purpose, it is exactly like that.
Likewise, the sense faculties [are non-existent], because they are instruments, like a disputant, a tree, or the act of taking up [an object].

Likewise, everything is non-eternal because it possesses a determined material cause, because it exists for the sake of an enjoyer, and because it is a means of enjoyment, just like a jar and other such objects; these reasons also apply to the fact that things possess the quality of being produced.

[61,5] Thus, because it is of intermediate magnitude, because it is susceptible to connection with numerous causes of destruction, because it serves as the locus for an enjoyer, because it possesses the nature of being the means for accomplishing actions and their fruits, and because it consists of many parts that are subject to being added to, diminished, filled, removed, burned, and split apart, the earth is perishable.
The primary elements, such as earth and the rest, are not imperishable like the body and so forth, because they possess the power to destroy one another, just like a weapon and a person.

In the same way, space possesses the properties of arising and destruction because it is contradictory [to be eternal], because it is the opposite of the Self (puruṣa), because it is a direct instrument [of perception], like a jar or similar objects, and because it is the substratum of qualities perceivable by the external senses.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord is established as eternal, possessing unsurpassed power, knowledge, and sovereignty.

To this it is replied: The referent of the word "Īśvara" is not omniscient, because he possesses the qualities of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), being a real entity (*vastutva*), being denotable by words (*śabdābhidheyatva*), having a self (*ātmatva*), depending on means of proof (*sādhanāpekṣa*), and being a perceiver (*upalabdhṛtva*), just like ourselves and others.
[61,15] Even the word "Īśvara" does not denote one endowed with unsurpassed knowledge, because it is a word, like the word "pot" and so forth.
The world is empty of an omniscient being and a supreme lord, because it is the locus of many living beings, like a kingdom with many mutually conflicting leaders.
[61,19] All living beings, being sentient, do not perceive an omniscient being in the past and future times either, just as they do not perceive one now, like ourselves and others.
The omniscient one and the supreme lord postulated by other disputants do not exist, because they are not perceived, like the horn of a hare.

Likewise, he would not be omniscient nor the Lord, because of being bodiless, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*). If he were to possess a body, then his having a body would depend upon factors such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth; and in that case, he would be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*), just like ourselves and others. If it is argued that he is indeed bodiless, then his status as the creator of the world, his role as a benefactor, and so forth, would be untenable, as demonstrated by the example of the liberated soul.

The occurrence of the specific arrangement of the world, which is fit for distinguished enjoyment, arises from its very nature (*svabhāva*), just like the sharpness of thorns or the closing and opening of the *kumuda* and *kamala* lotuses. Even the coming and going of the moon, the sun, the stars, and so forth, is natural, like the movement of iron toward a magnet.

To this it is replied: first of all, the arrangement of the earth and so forth does not exist by way of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*). There is simply no example that establishes such a proof. Furthermore, the sharpness of thorns and the like is not accepted as being intrinsic.

If it is argued that the arrangement of earth and so forth is like the heat and so forth of fire and so forth, because it is the nature of things (vastu-dharmatva) due to the reason [of being an effect], then [the argument] would be inconclusive (anaikāntika), because the arrangement of palaces and so forth is also the nature of things.

[62,5] Now, if it is argued that this is because [the world] possesses intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikatva*), then [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhatva*), because it is admitted that the arrangement of the world is impelled by the purpose of experiencing the fruits of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). The existence of the agent's merit and demerit will be proven later.

Therefore, the arrangement of the earth and so forth is not spontaneous, because it exists for the purpose of the enjoyment of living beings, like the arrangement of palaces and the like. The activity of the moon and other celestial bodies is not spontaneous, because it is an activity, like the activity of ourselves and others.

[62,10] If it is argued that the activity of ourselves and others is not inherent (*svābhāvikī*), we reply: no, because that would entail the consequence of its being eternal, like the heat of fire. For the heat of fire, while being inherent, does not require a fixed cause for its own acquisition, since it does not exist apart from the existence of the substrate (*dharmī*). However, in the case of the arrangement of actions, results, and so forth, there is a requirement for specific causes for their own attainment; therefore, they are not inherent.

If it is argued that even the requirement for a specific cause in the construction of palaces and the like is their very nature (*svabhāva*), let it be so; they possess such a nature. Nevertheless, the earth and other elements likewise possess a nature that requires a specific cause for their arrangement, just like palaces and such. Consequently, a disagreement regarding the name is not a fault, because it depends on a different perspective; thus, the proposition is merely a semblance of an argument.

The inferences stated by you are invalid because they contradict worldly experience, inference, and scripture. First, regarding the contradiction with inference, we point to such reasons as "possessing excellence" (*sātiśayatva*) and so forth. Regarding the contradiction with scripture, we cite passages such as: "He who is all-knowing, all-seeing, the one controller," and so on. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the entire world: everyone from the learned Brahmins down to the cowherds, while engaged in their daily activities, constantly direct their minds toward names such as Śiva and Nārāyaṇa; even when faced with those whose intellects are confused and who offer prohibitions, they do not even take note of the mere twigs of those prohibitions.
Bowing down, they worship the Supreme Lord with raised hands, offering handfuls of flowers and other such things; and they also pray for their rewards from Him alone.
Now, if he should say, "The other propositions are refuted by our inferences which establish the non-existence of an omniscient being," it is said in response: These are not valid inferences. How so?

First of all, the proposition itself is flawed. If you mean by "Lord" (īśvara) that which is intended by you to be an omniscient being, and you state that the referent of the word "Lord" is not omniscient, then you would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Even if it were that which we intend, nevertheless, for you there would be the fallacy of an unestablished subject (*asiddhaviśeṣyatā*).
Furthermore, if it is argued that the Lord lacks omniscience, even so, one is merely proving what is already established.

[63,8] Likewise, there is also a contradiction with one's own accepted tenets (*abhyupagama-virodha*). How so? Because sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and the state of being omniscient (*sarvajña-bījatva*) increase, their reaching a limit (*kāṣṭhā-prāpti*) must be admitted, just as it is in the case of measurement (*parimāṇa*). Similarly, the words "Lord" (*īśvara*) and "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) must be understood as denoting the attainment of such a limit. And this "attainment of a limit" consists in being unlimited (*niravadhikatva*), just as measurements and the like culminate in the infinite measurement of the self (*ātman*) and space (*ākāśa*). If this were not the case, there would be contradictions with inference (*anumāna*), with accepted tenets, and with one's own words (*svavacana*).

Furthermore, if one were to abandon the meaning of the word "Lord" (īśvara) as having reached the ultimate limit (kāṣṭhāprāpta), it would follow that one is merely propounding the word itself; for a word is never uttered when its denoted object has been partially abandoned.

[63,14] Now, if it is not accepted that even magnitude (*parimāṇa*) and so forth possess an ultimate limitlessness, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). For if the self (*ātman*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth lacked omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), there would follow the faults of having intermediate magnitude, non-eternality, and so on. Even if it is argued that the self is omnipresent because its effects are observed everywhere, in that case too, who could prevent the selves of birds and other creatures from being located within the space and so forth that fall within the range of human experience?

[63,19] If it is argued that [the self] is not established because it contradicts inference (*anumāna*), then one could likewise state the objection of contradiction with inference regarding the self and so forth, on the grounds of their being objects of cognition (*prameya*) and being entities (*vastu*), just like the earth and other elements. However, this does not constitute a contradiction with inference in this case, for if it did, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-existence of inference altogether.

[63,22] If it is argued that the very absence of inference is thus accepted, then there would likewise be no confidence in perception. Now, if the status of perception as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is due to the arising of a determinate cognition, then let inference also possess validity because of the emergence of a determinate cognition. If it is further argued that inference has only as its object smoke and so forth whose connection [with fire] has been observed, then even in that case, there is indeed an absence of inference: "A place possessing smoke is devoid of fire, because, while the connection with fire is not perceived through direct observation, it is a place, like a place currently perceived to be empty of fire."

[63,27] Now, if it is argued that inference possesses the status of an inference only when its object is a relation observed through corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then perception too would be a means of valid cognition because of its being a means of valid cognition, just like inference. Or else, it would be non-valid because of the absence of corroboration by another means of valid cognition, like "inference from general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) and so forth. Therefore, the validity of "inference from general observation" is not established as permanent; since it produces a determinate cognition, it cannot be refuted.

Furthermore, for one who does not accept the validity of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), fear of snakes and the like would be impossible, because the connection between one's own body and death has never been perceived before. Likewise, the application of medical treatment and other such measures for the remedy of disease would not be possible, due to the absence of any cause for the apprehension of death. Similarly, since birth is also unperceived, one’s own body would be considered unborn; consequently, there would be an absence of any necessity for avoidance or acquisition.

Therefore, because of the commonality of having a limited magnitude and so forth, and because of the commonality of possessing excellence, the proof of the infinity of God’s knowledge follows from that which is observed through general correlation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*).

Furthermore, because the omniscience of Īśvara is being negated, his existence must be admitted; for it is impossible to negate that which has not been accepted as an entity. Indeed, one does not employ the word "not" alone. It is said, "Īśvara is not omniscient"; thus, in that case, omniscience is in some sense admitted.

[64,12] For example, it is said that "the horn of a hare does not exist," "the son of a barren woman does not exist," or "a flower of the sky does not exist. In these cases, there is a negation of horns, sons, flowers, and so forth—which exist elsewhere—in relation to the hare and others; likewise, it would be the same here as well.

Furthermore, by negating the relationship between the meaning of the word "Īśvara" and omniscience through the statement that "Īśvara is not omniscient," one effectively accepts the omniscience of someone other than Īśvara; for it is impossible to negate a relationship without first accepting the two relata.

This very connection that has been proposed is being refuted, while an untenable one is being accepted; this is merely a waste of effort. For there is no refutation of the well-established entities of God and the Omniscient One. Indeed, it is not proper to refute the established infinite dimension of space by saying "space does not have infinite dimension," and then attempt to establish that [infinite dimension] in things like jars and the like, whose infinite dimension is not established.

[64,22] Now, if it is precisely the two related entities—the Lord and the omniscient one—that are being negated, then the proposition would be self-contradictory; for one accepts that the meanings of the words "Lord" and "omniscient" are the states of being the Lord and being omniscient. Indeed, it does not occur that "fire is not the meaning of the word 'fire'."

[64,25] Now, even if the words "Lord" (īśvara) and "omniscient" (sarvajña) have unestablished referents, the negation of their meaning is nonetheless untenable; for there is no possibility of obtaining an object that is unestablished. Indeed, nothing that is unestablished can serve to negate a ram's wife atop this mountain peak. Furthermore, the employment of these words would be purposeless, because their referents are unestablished.

[65,1] Now, if someone were to postulate a connection between the two words *īśvara* and *sarvajña*, whose meanings are well-established, with the limitless lordship and omniscience that are themselves unestablished—just as one might postulate a connection between the sky and flowers—even then, because it would be a negation of a meaning already accepted, the proposition (*pratijñā*) would be self-contradictory; for one has accepted that the referents of the words *īśvara* and *sarvajña* are the universals (*sāmānya*) characterized by multiple individual instances (*vyakti*) of lords and omniscient beings, both those possessing excellence (*sātiśaya*) and those without excellence (*niratiśaya*).

For it is well known in the world that the words "lord" (īśvara) and "omniscient" (sarvajña) produce cognitions directed toward multiple individuals characterized by varying degrees of excellence and deficiency. Indeed, those who are lords of two or three villages do not cease to be "lords" simply because they are not the successive lords of larger domains. Furthermore, even one who is the lord of a single household is not not a lord; rather, this word "lord" is meaningful when it refers to one who is like a surging wave upon the great ocean of bliss.

[65,9] Likewise, when it is said that "the grammarian is omniscient," he does not thereby become endowed with superior knowledge. One must either accept the meanings of the words "Lord" and "omniscient" as being either unlimited or limited; therefore, by negating those [meanings], the proposition would contradict one's own accepted tenets, just like the negation of the meaning of the word "large" as being the largeness of the self, space, and so forth.

[65,13] Now, if it were argued that "the Lord and the Omniscient One do not exist as limitless beings because they are not perceived, like a non-Lord or a second head," even so, because one has accepted the referent of the word [used in the argument], the proposition contradicts one's own tenet.

Because the unlimited sovereignty and omniscience [of God] are perceived through signs such as the seed of sovereignty and omniscience characterized by excellence and so forth—just like [the perception of] unlimited magnitude—the non-apprehension [of such qualities] is unestablished.

[65,17] Now, if it were asserted that the referent of the word "Lord" (īśvara), left unqualified, is not omniscient—on the grounds of such reasons as being a "real entity" (vastutva) and so forth, like ourselves and others—then the proposition would contradict all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is because the well-known referent of the word "Lord," which is characterized by non-ordinary omniscience, is established by all means of valid cognition. Just as if one were to say, "The referent of the word 'Lord' is not omniscient, because of being an object of knowledge (prameyatva) and so forth, like a jar and the like," I shall state exactly what one might say in response to that.

[65,21] Here, the world is empty of an omniscient being; or time, or the directions, or space, or a region containing living beings, or all living beings themselves, are empty of an omniscient being; or the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have the omniscient being as their object; or the cognizers (*pramātṛ*) do not comprehend the omniscient being—against such propositions, when an unlimited Lord or an omniscient being is being negated, one must state the faults of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) consisting in the contradiction with the accepted meanings of the well-known terms "Lord" and "omniscient."
But is it not the case that the world, or time, is empty because the son of a barren woman does not exist?

If it were being asserted [in that way], the aforementioned fault of the thesis would ensue; however, this fault does not apply here. This is because the meaning of the sentence—the negation of the existence characterized by the son of a barren woman—is unestablished, just like the referent of the word "omniscient God. Since there exists a function of negation directed toward a word-meaning whose mere presence is understood through the cognition induced solely by the words themselves, there is no admission of the existence (or non-existence) of the son of a barren woman. Therefore, the fault of negating what has not been admitted does not arise.

Now, even in the case of the claim that "the Lord is not omniscient," it is merely the concept of omniscience (*buddhi-mātra*) as it is being apprehended that is negated; it is not possible to negate a real entity (*vastu*) while it is still present, just as one cannot negate an elephant by means of a mere rival elephant. Furthermore, if the entity were to be excluded by the negative particle (*nañ*), then by the mere use of the negative particle, the proponent's position itself would be excluded. Therefore, in this instance as well, there is only a negation of the concept of omniscience; thus, the negation of what has been accepted is not a fault of the thesis.

[66,5] This is true; however, there is a distinction. A cognition whose object is a thing established by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is negated with respect to another thing or at a particular time, because it would otherwise apply due to the commonality of the thing—as when one says, "The jar does not exist. In some cases, even in the absence of an external object, the cognition itself is negated as it is brought into proximity by words and constructed as another thing—as when one says, "The son of a barren woman does not exist."

But even where there is the negation of an entity established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there too the fault of negating an accepted object remains. For example, in the case of the statement, "The referent of the word 'Īśvara' is not omniscient. This is because it is already established—by the mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the fact that the words 'Īśvara' and 'omniscient' denote universals (*sāmānya*) that follow after individual instances (*vyakti*) of Īśvara and omniscience as they increase—that these words illuminate the existence of an unlimited Īśvara and omniscience, just like words such as 'great', 'many', 'all', 'infinite', and 'measureless'.

Just as these words such as "the Great" (*mahat*) and so forth—while denoting universals (*sāmānya*) that follow after well-known, surpassable instances of the Great and so on—serve as indicators (*liṅga*) for the existence of unlimited, great, many, all, and infinite individual instances; because the universals of the Great and so forth, which follow after surpassable individuals, possess a power that is not exhausted by pervading unlimited individual instances of the Great and so forth. For it is not the case that an existing pervaded object is not pervaded by an existing pervading object. But from the unlimited...

Since there is no further pervaded [entity], there is the destruction of the pervader, namely the universal, because it is established as being known precisely through its relation to the pervaded object. Therefore, for one who seeks to prove the non-existence of the referents of the terms "Lord" and "omniscient" on the grounds that they are not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this is merely a negation of a previously accepted point; thus, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is flawed.

Furthermore, it is impossible to establish that the words "Lord" (īśvara) and "omniscient" (sarvajña) do not have those meanings or have some other meaning; for no one who is not insane would venture to deny the existence of an infinite reality consisting of the combined, ever-increasing degrees of power, knowledge, and sovereignty found in every individual. Thus, the proposition contradicts inference.

Furthermore, those who negate an *īśvara* (Lord) as imagined by others incur the undesirable consequence of [negating] direct perception and the minds of others. If it is argued that this is due to the words of another, we say no; for the words of another are not distinct from those that establish the marks (*liṅga*) proving an omniscient being, such as the possession of excellence and so forth. Moreover, in negating the meaning of such words, one negates what has been accepted [by oneself].
And as before, there is also a contradiction with inference.

Furthermore, reasons such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) are also unestablished (*asiddha*). Why? Because we accept that [the subject] is distinguished by unsurpassed knowledge and sovereignty. If, moreover, you yourself were to accept such [qualities], then the existence of an omniscient being would be established, precisely because it has been accepted.
Furthermore, another point: when such a negation is accepted—as in "a jar is not non-jar, because it is a real entity, like a cloth"—so too would it be here.

Furthermore—if an infinite regress is not admitted, then properties such as "being an object of cognition" (prameyatva) would lack the status of being a property of the subject (apakṣadharmatva) and would suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatva). For if that were not admitted, what could possibly be proven? For what would be achieved by one who says to a person already satiated, "Do not eat"?
Now, it might be argued: "I intend to negate the omniscience of God by referring to an unlimited [omniscience]. This too is not tenable, because omniscience itself is also unlimited.

Furthermore, because the terms "Lord" (īśvara) and "omniscient" (sarvajña) would be subject to deviation—since they could refer to degrees of excellence or lack thereof in sovereignty and omniscience—they cannot be the primary denotations of these words. Just as words such as "great" (mahat) are secondary when applied to jars and the like where greatness is variable, but not so when applied to space (ākāśa) and the like, so too here, since unsurpassed sovereignty and omniscience are non-deviating attributes, He alone is the primary referent of these words. Nor does the rejection of the primary meaning attain any merit.

Furthermore—just as you refute the omniscience of the Lord, who is established through inference and scripture, by means of the conceptual alternatives regarding properties such as being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), in that very same way, [the Lord] would also necessarily be insentient (*acetana*) like a jar or other such things due to those very properties such as being an object of knowledge; for there is no contradiction. Just as being an object of knowledge is pervaded by non-omniscience, so too is it pervaded by insentiency and the like.
If you say that there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), do you not even glance at the contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*) in this case as well?

Nor can anything be superimposed upon either the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) by means of the common property of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), because *prameyatva* and the like exist everywhere with respect to real entities (*vastu*). Thus, the mention of *prameyatva* and so forth is not for the purpose of deluding the intellect.

67.20 Now, if it is argued that [the Lord] is so because he possesses a self, then it would follow that your Lords are ignorant, just like liberated souls (muktātman). If you say this contradicts perception and other means of knowledge—here too, as before, there is a contradiction with inference and other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, the claim that there were no perceivers of God even in the past and future times is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the existence of perceivers among contemporary beings, such as those who possess life and so forth. Moreover, there were perceivers and will be perceivers of God in the past and future times as well—beings skilled in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—because they possessed excellence and other such marks, just like ourselves and others.

If it is argued that [the Lord] is not omniscient because he is bodiless, like liberated souls or space—[we reply: no, because he possesses a body. For the manifest and the unmanifest constitute his entire body; and since it has been stated that being bodied implies non-eternality due to dependence on merit (*dharma*) and so forth—[we reply: no, because he is actually bodiless. If it is argued that there is a contradiction between being bodied and being bodiless—[we reply: no, because we observe both bodiedness and bodilessness in the single Self who was once liberated and is now being liberated.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction there because the two states belong to different times—[we reply: no, for here too we accept that they belong to different times.

Furthermore—because of His very nature as the Lord (*īśvara*), the simultaneous occurrence of both is possible; both the state of possessing instruments and the state of being without instruments are appropriate precisely because of His lordship. Thus, the scriptures state: "The bodiless among bodies" (*Kaṭha Upaniṣad* 2.21); likewise, "He who dwells in all beings" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.15); and similarly, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.9), and so forth.

If it is argued that the scriptures do not establish the existence of God because they are intended for the purpose of resolving contradictions—no, this is not so—because they are not subordinate to anything else. For there is no authority whatsoever, such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, that establishes them as being subordinate to ritual action (*karma*).

If it is argued that [the injunction to meditate] is a subsidiary part of the New and Full Moon sacrifices and so forth because it is encompassed by the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), we say no; for there exists another injunction, just as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices. Just as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites—due to causes such as being treated in separate contexts (*prakaraṇa*)—do not stand in a relationship of mutual subsidiarity (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*), so too it is not logical for [the meditation on Brahman] to be a subsidiary to the Agnihotra and other rites, since its object is defined by such passages as "It is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).

If it is argued that there is no fruit [for such knowledge], we say no; for there is an injunction directed toward a specific fruit, as stated in passages such as: "He who, having not merely heard of that Self, knows it, attains all worlds and all desires" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

Now, if it is argued that even so, because this is a subordinate element of the injunction for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), it is merely a praise (*stuti*)—we reply: there can be no praise of that which is absolutely non-existent. For instance, in the statement "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity," there is no actual swiftness in Vāyu [in the literal sense]. If it is argued that praise and the like are possible even through something non-existent, we say: no—for what is employed here is that which is established by inference (*anumāna*).

Now, if it is argued that because the Lord is connected with the performance of all effects and instruments, He must be subject to the pleasure, pain, and so forth of all living beings—this is not so, because of the difference in the cause. For transmigrating beings, the connection with a body and other such things is caused by merit (*dharma*) and the like; from those causes of merit and so forth follows the union with pain and the rest. But for the Lord, there is no merit or the like, because His connection with bodies, effects, and instruments is due to His being the cause of unsurpassed sovereignty and other such qualities. It is just as in the case of a planet and the spirit possessing it.

68.22 If it is argued that, because they possess instruments such as the eye, there is a non-perception of all things—as is the case with people like ourselves—we say: no. For those whose instruments are capable of grasping all objects, there is an absence of obstructing causes. Indeed, for instruments that are all-pervading, their range of objects is restricted by the veiling influence of demerit (*adharma*) and the like. However, for one in whom there exists no obstruction in the form of a veil such as demerit, there is no fault in the claim that his instruments grasp their respective objects in their entirety, since that [obstruction] is absent.

Alternatively, by means of all the instruments of living beings, the Lord experiences everything—even in the absence of His own separate instruments—as if through a state of possession. Furthermore, no object exists that is devoid of living beings, because of the scriptural texts such as "He who dwells in the earth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3) and "He who dwells in the waters," which declare that the Lord, known as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), resides within all things.

Alternatively, even in the view that [the Lord] is bodiless and devoid of sense organs, the omniscience of the Lord is established as follows: every supreme being possesses the attributes of sovereignty over power and knowledge that surpass all others; because he is all-pervading like space, he is connected to everything; because he is the purpose of all, he illuminates all objects; and because he is free from dharma, adharma, and so forth, his power is unimpeded. Thus, the omniscience of the Lord is proven.

If it is argued that the mind’s capacity to apprehend form and so forth depends precisely upon the eye and other [faculties]—we say no—because this has already been refuted by the absence of both sovereign power (*aiśvarya*) and such qualities (*dharma*).

Furthermore, it is observed in the world that even what is perceptible by the eye is not grasped by the eye. All darkness, though it is perceptible by the eye, is perceived by those with healthy internal organs even when their eyes are closed; yet that very same dense darkness is not perceived at all by those whose eyes are wide open but whose minds are directed elsewhere, just as light is not perceived in space while it is being grasped [by the senses].
Furthermore, if one were to say that darkness is merely the absence of light and not a real entity—that too is not correct—because an absence lacks the capacity to conceal a real object.

Now, one might argue that the non-perception of jars and other objects is due solely to the absence of light—which serves as the cause for perception—and not because there is such a thing as "darkness" that conceals objects. This is not so; for since the eye is itself illuminating, it is illogical for it to require assistance from another light. In the absence of any object of a different nature to conceal them, objects would be illuminated by the eye to whatever extent their illuminability permits. Indeed, a lamp does not require a second lamp to illuminate.

Furthermore: if the eye were dependent upon the assistance of another light, then even at night, with the moon as its companion, there would be the undesirable consequence of the eye perceiving forms and so forth just as during the day, since there would be no reason for its concealment.

Furthermore: if darkness were non-existence (*abhāva*), then while the moonlight is present at night, darkness should not persist even slightly; for it ought to perish entirely because of the presence of light. For while a distinction such as dullness or intensity is possible in the case of lights because they are positive entities (*vastu*), such a distinction cannot exist in the case of non-existence, since non-existence is devoid of specific qualities.

Furthermore, the claim that the eye fails to perceive due to a lack of assistance and a lack of inherent capacity for perception is also subject to contradiction. For instance, even when there is the illumination of a lightning flash and the most intense play of lightning, why does one's vision not perceive it? Indeed, it is not logical to say that the non-perception of lightning is due to the eye being startled by it, as there is no contradiction between them.

Furthermore—In the science of medicine (*cikitsā-śāstra*), it is stated that "shadow is sweet and cool. For sweetness and coolness cannot belong to a non-entity (*avastu*). Likewise, it is said to be wholesome; for they would not ascribe wholesomeness or unwholesomeness to a mere absence (*abhāva*).

70.7 And because a shadow is perceived from a lamp. If darkness were non-existence (*abhāva*), how could there be a shadow of a lamp within the circle of the lamp’s radiance? If it is argued that even if it were a real entity (*vastu*), it is untenable due to contradiction—[we reply]: No; for it is possible, just as in the case of poison and a snake. Just as poison, though it causes the death of living beings, is not capable of causing the death of the snake itself, so too is it with the lamp and its shadow.

Therefore, darkness is a real entity (vastu), because it possesses degrees of intensity and deficiency, like light; because it can be removed by a contrary substance, like a jar; and because it acts as an obstruction to the perceiver, like a wall.

Furthermore, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is capable of grasping the objects of the senses even independently of the sense organs, because sound is perceived by one whose ear-cavity is covered. Nor can another auditory organ be inferred for one whose ears are covered, since even a deaf person does not perceive sound when their ear-cavities are covered.
Furthermore, even through the cognition of a proposition, the apprehension of form and so forth is observed to be independent of the sense organs.

Furthermore, there would be an impossibility of memory even if the mind possessed the capacity for superior apprehension independently of the sense organs; yet dream-memories have clear objects such as forms and so forth.

If the apprehension of form were produced even previously by the eye and the internal organ (manas) acting in conjunction, then it would have been apprehended by those very two acting in conjunction during dreams and so forth; however, this is not the case. It is universally established that the mind possesses independence in the apprehension of pleasure and the like.

Therefore, the sense organs serve as the illumination for the mind when it is independent in the apprehension of objects; this is stated [in the Yoga Sūtras] as "by means of the channel of the senses" (YS 1.7). Likewise, the Śruti also says: "For with the mind alone one sees, with the mind one hears" (BAU 1.5.3).

Now, it may be argued: "Just as the sense organs require light, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) must also depend on the assistance of the sense organs to be a perceiver. This is not so, because there is a deviation from this rule. For nocturnal animals, the apprehension of form occurs during the day even without the accompaniment of external light; and for owls and the like, there is no apprehension of form during the day, even though light is present.

Furthermore, even without the production of a cognition dependent on an instrument of proof, the knowledge of the measure of gold and so forth is observed through the mere sight of scales and the like.

Now, if he should say that the eyes and other senses are useless, he should be told: "The senses possess utility elsewhere, just as in the case of the scales and so forth. Just as, due to the excellence of the purity of the object of the scales and so forth, a person possesses skill in discerning objects such as gold through mere sight even without the instrument of the scales, in the same way, the capacity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) to grasp form and other objects is not obstructed by the excellence of its purity, even when it does not require the assistance of the eyes and other senses.

Furthermore, a collection of actions that must be accomplished by many is not necessarily not accomplished by one; for we see that while a rock or similar object is being lifted by many, certain unique individuals, such as elephants or men, lift it alone.

In the same way, forms and other objects being perceived by the internal organs of others through the assistance of the sense-faculties are perceived by the Supreme Lord’s consciousness alone, without any movement of the eyes or other organs, because the excellence of His stainless sovereignty has reached its ultimate limit.

Because it is inferior to that [of the liberated], the internal organ of transmigrating beings requires the cooperation of the senses for its sovereignty, power, knowledge, and so forth, due to the impurity of ignorance and other defects; this is like the lifting of stones and such by those of weak strength.

Furthermore, as for those such as the Buddha, Ṛṣabha, and others who, while remaining within saṃsāra, become lords, it is impossible for them to possess unsurpassed power, knowledge, and sovereignty, because they are delimited by time. And those who praise their vision admit that they are subject to the limitation of time.

Our Lord is not subject to limitation by time; rather, He is to be inferred solely through signs such as His unsurpassed sovereignty, which were unknown to those of the past, present, and future, including Buddha and others. He is not inferred by some as being of three kinds—having arisen at such-and-such a time, arising now, or yet to arise—for such [specification] would contradict His state of being unsurpassed.

71.25 Therefore, because [the attainment] of Buddhas and others depends upon prior accomplishment, and because earlier Buddhas have already occupied the full extent of time, even a Buddha of a later period cannot possess unsurpassed power, sovereignty, and knowledge. This is contradictory. If one were to argue that they possess equal power, knowledge, and sovereignty, yet exist at different times—just as kings of equal kingdoms do—even so, because the desire to pervade the interval between other Buddhas is frustrated, there is an absence of unsurpassed sovereignty and the rest.

For someone might desire to bring another Buddha under their control and to pervade his domain, since desire is unrestricted. Furthermore, if one were to gain mastery over another Buddha, one's universal sovereignty would be diminished.

Now, if it should be argued that because another Buddha cannot be assisted and because [the Tathāgata] lacks passion and so forth, there is no desire for the pervasion of his objective domain—therefore, it is said: just as the remaining for some time after having attained Buddhahood is preceded by desire, so too there must necessarily be a desire for remaining during the time of another Buddha.

Furthermore, because there exist other living beings to be favored, it is logical that [the Buddha] would desire to remain for a period of time; yet, not all living beings will be favored by the future Buddha.

Furthermore, even if Buddhahood were of the nature of suffering and so forth, because the Buddha’s abiding is for the sake of benefiting living beings, he must necessarily desire to remain for a long duration. Moreover, since his perfection was achieved prior to any consideration of ignorance and the like, and since they themselves have accepted that the essential nature of a Buddha consists of being free from suffering, emptiness, and so forth, it is impossible for there to be unsurpassed power, knowledge, and sovereignty arising from other teachers such as Buddha-Ṛṣabha.

However, because there is no temporal limitation, these defects do not apply to our Lord; for, since we infer that His power, knowledge, and sovereignty are unlimited, defects such as having degrees of excellence or being non-final cannot be suspected of Him, as they might be of things like the self or space.

And thus he demonstrates: "Inference has its utility exhausted by the subsumption of the mere universal. This means that inference has its utility exhausted (*kṛtopakṣaya*) when there is the subsumption of the mere universal of a particular person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) endowed with unsurpassed power, knowledge, and sovereignty; for it is because [inference] involves gradation (*sātiśayatvāt*). As it has been said regarding inference: "Where there is attainment, there is merely the movement [toward it]. Therefore, it is not capable of establishing the specific qualities and so forth belonging to the one designated as God (*īśvara*), even though they exist, because it is intent solely upon the subsumption of the mere universal.

This is what is meant: since even the qualities of those who exist are exhausted by the very act of being presented as generalities, inference is not a means of presenting them; how much less, then, could it be a communicator of such things as desire, cognition, dharma, adharma, and lack of sovereignty, whose presence is absolutely impossible and which are contrary to the properties of the object of inference?

For this very reason, a counter-argument based on a contradictory proof is impossible. Just as in the case of the inference for the existence of an omniscient being, an inference establishing its non-existence cannot function prior [to the former]. For an inference does not have the property of waiting for the statement of another; indeed, when inferring fire by the sight of smoke, one does not wait for the utterance of another speaker.

Furthermore, one does not personally raise the doubt as to whether an omniscient being exists or does not exist prior to [establishing] the cognition [of such a being]. This is because the actual existence of an omniscient being is not accepted by oneself, just like a jar or other objects. Indeed, no one doubts whether a horn exists or does not exist on a rabbit when the very nature of the rabbit has not been determined.

If it is argued that [the opponent] raises this doubt based on the words of another, then it must be explained how even the other person could have raised such a doubt when the existence of a Lord (Īśvara) is not established for them. If it is argued that the other person is under a delusion (*bhrānti*), we reply: no cause for delusion exists when a universal (*sāmānya*) is not perceived; indeed, a delusion that a cuckoo is present in a piece of mother-of-pearl never arises for anyone. Therefore, he says: "The understanding of specific designations and so forth is to be sought from scripture (*āgama*). That is to say, it is to be sought from scripture such as the Vedas, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Yoga, and Dharmaśāstras.

Even though there is no benefit for himself—since for him there is nothing further to be attained for his own sake—the purpose [of his activity] is the favoring of living beings who are submerged in the mire of ignorance, because there is no other teacher to instruct them in the boat that is the means for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.

The completion of the sentence is: "Thinking, 'I shall repeatedly rescue those who have no other refuge and who have surrendered their very selves to him with all their being by teaching knowledge and dharma,' he proceeds, being one whose nectar-like compassion has been aroused again and again, once the teachers—who possessed specific scriptural knowledge favored by Īśvara—have perished during the dissolution of the eon or the great dissolution."

And so it has been said: "the primordial knower" (*ādividvān*). The meaning is: one who was a knower from the beginning (*ādau vidvān*), whose knowledge was not overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*. Alternatively, he is the "origin" (*ādi*) because knowledge, virtue, and other qualities are derived from him; thus, he is both the origin and the knower—the primordial knower. Having presided over a "created mind" (*nirmāṇacitta*)—a yogic mind fashioned by mere volition—for the purpose of instruction, like a spirit possessing a person, the Blessed One, the supreme seer (*paramarṣi*), is the one of supreme vision. His supremacy is established through scripture.

The term "seer" (ṛṣi) is used here for one whose verbal root signifies either "seeing" or "going. It is the Supreme Seer, the Lord himself, known by names such as Kapila and Nārāyaṇa, who proclaimed [the doctrine] to Āsuri.

Therefore, the Lord (Īśvara) is established as distinct from both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa), being the cause of grace toward them through His knowledge of the manifestation of the fruits of the actions and dispositions of all living beings. One should not raise such objections as: "How can the Lord, who has taken up a wealth of preeminent *sattva*, be a creator? And how does He bestow grace? For it has been stated that [the nature of] the Lord is to be sought through scripture (*āgama*), and because inference regarding Him is impossible due to the failure to apprehend a specific relationship (*viśeṣasaṃbandha*). ||25||

That Supreme Lord, whose nature has been described, is the teacher even of the ancient teachers—those who taught the relationship between all the means and the goals to be accomplished, namely worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). The meaning is that He is the author of their instruction in knowledge as well, because all knowledge originates from Him, just as sparks, salt-crystals, and droplets of water originate from fire, salt, and the ocean.

And we have already stated that his primordial wisdom is unconditioned by time, because it is beginningless. Other teachers are limited by time, which is characterized by the passing, the future, and the present; but that Lord (Īśvara), being eternally liberated as the Lord, is to be inferred even by them, just as he is by us.

If it is asked: "Why, then, even though it is a real entity (*vastu*) and possesses the generality of weight (*gurutva-sāmānya*), is time not its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*? he replies: "Wherein time does not apply for the purpose of delimitation. With respect to that subject, the Lord (*īśvara*), time—which like a *prastha* measure acts as a delimitor for the purpose of delimitation—does not apply; that is, it does not take the Lord as its object by way of being a delimiting factor, even though it is a delimitator of all transformable things (*pariṇāmin*).

Now, one might object: "Since the Lord consists of preeminent *sattva*, and since that which is an effect of *pradhāna* is delimited by time, why is that *sattva* not delimited? For the nature of the *puruṣa* is indeed undelimited by time for everyone. This objection should not be raised, because the *puruṣa* is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*).
