Now, if you should think that God is independent of *sattva*, like the Lord (*īśvara*) well-known in other systems (*tantrāntara*), that is incorrect, because it is accepted that he takes up *sattva* as a preeminent material cause (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, if you should think: "It is time alone that delimits the effect already set in motion by the existence of God, not the existence of God itself"—that too is incorrect, because only that which is manifested is subject to delimitation, and the existence of God is indeed manifested.

Furthermore, if you should maintain that the *sattva* of the Lord exists only in its primordial state (*pradhānāvastha*), that is untenable because knowledge would be impossible [in such a state]. Alternatively, if you should argue that—due to the acceptance of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*)—the *sattva* of knowledge and other qualities exists even in the primordial state, just as the seed exists in the fruit or the tree in the flower and bud, that too is not correct. For [if they were already manifest], they would be fit for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Moreover, if that were the case, there would be no distinction between all things, since there would be no difference in their connection with the mere existence of knowledge and so forth, leading to the consequence that everything would be eternal.
Furthermore, if you should say that even though effects are manifest, some of them are delimited by time while others are not, that too is not tenable because it contradicts logic.

Furthermore, if you should object that the temporal limitation of the existence of Īśvara is established by scripture (*āgama*), that too is not valid, because the scripture is not illuminative [of such a fact].

Furthermore, if you were to say that scripture is the indicator of the fact that [the self], though existing, is simply not delimited by time because it is unknown, even that is not tenable; for since it would be the cause for the practice of cessation and so forth, it would follow that it is delimited by time, yet because it is stainless, it is not delimited by time—thus there would be a contradiction.
To this it is replied: there is no fault, because the state of being unconditioned by time depends upon the excellence of the purity of the Lord’s essence.

[75,14] Just as for other gurus, the excellence of their stainlessness (*vaimalyaprakarṣa*) is not delimited by time because it is caused by the performance of yoga, dharma, and so forth, it is not so for the Blessed One. How so? Because his *sattva* is like the nature of pure being (*sattvasvarūpa*), which—due to the eternal and absolute disappearance of *rajas* and *tamas*—is independent of causes such as dharma and the like, illuminates all objects, and is not delimited by time. Likewise, the excellence of its effect is also not delimited by time.

Just as heat and light in fire are not limited by time, so too the excellence of the stainless knowledge within the Blessed One’s being reaches a state of being unconditioned by time; it is with reference to this that it is said, "wherein time, whose purpose is limitation, does not apply. It is certainly not said with reference to something that is not an effect.

[75,22] For gravity has no limit. He says this very thing: just as at the beginning of this creation, the existence of those born at the start of the creation is established through inference by means of the excellence of the purification of knowledge, and is known from scripture (*āgama*), so too is there the establishment of those born at that time and even those prior to them in past creations; likewise, it is understood through inference and scripture even regarding the future time.

And this is the purpose of this sūtra: just as teachers are worshipped without ceasing by those who have no other refuge because they instruct in knowledge, dharma, and so forth, so too should this Blessed One—who is the teacher even of all teachers—be held incessantly within one's own heart by those whose minds have no other object, especially under names such as Nārāyaṇa and others.

Furthermore, even that service characterized by approaching the Blessed One and so forth, which is intended to be performed constantly with a mind undivided from Him—that too is not prohibited, because devotion to the Lord is well-established in both Śruti and Smṛti.

Just as those who have been seen by their gurus and brought face-to-face through service bestow grace upon those intent on serving them, so too does this Supreme Guru grant grace by mere meditation (*abhidhyāna*). And thus says the Śruti: "Whosoever has supreme devotion for the Divine, and for the Guru as for the Divine—for that great-souled one, these truths that have been told shine forth. The Smṛti also says: "He who performs my work, who regards me as the highest, who is my devotee, free from attachment, and without enmity toward all beings—he comes to me."
O Pāṇḍava! Thus [ends 1.26].

It has been stated, "From devotion to the Lord" (*īśvarapraṇidhānāt*). How is He to be devoted to? And what is the means for that devotion, by which the devotee performs that devotion? To explain the means for that devotion, he says: "The *praṇava* is His designator. The *praṇava* is the designator—the signifier—of that Lord whose characteristics have been described, just as the word "cow" is the signifier of an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth.

It is called *praṇava* because by means of it one is praised (*nūyate*) or extolled (*stūyate*) preeminently; or else, it is the *praṇava*, the syllable *oṃ*, because by it one praises (*praṇauti*) the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, it is so called because the Blessed One is directed toward (*praṇdhīyate*) by those who direct their minds toward him; or because by it they bow down (*praṇamanti*); or because by it one fixes (*praṇidhatte*) the Blessed One in the mind—this being derived from the root *dhā* with the addition of the letter *v*. For indeed, by means of sound, there is a mental fixing (*praṇidhāna*) of objects that are beyond the senses, just as when one thinks, "Meru is Indra."

And the denotation (*vācya*) of that syllable *oṃ* is Īśvara. Furthermore, there is an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) based on nine meanings: from the root *ava*, in the sense of "protecting" (*rakṣaṇa*) and so forth, with the suffix *maniṣṭi* and the elision of the *ṭi*. He protects those who apply themselves to him from *saṃsāra*; or he causes the transmigrating being to go to *nirvāṇa*; or he delights them beyond measure; or he causes them to realize the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) through the grace of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and other means—thus it conforms to such meanings. In every respect, however, it is most proximate to the name of the Blessed One as "the Beloved."

Therefore, when one constantly directs the mind toward Him, He becomes gracious. This is evidenced by numerous scriptural passages (*śruti*), such as "Oṃ Khaṃ Brahma," "Oṃ is Brahma," and so forth; and by traditional texts (*smṛti*), such as "Oṃ Tat Sat" and "Oṃ Viśvaṃ Viṣṇuḥ," and others. Because the word "Oṃ" ends in the letter *m* and is formed with a primary suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*), it lacks case endings, as its final syllable functions as a single phonetic unit.

[77,12] Is its status as signifier and signified established by convention (*saṅketa*), or does it exist inherently like the light of a lamp? What follows from this? If it was designated by that Blessed One or by others for the sake of worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*) with the thought, "Let this be its name," then since it was previously not denotable by the word *oṃ*, let those who were meditating or those who were reciting have done so either with the word *oṃ* or with some other name; let it be the same now as well. What is the point of this specific mention of the syllable *oṃ*? Or again—
Even though He exists like the light of a lamp, nevertheless, even upon the first hearing, God would be perceived, just as the sun is perceived through its light.

Furthermore, even a conventional designation (saṅketa) would be useless because the relationship [between word and object] is already established; or, if it were to be designated as something previously non-existent, one would incur the fault mentioned before—this is what is intended.

To this it is replied: the relationship between this signified object and its signifier exists whether the word be eternal or non-eternal; however, convention merely illuminates that very pre-existing relationship.

[77,22] But has it not been said that if [the relationship] were established, they would understand it even upon the first hearing? It is replied: although the relationship between the signifier and the signified—that is, between word and meaning—is indeed established, it is not perceived by the sense organs, unlike the case of the sense organs and their objects; for the capacities of the denoted and the denoter are imperceptible.

Consequently, the claim that an object is to be inferred from a word is incorrect, because the relationship [between the two] is not apprehended, and because the relationship is manifested by the employment of another [person]. For inference does not depend upon the employment of another.
Now, if he should say that the inference of an object follows from an inferred relation, he should be asked: "In what way is the relation between the word and its object inferred?"

If he should say: "Because one perceives an effect, one first cognizes the object and subsequently infers its connection [with the sense organ], just as, having perceived color with the eye, one infers the connection with the eye," he should be answered: "In that case, then, comprehension is established from the word alone, even without inference."

For if one has achieved his purpose through the cooking of a single grain of rice, what need is there for the cooking of a thousand? If it is argued that the relationship is grasped through repeated observation of the application—just as in the case of fire and smoke—we say no; for even in thousands of applications, the relationship between word and meaning is not grasped by perception in the way that the relationship between fire and smoke is grasped even at the very first instance. This same principle applies to the sentence as well.

Therefore, the convention merely illuminates the already established relationship between the denoted, namely Īśvara, and its denoter, the *praṇava*, just as it reveals an existing relationship between a father and a son. Because it depends upon the application of convention, the meaning is not understood from the first hearing, just as the eye [does not perceive form] in the absence of light.

[78,17] But surely, if the position is that sound is impermanent, how can there be an eternal relation when the relata are impermanent? For the relation between two impermanent things, such as a water-jar and a rope, cannot be eternal. It is replied: just as the relation between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge, between the sense organ and its object, and between actions and their factors remains established even though the related entities are impermanent—so too here, the relation remains established without deviation; and even at the beginning of creation, the convention depends upon the expressive power of the signifier and the signified.

Just as at the beginning of creation, the manifestation of form and the eye occurs precisely in dependence upon their respective capacities as the grasped and the grasper, so too here, the linguistic convention is established precisely in dependence upon the capacities of the signified and the signifier.

The followers of the Āgama, the proponents of the Veda, assert that the eternal correspondence between word and meaning is established through an eternal consensus based on the tradition of the elders alone, in the form of a relationship between signifier and signified, and not otherwise. And this consensus is the cause of the relationship between word and meaning; such is their position.

This is logical if it belongs to the category of future things; however, if it belongs to any other category, the relationship is established in every respect and is merely manifested by convention, just like that between a father and a son.

[79,12] However, if the relationship between the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka) were unstable, it would not be possible to say that "the Lord becomes manifest in the form of the syllable Om. For indeed, if the relationship between the cook and the act of cooking were not established, the employment of the cook and the fire for the purpose of cooking would not be appropriate. But since the relationship between the signified and the signifier is established, the employment of the syllable Om as the means for the propitiation of Your Honor is appropriate; it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the entire commentary [is composed]. 1.27.

[79,16] For the yogin who has thus understood the relationship between the signifier and the signified, how is propitiation of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) to be performed? To that end, he says: "The repetition of that and meditation upon its meaning. The repetition (japa) of that—the *praṇava*, which is the signifier of the Lord, consisting of three and a half measures or three measures—is its mental or whispered recitation (*āvartana*). And meditation upon its meaning (*tadarthabhāvana*) is the contemplation (*abhidhyāna*), the mental superimposition upon the intellect of the Lord who is presented by the signifier, the *praṇava*. The ellipsis of the sentence is: "This must be done."

[79,21] Thus, for the yogin who performs both, the mind becomes one-pointed. And he demonstrates that the attainment of one-pointedness is the fruit of propitiating Him; and so it has been said: "One should practice yoga from study. From study—meaning from the recitation of the *praṇava*—one should practice yoga while having a mind bowed toward the Lord. For that purpose, one should meditate upon the Lord (*dhyāyet*). And through meditation on His meaning, with an unshaken mind, one should contemplate the *svādhyāya*, the *praṇava*, and recite it mentally.

Mental recitation (*abhijapa*) is praised because it is closer to meditation (*dhyāna*) [than verbal recitation], so that the mind may not become inclined toward sense objects. Thus, the perfection of study and yoga consists in being unassailed by other mental states that oppose it; and through that perfection of the recitation of the *praṇava* and meditation on the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self (*parātmā*), the Parameṣṭhin, is revealed to the yogi. 1.28.

Furthermore, since it was stated in the preceding sūtra that "the mind becomes one-pointed," this constitutes one fruit; the word "kiñca" (furthermore) is used with reference to that. Is there yet another fruit, or is one-pointedness of mind itself the only one? To this he says: "From that, there is also the attainment of the inner consciousness and the absence of obstacles. From that—namely, from devotion to Īśvara—there is the attainment of the inner consciousness (*pratyak-cetanā-adhigama*).
The term *pratyak-cetana* refers to the Self (*ātman*), because it directs its own intellect inward; its "attainment" (*adhigama*) is the direct experience of its true nature as it really is.

[80,16] But surely the person is indeed apprehended within oneself through the notions "I am happy" and "I am suffering. Since this is well-established, what further qualification is being stated? True, it is so; however, that cognition is undifferentiated from the activity of the mind (*citta*). Furthermore, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the expressions "I am happy" and "I am suffering," and because here the notion of "I" has as its object a modification of the mind, its establishment is indeed based on ignorance (*avidyā*).

How is that higher knowledge? He says: Just as the Lord Puruṣa is pure, being devoid of the impurities of afflictions and so forth; for that very reason he is serene; for that very reason he is solitary, being free from the three guṇas; for that very reason he is free from calamities, being devoid of the three kinds of suffering, and is the perceiver of pre-eminent *sattva*—in the same way, this Puruṣa of mine also understands: "I am pure, serene, solitary, free from calamities, and the perceiver of the intellect (*buddhi*)."

By the presentation of the analogy and the thing illustrated through the expressions "as" and "so," the distinction between the Lord (Īśvara) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) is stated, as well as the logical justification for what has been said regarding the Buddha. Furthermore, because the Primordial Matter (Pradhāna) is established as being for the sake of another, and because the Knowers of the Field are likewise established, there is therefore a mutual distinction between them.

Furthermore, whatever obstacles there may be for him—such as those beginning with disease that will be mentioned hereafter—even these do not arise for him due to his devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna). (1.29) In this regard, what are those obstacles, and how many are they? To this he says: "disease, languor," and so forth. In terms of number, there are nine obstacles; in terms of their essential nature, they are disease and the rest. Disease is a disturbance of the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu).

The *dhātus* are wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*); their state of imbalance is *vaiṣamya*. This arises from the consumption of substances that predominantly increase wind, bile, or phlegm, and so forth. For when these [humors] reach their own respective sources, they are said to undergo increase. *Nutrient-fluid* (*rasa*) is a specific transformation of the food that has been consumed; it is called *rasa* because it is the effect of *rasa*. It is sevenfold, known as nutrient-fluid, blood, fat, muscle, bone, marrow, and semen. Its imbalance consists of increase or decrease, while the imbalance of the instruments [of perception] consists of blindness, deafness, and so forth.

[81,22] *Styāna* (sloth) is the mind's lack of serviceability, its state of stagnation. *Saṃśaya* (doubt) is a cognition that apprehends two contradictory alternatives, such as "Is it a post or a person?"

[81,24] Negligence (*pramāda*) is the non-cultivation of the means for achieving meditative concentration (*samādhi*), characterized by a lack of moral discipline (*aśīla*). Laziness (*ālasya*) is the failure to engage [in practice] due to heaviness of body and mind. Non-restraint (*avirati*) is greed, longing, or craving, which has as its intrinsic nature the association of the mind with sense objects, or is caused by such association.

Seeing things as they are not is erroneous cognition; it is a perverted engagement with the means for achieving yoga or with that path itself. "Not having attained the stages" (*alabdhibhūmikatva*) is the non-attainment of the stage of meditative concentration (*samādhibhūmi*). The "stages" (*bhūmayaḥ*) refer to the specific mental states such as applied thought (*vitarka*) and so forth, which have been mentioned and will be mentioned hereafter. Even when the stage of meditative concentration has been reached, if the mind somehow wavers from it, its subsequent settling back therein would indeed be [the attainment]; however, the failure to attain that is called "instability."

[82,16] Thus, these are the nine obstacles (*antarāya*). They are called "obstacles" because they come along creating an interval, a gap, or a separation; they are distractions, adversaries to the attainment of yoga, and calamities. And these exist together with the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*). They distract the mind toward sense-objects, thus they are "mental distractions. Once the mind is distracted, these—along with the fivefold fluctuations—exist in a state of mutual causality.

Now, in the absence of these—namely, in the absence of disease and so forth—the previously mentioned mental fluctuations such as the means of valid cognition do not arise due to the lack of their auxiliary causes. Because they exist only when those [auxiliaries] exist, it is said that the distractions of mental fluctuation have corresponding opposites. 1.30.

[82,22] Suffering is that by which living beings are struck and strive and exert themselves for its removal. And that is threefold. Internal (*ādhyātmika*): "internal" means pertaining to the self (*adhyātman*); that which exists therein is internal. And that consists of the bodily and the mental. The bodily is caused by the imbalance of the humors (*dhātu*) and so forth. The mental has as its cause the frustration of desired objects and the like. External to the elements (*ādhibhautika*): "external to the elements" means pertaining to the elements (*adhibhūta*); that which exists therein is external to the elements. And that consists of what has befallen one from animals, wild beasts, and so forth.

"Supernatural" (*ādhidaivika*) means "pertaining to the gods" (*adhideva*); that which exists therein is *ādhidaivika*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied here by the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "after *adhyātma* and so forth. Because it belongs to the class beginning with *anuśatika*, there is *vṛddhi* strengthening of both word-roots. And that [suffering] is caused by wind, rain, and so forth; though being one and the same, it is differentiated as having the form of *rajas* according to the difference in its causes.

[83,13] Dejection (*daurmanasya*) is the agitation and disturbance of the mind due to the frustration of one's desires; it is a state of being unsettled and wavering. That which causes the limbs to quiver and tremble is "the quality of making the limbs quiver. (And that is not...)

Now, this practice beginning with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) arises from repeated cultivation; it manifests like the surging waves of a great ocean of bliss. Furthermore, its emergence is as follows: *śvāsa* (inhalation) is the drawing in of external air, characterized by a predominance of the inhalation of external air and the cessation of exhalation. *Praśvāsa* (exhalation) is the opposite operation, which expels the abdominal air. These are "co-existent with distractions" (*vikṣepasahabhū*), meaning they occur only in one whose mind is distracted, together with those very distractions.

These do not occur for one whose mind is concentrated; that is to say, to the extent that the mind is concentrated, to that extent they do not occur. They are to be pacified by those very two—cultivation and detachment—and they require no other antidote.

[83,21] It is understood that no power arises from those dedicated to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) except through practice and dispassion. And by stating "the absence of obstacles," it is shown that even from previous devotion to the Lord, obstacles are suppressed. (YS 1.31)

It has been stated that "their cessation occurs through practice and dispassion. Among these, the object of dispassion has been explained. Now, concluding the discussion on the object of practice, he says: "Practice of a single principle for the sake of its prevention. For the sake of preventing those distractions—that is, for the sake of their prevention—one practices a single principle (*ekatattva*). And that single principle cannot be practiced because it is a real entity (*vastu*); for it is not possible to speak of the cultivation (*śīlana*) of entities such as the Self (*ātman*) and so forth. Indeed, those [entities] abide by virtue of their own inherent majesty (*māhābhāgya*) and are not merely the mind.

However, he will later refute the dependence of objects upon the mind with the words, "And an object is not dependent on a single mind," and so forth. Therefore, anticipating this objection, the author of the Commentary says, "One should practice the mind having a single reality as its object. This very meaning is already contained within the compound "practice of a single reality" (*ekatattvābhyāsa*) in the aphorism itself.

[84,1] Is it not the case that no single, persisting mind exists for which a cognition could have a single reality as its object? The mind is nothing but cognitions, and those cognitions are restricted to their respective objects and perish in every moment. Furthermore, the instability of cognitions is directly experienced by oneself. Nor is there a persisting cognizer distinct from the cognitions, because [the notion of identity] falls within the same mental continuum and is based on similarity—just as one says, "that is the same lamp" or "those are the same hairs."

Regarding this, it has also been said: the cognizer (*pratyayin*) is distinct from each and every cognition (*pratyaya*), because it is not other than those cognitions which are mutually distinct and separate. The cognizer, existing as the object of the "I"-cognition in its own nature within each single cognition, is distinct from the cognizer that was the object of the "I"-cognition in past and future times, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, just like a jar and a cloth. Alternatively, it is like a present jar being distinct from a destroyed jar and a future jar, because they belong to different times.
All cognitions of "I" have distinct objects, because they are cognitions, like cognitions whose objects are jars, cloths, and so forth.

To this it is replied: one who speaks thus would indeed contradict his own treatise. For he says: "For one whose mind is momentary, every single mind is one-pointed precisely because of the absence of distraction; there is no such thing as a distracted mind. Since all minds would be one-pointed and since the state of distraction would be non-existent, the instruction of the treatise for the purpose of prohibiting distraction would be useless. Yet there exists the instruction on loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth for the sake of purifying the mind.
That [instruction] would be contradicted by one who accepts that the mind has such a nature.

[84,27] But surely, for you as well, since there is no difference between the activity and that which possesses the activity, distraction is untenable; therefore, the instruction for its negation would be purposeless. This is not a fault, because we accept the existence of both the activity and that which possesses the activity.

If the modes themselves were mutually distinct and arose as entirely different from the possessor of the modes, and were restricted to their respective objects, then this fault would arise; however, it is not accepted that this is the case.

[85,7] How, then, is it that by means of its modes (*vṛtti*), the one [mind] possesses multiple objects and remains stable through the diversity of those objects? Because we do not admit the reversal of existence and non-existence, he thus demonstrates the consistency of his own position (*ātmapakṣa*). Furthermore, if this mind—which has spread out in many ways according to the distinction of its modes—were, like the proponents of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, withdrawn from all objects everywhere and, having been turned back, concentrated and fixed upon a single object such as the Self (*ātman*), then it would become one-pointed (*ekāgra*).
The meaning is that it is worthy of being accomplished through human effort.

[85,12] Therefore, the instruction of the treatise is for the purpose of its refinement. (Hence it is not perception. For this reason—namely, because of the instruction in the treatise concerning the refinement of that [mind]—even for the proponents of momentariness, like the Sāṃkhya and Yoga teachers, the mind is not one, nor does it have multiple objects, nor is it stable.

Or rather, it must be accepted later as being restricted to each respective object; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the treatise (*śāstra*). As for one who considers the mind to be "one-pointed" (*ekāgra*) because it is a flow of similar cognitions—meaning that in a single continuum, the flow of cognitions is similar or identical—that which is the opposite of this, having a flow of dissimilar cognitions, is "distracted" (*vikṣipta*). Thus, since one-pointedness is established by the negation of distraction, and the teaching of its purpose [is likewise established], how could there be a contradiction with the treatise?

The other says: No, because we do not admit a single substratum (*dharmin*) consisting of a mental continuum (*pravāhacitta*). For one does not admit a so-called "mental continuum" as a single substratum for past, present, and future moments of consciousness. If one were to admit such a thing, one’s own position would be abandoned. Why? Because the mental continuum is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*); that very thing which is a single entity does not exist, whose property (*dharma*) could be one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
For he accepts that these very conditions, joined together with one another like a row of ants, constitute [the world].

Now, if it is thought that although there is no single entity, nevertheless the property of one-pointedness belongs to all those conditions that flow in a similar stream—just as illumination belongs to the flames of a lamp—the author replies: a collection of things that arise and perish at non-simultaneous times is impossible. Furthermore, the example is devoid of the probandum; for there is not one single illumination belonging to many flames, since illumination differs with each individual flame, nor is there a single property common to both the illumination and the flames.

[86,9] Furthermore, if it is thought that one-pointedness is a property belonging only to a certain portion of the mental stream (*pravāha-aṃśa*), just as in a single row of ants there might be even one red ant—this is not so, because it is beset by the same faults mentioned previously. Every portion of the mental stream, whether carrying similar or dissimilar contents, is necessarily restricted to its own object (*pratyarthaniyata*) just as before, and thus would be one-pointed; consequently, there would be no possibility of a distracted mind. Therefore, one must admit that the mind is a single entity, manifold in its objects, and stable, provided that the treatise teaches the cultivation of the mind.

Furthermore, if cognitions were to arise as distinct by nature through an instrument that is not connected with a single mind, then tell me: how could one cognition be the rememberer of what was seen by another cognition, just as Yajñadatta cannot remember what Devadatta saw? Or how could one cognition be the experiencer of the latent deposit of karma accumulated by another cognition?

[86,17] For one who is to become a son in the future would not experience the fruit of accumulated karmic predispositions, such as rebirth in heaven. Now, if it should be argued that the perishing active consciousness deposits some kind of latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) for the sake of the cognition of the specific future son—this is not so, because of the absolute difference between the storehouse consciousness and the active consciousness, and because [the latter] lacks substantial reality.

[86,21] If the evolving consciousness does not arise from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), then it would be that very same thing with only a difference in name; and in that case, because it would lack the application of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), memory would be impossible. Alternatively, if it were something else, even so, one evolving consciousness would not deposit a formative force in the storehouse-consciousness, because they are distinct, just as [one] storehouse-consciousness does not [deposit a force] in another stream of consciousness.

Furthermore, even if it were to deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—being impressed by the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—would be incapable of reaching another place or time, because its momentariness is admitted; and as it perishes right then and there, it is not sufficient to benefit a subsequent consciousness. If it were to benefit [a future state] separated by space and time, then it would have to benefit [states] arising in other, distinct continua as well.
[87,1] Now, if it were to persist for a period of time, then its momentariness would be lost. If it were to remain for another moment, who would find fault with its persistence over a long duration?

[87,3] Furthermore, even if it is argued that the prior *ālayavijñāna* perishes after having deposited its impressions (*saṃskāra*) into a future *ālayavijñāna*—which is similar to itself, arises in the interval, and is distinguished by the impressions of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—that is not so, because there would be no other impression [to receive them]. If such an impression exists, it leads to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, there is no substratum (*ādhāra*), then what [is the case]?

The assumption of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) for the sake of depositing impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is unnecessary; for just as the storehouse-consciousness deposits an impression in the storehouse-consciousness that is about to arise but is non-existent at that moment, so too let the active consciousness itself deposit an impression in the active consciousness that is about to arise but is non-existent at that moment, without depending upon the storehouse-consciousness.

Furthermore, it is not observed that a perishing [entity] imparts a conditioning (*saṃskāra*) to another entity that is yet to arise and does not exist at that time. Nor could the future entity itself perform the conditioning; for it is contradictory to say that the former is conditioned by the future, and that it will be in the future. If the future, being non-existent at that time, were to be conditioned, then why—given the lack of distinction in the absence of a connection—should one postulate a distinction between similar and dissimilar successions? For in that case, everything would be conditioned by everything. Nor can there be simultaneous arising and perishing of the future and the perishing [entity], as that would entail the consequence of their being non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).

If it is argued that, as with the two ends of a balance scale, the destruction of the former and the production of the latter might occur simultaneously for two entities, this is not so, because it contradicts your own tenets. For the proponent of momentariness (*vaināśika*) does not accept any effect other than the very acts of production and destruction themselves; and if such an effect were accepted, it would contradict the established doctrine.

Furthermore, as long as the action is arising, the causal factor must persist; consequently, there would be a loss of momentariness. And if it does not persist, then its appropriation for the sake of the action is purposeless.

Furthermore, if the agent were nothing other than the action, and the action were nothing other than the agent, then the words "action" (*kriyā*) and "agent" (*kāraka*) would be synonyms. Consequently, in the expressions "the sprout arises" (*aṅkuro jāyate*) and "Devadatta arises" (*devadatto jāyate*), the terms "sprout" and "Devadatta" would be synonymous, because both would consist merely of the act of arising.

[87,23] Now, if it is argued that the act of production is distinct when qualified by Devadatta and distinct when qualified by a sprout, then it must be admitted that the causal factor (kāraka) is [defined] by its qualification; for nothing could be qualified in itself without some distinction.

[87,25] Now, if it should be argued that the act of arising (*utpatti-kriyā*) is distinguished by its own nature from another act of arising—just as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—that too is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence of identity between existence and non-existence. Here, one says "the sprout arises" and "the sprout perishes"; since that very thing which arises is the very same thing that perishes, it follows that the production of the sprout is the destruction of the sprout; thus, production is said to be destruction. For the sprout itself would then have to be called both the action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kāraka*). (Citaḥ)

Furthermore, it might be argued that the activity of producing the sprout is indeed distinct from the activity of destroying the sprout; even so, this would entail the consequence that the production of the sprout is eternal, precisely because destruction is something other than it.

Moreover, even if it were the case that a thing is variegated like destruction and production, then it would follow that non-existence (*abhāva*) itself must be variegated. How so? For even in the absence of an agent distinct from the action, one might claim that destruction alone possesses production and destruction, or that production alone possesses production and destruction. Indeed, no specific quality such as variegation can belong to non-existence because it is devoid of all attributes;
furthermore, since there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence, neither perception nor inference would be applicable.

[88,14] Furthermore, as for what is said regarding the lowering and raising of the two ends of a scale: in that case, it is logical that because the two ends of the scale exist at the same time, the depression of one end is caused by the weight of another object, while there is a corresponding elevation of the other. Here, however, the destruction of the past consciousness and the arising of the future consciousness do not occur simultaneously, like the depression and elevation of a scale, because there is no third cause; [if they were simultaneous], it would be impossible. A consciousness that is perishing produces its own likeness, since it does not possess duration due to its very destruction.

[88,20] Now, if it is argued that it is just as a lump of clay perishes while producing a jar, that is not so; for it is precisely the parts of the clay that undergo transformation into the form of the jar. Indeed, the single lump of clay is the substratum of many properties, such as being a lump or being a jar.

Furthermore, as for the claim that when seeds are perfumed by a perfuming substance (*vāsakadravya*), the perfumable substance conforms to that perfuming substance—that too is not a valid reason, because the perfumable and the perfumer remain distinct. For it is precisely the sprouts and so forth, which remain distinct from the seeds, that are perfumed by the perfuming of the seed. Since they are other than the perfuming substance, subtle parts of it indeed exist within them without having entered into their constituent parts.

Therefore, it is logical that only existing things, such as sprouts and the like, are perfumed by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the seed; for there is no arising of non-existent things, such as a rabbit’s horn. If non-existent things were to arise, then because the object to be perfumed (*vāsya*) and the perfumer (*vāsaka*) would have perished—and since they would be indistinguishable in their lack of existence—the [result] would not arise conforming to the substance of the perfumer, or else something entirely different, such as a hand, would arise.

Or if even something absolutely non-existent, such as a hare’s horn, were to arise, then there would be no distinction between the three types of non-existence when the seed has been perfumed. Therefore, one must admit that the causal agent is stable and possesses activity across multiple times—past and future. Otherwise, for one who attempts to establish that the mind is merely a collection of conditions and momentary, even their own argumentation falls into the "cow-dung-and-milk" fallacy.

Just as cow-dung cannot be turned into milk-porridge, even by one who exerts great effort and employs numerous reasons such as its being a product of a cow, so too it is impossible for a momentary mind to accomplish recollection and the like.

Furthermore, if the mind were something other [than the self] and were merely a momentary cognition, it would not remember what was seen by another; thus, it would deny what was experienced by its own self.

[89,18] However, when asked "Did you see it?", even though he has seen it, he would say, "I did not see it. For indeed, on his view, that object is seen by another; and if he denies it, how could there be a cognition of what was experienced? How could there be the realization: "What I saw, that very same thing I touch," or "What I touched, that very same thing I remember"? This realization occurs only when there is a single agent for both the cognition and the memory.

Otherwise, one would have such recollections as, "I touch that which was seen by one similar to me," or "I remember that which was seen by one similar to me. Furthermore, for every person, the notion of "I" arises in relation to both the cognition of memory and the cognition of perception; and this notion presents itself as immediate and direct only when there exists a single, non-different cognizer who is the agent of those various cognitions.

[89,89],26 But surely, even if there is oneness of the object of a single cognition, there should not be the notions "I perceive" and "I remember" regarding the agent, since there is a difference in the cognitions and the remembrances due to the difference in words such as "perceiver" and "rememberer. To this he replies: "No, because it is perception. He demonstrates that very point: "And this cognition 'I am' is graspable through one's own experience because of non-difference."

If it is argued that the object of the "I"-cognition is distinct [from the self] because of the difference in words—such as "the cognizer" versus "the remember"—and because of the difference in cognitions, [the author] says: "For the greatness of direct perception, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*), is not overridden or sublated by inference, just as [the perception of] color is not sublated by the eye."

Furthermore, this cognition "I" is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); it does not function as a general [cognition] occurring in a single agent among those cognitions that are recollections (*smṛti*).

If that which has become a direct perception were to be sublated by inference (*anumāna*), then at that time even inference would lose its status as a means of valid cognition, because inference is rooted in that [perception]. This very point is stated: "And another means of valid cognition [is established], and the defect in the opponent's thesis regarding the means of valid cognition has been explained through contradiction with inference."

[90,14] The substratum of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) of present conditions is not other than the substratum of the formative impressions of past and future conditions, because, while being connected to a single continuum, it has the nature of consciousness, just like the essential nature of the self (*ātman*).

[90,16] The substratum of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of past and future cognitions is distinct from the substratum of the mental impressions of present cognitions, because it possesses the nature of consciousness (*bodhātmakatva*) through its connection with a single continuum (*ekasantāna*), just like the self (*ātman*) by virtue of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). The subject of the present "I"-cognition is non-different from the subjects of past and future cognitions, because it is a cognizer (*pratyayin*) when connected with a single continuum, just like its own essential nature.

The present cognition of "I" is not distinct from past and future cognitions of "I," because, when they belong to a single continuum, they are cognitions [of the same subject], just as [the cognition of] one's own nature is not distinct from itself.

[90,20] A present cognition is distinct from past and future cognitions, provided there is a connection within a single continuum, because it has the nature of consciousness, just as [the self is distinct] from the nature of self-love and so forth.

[90,22] The present cognizer is not other than the past and future cognizers, because, while being connected to a single continuum, it has the nature of consciousness, just as the self is not other than its own essential nature.

[90,24] Since mutual recollection, reconnection, and so forth are not observed among distinct mental continua (*santati*), whereas recollection and the like are indeed observed within a single continuum, the fact of having a single agent is established. Thus, regarding this matter, there is nothing to be proven by inference, since perception (*pratyakṣa*)—the most authoritative of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is available. For no one takes up a mirror with the desire merely to see the mark on their palm. Nevertheless, some, unable to endure the foul-smelling inferences fabricated by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*), [proceed as follows].

They demonstrate clever counter-arguments. And so it has been said: "Therefore, the mind is one, manifold in its objects, and stable; it is for this [mind] that the purification of the mind is taught by the treatise. This indicates that the connection with the instruction of the treatise is the reason for the stability of the mind. For indeed, no refinement such as washing or turning over is performed upon a jar while it is being carried about. (1.32)

How is the purification of the mind described? It has been stated that it is "the practice of a single reality. What, then, is that single reality which is the object of this practice? To this he says: "The cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward objects that are happy, suffering, virtuous, and non-virtuous, respectively, results in the clarification of the mind. Loving-kindness is the cultivation directed toward friends; it is such that one rejoices in the happiness of those who are happy, being free from envy and other such faults.

Likewise, one should cultivate compassion (*karuṇā*) toward those who are suffering, understanding it as pity for their pain; joy (*muditā*) toward those whose nature is merit, understanding it as an appreciation for their virtuous character; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward those of non-meritorious character, understanding it as indifference toward their non-virtuous activities—this is to be supplied as the conclusion.

[91,25] For one who cultivates this in every respect, there is purity; "white" refers to the pure dharma resulting from the avoidance of harming living beings and so forth. Then, being born from that dharma, it clarifies the mind. By means of that clarity, the mind attains a state of one-pointed stability. The meaning is that through one-pointedness, one becomes concentrated (*samādhīyate*). Thus it has been said: "For the intellect of one whose mind is clear quickly becomes established."

In this regard, since equanimity (*upekṣā*) is by nature a state of non-action and thus not a cause for [wholesome] phenomena, why is its inclusion mentioned here? If equanimity were not included, the mind might engage in activity even toward those of unwholesome conduct (*apuṇyaśīla*). Consequently, due to the turbidity caused by that engagement, one would not be fit for the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables]. Furthermore, so that demerit (*adharma*) does not arise from the activity of the aspects of cause and effect associated with unwholesome conduct, the stability of the mind itself is equanimity; therefore, it is included. And in this context, the stability of the mind is what is intended.

Therefore, for one whose mind is thus concentrated and who cultivates a mind focused on a single reality such as loving-kindness or compassion, the previously mentioned obstacles will not arise. (1.33)

[92,16] Or, by means of exhalation (*pracchardana*) and retention (*vidhāraṇa*) of the breath. The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate an alternative to other means, such as the cultivation of friendliness (*maitrī*) and so forth. The meaning of the context is that the stability of the mind (*cittasthiti*) is to be accomplished by any one of the various means, beginning with the cultivation of friendliness. The demonstration of multiple means is intended to show that for some person, in a certain situation, a particular method may be easier to perform. Exhalation and retention may be practiced either separately or combined. Exhalation is the gentle expulsion of the abdominal air through the nostrils until it reaches the limit; retention is—

Prāṇāyāma is indeed [to be performed] until exhaustion. Although the breath is also extended by means of exhaling (pracchardana), nevertheless, because the external function is not suppressed, it is specifically defined as prāṇāyāma through the term "retention" (vidhāraṇa). ||1.34||

"Or, an activity possessing objects has arisen as the basis for the stability of the mind"—this is the completion of the sentence. That yogic activity which possesses objects—namely, that characterized by the perception of odors and so forth—is called "possessing objects," because odors and the like have become its objective supports (*ālambana*).
"Activity" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the first manifestation of yoga as it becomes present for a practitioner who is training in yoga.

It is the initial appearance of yoga that produces conviction and generates enthusiasm for the practice of yoga, like the emergence of smoke from a fire being kindled. When such activity has arisen, it gladdens the mind of the practitioner through the production of conviction and binds it to stability.

For one who fixes the mind on the tip of the nose, there arises the perception of smell—the experience of exhilarating, fragrant odors—which, due to its uninterrupted nature, is described as being like a constant union. That is the manifestation of smell. The same applies to the tongue and other senses; the word "fixing" is understood to apply to them as well. These manifestations bind the mind to its state of stability, dispel doubt, and serve as gateways to the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

By this it should be understood that for one who fixes the mind on rays of light, the moon, the sun, planets, lamps, and so forth, or who fixes it within the heart-lotus, the occurrence of an appearance in the form of rays, the moon, and so on, arises due to a state of imbalance; it is simply a manifestation possessing an object.

[93,23] Even if the reality of an object has been understood from scripture, inference, or a teacher as being exactly so, with an unerring nature—since those sources do not teach anything otherwise—even so, as long as even a single part is not cognizable through its own cause and is not directly perceived, then for one who has not directly perceived even a single part of the meaning taught by scripture, no firm conviction will arise regarding all such subtle matters, such as liberation and the like, which remain as if beyond perception.
Therefore, for the sake of corroborating scripture, inference, and the teacher, some particular [instance] must necessarily be perceived through direct perception.

In this regard, when one has directly perceived even a portion of the objects taught in the scriptures and so forth, one gains conviction in everything, including subtle objects, until final liberation (*apavarga*). It is for this very purpose that this "purification of the mind" (*cittaparikarma*) is taught—beginning with the section on friendliness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and so on, and ending with the statement that "its mastery extends from the atom to the infinitely great"—for one who is distinguished by the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and postures (*āsana*).

This is what is meant: by the practice of any one of the means taught in this section, and because a portion [of reality] has been directly perceived, one’s doubts are dispelled; until final liberation (*apavarga*), with faith and other qualities firmly established, with external mental fluctuations stilled, and possessing the detachment characterized by the realization of mastery, one becomes capable of directly perceiving each respective object—such as the three types of transformation taught in the third chapter—for the sake of attaining the powers of knowledge and so forth.

And thus, the meaning of this section is that the cultivation of the mind is taught for this very purpose. And the author of the Commentary has demonstrated this with the words, "It is for this purpose alone that there is this cultivation of the mind," and so forth. (1.35)

"Or, a sorrowless, luminous activity of the mind has arisen which serves as a basis for stability"—this connects with what was previously stated. That activity in which light exists is "luminous" (*jyotiṣmatī*); and because it removes sorrow, it is called "sorrowless" (*viśokā*).

And how does that arise? He says: for one who holds [the mind] within the lotus of the heart, there occurs the consciousness of the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the self-awareness of its own nature. For what is the form of the *sattva* of the intellect? He says: the *sattva* of the intellect is luminous, having the nature of shining, resembling space, and all-pervasive; "wherein" means in that *sattva* of the intellect.

"Because of the dissimilarity of stability" means because the identity with the nature of the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*) has not been attained. For one who maintains concentration precisely within the heart-lotus, the active light becomes manifest and is differentiated in the form of the radiance of the sun, moon, and jewels. Thus, when the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*) reaches the state of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*) within the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), it attains its own essential nature; through the attainment of identity, it becomes like a great ocean without waves—tranquil, infinite, and consisting of pure "I-am-ness" alone.

Regarding that which was stated: "In that state where there is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sense of 'I-ness' (*asmitā*), having found—that is, having reached—this very subject under discussion, the subtle self (*ātman*) which is the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) characterized by 'I-am-ness,' he perceives it simply as 'I am. He perceives only so much as the nature of the objective support. Because it conforms to that, it is delimited by the very nature of the ego-sense, just as a crystal gem is colored by the form of an adjacent object. Thus, there are two types of sorrowless activity: that which possesses objects and that which consists of mere 'I-ness'."

All [the forms of concentration] beginning with the perception of smell and ending with the mere sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātra) are indeed free from sorrow (*viśoka*). However, *jyotiṣmatī* is other than the fivefold activity beginning with the perception of smell; whereas *viṣayavatī* occurs even prior to the mere sense of "I-am-ness. Such is the division of the objects. By means of that sorrowless *jyotiṣmatī*, the yogi’s mind attains a state of stability. (1.36)

[95,24] Or, "the mind has as its object one free from passion" (*vītarāgaviṣayaṃ cittaṃ*): that condition (*pratyaya*) from which passion has departed is "one free from passion," meaning one devoid of passion. That very [condition] is the object (*viṣaya*), the focal point (*ālambana*), of that mind; thus, it is "that which has as its object one free from passion. Furthermore, a person free from passion is well-known in the world. For even among those possessed of passion...

Even regarding an object that is a cause of passion for a person—such as a woman, a mother, or others—it is precisely that mental representation (*pratyaya*) which one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) should practice as the objective support (*ālambana*), and not the object itself which serves as the support. This is because objects are inherently treacherous. That mind, colored by the objective support of the representation of one free from passion, likewise becomes free from passion, exceedingly serene, and attains a state of stability. For a mind corrupted by passion wavers like a horse that has been broken in by a harsh bridle. (1.37)

[96,18] Or, it has as its objective support the cognition of dream-sleep; that is, the mind has as its objective support either the cognition of a dream or the cognition of sleep, and thus it takes on that very form. For such is the nature of the mind: whatever it takes as an objective support, it becomes the form of that. And in a dream, there is a cognition devoid of objects such as sound and so forth. Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of cognition is luminosity (*avabhāsakatā*); even in that case, it takes as its objective support only the own-form of the cognition itself, and not the actual nature of an object being remembered.

Indeed, even by an object that is being remembered, a state of mental impairment is observed. However, the cognition of sleep consists of the non-perception of particulars; it has the notion of non-existence as its support, and is experienced as peaceful, infinite, and characterized by a lack of movement. Therefore, it is logical that the mind, having that as its support, attains a state of stability. 1.38.

[96,25] Or, from meditation on whatever is desired; "whatever is desired" is said with reference to the stability of the mind, because the stability of the mind is the subject at hand, and not with reference to pleasure and so forth, since that has been prohibited by the statement: "One should by no means hold the mind after it has reached sense objects. In that state, having attained stability and being pliant (*karmanya*), it also attains a state of stability in other scriptural [meditations]. (1.39)

[97,14] Its mastery extends from the atom (*paramāṇu*) to the ultimate limit of greatness (*paramamahattva*). The word "limit" (*anta*) is connected with each term. For the yogin who enters into subtlety—that is, who enters into dimension and contracts [the object]—at the time of illumination, he observes it as small and increasingly smaller in succession until it is contracted down to the atom. And that atom is the limit of the contraction of the mind. Therefore, that is the state of stability ending with that.

[97,18] Thus, for the mind that pursues both extremes and experiences both contraction and expansion, that non-obstruction by another contrary cognition is the supreme mastery (*vaśīkāra*). The former [mastery] is also indeed [a form of] the latter; nevertheless, this is its distinction: because of that mastery, [the mind] becomes complete, unbroken, and has attained stability, such that it no longer requires further preparatory cultivation (*parikarma*) performed through practice. The former [states], however, still require some degree of further preparatory cultivation.

In this regard, there are three types of concentration (*dhāraṇā*): the contracted (*saṃkṣiptā*), the expanded (*viśālā*), and the transformative (*vikaraṇī*). Among these, the transformative touches both extremes; the expanded touches the limit of supreme magnitude; and the contracted touches the limit of the smallest atom. And all three of these are included here in the Sūtra. 1.40.

[97,25] Now, regarding the mind that has attained stability: since it has been stated that stability is attained by means of one or another of the aforementioned methods, this Sūtra was composed to demonstrate what the nature and what the object of that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are: "For one whose fluctuations have ceased, there is, with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, a state of being established in them and a state of being colored by them, like a precious gem of noble birth."

[98,10] But will you not state the object of *samāpatti* in the third chapter with the words, "From *saṃyama* upon one's own nature, through its being for the sake of another, there is knowledge of the Puruṣa," and so forth? And the nature of *samāpatti* will be established by the very accomplishment of the effects of *saṃyama*. Therefore, this sūtra is useless. This is not a fault, because its purpose is to demonstrate the efficacy of the mastery over the means previously mentioned.
For it is thus that this mastery over the mind occurs: the mind, having attained *samāpatti* upon objects such as the grasper and so forth, becomes their manifestation.

Furthermore, it was stated that [the samādhi] is "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) because it is accompanied by *vitarka* and so forth; therefore, the nature of *vitarka* and the rest must be shown here. Since the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) has not yet been described, it would be impossible to show the nature of *vitarka* and so forth by saying, "The meditative attainment consists of phenomena such as *vitarka*. The phrase "of one whose fluctuations have ceased" (*kṣīṇavṛtteḥ*) means of one for whom cognitions such as external means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) have subsided.

[98,18] But surely all conditions have completely subsided; for when all conditions have subsided, consciousness, having completed its function, does not take as its object anything gross, subtle, or otherwise.

The phrase "like a well-bred gem" is an illustration. Just as a crystal, due to the difference in its proximate supports, appears in the form of those various supports when colored by this or that color; so too, the mind, colored by the object of perception (*grāhya-ālambana*), having merged with the perceived object, appears in the form of the very nature of that perceived object.

In that same way, when colored by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the mind, having attained the state of identity with the subtle elements, appears as a manifestation of the very nature of those subtle elements.

[98,25] In the same way, when colored by a gross object of perception, it becomes absorbed in a gross form and appears as a gross form; likewise, when colored by the diversity of the universe, it becomes absorbed in the diversity of the universe and appears as the universal form.

The same should be understood regarding the objects of apprehension and the sense faculties as well: colored by the object of apprehension and having attained the state of apprehension, it manifests in the form of the very nature of that apprehension.

The meaning is that, in this way, the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), which makes [the object] known, becomes identified with the person who is the grasper; it manifests in the form of the grasper’s own nature.

Likewise, it is colored by the latent impressions of the liberated person. When that very intellect (*buddhi*) is no longer the perceiver of objective modifications, then there exists the state of the mere discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa.

When one is called an "indifferent person" (*udāsīna*) or a "liberated person," it is because the mind is freed from all afflictions and the like; for that very liberation of the mind from afflictions and so forth is what constitutes the liberation of the *puruṣa*. For this very reason, the Sūtra employs the term "grasper" (*grahītṛ*); here, the "grasper" intended is specifically the liberated *puruṣa*.

[99,15] For just as when one performs the very grasping of the Person (puruṣa)—once the realization of mastery over the other has arisen—there is no further connection with saṃsāra; so too it has been said: "As soon as there is a connection between the mind and the sattva, because of the absence of connection with the afflictions and so forth, he is forever liberated and forever the Lord."

Therefore, [the mind], colored by the reflection of the liberated person and having attained the state of the liberated person, manifests in the form of the liberated one's own nature. For it is incorrect to think that [the mind] manifests in that very form even when it has not attained the state of the liberated person—though the connection with *sattva* has ceased—for that would entail the consequence of the mind's own dissolution.

[99,22] Furthermore, the *puruṣa* is subtle and beyond all comparison; the *pradhāna* is equally subtle, as is the *sattva* which is the cause of its effects. When the mind (*citta*) enters into *samāpatti* with either the *pradhāna* or the *puruṣa*, it is not capable of entering while remaining in its own established form. For a jar does not enter into the state of clay without abandoning its own specific nature.

[99,25] But surely, even by means of the effect, which is the existence of the yogi, the Great Principle (mahat) and the I-principle (ahaṅkāra) are said to be cognizable? Regarding the Great Principle first, there is a dispute as to whether it is cognized or not. For when its state of being cognizable is established—just like the nature of the liberated perceiver—a specific relation is possible for both the Great Principle and the I-principle as well.

For those two [the intellect and the ego] exist in manifestation; therefore, a specific relationship is possible. And from that specific relationship, just as one's own person is perceived—both as the perceiver and as the perceived—due to its connection with specific mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), so it is here. However, there is no perception of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) in their entirety, because of their vastness.

If those two as well—the mind and the sentient being—were grasped in their entirety, they would arise as having the nature of mere mind and mere existence; and that being the case, there would be no apprehension of their objects at all. Furthermore, because the primary matter (pradhāna), the spirit (puruṣa), and their connection are by nature absolutely unmanifest, there can be no apprehension of their own essential forms.

[100,7] But is it not the case that Īśvara would be non-omniscient, since the primary matter (pradhāna), the person (puruṣa), and their connection are not perceptible? It is said in reply: everything other than the primary matter, the person, and their connection [is known by him].

Regarding the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), there is no disagreement, because we accept the existence of perception that is unlimited in scope. However, as for that which is beyond our own range—namely, that which is the domain of inference—it is He alone, the Lord, who is capable of knowing it. It is certain that if there is anything to be known, He knows all of it, whether in this way or that; for it is impossible for something to be an object of knowledge if it lacks a knower.

Furthermore, if both primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) were to become objects of knowledge in their own right, then, like the intellect (buddhi), they would fall into the predicament of being objects of experience. Consequently, they would also be for the sake of another, and yet another "other" would have to be postulated.

[100,14] Now, one might object: "Since persons are objects of enjoyment for one another, a 'Supreme Enjoyer' need not be postulated. This is not so, because since all persons are equal, it is impossible for them to stand in the relationship of subject and object. Indeed, two lamps do not illuminate one another. Furthermore, if a person were an object of enjoyment, it would follow that the person possesses the nature of pleasure and the like; and if that were the case, it would follow that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) would be without a cause. Such are the many further defects.

[100,18] But surely it will be stated that "from saṃyama upon the self-interest resulting from the interest of another, there is knowledge of the Puruṣa," which establishes the perceptibility of the Puruṣa. True, this has been rightly said. For this very reason it is said that the Puruṣa does not become an object by its own nature. It is for this reason that it was stated therein: "The Puruṣa is not seen by means of the cognition of the Puruṣa, which is essentially the *sattva* of the intellect; rather, the Puruṣa itself..."
It perceives its own object as a condition; for thus it has been said: "O Maitreyi, by what means could one know the knower?"

[100,23] But surely, the mind colored by having the Puruṣa as its object is the object of the Puruṣa; and this being so, the Puruṣa would be directly perceived (pratyakṣa). Just as when a cognition colored by having a jar as its object is apprehended by the Puruṣa, the jar is said to be directly perceived—this is not a fault, because the Puruṣa is not pervaded by the mind in the same way that a jar is. For external objects such as jars are pervaded by the mind, but the Puruṣa is not.
The person [is infinite] because of infinity.

For a limited mind, when taking as its object [the Puruṣa], is not capable of pervading the infinite subject, the Puruṣa. If it were to pervade the Puruṣa, it would likewise have to pervade the Pradhāna.

Therefore, just as a face is perceived in a mirror in the form of a reflection, so too is the cognition—which has transformed into the form of the reflection of the Puruṣa—perceived by the Puruṣa. And thus Vyāsa says: "Just as one sees the Self within oneself, as if in the surface of a mirror."

But there is no door for transformation into the form of another person who is liberated. If it were to transform into that other's form, then even for the liberated one, that [other] would be his own and thus would become an object of perception. For there is no such thing as a distinctness in the transformations of the mind. Indeed, when the mind has transformed into its own form, the Puruṣa does not fail to see the mind; rather, because of the relationship of ownership existing toward one's own Puruṣa, there is the door of transformation.

How, then, is the perception of another person—who is distinct from one's own self and lacks any inherent connection to it—explained? Just as one sees another’s face by means of another’s mirror, so too the Puruṣa, seeing his own being transformed into the form of another sentient being which stands in the place of a mirror, knows that other person as well.

[101,18] Regarding this [Self], the notion "this is his Self" or "this is my Self" is understood through inference alone, based on the perception of specific differences existing in other sentient beings as distinct from one's own. Since sentient beings consist of the three *guṇas*, they necessarily possess such distinctions. However, because *puruṣas* are devoid of distinctions, their differentiation by way of their own essential nature is indeed difficult to perceive.

Therefore, for the mind—which is like a noble jewel—there is "abiding in them and being colored by them" (*tatsthatadañjanatā*) with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, which constitute the person, the sense-faculties, and the elements. It "abides in" those things, such as the grasper and so forth; thus it is "abiding in them" (*tatstha*). That which is characterized by this state of abiding in them—the coloring by the grasper and so forth—is precisely what is called "attainment" (*samāpatti*), defined as the assumption of their form by that which abides in them.

Right attainment is *samāpatti*, and that is such [an attainment] only for one whose outward mental activity has ceased. Although there is also an attainment for one whose mind has emerged from concentration, nevertheless it is not more perfect, because the quality of purity (*sattva*) of the mind is utterly overwhelmed by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*). (1.41)

This attainment is fourfold. Therein, he explains the first attainment: "The attainment associated with discursive thought (*savitarka*) is that which is intermingled with the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and knowledge. Word, object, and knowledge are "word-object-knowledge"; their conceptual constructions are "conceptual constructions of word, object, and knowledge. That attainment which is intermingled—that is, mixed—with conceptual constructions whose objects are the things to be expressed, and which is perceived through mutual cognition, is the "intermingled attainment" (*saṃkīrṇa-samāpatti*).

But is it not the case that word, object, and cognition have mutually exclusive natures, while the yogi takes a single entity as his object of meditation—whether it be a word, an object, or a cognition? In that case, what confusion of the conceptual constructions of word, object, and cognition could there be?

It is just so. Nevertheless, this very conventional usage in the world consists in apprehension without differentiation. For example, in the world, the apprehension of the word "cow," the object "cow," and the cognition "cow" is seen as undifferentiated. For thus the world designates all three simply as "cow. Likewise, when one of them is apprehended, there is also recollection of the remaining two.

But is it not the case that this entity is not actually such [as it appears], because it arises only after the apprehension of the linguistic convention for the word's meaning? Yet, even prior to the convention, one certainly determines some kind of general term, since we observe the apprehension of things even when they are distinct. Furthermore, there are other properties of the sound, such as the phonemes *ga* and so forth, acute (*udātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), fast, medium, slow, and the auditory perception itself; these do not belong to the object or the cognition. Likewise, there are other properties of the object, such as the observation of the dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns; and similarly others.

The properties of the conditions—such as being graspable by the person, having the nature of appearing as such, and producing mental impressions—and so forth, do not belong to the word and its object. Therefore, even the slightest scent of a mutual confusion of their properties does not exist in ultimate reality. Consequently, the path of these two is distinct.

In this regard, when one has attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on any object whatsoever, if that very object which has ascended upon the wisdom of concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) is permeated by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of the knowledge of words and their referents—that is, produced by the conventional association of words and referents and characterized by the mutual recollection and interpenetration of these—then if the object appears as qualified by those [concepts], that is a mixed attainment, called "with discursive thought" (*savitarka*).

Because they are distinguished by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of knowledge regarding the conventions of words and their meanings acquired over the course of many previous births, even the first meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of a yogin is not distinct from that of ordinary people. However, this is the distinction: because the mind of the yogin has attained a stable foundation, there occurs a continuous flow of identical cognitions. (1.42)

[103,12] Now, the attainment free from discursive thought (*nirvitarkā samāpatti*) is described. When, moreover, there is the purification of the memory of verbal conventions (*śabda-saṅketa-smṛti*): verbal convention is the understanding of the agreement that "this is the designator of this" and "this is the designated by this. The memory produced by that is the "memory of verbal convention.
Its purification is the turning away from falsity; it arises from the subsiding of *rajas* and *tamas*.

Knowledge derived from scripture (*āgamika*) is that of hearing (*śruti*), while worldly knowledge is that of inference (*anumāna*). Both of these—inferential and scriptural knowledge—have only the universal (*sāmānya*) as their object. For their conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists precisely in the superimposition of particulars (*viśeṣādhyāropa*). When the yogin’s wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhiprajñā*) is devoid of such superimposition—that is, when it is free from the superimposition of inferential and conventional knowledge—it grasps the object in its mere essence alone. This means that it is distinguished even from direction, space, time, and experience; thus, it is exalted by its own attributes through its state of being that very essence.

In this way, the wisdom of the yogin is uninterrupted by the mere intrinsic nature of that object; the meaning is that it does not perceive anything external to that object, such as space, time, or the like.

Even its own nature as a perceiving subject, that wisdom does not perceive, because it is exceedingly pure. It is distinguished only by the object of perception alone. And such is that attainment free from discursive thought (*nirvitarkā samāpatti*). "Free from discursive thought" means that discursive thought has departed from it; discursive thought is superimposition (*adhyāropa*), and that is absent in this state.

This very [cognition] is supreme, most excellent, pure, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not the other kind of direct perception; it is common to all and was previously recited in the midst of the functions as belonging to the yogin alone. It is the seed of both scripture (*śruta*) and inference (*anumāna*). Although what was stated previously is also indeed the seed of scripture and inference, nevertheless, while those two—scripture and inference—may arise even from that which is devoid of deliberation (*nirvitarka*), they do not arise from that which originates in direct perception born of *nirvitarka* samādhi. Therefore, he says: "From that, scripture and inference arise."

And that vision is not co-existent with the knowledge derived from scripture or inference; rather, it has an object different from the objects of scriptural and inferential knowledge. For that vision has particulars as its object, whereas scriptural and inferential knowledge have universals as their objects. Therefore, the vision of the yogi born of *nirvitarka* (non-discursive) concentration is unmixed with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By this, the definition of this *nirvitarka* attainment is illuminated by the Sūtra: "When memory is purified, [the mind], as if empty of its own form, shines forth as the object alone; this is *nirvitarka*."

[104,14] When there is purification of conceptualization through memory regarding linguistic conventions, auditory knowledge, and inferential knowledge, that very conceptualization of linguistic convention, conceptualization of auditory knowledge, and conceptualization of inferential knowledge constitute memory. For it is by means of memory that the property of one thing is superimposed upon another; indeed, a real entity cannot be superimposed upon another real entity in its own essential nature. But how can what is heard or inferred be superimposed upon what is perceived? Is it not well known that superimposition occurs? Thus one perceives: "This was heard by me," "This was inferred by me," and "This [is seen]."
