[104,20] Is it not the case that the very same thing which is being perceived is also what was inferred and heard? No, because of the distinction between the universal and the particular. What is heard or inferred is the universal, whereas the particular is the object of perception; and the superimposition of that universal upon the latter is indeed well-established.

The wisdom (*prajñā*) of the yogi, colored by the object of apprehension (*grāhya*), thus abandons its nature as an act of grasping and becomes one whose very essence is the mere thing (*padārtha*), as if it had assumed the form of the object itself. By the word "as if" (*iva*), it is indicated that it does not abandon its nature as an act of grasping; for a crystal, when serving as a substrate for an adjunct (*upādhi*), does not lose its own transparent nature. Furthermore, it is thereby stated that the object of apprehension exists as a distinct entity separate from the act of grasping.

That is the attainment free from discursive thought (*nirvitarkā samāpatti*). And it has been explained thus: for its objective essence (*arthātmā*) is approached by a single cognition. That which is approached by a single cognition is "approached by a single cognition" (*ekabuddhyupakrama*), meaning it is delimited by a single cognition. "Objective essence" (*arthātmā*) means the essence of the object of awakening (*bodhyātma*).

The object is the cow and so forth, or the jar and so forth; it is not consciousness itself that has the form of a cow or the like as its object. That which consists of a specific aggregation of atoms—that is, whose nature is a particular accumulation of atoms composed of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—is the cow, the jar, or whatever serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) of cognition. And that object is a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*), for those subtle elements of the primary constituents (*bhūta-sūkṣma*) are indeed situated in such a manner.

This is what is meant: the common property of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is their very self-nature, not something separate from them, just as the expansion and coiling of a serpent are not distinct from the serpent itself.

Furthermore, for those who hold that the effect is something entirely distinct from the cause, it would follow that the effect lacks dependence upon the cause. For a thread is dependent on its own fibers, and cloth is dependent on threads; however, when there is absolute non-distinction, the dependence of one thing upon another is not observed, just as a lump of clay does not depend on threads, nor do threads depend on a lump of clay.
Furthermore, it is not possible for there to be a destruction following the destruction of that [cause], for a cloth does not perish following the destruction of its shards.

Now, it might be argued that the relation is the cause. For, in the case of a cloth, the threads are its constituents, and in the case of the threads, the filaments are their constituents; thus, the relation is there the cause, because [the existence and destruction of the whole] depend upon and follow the destruction of those [parts].

To this it is replied: the same undesirable consequence would apply even in the case of Caitra’s relation to his field and so forth; for, due to that specific relation, it would follow that the field and other such things are dependent upon Caitra and that they perish along with him.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) is the cause; however, because its status as a relation is no different [from other relations], it cannot be the cause. Just as other relations are not causes because they depend on one or both of the related entities (*saṃbandhin*), so too the relation characterized as inherence, being a relation, is likewise not a cause due to its dependence on one or both of the related entities.

Furthermore, since a relation must depend on one or both of the related entities, if this were the reason [for its existence], then inherence would require another inherence, and that too yet another, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Just as qualities and the like depend upon substance by virtue of their relation characterized as inherence, so too, if inherence were distinct from substance, another inherence would have to be postulated for the sake of its dependence on substance; and for that another, and for that another—thus there would be an infinite regress.

Because the effect does not exist prior to its production, a connection with the cause is logically untenable; moreover, the non-existence of a hare’s horn and that of a jar are indistinguishable. In that case, one must state the reason why the cause is connected specifically with the jar and not with things such as a hare’s horn.

[106,4] That which does not exist previously would arise like the horn of a rabbit. But that which is other than the threads does not arise from the threads, because it is other than the threads, just as a jar [does not arise] from the threads.

The other says: Even if it existed previously, it does not arise because it already exists, like a pot that is currently being perceived. That which is non-different from something else also does not arise from it because it is already present, just like its own essential nature.

Another says: If it is said that "what exists does not arise," then this would be stating the absence of arising for that which already exists, which would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). If, on the other hand, it refers to the absence of manifestation, then there is a lack of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*).

As for what is also said—that "whatever is non-different from something else [is that very thing]"—in that case too, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) and a lack of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*). For manifestation occurs precisely from its own nature; indeed, if the manifested nature does not exist, manifestation cannot be produced even by a thousand manifestors.

Furthermore, there would be the abolition of all worldly conventions (*sarvavyavahāralopa*). How so? Suppose Devadatta’s cow or horse, having its ears and tail intact in the morning, were to go again into the forest and have its ears or tail cut off by someone. In that case, because of the disjunction of its former parts, it would be considered destroyed; yet another new animal with its ears and tail cut off would arise as ownerless and could be taken up by anyone. Since such a disjunction of parts is possible everywhere, and because there would be no fixed rule regarding the relationship between property and owner, there would be the abolition of all worldly conventions. Now, one might say:

It is not the case that a new whole is produced from previously acquired parts such as a severed ear and tail; for we do not observe anyone now producing another distinct whole with a severed ear and tail apart from the mother, father, and so forth.

Furthermore, that [animal] whose ears and tail have been cut off in a certain field would belong to the owner of that very field, and not to the one who possessed its previous parts, just like the grass, leaves, and so forth produced in that field.

Just as seeds belonging to another field, having been carried by a flood of water onto one's own field, result in a crop that belongs exclusively to the owner of the field and not to the owner of the original seeds; and even though he is wise, he does not claim, "This crop has been produced from my seeds, so I shall take it," nor does he obstruct the other.

Likewise, even when the ears and fingers have been cut off, the owner of the field alone shall take possession; in that case, no objection should be raised on the grounds that "this whole has been produced from my own parts."

Even for those who hold that when one [part] is grasped—such as when a horse has had its ears and tail cut off, and it is seen in its own field—it would be the same horse-giver who might take it away, thinking, "This is another; this is not the very same great horse given by me. If he were to take it, there would follow the consequence of the collapse of worldly linguistic conventions (*satvavyavahāra*) and the contradiction of the treatises (*śāstra*). Therefore, it is established that the whole (*avayavī*), which is the effect, is distinct from its parts, which are the causes.

As for what is also said—that [the self] is "other" due to the distinctions of word, cognition, and attributes—that too has been answered. For even when there is a distinction of words and so forth, non-otherness is observed. For example, "hand," "arm," and "palm" are distinctions of words for one and the same thing; "fatherhood" and "sonship" are distinctions of cognition for one and the same person; and "bound," "then released," "standing," and "gone" are distinctions of time for the same entity. Likewise, "burning-ness" and "cooking-ness" are distinctions of attributes. As for distinctions of direction, location, and so forth, they are simply unproven. Therefore, he says: "being of the nature of the self."

And that [cause] is inferred by its own manifest effect—namely, the effect consisting of the carrying and holding of water, or the capacity for such actions. For when an effect, which is its product, is perceived as manifest, there is the certainty that "it exists. The term "inferred" is stated using a common word or in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) with respect to those who hold contrary views.

That very [entity], though imperceptible, is inferred even prior to its manifestation—namely, during the state of clay and so forth—as existing by means of its effect, the fruit called "jar," which is manifested through the operations of causal factors such as the staff, the string, and the potter; it becomes manifest when manifested by those very causal factors like the staff which serve as its revealers, and it disappears upon the arising of other properties. That same [entity], which is the property of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), is called the "composite whole" (*avayavin*).

This is what is meant: since atoms are imperceptible, their manifestation and disappearance are not tenable. Therefore, that which manifests upon the arising of a different property and disappears due to its contradiction with it—and which depends on manifestors and the like during its manifestation—is called a "whole" (*avayavin*). And that property which is thus characterized is distinct from the atoms.
Furthermore, these other reasons for the existence of the whole (*avayavin*)—namely, that it is one, large, minute, characterized by activity, and impermanent—are each individually reasons.

Furthermore, in the expression "one jar," there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because that which is denoted by the word "jar" is one; and this coreferentiality exists in the case of "that which is one. For it is not possible for many atoms to be established as having coreferentiality through oneness.

Likewise, it is not tenable for atoms (*aṇu*) that are not large to possess largeness as a common locus; similarly, it is not tenable for them to possess minuteness (*aṇīyastva*). For it is not possible for atoms to be minute in relation to other atoms, since they are all equally minute. Furthermore, minuteness is not perceived in atoms themselves; rather, minuteness would only be established in respect to another entity that is smaller than the atoms.
Furthermore, what is meant by "having the nature of activity" (*kriyādharmaka*)? That which has activity as its property is "that which has the nature of activity.

This means that it brings about the accomplishment of an operation that results in a fruit. For it is not logical that atoms should bring about the accomplishment of an operation resulting in a fruit, because they cannot be set in motion by people such as ourselves. Moreover, because of their impermanence; for the impermanence of atoms is not perceived.

Furthermore, because it is visible. For atoms are not visible; likewise, because they are tangible, and because there is abandoning, taking up, and supporting—such things as these. Therefore, worldly transactions are carried out by means of the whole (avayavin), and not by means of atoms.

Furthermore, for one who holds that the whole (*avayavin*)—which, though its existence is thus well-established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is actually a non-entity (*avastuka*) consisting of a particular accumulation—and whose subtle causes, such as atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth, are imperceptible, there arises false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) because it is not established upon the nature of those [causes], due to the absence of the whole. Thus, for such a person, object-cognition is generally attained as being nothing but false cognition.

[108,24] Consequently, every cognition arises with the form of sound and so forth, the form of pleasure and so forth, and the form of that [corresponding] cognition itself. Yet, sound and the rest—which are considered to be the parts that produce the form of the cognition—are not admitted [to exist as external objects]. Pleasure and the rest, too, because they are objects, belong strictly to the category of parts. Likewise, since that very cognition produces its own form, it follows that even its own nature is false; thus, all cognition whatsoever becomes false cognition.
Consequently, he has effectively admitted that even perception and inference are merely fallacious, because they too have sound as their object.

Even that omniscient knowledge which has as its object [the truths of] impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth—since even that lacks an objective referent, it too would result in being false knowledge. Consequently, the independent non-Buddhist teacher (tīrthakara) would lack authority, and therein the teacher’s absence of a valid dharma is admitted; for there is no distinction in their both being objects of valid cognition, just like sound and other such phenomena.

This demonstrates the following: could even correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) exist, given the absence of objects? For whatever is perceived is apprehended as a composite whole (*avayavin*); since there is no distinction in their capacity to impart their own forms (*svākāra*) to cognition, and since you do not admit the existence of any such entity that imparts its own form, it follows that all cognition of an object is rendered false by that [absence].
And likewise, what would right cognition be such that, in relation to it, false cognition is intended?
And when one denies the whole (avayavin), which is established by all valid means of cognition and by perfect omniscience, then it is impossible to establish the object of correct knowledge.

And when one does not perceive the further shore, how could one then conclude that "everything is false"? False cognition attains the state of falsity only in relation to right cognition, because right and false cognitions are relative to one another.

Furthermore, for one who considers that cognition which has no object is "correct," its existence is untenable because its own nature cannot be apprehended. If it is apprehended, then, by virtue of being an object, the whole (avayavin) must be false; and because that [whole] is false, the cognition of it is false, and likewise the cognition of that [cognition] as well—thus, the falsity of reality has already been stated previously.

Furthermore, if the correctness of knowledge consists in its being objectless, then since all knowledge would not admit of objects, it would follow that objectlessness itself constitutes correctness. Even so, one must explain what false knowledge could possibly be, given that all knowledge is correct.

Now, one might argue: "That which appears as if having an object is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), whereas that which is entirely without an object is correct [knowledge]. Even so, the fault already mentioned remains: there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its existence. Therefore, the whole (*avayavin*) must necessarily be accepted as the object of correct knowledge. Thus he says: "Therefore, the whole exists, which, having entered into common usage due to its magnitude, becomes the object of the non-discursive meditative attainment (*nirvitarkā samāpatti*). (1.43)

By this very [explanation], the subtle objects, both with and without discursive thought (*savicārā* and *nirvicārā*), have been explained. In that regard, among the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) which possess manifest properties and are delimited by the experience of place, time, and cause, there is the "sound delimited by place. For every object, being delimited by place and so forth and being connected by the knowing subject who possesses the capacity for cognition, becomes fit for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*).

When those [objects] are thus [perceived], that meditative attainment which is likewise constituted and directed toward conceptual constructions of place and so forth is called "with deliberation" (savicārā). Consequently, it is established that "with deliberation" is not distinct from "with discursive thought" (savitarkā).

[110,16] How so? Because here too there is no difference in superimposition (*adhyāsa*). However, this is the distinction: all superimpositions—of linguistic convention, the knowledge of objects, place, and so forth—occur in the stage accompanied by discursive thought (*savitarkā*).

Furthermore, in this case, because verbal conventions are not established regarding those subtle dharmas consisting of "that-only" (tanmātra), there is no superimposition of knowledge of specific names and conventions, nor is there superimposition of place and so forth; or rather, the object is subtle—thus is the non-distinction from *savitarka* established.

In that case as well, it is the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*)—which is apprehended by a single cognition and is distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, or distinguished by the aforementioned qualities of place and so forth, or distinguished by emergent qualities—that becomes the object of focus; it is not the case that cognition itself, being devoid of an object, presents itself in the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhiprajñā*).

Furthermore, when—in every way, in every manner, from every source, and everywhere—those phenomena which are quiescent (*śānta*), arisen (*udita*), and indescribable (*avyapadeśya*) are [present], they are the "quiescent, arisen, and indescribable phenomena. Within those that are not delimited by these: a phenomenon that has performed its activity and ceased is "quiescent"; one that has entered into activity is "arisen"; and one that is neither quiescent nor arisen, nor possessing a manifestly perceived characteristic, is "indescribable."

For example, gold possesses powers for the production of various unperceived and unheard-of forms; these are indeterminate properties (*dharma*). When the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*)—which follow after all things and are not delimited by those [powers]—are present, they follow after all things because they are the originators of all specificities (*viśeṣa*). Since the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are infinite with respect to all objects because they possess the nature of everything, the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) directed toward them is "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*).
Whatever characteristics belong to "without reasoning" (*nirvitarkā*) are all to be understood here as belonging to "without deliberation."

He demonstrates this: for that subtle element (bhūtasūkṣma), being of such a nature—characterized by this very essence which is devoid of distinctions such as place, time, and causal conditions, which is all-pervasive, and which conforms to all attributes—becomes the objective support (ālambana) that colors the wisdom (prajñā) of samādhi.

And when wisdom (prajñā) becomes empty of its own form and consists of the object alone, then it is "without deliberation" (nirvicārā). In that state, it is indistinguishable from "without conceptualization" (nirvitarkā). He shows this by himself: "having the Great Reality as its object. The compound *mahadvastu* means "the Great Reality" (*mahataḥ vastu mahadvastu*), just as in the case of *rāhuśiras* ("the head of Rāhu"). That which has this as its object is "having the Great Reality as its object"; thus, both the state with conceptualization (*savitarkā*) and without conceptualization (*nirvitarkā*), as well as the state with deliberation (*savicārā*) and without deliberation (*nirvicārā*), have subtle reality as their object.

By this very twofold attainment, known as "with discursive thought" (*savitarka*) and "without discursive thought" (*nirvitarka*), the twofold attainment of "with deliberation" (*savicāra*) and "without deliberation" (*nirvicāra*) is explained. Of these two—the "with discursive thought" and the "without discursive thought"—the elimination of discursive thought is explained by this very "without discursive thought" attainment, and the "without deliberation" attainment is likewise explained. By implication, the "with deliberation" attainment is explained by the "with discursive thought" attainment, because their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the same in both cases. And the distinction has been stated: ||1.44||

It has been stated that the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)—both with and without deliberation (*savicārā* and *nirvicārā*)—has a subtle object (*sūkṣmaviṣaya*). In connection with that, this is now considered: what is the "subtle object" that constitutes the final limit? And the state of having a subtle object culminates in the absence of any further mark (*aliṅgaparyavasāna*). For the atom of earth (*pārthivasyāṇoḥ*), which consists solely of the nature of smell alone, is a subtle object when compared with the earth as a whole.

Even for that which consists of the mere nature of smell and so forth, the subtle object is the *liṅgamātra*, the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*). From that Great Principle, the *tanmātras*—along with egoity (*ahaṅkāra*)—are produced; it is called *liṅga* because they go to dissolution (*laya*) therein, or because they return from the unmanifest (*pradhāna*) to the *liṅga*. Its opposite is the *aliṅga*, the Unmanifest (*pradhāna*), which neither goes to dissolution nor returns from any other state of dissolution. The subtle object of the *liṅgamātra* is the *aliṅga*.

And there is nothing subtler than the unmanifest (*aliṅga*). "Subtle" refers to a cause in relation to its gross effect, and that [causal series] culminates in the unmanifest. There is no other cause subtler than the unmanifest, which is the primary matter (*pradhāna*).

[Objection: "Is it not the case that [the question] 'Is it the Puruṣa? [is inappropriate]? [Response: Indeed, in that context, there is no suspicion whatsoever regarding the Puruṣa, because the discussion proceeds by way of the subtlety of cause and effect; thus, this is not a fault. For some indeed accept that the Puruṣa also possesses causality. It is precisely out of such suspicion that this is said: "Is it not the Puruṣa? This is true: the state of being without marks (aliṅga) is the subtlety of the unmanifest (aliṅga). Why? Because the unmanifest is the cause of the manifest (liṅga). That which is its inherent cause is, in relation to it, subtle—this is the subject under discussion.

[Objection: But surely the *puruṣa* is also essentially without *liṅga*. [Reply: This is not a refutation; however, the *puruṣa* is not subtle in relation to the *liṅga*. Why? Because even though the *puruṣa* is essentially without *liṅga*, he cannot be the pervasive cause (*anvayi-kāraṇa*) of the *liṅga*, since the effect is not connected with consciousness (*caitanya*). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the *puruṣa* himself would be an object of experience (*bhogya*). Consequently, the *pradhāna* (or the *puruṣa*) would be for the sake of another, would consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and would be without a cause. And this contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, he says: "But there is a cause."
The meaning is that it serves as the cause for the activity of the *pradhāna* by way of being the enjoyer. Therefore, the unsurpassed subtlety of the *pradhāna* has been explained. 1.45.

These very [four attainments] constitute seeded concentration (*sabīja-samādhi*). Since the four attainments have external objects as their domain, this "having external objects as their domain" is the reason for their being seeded. Concentration is also explained as "seeded" when it is accompanied by discernment (*samprajñāta*), because it follows the forms of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*); and it is further explained as "accompanied by discernment" according to the aphorism defining the characteristics of applied thought and the rest: "With respect to a gross object, it is with applied thought and without applied thought; with respect to a subtle object, it is with sustained thought and without sustained thought" (YS 1.42–44).

[113,19] When there is confidence (*vaiśāradya*) in the state free from deliberation (*nirvicāra*), there is internal clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*). For one who is freed from the impurity that is the obscuration—the very impurity which is the obscuration, namely the stain consisting of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth—there arises for the luminous *buddhi-sattva* a clear flow of stability, unoverpowered by *rajas* and *tamas*; this is confidence. When this confidence in the samādhi free from deliberation is produced, then for the yogin there occurs internal clarity, which is the discernment of knowledge regarding the self and other principles.

This is its very explanation: the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*)—wisdom itself being the light—is that which has the true nature of things as its object, conforms to the sequence, and follows the progression until the destruction of the afflictions; it is "conforming to the sequence" because it is clearly distinct, more refined, and purer in nature. By means of that, one knows things as they truly are.
And so it has been said: "Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man does not grieve for grieving people; standing on high ground, he looks down upon all those on the earth. (1.47)

[114,16] Therein lies the wisdom that bears the truth (*ṛtaṃbhara*). For one who is concentrated, when that light of wisdom—the internal clarity—has arisen, there arises a wisdom born of discrimination; this wisdom born of discrimination receives the name "bearing the truth. It is indeed literal: it bears only the truth, and therein not even a trace of erroneous cognition exists. For it arises for one whose stains of all error have been destroyed; and as it arises, it sweeps away the dust of the objects of sense.
And so it has been said:

"By means of scripture, by inference, and by the delight in the practice of meditation—cultivating wisdom in these three ways, one attains the supreme yoga. Thus, he divides the wisdom that constitutes the limbs of yoga into three parts: therein, one part follows the meaning of the subjects taught in the scriptures and traditional practices; the second is devoted to correctly establishing that very same subject by means of logical inference, preceded by the refutation of anything that contradicts the meaning of the scriptures; while the third, however, takes as its object the meaning correctly established through both authentic scripture and inference.
The cultivation of the causal condition is conducive to the attainment of the flavor [of liberation]. Thus, by practicing in these three ways, the yogi attains yoga. (1.48)

Furthermore, that *ṛtambharā* wisdom has an object other than the objects of the cognitions of ordinary persons; thus it is said: "It has an object other than the wisdoms of scripture (*śruta*) and inference (*anumāna*). Because particulars are infinite, they cannot be designated by convention; for a word is applied by means of a universal (*sāmānya*). Consequently, one who has not grasped the convention regarding a particular is unable to express or communicate that particular.

Likewise, inference has only the universal as its object. This too has already been stated: "The functioning [of the mind] is primarily characterized by the determination of the universal. This has also been demonstrated through an example: "Where there is attainment, there is movement; where there is no attainment, there is no movement. Thus, the application of the universal occurs through inference. It is only the universal that is applied by means of inference. Therefore, there is no particular whatsoever that is the object of the cognition derived from scripture or inference.

If it is argued that, in this way, no distinction residing in subtle elements or in the person would be perceived through worldly direct perception (*lokapratyakṣa*), and that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apart from the three [accepted] means by which we could cognize that distinction—[the author] replies: "There is no apprehension of this object, whether subtle, concealed, or remote, by means of worldly direct perception; nor is there an absence of this distinction simply because it lacks a [worldly] means of valid cognition."

For an entity exists and ascends to the royal highway only when its form is apprehended through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the specific distinction—whether pertaining to the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) or to the person (*puruṣa*)—is to be grasped solely by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

[116,13] But surely those subtle, specific features (*viśeṣa*) are apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is asked, "By what has this been made known? Are they apprehended because they are real entities (*vastu*"?), the answer is: they are indeed apprehended as existing through scripture (*āgama*) and inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule that they must be grasped by direct perception alone; for not all specific features, even those located on the palm of one's hand, are perceived, since the perceptibility of the specific features of other objects is itself something to be inferred.

How does he think thus? [He thinks that] the specific qualities derived from the subtle elements are perceivable by someone because they are specific qualities of an effect, like the specific qualities perceived in one's own hand. Therefore, that wisdom is of a different object than the wisdom arising from scripture and inference, because its object is the specific qualities; for its object is indeed the specific qualities. 1.49.

Upon the attainment of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), a new formation (*saṃskāra*) produced by wisdom arises for the yogin. For it is established that wisdom initiates formations; because wisdom is novel, its corresponding formation is known to be fresher—this is the distinction. Its possession of novelty, however, is due to its having a different object than others.

The impression produced by that [meditative state] is an impediment to other impressions; the impression arising from the wisdom born of the "season-bearing" (ṛtambhara) [intuition] obstructs and suppresses the latent tendency of the impressions of the emergent state, because it originates from a subject matter characterized by excellence. This storehouse of impressions persists until liberation.

[116,26] Because the latent impressions of emergence are overcome—that is, because the substrate of the latent impressions of emergence is overcome by the latent impressions of meditative concentration and wisdom—the conditions arising from them, namely those produced by the latent impressions of emergence, no longer occur. When conditions cease—meaning when the conditions for emergence cease—concentration becomes established as if it were "cognitive" (samprajñāta). From that, there arises wisdom born of concentration; from that, there arise latent impressions produced by wisdom. In this way, the new substrate of latent impressions increases. And from that, wisdom arises; and from that, latent impressions arise.

Regarding this, it is said: "The latent disposition of formative forces (*saṃskārāśaya*) arising from meditative concentration and wisdom is the cause for the mind’s engagement with its specific task, because it originates from conditions, just like the latent disposition of formative forces arising from emergence [from meditation]; and likewise, because it is a formative force of the mind. This shows how that latent disposition of formative forces will not fail to make the mind possessed of its task and endowed with formative forces.

This is not a fault, because it is contrary to that. How so? Those *saṃskāras* do not cause the mind to become oriented toward its specific objective (*adhikāra*) because they are causes for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*). For while *saṃskāras* arising from the conditions of emergence (*vyutthāna*) have as their cause the afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and thus function as the cause for the mind’s orientation toward *saṃskāras*, those *saṃskāras* born from the conditions produced by meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—because they arise from conditions contrary to those [afflictions]—do not serve as the cause for the mind’s orientation toward its objective.

Furthermore, they cause the mind to decline from its own activity—that is, they cause it to cease—from those functions directed toward the formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*). For the fluctuations of the mind culminate in manifestation (*khyāti*);
thus, it is a contradiction to say that the manifestation of the Puruṣa has arisen while the formative predispositions still persist.
For he whose accumulation of craving has departed does not thirst for water. This alone is what must be done by a person with the mind; for no one desires to do again what has already been done. 1.50

Moreover, upon the cessation of that as well, there is the seedless samādhi because of the cessation of everything. The word "iti" (thus) indicates completion. When there is the cessation of even that new *saṃskāra* produced from samādhi and wisdom—by the force of the word "api" (also), it implies the cessation of samādhi and wisdom which are the causes of that *saṃskāra*—there occurs the cessation of everything. Thus, the two means for its cessation have been stated: namely, the practice of the cause of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*) and supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*).

Furthermore, how is it that all those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by truth-bearing wisdom (*ṛtambharaprajñā*) bring about the cessation of the wisdom of meditative absorption (*samādhiprajñā*)? Just as that truth-bearing wisdom brings about the cessation of the wisdom of meditative absorption itself, so too does it become an obstruction to—and the cause of the cessation of—the latent impressions that are of the same nature as the self, which were produced by their own causes, namely, the wisdom [of the previous stage].
Through this cessation, [the yogin attains isolation].

Why is it that the formation born of cessation (*nirodhaja-saṃskāra*) exists? Because when the concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the formation produced by them cease, another formation—which is the "cessator" (*nirodhaka*)—arises, distinct from the formation produced by the concentration and wisdom.

Furthermore, because that [cessator] does not allow for the arising of anything that has not set aside the concentration, the wisdom, and the formations produced by them, therefore that formation born of cessation sublates the formations born of concentration.

How, then, is it understood that this formation born of cessation exists? Even while it is present, it acts as an obstacle; to this he says: "by experiencing the sequence of time in the duration of cessation. The duration of cessation is its time, and that time is experienced sequentially because it increases through repeated practice. Therefore, by that experience of the sequence of time in the duration of cessation, the existence of formations produced by the mind in the state of cessation—that is, produced by the mind in the state of cessation—is to be inferred.

[119,10] Through the latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) produced by the meditative absorption of emergence (*vyutthāna-samādhi*) and those produced by the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), together with the latent impressions conducive to isolation (*kaivalya-bhāgīya*), the mind—its task having been completed—dissolves and sets into its own source, the egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), which is its own nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, those latent impressions born from discriminative knowledge and cessation are opposed to the mind's functional mandate; they do not become causes for its continued persistence.

Because the mind, having completed its office along with the latent impressions conducive to isolation (*kaivalya*), ceases its activity for that person whose purpose has been fulfilled; when that [activity] has ceased, the person is said to be established in his own nature alone, solitary and liberated. Thus, liberation is simply the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. (1.51)

Thus ends the first chapter, the Samādhipāda, in the *Śrīpātañjalayogaśāstrasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇa*, the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, a disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda and a wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) of the supreme order (paramahaṃsa).

[121,10] Now, the second book, the Sādhanapāda, is commenced. Right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is the means for achieving isolation (*kaivalya*). Furthermore, the means of yoga are themselves the means for achieving right vision by way of yoga. Since these are primarily expounded in this book, it is called the Sādhanapāda.

Likewise, because it primarily expounds the incidental manifestations (*vibhūti*) for one engaged in the practice of the means of yoga (*yogasādhana*), the third is called the *Vibhūtipāda*. Similarly, because it primarily demonstrates isolation (*kaivalya*) by way of the withdrawal of all things for one who is dispassionate toward all the powers and manifestations of yoga, the fourth is called the *Kaivalyapāda*.
[121,15] Likewise, since concentration (samādhi) is to be attained primarily at the outset, this is called the first "limb of concentration" (samādhipāda).

This is what is stated: "Yoga has been taught for one whose mind is concentrated" means for one whose mind is fit for action (*karmaṇya*). For the yogin who has attained and remains established in the means such as the cultivation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*)—which is accomplished through the causal condition of cessation (*virāma-pratyaya*) and supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*)—has been taught. How might even one whose mind has emerged from meditation be joined with yoga? How indeed might even one whose mind is distracted become fit for concentration? It is for this reason that the following is commenced.

The means of practice, beginning with austerity, are now set forth: austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya), and devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) constitute the yoga of action (kriyā-yoga). But one might ask: since austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord will be mentioned among the observances (niyamas), for what purpose are they stated here?
But is it not precisely this the purpose that was stated: that even one whose mind has emerged from concentration may still be joined with yoga?
This is not the case; for wherever the restrictive rules (niyama) are recited, it is precisely there that this purpose is accomplished.

If it is argued that [the mention of austerity and so forth is] for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions (*kleśa*), that too has already been stated in that very same context, namely: "From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity. And impurity consists of the afflictions and the like. Furthermore, the practice of the limbs of yoga will indeed be taught for the purpose of meditative cultivation at the transition [to the next life], as in: "The perfection of tranquility and concentration arises from devotion to the Lord. Therefore, the enumeration of austerity and the rest here is redundant.

[122.7] This is because the purpose [of this section] is to demonstrate that the practice of the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), which is the means for right vision (*samyagdarśana*), is preceded by right vision. And all the limbs of yoga, being means to right vision, belong to the time prior to right vision. Furthermore, only a single portion of their restrictive rules (*niyama*) is recited here as an illustration of their belonging to the time prior to all means. Although their priority in time is established by implication from their very nature as means, it is nevertheless stated explicitly so that clarity may be achieved.

[122,11] But even so, should it not be stated that [the practice of austerities and so forth] is to be recited immediately after right vision? No; for right vision alone is the direct antidote to the afflictions and the like. Ignorance (*avidyā*), indeed, is the root of all misfortune, and it is eliminated directly by right vision, which stands as its opposite. If the practice of austerities and so forth were recited immediately after that, there would be an intervention between ignorance and right vision. Consequently, one might suspect: "Is the practice of austerities and so forth the direct antidote to ignorance, or is it right vision itself?"

Furthermore, the object of the treatise on right vision must first be presented; and that object is the person who is overwhelmed by afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its maturation (*vipāka*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*). Just as one afflicted by disease is the object of the science of medicine, if the subsequent enumeration of the "means" (*tapa*) and so forth were placed immediately after that, then the object and the subject would be separated, and it would not be clearly distinguished that "this is the object" and "this is the subject."

Furthermore, by reading it at the beginning of the [first] quarter, its status as a means to right vision (*samyagdarśana*) is established, and the connection with the first quarter would be explained; for while yoga has been taught for one whose mind is concentrated (*samāhita*), how could one whose mind is emergent (*vyutthita*) be joined to yoga through the practice of austerity (*tapas*) and other means?
Furthermore, it must be shown that austerity and the other practices serve the purpose of cultivating meditative concentration and attenuating the afflictions.

But will he not state later on: "The perfection of tranquility and concentration comes from devotion to the Lord" (YS 2.45), and "The perfection of the body and the senses comes from the destruction of impurity through austerity" (YS 2.43)? In this way, he will describe the perfection resulting from each individual means.

This is not the case for those who have already attained realization, because here there is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of praising the means; for it is stated here that they are for that very purpose. Thus he said: "They are for the sake of cultivating tranquility and meditative concentration, and for the sake of attenuating the afflictions" (YBh 2.2). For in that context, they are restated for the purpose of praising the means.

[123,10] Now the words of the Sūtra are being explained: austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*)—these are "austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord. These very things constitute *kriyāyoga*, which is yoga in the form of action. Furthermore, actions such as austerity are called "yoga" because they have yoga as their purpose. For yoga is concentration (*samādhi*), which is a property of the mind; this *kriyāyoga* has that [concentration] as its goal. Therefore, by means of this *kriyāyoga*, one is a "yogi."

Austerity (*tapas*) consists of practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, as well as endurance of the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of the *praṇava* and of the purifying scriptures of liberation, beginning with the *Upaniṣads*. Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of one's actions to the Supreme Teacher, the Lord; or it is the renunciation of their fruits by surrendering them to the Supreme Lord.

But how is it that asceticism (tapas), consisting of bodily mortification and so forth—which is remote from the concentration of the mind—is considered a "yoga," whereas self-study (svādhyāya) and devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) are rightly called "yoga" because they are internal? To address this point, he says: "Yoga is not accomplished for one who lacks austerity."

For one whose mind is intent on nourishing the body and so forth, who does not avoid physical and mental exhaustion, who perceives the body and so forth as being ultimately the self, and who considers himself extremely delicate, yoga is not accomplished; therefore, the undertaking of austerity is prescribed.

Furthermore, variegated by beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and fashioned into diverse states by the habitual tendencies of grasping objects since time without beginning, the mind—being like a fish—is caught by the net of present objects. This "net" consists of the very objects of the present; and because that mind, which has this present-object-net as its snare, meets with dissolution and destruction unless it is pierced by the heat of asceticism (*tapas*), it is therefore called "unawakened. Since she [the mind], while having the present objects as her net, undergoes such a fate, [asceticism is necessary].

"How can there be concentration for a mind that is unpurified and undifferentiated?"—it is for the sake of differentiating it that austerity (tapas) is undertaken. And the practitioners of yoga (yogins) maintain that this austerity should be practiced so as not to obstruct the internal factor of concentration, which is the clarification of the mind; for since the purpose of austerity is the clarification of the mind, if it were to obstruct that very clarity, its own purpose would be lost. (2.1)

Regarding the purpose for which that yoga of action exists, he says—in order to demonstrate its subservience to another end—that it is "for the sake of cultivating meditative concentration and for the attenuation of the afflictions."

[124,19] But how is there this twofold purpose? He says: for when practiced, it cultivates meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Accompanied by the other limbs of yoga, it cultivates meditative absorption and attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*). And he will say: "From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to the discriminative discernment" (*Yogasūtra* 2.28). This is what he means by saying "the attenuated afflictions."

By means of analytical meditation (*prasaṃkhyāna*), because the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been attenuated, and through the cultivation of right view (*samyagdarśana*), he will render them like burnt seeds—seeds whose power to sprout has been destroyed, and for that very reason, whose nature is no longer to produce. Those from which no production exists are "non-producers" (*aprasava*); being non-producers and possessing such a nature, they are "of a non-productive nature" (*aprasavadharmin*). (Or this should be understood as applying to all seeds and so forth. He will make them non-productive; he will deprive them of their power to produce.

Following the attenuation of those [afflictions], there arises a manifestation consisting merely of the distinction between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which is no longer touched by the afflictions; this wisdom, having fulfilled its purpose, will lead to withdrawal and will no longer be conducive to facing toward *saṃsāra*.

[125,10] Even though the mere discernment of the difference between the sattva and the puruṣa arises through the instruction of the scriptures and teachers even without the practice of the limbs of yoga, nevertheless, that discernment does not arise having completely overwhelmed the afflictions, demerit, and so forth; thus, it is repeatedly assailed by the afflictions and the rest.
This is what is shown by the phrase "not again assailed by the afflictions" (punaḥ kleśair aparāmṛṣṭā). [Yoga Sūtra 2.2]

[125,14] What are these afflictions (*kleśa*) in their essential nature, or how many are they in number? To establish their number and essential nature, the following aphorism (*sūtra*) is formulated: "Ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and clinging to existence (*abhiniveśa*) are the afflictions. Since the definition of each one of these will be explained by the aphorisms themselves, no further effort is made here regarding that which is to be explained; for that which is to be explained is only this much.

Just as valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, and so forth are mutually distinct, there is no such distinction among the afflictions from error; rather, these are simply divisions of error itself. Why? Because they arise only when error exists. This is what is meant by the statement, "there are five errors."

[125,21] But surely, just as in the explanation of the divisions of mental functioning (*vṛtti*), the threefold division of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—namely, perception, inference, and verbal testimony—was explained right there, why was the fivefold division of this misconception (*viparyaya*) not also explained in that very same place? For it has been stated that misconception is indeed a modification of the mind (*cittavṛtti*). And thus it was illustrated: "The vision of two moons is sublated by the vision of a single moon regarding the object of the senses."
This is not a fault, because the afflictions (*kleśa*) do not constitute a functioning state. For the afflictions are not merely conditions;

rather, it is the functions that are merely conditions. The afflictions, however, are a stain upon the mind, just as cataracts are a stain upon the eye. When the mind is separated from the stain of the afflictions, there is an absence of the conditions for erroneous cognition.

For if the cognitive condition (*pratyaya*) itself were the error, then just as the yogin possesses cognitive conditions based on memory and valid cognition even when afflictions have ceased, so too would there be error; yet there is no error for those whose afflictions are exhausted. Therefore, error is said to be the impurity of the cognitive condition, which is the cause of apprehending things incorrectly, just like a defect in the eye.

Furthermore, since that [nature of the afflictions] cannot be understood or expressed apart from its conditions (*pratyaya*), it is expressed by means of those very conditions as "the functioning of perversion. Likewise, the functions (*vṛtti*) are specified as "afflicted and unafflicted," being distinguished by the term "affliction" (*kleśa*). Nor is it logical that the mere state of being a function should itself be the qualification of the functions. Similarly, they are explained as "having affliction as their cause"; yet it is not logical that the functions themselves should have the functions as their cause.

And because they do not function as such, the afflictions (*kleśa*) have not been explained there as being a specific type of mental modification (*vṛttibheda*). Thus it has been said: "They will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind. This is with the intention that the afflictions do not possess the status of a mental modification, but rather the status of an impurity (*mala*) alone. However, through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of non-difference, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by means of the term "cognition" (*pratyaya*), just as smoke [indicates] fire, or as the embryo exists within the womb; so too is it here.

[126,21] He states their contrariety to conditions with the words "those which are vibrating," and so forth. "Vibrating" means appearing by way of conditions; for they have no movement of their own, like the dyeing of cloth and other such things. They "strengthen the authority of the qualities" (*guṇa-adhikāram*), meaning they solidify the activity (*pravṛtti*) and the state of being that which is to be performed (*kartavyatva*) of the qualities. For when those [qualities] are vibrating, the mind does not become devoid of that which is to be performed.

They establish transformation, meaning they cause it to transform again and again. They elevate the stream of causal activity and sustain the stream of the functioning of the body’s instruments, such as the eyes and other sense organs. To the question "How so?", he says:
"By becoming mutually dependent through the relationship of cause and effect among ignorance and the other factors."
Furthermore, they bring about the results of karma; karma is threefold, and its results consist of birth, lifespan, and experience. (2.3)

Ignorance is the field for the subsequent [afflictions]—whether dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active. How is it that egoism and the others are misconceptions? This is demonstrated by the Sūtra itself: Ignorance is the field, the ground of production, the field for the acquisition of their own nature; just as the earth is the field for grasses, creepers, shrubs, and climbing plants which are not distinct from its own self, so too ignorance is the ground of production for the four misconceptions beginning with egoism, which are not separate from it, and which are each fourfold according to whether they are dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active. Thus, ignorance is the field of production for these four types of misconceptions.
For the misconceptions, depending upon that [intellect], acquire their own nature; therefore, the intellect itself undergoes transformation into the fourfold form consisting of egoism and the rest.

In this regard, what is meant by "dormancy"? Dormancy is said to be a state belonging to egoism (*asmitā*) and the other [afflictions], but not to ignorance (*avidyā*). This is because ignorance is the cause [of all afflictions]. Since it persists through all the various modifications of egoism and the rest, it is always awakened and never dormant; for there is no absence of its activity even in sleep. When any one of egoism and the others is dormant, at least one of them must necessarily remain present; otherwise, the emergence of another affliction would simply not occur. Therefore, only the four beginning with egoism possess the fourfold states, such as dormancy.

He provides the explanation of the phrase "establishment as mere potentiality in the mind" by saying "attaining the state of being a seed. Just as a seed, although not yet sprouting, remains within the earth while still existing, so too do egoism (*asmitā*) and the other afflictions abide in the mind in the form of potentiality, their nature as sprouts remaining unmanifest.

"Awakening of that" means the awakening—that is, the emergence—of those afflictions such as *asmitā* (egoism) and so forth; it is their manifestation toward an object of perception (*ālambana*), which is the domain of their own manifesting cause.

In this regard, it might be thought that the state of being a seed and the awakening of the affliction (kleśa) would necessarily occur at all times. To this he replies: For the yogin who possesses discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), who practices right vision (*samyagdarśana*), and whose seeds of affliction have not yet been burnt, even when an object of perception (*ālambana*) is present, there is no such attainment of the state of being a seed. Because it has been burnt, how could there be an awakening or a resurgence?

For while a seed that exists may sprout upon obtaining the causal conditions such as the union of earth and water, this is not the case for the power of a burnt seed; the same applies to the affliction.

[128,15] If this is so, why is this fifth state not mentioned among those that are "burnt, dormant, attenuated, interrupted, and extensive"? It is because it is not common to all; for this fifth state of affliction is not common to all embodied beings. Indeed, it belongs only to the yogin; therefore, it is not recorded by name [among the general states].

Or how is it uncommon? To this he says: in that very state, she (Ignorance) is burnt only by one who possesses the practice of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), and not elsewhere. One whose afflictions are exhausted, who is virtuous, and for whom this is the final body—such a person is called a yogi possessing right vision. Only in that state is she burnt, her seed-nature destroyed.

The fifth stage is that of the afflictions (*kleśa*). At that time, the capacity of the seeds of those existing afflictions is destroyed, just as the seed-capacity of existing barley and other seeds is burnt when they are parched. Even when an object is present before them, there is no awakening of these [afflictions] for one who possesses right vision (*samyagdarśin*), because they exist merely as residual impressions (*saṃskāra-śeṣa*), like an arrow that has already passed its mark.

[128,24] Dormancy has been explained. Furthermore, it was stated that for the yogin, there is no awakening of the afflictions (*kleśa*) which are like burnt seeds. Now, attenuation is being discussed: the afflictions are called "attenuated" when they have been struck down by the cultivation of the antidote—that is, when they have been weakened and rendered of feeble power through the cultivation of the antidote, such as the perception of the defects in the body and so forth.

Likewise, having been interrupted again and again during the intervals between the arising of other objects, they do not manifest their own nature; rather, they proceed by that very same nature and re-emerge in the form in which they were previously perceived—thus they are "interrupted."

Or else, having been interrupted again and again, at the time of interruption they do not manifest with their distinct nature—that is, with their own essential form—as they did in the preceding and succeeding moments.

In this regard, the illustration is as follows: how is it that at the time of passion (*rāga*), anger (*krodha*) is not observed? For indeed, at the time of passion, anger does not manifest. Why? Because of the mutual opposition between the intensifications of their respective modes of activity (*vṛtti*). For that [anger], having been obscured by the arising of passion, persists in another unmanifest form; thus, it is interrupted.

Likewise, passion (*rāga*) being observed in one instance does not mean it is absent in another object. Why? Because in this case there is no contradiction with the object, whereas in the previous case there was a non-manifestation of anger due to its contradiction with passion. Here, however, it is because objects are mutually contradictory. For an object that produces passion in one instance is not necessarily the producer of that same passion in another object.

For example, when Caitra is attached to one woman, he is not thereby detached from others. Rather, in that case, passion has attained its manifestation (*labdhavṛtti*) toward the woman to whom he is attached; whereas toward other women, it possesses a future manifestation (*bhaviṣyadvṛtti*). For that specific future manifestation of passion is then either dormant (*prasupta*) or attenuated (*tanu*) with respect to those other women.

[129,19] But as for the commentary beginning with "Is it not the case that passion (*rāga*) is observed in some instances?"—for what purpose is this? Is it not an explanation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of passion? [The opponent replies: True, it explains how passion acquires its future functional nature through the distinction of objects; nevertheless, it is of no use to the present context. For what has been introduced here is an explanation of disjunction (*viccheda*), and this is not an explanation of disjunction. Nor does it have a connection with the forthcoming extensive explanation, because that [extensive explanation] is self-contained (*nirākāṅkṣa*).
If that is so, then this is merely a continuation of what preceded. How can one think thus?

Apart from being dormant (*prasupta*), attenuated (*tanu*), or extensive (*udāra*), there is no such thing as a distinct state called "interruption" (*vicchitti*) as a separate quality. How so? It is said that as long as it has not yet attained its functional activity (*labdhavṛtti*), it is "dormant. When its activity is weakened by the cultivation of the counter-measures (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), it is called "attenuated."

Furthermore, that which has attained its activity is called "exalted. That which is termed "interrupted" is that which, having been perceived in one place, is perceived again; such as the stream of the Sarasvatī river. For anger is never seen to arise when passion is present. Therefore, there is no such thing as an eternal property called "interruption," because it is not observed.

To this it is replied: If there is no cessation [of passion] due to its non-perception, then let there be an absence of passion when it is seen in one place but not perceived elsewhere. But surely, let there indeed be an absence because of its non-perception elsewhere? No, indeed. Why? Precisely because it is seen in some place. For just because it is not directed toward another object does not mean it is absent from the mind, which is the locus (*dharmin*) of that passion. For just because the eye is at some time not directed toward an elephant does not mean that, while engaged with a jar, it is non-existent.
Simply because it is seen facing a jar; this is what he says: "In some cases, being seen, [the cognition] does not exist in another object," and so forth.

In the same way, anger also, being overwhelmed by an arisen passion, will have its manifestation interrupted, just like the current of the Sarasvatī river. For it is either dormant or attenuated with respect to another object, because its specific characteristics are not perceived when directed toward that other object.

What, then, is the distinction between dormancy (*prasupti*) and interruption (*viccheda*), given that non-perception (*adarśana*) is indistinguishable in both cases? It is said: because the continuity of the manifestation of activity is bound by something internal that does not oppose it, non-perception is "interruption" (*vicchitti*) for that which has not been burnt away.

But surely, this being the case, it is contradictory to say that at that time [the passion] is either dormant (*prasupta*) or attenuated (*tanu*), for the non-occurrence of its activity is observed due to another object, since what is intended is the state of being directed toward another object. That which is called "being directed toward another object" is indeed a property (*dharma*) of passion; it is that which is then dormant or attenuated. It is not that passion itself is never perceived by its own nature; rather, at the time of passion, it is not perceived with respect to all objects.

Alternatively, the commentary beginning with "And attachment in some cases" (*rāgaś ca kvacid*) is intended precisely to demonstrate another example of interruption. How will you show that there are two kinds of interruption? First, there is the non-perception [of a cause] everywhere due to its being overcome by an adversary when the continuity of its manifestation has already begun; as has been shown, for instance, by the non-perception of aversion at the time of attachment.

[130,27] Likewise, this is another case where, although a particular object is being perceived, there is a non-perception of that which serves as the cause for its attainment in another object. For example, just as Caitra, though attached to one woman, does not manifest attachment toward other women even though they exist—therein, that which has attained its functional state in one place is not seen elsewhere—it is said that "it is either dormant (*prasupta*) or attenuated (*tanu*). However, neither dormancy nor attenuation is what is intended to be expressed; rather, let it be either way, what is intended by the non-perception in that context is its interruption (*viccheda*).

That which has attained its functional activity (*vṛtti*) with respect to its object is "intense" (*udāra*). But is it not the case that those [afflictions] which are dormant (*prasupta*), attenuated (*tanu*), or interrupted (*vicchinna*)—being incapable of producing an effect—are not truly afflictions? For one who is dormant, attenuated, or interrupted is not capable of performing an action during the state of dormancy, attenuation, or interruption. Indeed, an unborn enemy is not capable of inflicting harm; nor can one bathe in a stream at a place where the flow has been interrupted. Therefore, let it suffice to say simply that "ignorance (*avidyā*) is the field for the subsequent [afflictions]. What is the point of teaching those [afflictions] that are incapable of action—namely, the dormant, the attenuated, and the interrupted?
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And all these do not transcend the domain of the afflictions (kleśa). For an enemy, whether asleep or yet to be born, will not fail to cause harm."

[131,19] What then is a defilement that is interrupted, dormant, subtle, or gross? Such a statement in terms of these distinctions is not appropriate; let there be only one example. Furthermore, it will not perform its function in any state other than the gross one.

[131,21] This is indeed true; nevertheless, a rebuttal is stated: however, it is only for these [seeds] that possess the specific cause consisting in the non-abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) as previously described that there is the state of being interrupted and so forth. Even in the state of being interrupted and so forth, they do not lose their capacity to act as the producer of emergence; thus, there is no fault.

If it is argued that [the opponent's capacity] is at that time incapable of producing its effect, we say no; for the purpose of the statement is to prescribe an antidote. Indeed, one must not fail to counteract an enemy simply because he is invisible, asleep, or yet to be born.

It is also heard that Indra split the womb of Diti by means of his adversary; he himself reveals the reason for this: just as there is cessation through the cultivation of an adversary, so too is it manifested by its own manifesting agent, such as the sense objects and so forth.

Since they manifest again, become concealed again, and will manifest once more, therefore even the states such as "flowing forth" (prasuta) must indeed be described for the purpose of establishing their antidotes, because they do not transcend the nature of affliction (*kleśa*).

[132,12] Now he concludes: All these afflictions are indeed varieties of ignorance. Why? Because in all [afflictions] such as the sense of "I" (asmitā) and the rest, ignorance alone is seen to overflow, to spread, and to arise.

Furthermore, whatever entity is produced and conceptualized by ignorance (*avidyā*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth adhere to it and arise with that as their object. For example, even though a physical aggregate such as a woman is something to be abandoned, one conceives through ignorance the notion "this is an object of enjoyment," forms the conceit of a self, and becomes attached. Likewise, having falsely conceptualized the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), one feels aversion.

How, then, do these very [afflictions] lie latent? Because they are perceived precisely at the time when the conditions for error exist. Furthermore, there is a distinction among the forms of ignorance (avidyā), because the afflictions perish following the destruction of ignorance. For the afflictions, such as egoism (asmitā) and the rest, perish along with the destruction of ignorance; indeed, no affliction whatsoever can exist in the absence of ignorance. (2.4)

In this regard, he states the essential nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). What, then, is the purpose of explaining the essential nature of ignorance? The author of the commentary himself will explain this by saying, "Ignorance is the root of this continuum of afflictions," and so forth. Since it is impossible to uproot that which is based upon it when the essential nature of the root of the continuum of afflictions is unknown, its essential nature is now explained.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, suffering, and non-self. How is there the perception of permanence in an impermanent effect? It is the cognitive distortion (*viparyayabuddhi*) that thinks "it is permanent," such as: "The earth is eternal; the moon and stars are eternal; the heavens are immortal."

[133,12] But surely, from this mantra, the permanence (*dhruvatva*) of the earth and the other elements is understood. In that case, how can their being effects (*kāryatva*) be asserted? There is no fault here, because it is relative. Relative to humans and so forth, the earth and the others are permanent. However, their being effects and their impermanence (*anityatva*) are established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as proven by statements in the Vedas such as, "At first there was neither heaven nor earth, nor the intermediate space," and so on.

[133,16] Likewise, regarding this body—which is impure, a most contemptible vessel for seeds, a source of supreme agitation, an absolute object of loathing, and as impure as a heap of excrement—how can it not be considered disgusting? To this he says: it is impure because of its carriage; it is impure because of its location in the womb; it is impure because of its seed, for the body has semen and blood as its seed; and it is impure because of its support, namely, the support provided by wind, bile, and phlegm. And their impurity is as follows:

It is well known: from "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), meaning from the outflow of impurities such as sweat, urine, feces, and so forth; and also from "deposition" (*nidhāna*), meaning from death. For those related to the deceased, there is the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of impurity (*āśauca*) lasting ten days and so on.

[133,22] But surely, if the body is impure by its very nature, then the prescription for its purification would be rendered useless; therefore, he says: "because purity must be applied to the body. This means that purity must indeed be established in it through scriptural authority, for it does not exist there inherently.

Alternatively, because the instruments—the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—are pure by virtue of their *sattva* nature, they are to be placed within it; therefore, due to its purity, this [purification] also belongs to it. This is because one perceives extreme impurity when there is a separation from the objects to be placed, such as the *sattva* of the intellect.

Therefore, the wise know that a composite mass is indeed impure. The mention of "grasping at a composite mass" is for the purpose of demonstrating the grasping at purity by those whose intellects are perverted. For those with inverted minds, the appearance of purity is seen in what is impure.

[134,12] Is it not indeed so? This lovely girl is like one fashioned from the limbs of nectar; she appears as if she has emerged after piercing the moon. With eyes like the petals of a blue lotus, she seems to comfort the world of the living with her two glances pregnant with emotion. What connection can there be between this and what? Where is the true nature of the body and such things, and where is this notion of purity regarding that which is thus impure? It is merely a perversion of purity in relation to the impure.

By this, the notion of merit regarding what is non-meritorious—such as that held by those who seek liberation from cyclic existence—is explained; likewise, the notion of benefit regarding what is harmful is explained, such as that held by thieves.

Likewise, I shall explain the perception of happiness in what is actually suffering: "To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of transformation, pain, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the modifications of the guṇas. In this context, the perception of happiness within the entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), which is in fact suffering, is ignorance (avidyā).

Likewise, the manifestation of the self in what is not-self occurs in external instruments—whether sentient or insentient, such as cattle, water-jars, and so forth; or in the body, which is the locus of experience; or in the mind, which is an instrument of the person. Thus, it is the manifestation of the self in that which is not-self.

To this it is replied: "But whose mental state is it that consists in the manifestation of a self within what is non-self? Is it not the very mind itself that manifests? Why is this questioned, since it has been stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a cognitive fluctuation (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of error? It is the mind alone—which, by virtue of having assumed the form of the apprehension of consciousness—that conceives of itself as the conscious Self, thinking "I am the seer," "I am the hearer," and so forth, without distinction, thinking "this is mine."
In this regard, concerning this very point, it has been stated here whether it be manifest or unmanifest.

Whatever manifest reality—from primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, including the body, the senses, and everything down to specific objects—be it perceptible, inferable, or known through scripture, or even the unmanifest *sattva*, if one regards that as the self, accepts it as such, and rejoices in its prosperity; if one exults in the success, the abundance, and the manifestation of that which has been understood as the self in its manifest and unmanifest forms, thinking "I am enriched by this prosperity" and "this prosperity is mine," [then one is bound].

Thinking thus, he grieves over the misfortune and the destruction of that [other], thinking, "This is my misfortune; it is I myself. All such conceits are indeed the lack of awakening of the ignorant one.

This ignorance consists of four factors. Now, one might object that since there is the perception of merit in what is non-meritorious and the perception of non-merit in what is meritorious, there should be six factors rather than four; however, this is not so, because these two are included within the four as appropriate. Ignorance is the root and the seed of production for this continuum of afflictions—the incessant operation of the afflictions beginning with dogmatic adherence.

Furthermore, it is the cause of the entire cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), including the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) of three kinds, together with its threefold maturation (*vipāka*) characterized by birth, lifespan, and experience. This is the meaning.

And regarding that ignorance, its reality as a distinct entity and its reality as a separate thing from the object should be understood, like the cases of an enemy or a cow’s footprint. Why is this stated? For, since it is called "misapprehension," its reality as a distinct entity has already been established.

This is the intended meaning: "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), specifically a *tatpuruṣa*. And that [compound] would either be one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant, as in "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*); or else it would be one in which the meaning of the prior member is predominant, as in "half-a-pepper" (*ardhapiṣpalī*).

In that case, if the first member of the compound were predominant, then there would be an absence of valid cognition (*vidyā*). Consequently, wherever there is an occurrence of *vidyā*—due to its commonality of function—it would be understood as occurring in other functions such as memory (*smṛti*) and so forth; thus, the object would be perceived as having an undetermined particularity. As for that which was previously called "ignorance" (*avidyā*), namely the perception of things in a contrary manner (*viparītakhyāti*), that would be merely a technical designation (*pāribhāṣikī*).

[136,7] What fault would there be in this? There might be doubt upon hearing the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Is the meaning of the word merely that which is already well-known, designated for the sake of technical usage in the treatise—just as it is said in the *Śābarabhāṣya* (1.1.1): "One should understand that those words which are well-known in common usage for certain meanings are to be understood in the Sūtras as having those very same meanings, provided it is possible"? Or is it something other than the well-known meaning, as in the case of the rule "guṇa and vṛddhi substitute for *ik*" (Pāṇini 1.1.3)? Consequently, if the meaning of the term were not determined, no technical usage could be made with the word "ignorance."

[136,12] Now, because of their grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatva*), the predominance belongs to the meaning of the latter member, as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). In that instance as well, since there is no contradiction between the referents of the words "blue" and "lotus," a relationship by way of the qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa*) relation is appropriate.

[16,14] Here, negation is expressed by the particle *nañ*. The word "knowledge" (*vidyā*) also denotes knowledge. In that case, if the negative particle were subordinate to the primary meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), it would effect the non-existence of that very subsequent member; in that event, its status as a subordinate element would be lost, and the primacy of the other [the subsequent member] would not be established either.

For when someone who has set out to produce something should instead destroy that very thing to be produced, he possesses no quality (*guṇatva*) with respect to what was to be produced, nor does that which was to be produced possess primacy (*pradhānatā*). Likewise, a subordinate element (*guṇa*) must be subject to the principal element (*pradhāna*). Therefore, since there is an absolute absence of anything subsequent to knowledge (*vidyā*), the negative particle (*nañ*) alone would be a mere restatement of the eternal; thus, only knowledge itself would be understood.

Having established it in this way, it is said: "And its reality as a substantial entity should be understood to be like that of a non-friend (*amitra*) or a non-cow’s footprint (*agoṣpada*).
