Just as a "non-friend" (*amitra*) is not the mere absence of a friend, and just as in the case where the meaning of the first member of the compound is predominant, as in *ardhapippalī* (half-a-pear), it is not merely the absence of a friend; so too, as it has been stated regarding the predominance of the meaning of the second member, there must be a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) that functions under the influence of the principal element (*pradhāna*). It is not [merely the absence].

"By the destruction of the principal [element]"—and thus it has been stated in the *Nañ-vārttika*: "When it is said, 'Bring a non-Brahmin,' it follows that any Brahmin whatsoever should be brought, because under the view that the meaning of the final member is predominant, the negative particle (*nañ*) is merely a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*). The same applies to the term *amitra*, and likewise to *avidyā* and so forth.

Or, for example, "not a cow’s footprint" (*agoṣpada*) is neither the absence of a cow’s footprint nor merely a cow’s footprint; rather, it is a distinct entity, a specific location, that is different from both that absence and that mere footprint. [How can this be so? Since it is heard as being merely a cow’s footprint and its absence, it is said: precisely because of the force of the linguistic usage (*prayoga*), there is the cognition of the meaning of an absolute non-cow’s footprint.

[137,11] How, first of all, is the meaning of the negative particle (nañ) one that is opposed to existence, such that when it is employed together with something else, it expresses the non-existence of that thing?

[137,12] Consequently, regarding the expression "not a cow's footprint" (*agoṣpada*), three meanings appear: an object that is the locus of a cow's footprint, something merely the size of a cow's footprint, and something contrary to a cow's footprint. Among these, if it were merely the size of a cow's footprint, then the employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) would be entirely purposeless. If, on the other hand, the negative particle applied to "cow's footprint" were intended as a restatement of the absence of something else, even so, it would still be entirely purposeless.

[137,15] Now, even if it were connected with the sense of "cow's footprint," it would still not apply to the primary meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), because the state of being "never frequented by cows" has not been expressed. For if there were a state of having been frequented, the use of the word would be appropriate even for the three times (past, present, and future). And that is called the primary meaning where [the place] was not frequented by cows in the past, is not being frequented now, nor will it be frequented in the future.

Therefore, when possible, it is logical that the meaning of the negative particle is precisely that; thus, neither the mere possibility of being frequented nor the mere fact of being frequented is intended. By the word *agoṣpada*, a place that is the very opposite of being frequented by cows is denoted.

[137,21] But how can there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified, as in the case of a "blue lotus," given the contradiction between existence and non-existence in a single entity? For if one merely establishes its non-existence, conventional discourse would become impossible; rather, when the non-existence of something is asserted regarding a particular object, that very thing is understood as a distinct entity. As it has been said: "The footprint of a cow [is used] as a measure for what is frequented and what is not frequented."

[137,24] Furthermore, if the term *asevita* is understood here as a gerund (*kriyā*), this compound is to be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi*: "that which has not been cultivated is 'uncultivated' (*asevita*). Therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) is neither a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) nor an absence of a valid means of knowledge; rather, it is a different kind of cognition that is contrary [to reality]. || 2.5 ||

[137,27] *Asmitā* (the sense of "I-am-ness") is the apparent identity between the power of seeing and the power of vision. Now, he explains the misconception (*viparyaya*) called *asmitā*. "Seeing" (*dṛk*) is perception; it is the *puruṣa*, and that alone is the power (*śakti*). "Vision" (*darśana*) is that by which one sees; it is the power consisting of the determinative nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The "apparent identity" (*ekātmatā*) of these two powers—seeing and vision, whose natures are perception and determination—is as if they were one. It is a single self (*ātman*), like a wave surging upon the great ocean of bliss; the state of being that is "oneness of self" (*ekātmatā*).
By the word "iva" (as if), he expresses absolute distinction; the affliction called asmitā is said to be like the attainment of a single nature.
That notion of "I" in which the distinction between the mind and the person is not perceived is this very notion of "I," called the affliction known as *asmitā*.

In the previous case, however, it was stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is simply a perverted vision (*viparītadarśana*), consisting in the manifestation of the self (*ātman*) in what is not the self—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is an instrument of the person (*puruṣa*). Here, by contrast, the distinction is that *asmitā* is the vision of non-difference between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person, appearing as if they have attained a single nature.

This is what is meant: when there is, as it were, a state of non-differentiation between the power of the enjoyer and the power of the object of enjoyment—which are in fact utterly distinct and utterly unmixed—then experience (bhoga) is conceived. The meaning is that the affliction called *asmitā* (the sense of "I-am-ness") is the cause of experience. For when the notion "I" exists, there occurs a connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth, such that one thinks, "I am happy" or "I am miserable. Therefore, it is thus.

But when there is the attainment of their own true nature—that is, when, through their distinction, the realization of the true nature of both intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*) occurs as "I am not" and "there is nothing mine"—then isolation (*kaivalya*), which is indeed non-mixture, comes to pass. How could there be experience? For while the cause exists—namely, the notion of "I" which is undifferentiated—the effect, experience, exists; when that cause is absent, there is no experience. Indeed, it is not possible to perceive happiness or suffering in the mind without superimposing consciousness upon it.

For the "I" is the object of the notion [of ego], being the substratum for the notions of pleasure and pain; this is because of the grammatical coreferentiality [expressed] in such statements as "I am happy" and "I am miserable. Therefore, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), known as "I-am-ness" (asmitā), is the cause of experience.

And so it has been said: "The Puruṣa is distinct from the intellect; he is distinguished from the intellect as being separate and of a different character. By what qualities is this distinction made? He says: by form (ākāra), character (śīla), and knowledge (vidyā). By form, that is, by the nature of its functioning (vṛttyārūpya); by character, that is, by being experienced through the intellect; and by knowledge, that is, by having consciousness as its essential nature (caitanya-svarūpatā). Alternatively, by form, insofar as its essential nature is pure and infinite; by character, because of its unchangeability and lack of transition; and by knowledge, because its essential nature is the power of consciousness (citi-śakti). Thus, by these attributes, there is a distinction from the intellect.

Likewise, the distinction of the intellect (*buddhi*) from the Person (*puruṣa*) is by way of its form—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion; by way of its nature—consisting of determination, activity, and stability; and by way of knowledge (*vidyā*), which consists of the ascertainment of all objects. Thus, not seeing the Person as distinguished from the intellect by these mutually distinct forms, characteristics, and natures, the world, through delusion, forms the notion of self and the conviction of "I" with respect to that intellect. This illustration refers to this aspect: that there is, as it were, a non-distinction between the intellect and the Person, though they are absolutely distinguished by their natures of knowledge and determination.

As for the statement that "one might act while not seeing [the distinction], thereby forming the notion of self [with respect to the mind]," that is precisely the aforementioned ignorance (*avidyā*). Alternatively, since "not-seeing" (*asmitā*) is a specific variety of ignorance, every example applies. "One might act while not seeing" refers to the non-perception of the true nature of the Puruṣa; this is the cause and reason for ignorance and for "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*), namely, the mind's being colored by both the seer and the seen. However, the non-perception of the Puruṣa occurs precisely because he is the Seer. (2.6)

Attachment (*rāga*) is that which arises following pleasure and lies latent within pleasure. "Arising following" (*anu-janman*) means its production (*utpatti*). Others read the text as "lying latent within pleasure" (*sukhānuśayī*) and likewise "lying latent within suffering" (*duḥkhānuśayī*). They explain: attachment is that which lies latent within pleasure, and aversion (*dveṣa*) is that which lies latent within suffering. Their nature is such that they have the habit (*śīla*) of experiencing pleasure; thus it is "that which lies latent within pleasure," and similarly for "that which lies latent within suffering. In both cases, it is precisely by way of arising following [pleasure or pain] that this habit is established. And so he will say later: "From dharma comes pleasure; from pleasure, attachment."

How is it that pleasure has a latent tendency (*anuśaya*)? To this he says: "For one who possesses higher knowledge of pleasure" (*sukhābhijñasya*). One who has higher knowledge regarding pleasure is "one possessing higher knowledge of pleasure" (*sukhābhijña*); that is, one who has experienced pleasure. For such a person who possesses higher knowledge of pleasure, there is a recollection of pleasure (*sukhānusmṛti*). Recalling former pleasure—that which was previously experienced—one becomes attached to pleasure, to delight, or to its means, such as agallochum, sandalwood, and so forth. In that regard, whatever craving (*gardha*) there is, that is called thirst (*tṛṣṇā*), greed (*lobha*), and passion (*rāga*). (2.7)

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is that which arises following suffering and lies latent within suffering. It has been stated that "suffering" refers to that by which living beings are struck and strive to inflict injury upon it. The explanation regarding "one who has experienced suffering" is as before. Hatred is the resentment, the desire to abandon, the impulse to strike out, or the anger felt toward one who has previously caused suffering, or toward the means of that suffering, such as thieves and the like. The entire explanation is the same as for attachment (*rāga*). (2.8)

[140,16] "Flowing by its own natural force" (*svarasavāhī*): even for the wise, such deeply ingrained clinging (*abhiniveśa*) flows by its own natural force—that is, by its very nature—having the habit of proceeding toward ignorance alone in the mind. This is because we see that the root *vah* is used even when it is intransitive, as in the expression "the river flows. Alternatively, "flowing by its own natural force" means having the habit of cognizing its own natural state (*svarasa* = *svabhāva*). The word "even" (*api*) implies that fear of death is appropriate only for the ignorant who conceive of the self as being annihilated; this is the intended meaning. Even for the wise, despite their correct vision (*samyagdarśana*), [this fear persists]. The sense is that even for the ignorant, fear of death is indeed logical if they imagine the self to be subject to destruction.

For one who possesses right vision and believes that the self is not annihilated, this [fear] is improper. Likewise, among those of even more deluded intellect who perceive the annihilation of the self, this intention—the fear of death—is deeply rooted, firmly established, and stable; in that very same way, although it is improper for the wise man as well because he perceives the non-annihilation of the self, it remains deeply rooted.

Why, then, does this fear of death arise so naturally? Because for every living being, there is this constant aspiration for the self: "May I not experience death; may I not meet with annihilation. Or rather, the aspiration is: "May I be endowed with auspicious qualities; may there be no separation from them. Among the deluded, what is prayed for is the non-interruption of the self along with the abundance of enjoyments.
What is understood by this prayer? He says: "And this prayer for oneself does not occur for one who has not experienced the nature of death. And by this prayer for oneself...

The experience of a previous birth is perceived. This is what is meant: for there is no longing for pleasure that has not been experienced, nor is there a desire to avoid suffering that has not been experienced. Even for one who has not experienced the suffering of death through perception or inference, a previous experience of death is inferred by this self-aspiration; and since that too cannot occur without a birth, it is an experience of birth. Thus, the successive experiences of birth and death in the past are considered to be beginningless.
And this attachment is a defilement that exists even in a worm as soon as it is born.

[141,17] He explains the cause for the experience of death: the fear of death, which is impossible according to perception, inference, and scripture, consists of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and serves as the cause for the realization that the self and its enjoyments will be annihilated.

This infers the suffering of death experienced in a previous birth. Just as this affliction is seen even among those who are utterly deluded, such as worms and the like, so too it exists even for the wise person who understands the prior and subsequent limits—wherein the prior limit is bondage and the subsequent limit is liberation—or for one who has realized the limits of birth and death; it is firmly rooted [even in them].

But why is this [impression] firmly rooted in the wise man just as it is in the deluded? To this he says: "For this impression of the fear of death is common to both the ignorant and the wise, because they both experience death" (2.9).

[141,24] It will be stated that the latent disposition (*āśaya*) has its root in the afflictions (*kleśa*), and that when the root exists, there is its maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore, those afflictions must be abandoned. And they have been demonstrated for the purpose of their abandonment. Furthermore, he will state the means for their abandonment: "Their activities are to be abandoned by meditation" (*dhyāna-heyās tadvṛttayaḥ*). In this regard, it is not known what the object of the application of meditation is—whether its object is the karma and afflictions whose seeds have been burnt, or whether it has all things as its object. For the sake of distinguishing these objects, this sūtra is commenced: "They are to be abandoned by regression; they are subtle."

Those five afflictions, resembling burnt seeds, perish along with that mind when the mind’s functional activity has ceased for the yogin. This is what is meant: through the dissolution—that is, the complete cessation—of the mind whose purpose for the person has been fulfilled and whose essence as seeds has been burnt by the fire of the practice of right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), the afflictions likewise perish.

Because dissolution arises [spontaneously], there is no dependence on the means of meditation. For that which is already burnt does not require further burning, nor does that which is already ground require further grinding. But the mind, because its purpose for the person has been accomplished and because there is no longer any cause for its continued existence, ceases of its own accord. (2.10)

Furthermore, for what kind of beings is there an expectation of the means such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? To this it is said: "But for those who are established, having attained the state of being seeds."

Those functions of the afflictions which are to be abandoned by meditation (*dhyāna*) were previously attenuated by the coarse counteragent known as the yoga of action—namely, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*). Now, because they have been attenuated, they exist in the state of the potency of the seed; these must be eliminated by means of the powerful counteragent of great meditation (*dhyāna*), characterized by a specific proficiency arising from the practice of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). This continues until they are rendered subtle—that is to say, until they are like burnt seeds, until they are rendered seedless.

What is this like? Just as the coarse dirt on clothes is washed off first, whereas the subtle dirt caused by oils and the like is removed later with effort and skillful means such as alkaline substances and specific techniques; so too, the gross fluctuations of the afflictions have weak counteragents, being countered by the practice of the limbs of yoga such as austerity, self-study, devotion to the Lord, and the observances and restraints. However, the subtle fluctuations have powerful counteragents.

These [subtle afflictions] are subtle, depend upon the potency of their seeds, and are great adversaries to right vision—right vision which is unimpaired and possesses the excellence of radiance attained through the practice of austerity and Vedic study. ||2.11||

[143,16] For what purpose, then, does one strive for the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*)? To this he says: because the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*), which is to be experienced in seen and unseen births, has its root in the afflictions. The "afflictions" are ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest; that latent deposit of karma whose root—its cause of birth—is these afflictions is called "having the afflictions as its root. It is called a "latent deposit of karma" (*karmāśaya*) because it lies within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) until the fruit of the action is bestowed; it consists of both white and black natures. "Seen" and "unseen" refer to the two types of births; that which is to be experienced or felt in those two is "to be experienced in seen and unseen births."

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: that karmic latency (*karmāśaya*) whose fruit is to be experienced in either the present or a future life is the root of the afflictions (*kleśa*), provided that the karmic latency which has as its fruit to be experienced the results of actions performed in the present or future lives is indeed the root of the afflictions.

That accumulation of karma, whether meritorious or non-meritorious in nature, whose fruition is accomplished in a particular birth, has its fruit to be experienced in that very birth; this is "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*). However, that accumulation of karma whose fruit is to be experienced in another birth is "to be experienced in a future life" (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*).

[143,25] Now the commentary is being explained. In that context, the statement "the latent disposition (*āśaya*) of meritorious and non-meritorious karma arises from greed, anger, and delusion" indicates that its root is the afflictions (*kleśa*). The latent disposition of meritorious karma arising from greed is, for example, the desire for heaven or for a son, such as when one thinks, "I shall experience a pleasant fruit here or in heaven. That arising from anger is, for example, the case of Viśvāmitra and Ambā. That arising from delusion is, for example, the case of Draupadī and Kumbhakarṇa.

[144,6] Even a non-meritorious latent disposition (*apuṇyakarmāśaya*) originates from greed (*lobha*), as when one kills a leopard for its skin or an elephant for its tusks; or as Karna spoke untruth out of greed for knowledge of the scriptures (*śāstrajñānalobha*). That which originates from anger (*krodha*) is, for example, the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*), as well as that of Aśvatthāman in the *Mahābhārata*. That which originates from delusion (*moha*) is, for example, that of the "liberators from saṃsāra" (*saṃsāramocaka*) and others, and of Nahuṣa.

The connection of the two—egoism (*asmitā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—is with each of greed, anger, and delusion respectively. How so? One becomes angry thinking, "I have been insulted"; one becomes greedy thinking, "I shall experience pleasure"; and one becomes deluded thinking, "I am being deluded."

Ignorance (*avidyā*) also, characterized by perverted vision, is connected with all [the afflictions]. For in the absence of ignorance, there is no possibility of the existence of egoism (*asmitā*) and the others. Attachment (*rāga*), however, is simply greed (*lobha*); aversion (*dveṣa*) is anger (*krodha*); and clinging (*abhiniveśa*) is included within delusion (*vimoha*).

As for the statement that "delusion is again ignorance," this is said because of their commonality as ignorance alone. However, greed, anger, and delusion are independent factors that serve as the gateway for the production of merit and demerit; and thus he will say later: "preceded by greed, anger, and delusion."

That latent predisposition of karma (*karmāśaya*), which arises from greed, anger, and delusion, is both to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) and to be experienced in a future life (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*).

Furthermore, since the intrinsic nature and causes of actions are identical, how is it that for some there is experience in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyatva*) and for others experience in a future life (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīyatva*)? To this he says: It is produced either through intense application—that is, through intense effort by means of mantras, asceticism, and meditative absorption performed in their well-known forms with intense urgency—or through the propitiation of the Lord, deities, great sages, and those of great spiritual power.

It has been said that for Īśvara, the deities such as the Ādityas, and the great seers such as Bhṛgu—who possess great majesty and whose minds are devoted to the knowledge of Dharma—it is precisely these [deeds] that, when fully accomplished through more intense propitiation, ripen immediately;
they ripen in that very same birth, as was the case with the youth Nandīśvara.

Likewise, when harm is committed repeatedly and persistently through intense affliction—such as the excess of greed and so forth—toward those who are fearful, diseased, or miserable; toward those who have placed their trust in one; or toward those of great majesty, such as ascetics whose minds are devoted to knowledge and the Dharma, that latent disposition toward evil karma ripens and bears fruit immediately, as in the case of Nahuṣa.

In the world as well, the proximity of fruits such as trees to their causes is well known through the specific cultivation of the field and the seed, as established by the science of arboriculture (*vṛkṣāyurveda*). Likewise, in actions such as going (*gam*) or cooking (*pac*), one observes the proximity or remoteness of the result depending on the distinction between intense or mild performance.

In this regard, he provides an illustration of the latent impression of meritorious karma: just as the youth Nandīśvara, having abandoned his own human transformation, was transformed into a deity through a birth brought about by the performance of intense austerities aimed at propitiating Maheśvara.

Likewise, Nahuṣa is an illustration of one whose latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) consist of non-meritorious actions. He was the Indra of the gods; having abandoned his own transformation, through the force of his latent impressions produced by the performance of extremely deluded acts, he was transformed into the state of an animal.

The examples for anger and the other [afflictions], by virtue of being experienced in either the present life or a future life respectively, have already been explained previously. By this same principle, the accumulations of meritorious and non-meritorious karma produced by the practice of afflictions such as greed—whether mild or more mild—are explained as being experienced in a future life, just as in the world. Regarding that, it is further said:

In that regard, for those hell-beings who have not performed actions specifically for the sake of attaining hell—namely, those characterized by killing a brahmin, violating the teacher’s wife, and so forth—for those hell-beings, based on the fact that their state as hell-beings is the result of unwholesome cultivation, there exists no karmic intention whose fruit is to be experienced in the present life, by which a [new] fruit would be initiated.

But how is it that there is the undertaking of karma by hell-beings, animals, and so forth, as well as by gods and humans, while it is said that this alone is the "land of karma" (karmabhūmi) and not the hells and other realms? It is not so, because the performance of karma is observed among Nahuṣa and others. Moreover, it is heard that even Śakra incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin through the slaying of Vṛtra and others, and there is also the scriptural report of his practice of yoga and other disciplines.

That which is called "the sphere of action" (*karmabhūmi*), where humans possess the authority over karma, is said with reference to the swift attainment of results therein. As it has been stated: "For in the human world, success born of action is indeed swift" (BhG 4.12). Furthermore, from Vyāsa’s recollection of the narrative of the worm (*kīṭopākhyāna*), it follows that even animals are capable of performing karma.

Furthermore, because action is possible for one who possesses a body, sense-faculties, and so forth, and because actions originating from body, speech, and mind bring about results due to being preceded by afflictions (*kleśa*).

Even for those who have exhausted their afflictions (*kleśa*) and possess right vision, there is no *karmāśaya* to be experienced in a future birth, precisely because of the absence of afflictions. For one free from passion (*vītarāga*) is never seen to be born again. Since afflictions are the cause not only for the initiation of karma but also for the initiation of the fruits of karma, it is possible for a *karmāśaya* to be experienced in the present life even for one whose afflictions are exhausted, provided it was initiated prior to the attainment of knowledge;
this is because its fruit has already begun to manifest, like an arrow that has been released. (2.12)

Furthermore, when the root exists, its maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. For the root of actions is the afflictions (*kleśa*). "When this root exists" means when the afflictions exist. The maturation—meaning the production of the fruit—of that latent deposit of meritorious and non-meritorious action arising from greed and anger is "its maturation. What, then, is that fruit? He says: birth, lifespan, and experience.

[146,26] "When the afflictions (*kleśa*) exist, the latent impression of karma (*karmāśaya*) begins to produce its fruition (*vipāka*), but not when the root of the afflictions has been severed"—this is the explanation of the "root. Regarding that statement, "when the afflictions exist, the latent impression of karma begins to produce its fruition," he provides an illustration: "Just as rice grains covered by husks, whose seed-nature has not been burnt."

Even when covered by husks, seeds whose nature has been scorched are never capable of sprouting; likewise, even when their husks have been removed, seeds whose nature has been scorched are not fit for sprouting. This distinction in the illustration is intended to demonstrate both aspects of the point being illustrated.

How is it that the latent predisposition for action (*karmāśaya*), when enveloped by afflictions (*kleśa*), results in the growth of maturation (*vipāka*)? It is like rice grains (*śāli-taṇḍula*) enveloped by husks; as long as the afflictions remain bound, they produce maturation. However, one whose afflictions have been removed—or whose seeds of affliction have been burnt away by higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*)—is not like this. Just like rice grains from which the husks have been removed, one whose afflictions have been removed does not result in the growth of maturation.

For yogins who possess right vision preceded by the exhaustion of the afflictions (*kleśa*) through the practice of the limbs of yoga, even if the afflictions have not yet been entirely removed, the capacity of the seed is burnt—just as a grain of rice whose husk has been removed and whose seed-power is burnt—and thus, its power being burnt by the fire of absolute right vision via the channel of the practice of the limbs of yoga, it does not sprout as a fruition.
And likewise, Vyāsa demonstrates a separate liberation for both the followers of Sāṃkhya and the practitioners of Yoga.

"Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so too the self is not reborn when the afflictions have been consumed by knowledge. (Mbh 12.204.16) Likewise, it is said that "the yogi who has transcended the sovereignty of yoga shall be liberated," and so forth; and here too, he will state that liberation belongs to both the one who has attained sovereignty and the one whose yoga has reached its consummation.
As to how many kinds this maturation (*vipāka*) is, he says: "And that maturation is threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience."

In this regard, the following is investigated: what, then, is the result of this investigation? It is said that within a single lifetime, a single sentient being performs a great many actions with mutually contradictory results. As it is said: "Through the defects of actions born of the body, a person goes to the state of an immobile being; through those of speech, to the state of a bird or a beast; and through those of the mind, to the state of a low-born caste."

[148,7] Furthermore, people perform actions for the sake of heaven as well as those that lead to hell. In this regard, it is heard in scripture that a single act, such as the killing of a Brahmin, causes multiple births, according to the Smṛti beginning with "as a dog, a pig, a donkey, and a camel," and so forth.

[148,9] Furthermore, if actions that possess contradictory locations, times, causes, and ripenings were to initiate a single birth, their state of having contradictory ripenings would be lost. Consequently, the injunctions regarding the purpose of those actions would be subverted.

[148,11] Now, if it were generally the case that the commencement of birth results from actions because they are innumerable—such that the fruit is commenced by some alone and not by others—then a fixed rule would be untenable as to which [action] has commenced it and which has not. Furthermore, there would be a collapse of enthusiasm among agents regarding the fruits of their actions, leading to a failure of engagement in activities directed toward worldly prosperity and the supreme good.

[148,15] Now, if it is argued that by means of one [cause] there is indeed the destruction of the others, even so the same fault remains, because there is no fixed rule as to what is destroyed and what is the originating cause.

[148,17] Now, even if there were indeed no destruction, there would still be an absence of the time for the commencement of what remains, and consequently an absence of liberation. Therefore, this is investigated in order to demonstrate that the scriptures concerning engagement and cessation possess purposeful meaning.

[148,19] Is a single action the cause of a single birth, given that there exist many actions which serve as the causes for attaining heaven and so forth? Thus, the first inquiry is whether one action projects multiple births; for an inquiry must indeed be directed toward two opposing positions.

The second investigation is as follows: Does multiple karma produce multiple births—whether of contradictory or non-contradictory results—or does multiple karma produce a single birth—whether of contradictory or non-contradictory results?
Furthermore, what follows from this? First of all, a single karma is not the cause of a single birth. Why? Because when many karmas exist, why does only one karma not initiate a single birth?
If the initiation of birth belongs to only one [individual], then, because saṃsāra is beginningless and has been accumulated over beginningless time, an incalculable amount of karma—
both that which yields contrary results and that which yields non-contrary results— is accumulated by each individual person in every single birth.

In this regard, since there is no fixed rule for the sequence of the results of the remaining mass of karma—comprising the countless actions accumulated over many previous births that are distinct from the karma initiating the present birth, as well as the present karma accumulated in the current life whose effects have not yet begun—it would be uncertain whether some portion of the mass of karma accumulated in previous births will initiate the future birth, or whether some portion of the mass of karma belonging to the present life will do so. Consequently, the world would lack confidence.

[149,18] Would the fruit be produced by past karma, whether defiled or undefiled, or rather by present karma, whether defiled or undefiled? Because of this uncertainty, no one would perform the *agnihotra* and other rites, nor would anyone strive for liberation; thus, a lack of confidence would result, which is undesirable.

[149,21] Now, in the first investigation, he refutes the second position: "And a single karma is not the cause of multiple births. Why? Because in each individual birth, many karmas are performed; if among them only a single karma were to be the cause for the maturation (*vipāka*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*) of multiple births, then it would follow that there would be no time for the maturation of the remaining karma other than that which has already begun its effect, and that too is undesirable. Furthermore, there would be no fixed order of the results.

The aforementioned fault also applies here. One should not accept such an undesirable consequence. As for the fact that each individual act, such as the killing of a Brahmin, initiates multiple births, this is accepted precisely because it falls within the scope of the scriptures; thus, it is understood to have the killing of a Brahmin and so forth as its specific object.

In this second investigation, the first position is now refuted: "Nor is a plurality of karmas the cause of a single birth. Why is it not accepted in this way? To that it is said: that very plurality of births occurring simultaneously is not possible for a single non-omnipotent being. And if it is stated that they occur successively, does one [karma] initiate multiple births? In that case, there is the persistence of the previous fault; everywhere there is the persistence of the first fault, namely, a lack of confidence due to the absence of a fixed order in the sequence of results.

Therefore, since these three positions are untenable, he now concludes the established doctrine: "In the interval between birth and death"—that is, in the middle between birth and death—the accumulation of meritorious and sinful karma performed is that which is to be experienced in a non-contradictory birth and whose fruition is not restricted to a specific time. He will explain its threefold application; therefore, this rule is stated specifically for the accumulation of meritorious and sinful karma whose fruits are non-contradictory.

[150,19] Variegated by accumulation: because it is accumulated by many actions, both similar and dissimilar, it is variegated through accumulation. It exists in the relationship of primary and subordinate; some action is primary with respect to one action, yet subordinate with respect to another, and what is subordinate may also be primary—thus it exists as a mixture of many diverse actions.

Manifested at the time of death: just as the conjunction of the seed, the field, and the preparation of the soil is the cause for the manifestation of the state of the sprout, so too is death the instrumental cause for the manifestation of those karmas that are not mutually contradictory. Combined through a single-pointed focus and unified by being merged into one, it brings about only a single birth.

And that birth, having obtained its lifespan through that very karma whose nature was manifested at the time of death, results in experience during that lifespan by means of that same karma by which the birth and lifespan were produced. It is just as the sprout is produced from a certain seed, and from that very same [seed], the fruit, flowers, and so forth are also produced.
By that very action, the production of wealth and life-span indeed occurs; this is what is being determined.

However, the status of other causes of life-span, wealth, and so forth—such as sacrifices performed with the desire for sons or cattle—as the cause for obtaining sons, life-span, and the like, is not being denied. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with all the Śrutis and Smṛtis. Therefore, by the phrase "by that very action," once birth has been brought about, since its purpose has been fulfilled, a mere negation of the possibility of cessation is made.

Because this latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience, it is designated as "having three maturations" (*trivipāka*), since its maturations—birth and the others—are threefold. This is called the "single-birth" (*aikabhāvika*) latent deposit of karma; it is "single-birth" because its purpose is fulfilled within a single lifetime.

[151,14] However, karma to be experienced in the present life initiates only one ripening (*vipāka*), such as the sacrifice for the sake of a son, a village, and so forth; or it initiates two ripenings, because it serves as the cause for both enjoyment and lifespan, such as the sacrifice for the sake of longevity and so forth; or it initiates three ripenings, as in the cases of Nandīśvara and Nahuṣa.

[151,17] But is it not a contradiction that for Nandīśvara and Nahuṣa there is both experience in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīyatva*) and the commencement of the threefold ripening (*trivipākārambhitva*)? For the birth of Nandīśvara as a human is indeed seen; however, that which is Nandīśvara’s divinity and Nahuṣa’s state as a serpent—both of these are unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Indeed, divinity is not experienced by Nandīśvara while he is still in the state of humanity, nor is the state of being a serpent experienced by Nahuṣa while he is still in the state of divinity. How, then, can there be both the commencement of the threefold ripening and experience in the present life?

This is not a fault. It is precisely the body, characterized by its currently perceived genus, that has undergone transformation into another genus for those two. And it is not the case that, as with others, the attainment of another genus occurs through the destruction of a body characterized by its perceived genus, depending on causes such as the infusion of semen; such is not the case for Nandīśvara and Nahuṣa. Therefore, it has been illustrated that there is both the commencement of a threefold fruition and the state of being experienced in the present life.

In this regard, the mass of karma is threefold: that to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*), that to be experienced in a future life (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*), and that which is indefinite as to its ripening (*aniyatavipāka*). As for that which is to be experienced in the present life, its ripening is not fixed. Sometimes it has only one ripening, being the cause for experience (*bhoga*) alone. Sometimes it has two ripenings, because it is the cause for both experience and the life-span (*āyus*). Sometimes it has three ripenings, because it is the cause for birth (*jāti*), the life-span, and experience, as in the cases of Nandīśvara and Nahuṣa.

However, that which is to be experienced in a future birth (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) is of two kinds: that with determinate fruition (*niyatavipāka*) and that with indeterminate fruition (*aniyatavipāka*). That with determinate fruition has already been shown by the passage beginning with "therefore, performed between birth and death" (*tasmāj janmaprāyaṇāntare kṛta*); as for that with indeterminate fruition, it will be described as being of three types.

Now, however, another mass of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the maturation of karma is described. By those latent impressions—which are brought about through the experience of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and maturation; and which consist of the experience of afflictions, the experience of karma, and the experience of maturation—this mind, which has been coagulated since beginningless time, is made variegated as if by a painting on a cloth or a wall, and is spread and pervaded everywhere like a fish-net with its knots.

[152,15] Now, in each single birth, the latencies (*vāsanā*) preceded by many previous existences operate within both karma and its maturation (*vipāka*) by becoming its constituent parts. For if the latency were not a constituent part of the karma and its maturation, it would be impossible for a newborn fawn to exhibit a sudden outburst of rage and an attack toward a young bull. Nor could that [intensity] be possible through the mere latency of a single experience.

However, this *karmāśaya* which is performed during the interval between birth and death, which serves as the cause for a future birth that is obstructed [by other karma], and which initiates three types of maturation (*vipāka*) through the relationship of primary and secondary factors—this alone is called "belonging to a single existence" (*ekabhavika*). It is not [karma] to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*), nor is it [karma] with indefinite maturation (*aniyatavipakti*) to be experienced in a future life (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*), nor are they the latent impressions (*vāsanās*).

[152,22] First, as for their essential nature: those formative factors (*saṃskāra*) which are the causes of memory are the latencies (*vāsanā*); and they are beginningless, because this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), consisting of the experience of the results of afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, is itself beginningless.

[152,24] But regarding that aforementioned *ekabhavika* (single-birth) *karmāśaya*, which resembles a wave upon the great ocean of bliss (*ānanda*), its exception (*apavāda*) is now stated for a specific portion. How is it both of determinate ripening (*niyatavipāka*) and of indeterminate ripening (*aniyatavipāka*)? What is this determinately ripening [karman]? It is that which, manifested at the time of death, initiates its effect; and that alone is the *ekabhavika*.

However, that which has contradictory cognition, place, time, or cause is of indefinite fruition (*aniyata-vipāka*), even though it shares the commonality of being experienced in an unseen birth (*adṛṣṭajanma-vedanīyatva*). Why? Because of its contradiction with that which has definite fruition (*niyata-vipāka*). Nor is this [indefinite karma] restricted to a single existence (*ekabhavika*), precisely because of that same contradiction. As for what was said regarding its being "restricted to a single existence"—namely, that "this is the karmic latency (*karmāśaya*) restricted to a single existence"—that was stated by way of the commonality of being experienced in an unseen birth.

But surely, if this were so, it would contradict such rules as: "The latent deposit of meritorious and demeritorious karma performed during the interval between birth and death—variegated by its accumulation, existing in a relationship of primary and secondary factors, manifested at the time of death, and coalesced into a single whole—produces a single birth. And so forth.

Why [is this so]? Because death manifests all previous karma; and because a new latent disposition (*āśaya*) arises through the destruction of the substratum of the prior disposition. On the substratum of human dispositions, there previously existed the dispositions of divine and animal births; and at the time of death, when that substratum is destroyed, since death is common to all as the cause for manifesting all karma, there is no reason why only some of the dispositions of divine and animal births should be manifested and not others. For a lamp does not manifest an object that has come within its range by abandoning one part of it.

To this it is replied: this is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence that actions are purposeless. For indeed, many kinds of mutually contradictory actions are performed. One who has performed an action for the sake of heaven might perform another action for the sake of cattle, villages, and so forth, and then again perform a powerful action for the sake of killing a Brahmin or for the sake of attaining the state of an immobile being; in that case, for one who has attained the state of a hell-being or an immobile being, the attainment of cattle, villages, and the like is impossible.
Consequently, the purposelessness of those actions would follow.

[153,18] Now, if it is argued that even there the pleasure of obtaining a village and so forth exists, we say no; for when one says "desirous of a village," what is intended is not the state of possessing the pleasure of a village. Indeed, one who has attained the pleasure of a village is not said to have merely "attained the village."

Furthermore, all the treatises would be contradicted; moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence that heaven, hell, and so forth—which are not perceived—would consist of nothing more than pleasure and pain. Consequently, the Vedic revelations (*śruti*) and traditional codes (*smṛti*) which declare the existence of the remainder by the phrase "by the remainder" would be subverted. Therefore, not all karma is manifested at the time of death. For otherwise, there would result the futility of those karmas that are utterly opposed [to one another], and if the science of karma were rendered purposeless, there would follow a lack of confidence even in the science of liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*).

[153,24] Furthermore, among manifestors as well, we observe the deviation that while some possess the capacity to manifest, others do not. For example, although the eyes of Caitra and the eyes of an owl both manifest color-form (*rūpa*), they mutually deviate with respect to day and night. And although light equally serves as a cooperative cause for all eyes, it does not serve as a cooperative cause for the eyes of an owl.

Likewise, even though a single physical body, such as that of a woman, is the cause for the manifestation of pleasure, pain, and delusion—all of which may be manifested therein—only one of them is actually manifested in a given case.

If it is argued that there is no fault here because of the contradiction with karma and so forth, then in this case as well, there is a non-manifestation of all karmas due to contradiction. Furthermore, even when the field that serves as the receptacle for seeds is being destroyed, despite the presence of conditions such as water, those seeds contained therein do not initiate their effects, such as sprouts, if they are of a contradictory nature. Likewise, even when the receptacle for the latent dispositions (*āśaya*) belonging to the human state is being destroyed, there is no simultaneous acquisition of activity by all the latent dispositions of a contradictory nature belonging to divine or animal births.

Furthermore, death alone is not the manifestor of karmas, because we observe that those karmas which are to be experienced in the present life exist for the sake of enjoyment. If it is argued that for those karmas for which death alone is the manifestor, there must be the manifestation of all of them, we say no, because of the contradiction with the dispositions (*āśaya*) belonging to divine, animal, and human births.

Furthermore, because death (*prāyaṇa*) occurs with specific distinctions of time—past or future—it cannot be the manifestor of all karmas simultaneously. Moreover, there is a distinction in death due to the scriptural mention of specific types of death; as it is said, "Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end" (*BhG* 8.6), there is a distinction in death based on the distinction of specific memories. Therefore, death is not eternally the manifestor of all karmas, for otherwise, the qualification [of the scripture] would result in meaninglessness.

Nor could the specific qualification of "recollection" and so forth result in the alteration or destruction of the primary subject. For if it were to cause that destruction or alteration, recollection would no longer function as a cooperative factor for the primary karma; rather, it would become independent. And in that case, the performance of the action would be rendered futile.

Furthermore, there would follow the absurd consequence that beings in the embryonic stages, such as the *kalala*, would attain liberation, because they do not initiate action. If it is argued that these stages possess the nature of action just as they possess the nature of fruit, we say no, because the arrangement of the instruments has not yet occurred. For it is only when the instruments are arranged that actions acquire their functional activity and the status of being fruits; at that time, such an arrangement is not possible.

If it is argued that [the dreamer's actions do not persist] because they are like a dream, we say no; for even there, action is not admitted. Furthermore, the Śruti states: "Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it" (BAU Bh), showing a lack of connection with the karma produced by the dream-vision. No one is guilty of a transgression on account of dreams, since [dreams] show the performance of acts such as the killing of a Brahmin. If it is argued that this is not so because of the observation of expiations for spilled semen and the like, we say no; for that expiation is caused by the spilling of semen.

Therefore, even if one accepts that a fruit exists during the stages of the embryo (kalala) and so forth—just as it is accepted in states such as dreaming—nevertheless, because there is an absence of the operation of the instruments (karaṇa), that is merely a fruit like in the state of dreaming;
it is not the state of being an agent of action (karmakartṛtva). Thus, the consequence of liberation would indeed have occurred for those who have entered the womb.

Therefore, because there is the possibility of specific distinctions among those deaths (*prāyaṇa*), the capacity of deaths to manifest all karma is not eternal. For this reason, it is stated in the commentary: "In that regard, this restriction applies only to that which is to be experienced in a future birth (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) and has a fixed maturation (*niyatavipāka*), namely, that which was performed between birth and death," and so forth; by such words, the restriction regarding the commencement of the three types of fruition is stated, but not for that which is to be experienced in a future birth and has an unfixed maturation (*aniyatavipāka*).
Why? Because for that which is to be experienced in a future birth and has an unfixed maturation, there are three possible courses.

How can there be the destruction of an unripened action? It is the destruction of that which has not yet reached the time of its own destruction, just as there is the destruction of an action that has been prohibited by means of expiation and the like.

[155,15] Regarding the primary karma, there is the "entry into the sowing" (*āvāpagamana*). When the primary karma is fixed as to its experience (*niyatavedanīya*), there occurs the "attainment of sowing" (*āvāpāpatti*); even while bypassing the fruit of the primary karma, it itself brings forth its own fruit very gradually by entering into the midst of the intermediate [karma]. Just as when whole grains of rice are being sown, even incomplete grains of rice that are sown produce their own small measure of efficacy. Or, there is the state of that which is overwhelmed by a primary karma of fixed ripening; this refers to that which has a fixed ripening (*niyatavipāka*) [but remains suppressed].

The primary karma whose fruit has already begun is suppressed and set aside for one who is overcome by another; this is because its fruition is obstructed by contrary place, time, and causal conditions. It is just as when, between two contenders for sovereignty, one who is defeated by the other who has already established his kingdom remains in wait, depending upon place, time, and causal conditions.

In this regard, the destruction of what has been done but not yet ripened is as follows: through the arising here and now of pure karma characterized by austerity (*tapas*), sacred study (*svādhyāya*), yoga, and so forth, there occurs the destruction—prior even to its attaining fruition—of impure black karma characterized by violence and the like, such as that consisting of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). The phrase "here and now" (*ihaiva*) is not intended to be restrictive, since destruction is logically possible even in another birth prior to the attainment of fruition; for example, specific sins that cause physical marks such as deformed nails are destroyed by means of expiation once they have been recognized by those very signs.

This he explains by means of an illustration established in another system (*tantrāntara*), wherein it is said: "In birth after birth, there are indeed two pairs of actions, white and black, for the practitioner, the person who is subject to authority. One heap, created through the merit of Vedic study and other such acts, destroys the other heap created through demerit. Or rather, for the meritorious person, the heap of white action destroys the heap of black action. Therefore, you yourself should perform your own white actions."
Why? Because right here, in this very place, the seers—those who know the distinctions of the ripening of karma—declare and make known your ultimate refuge and peace.

The entry into the primary action is demonstrated by way of an illustration: "with little admixture" means a very slight opening for fault. Why? Because it is "with a remedy," that is, accompanied by a remedy. It requires a remedy, but is not already remedied. The meaning is that it rests upon the same basis as the knowledge of the power and means of the remedy. It is "with reflection," that is, with careful consideration. How so? In times of distress, one reflects: "How am I performing what should not be done? When indeed shall I emerge from this? I shall not do it again."

For one who has engaged in action for the sake of sustaining life and so forth, who is skilled and wise—being expert in the discernment of how to avoid the defects of the fruits of action—this slight mixture is not sufficient to cause a diminution; it is not capable of detracting from the much greater fruit of merit resulting from his engagement, nor of diverting him from that fruit to employ him in its own (the mixed action's) purpose. Or rather, this [mixture] is not even sufficient to diminish the wholesome action itself. Why? Because he thinks: "This wholesome action is indeed mine, and it is truly effective. Thus does the practitioner reflect.
"Because I possess much other merit, into which this [transgression] has fallen as a small admixture among many virtues; thus, even in heaven, it will cause only a slight diminution."

Or, it refers to the state of being overwhelmed by a primary karma of certain ripening. How so? This is a question arising from a malicious intention. How is the subjugation of one whose sovereignty has not yet commenced by another whose sovereignty is already active logical, given that the commencement of sovereignty occurs through different causes?

But here, death is the manifesting cause (*nimitta*) common to all karmas; since that cause exists, it is logical that all karmas obtain their functional activity (*vṛttilābha*). Therefore, one considers it improper that only the primary karma manifests while the other does not. Consequently, let there simply be the descent into a new womb (*avāpagamana*).

To this it is replied: In that regard, death has been stated to be the common cause of manifestation for many actions—whether meritorious or non-meritorious—that are to be experienced in a future birth (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*), whose ripening is determined by factors such as place, time, and circumstances, and whose fruition is fixed. It is not, however, the cause for actions to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) concerning objects such as sons or villages, nor for those actions to be experienced in a future birth whose fruition is undetermined, as previously explained.

As for that [karma] which is to be experienced in a future birth and whose ripening is indefinite, it may perish like water in a desert, or it may be suppressed and remain latent for a long time; yet it will eventually arise whenever there appears a manifesting cause—namely, an action of a similar kind that is compatible and not contradictory. For when an action of a similar kind is undergoing ripening, it brings this [indefinite karma] to the fore.

It is precisely the ripening of that very karma whose ripening is indefinite; for there is no determination of place, time, or cause, as one cannot determine: "In what place, at what time, or by what cause will that karma become oriented toward its ripening? This course of existence is variegated and difficult to know. It is variegated due to the diversity of destruction, acquisition, suppression, and so forth; it is difficult to know because of the lack of determination regarding place, time, and cause.

[158,10] If it is objected: "But was it not stated that karma to be experienced in a future birth, when manifested at the time of death, produces only a single birth—that is, it initiates only one lifetime? Would this not now be contradicted by the statements regarding its destruction, suppression, subdual, maintenance, and so forth? [Response: No, because the answer has already been established. This rule applies specifically to karma to be experienced in a future birth whose fruition is fixed (*niyata-vipāka*). Therefore, the general rule (*utsarga*) is not set aside by this exception (*apavāda*) concerning the lack of necessity.

How is there no cessation? The meaning is that there is no cessation because the latent disposition of karma belonging to a single birth (*ekabhavika*) is difficult to discern; thus, even for karma with indefinite fruition (*aniyatavipāka*), its initiation within a single lifetime is not prohibited.

Alternatively, considering that the cessation of a general rule occurs through its exception (*apavāda*), the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the phrase "the latent predisposition (*karmāśaya*) of a single lifetime is difficult to know. Since an exception to one part of a general rule effects its cessation rather than the whole, therefore, the latent predisposition of karma that is eternal, fixed in its ripening, and belonging to a single lifetime is indeed easy to know.

Another interpretation: here, the subject under discussion is that the course of karma is to be known; this [present statement] is an exception to that, namely, that the latent disposition (*karmāśaya*) of a single existence is difficult to know. In this context, the word "iti" has the sense of a reason. Because of which reason the general course of karma must indeed be understood in that way—[it is said] that it is "difficult to know," meaning it is to be known with difficulty, that is, with great effort. (2.13)

The latent deposit of karma has been explained as being both to be experienced in the present life and to be experienced in a future life. Its fruition is also threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience; these have pleasure and pain as their results because they have merit and demerit as their causes. Pleasure is happiness (*sukha*), and pain is suffering (*duḥkha*); "pleasure and pain" refers to both together, and those whose fruit consists of these are "those having pleasure and pain as their results. Likewise, merit and demerit are "merit and demerit"; those whose cause consists of these are "those having merit and demerit as their causes. The state of being such is "having merit and demerit as their causes," and it is from that [state] [that the fruition arises].

Because they have merit and demerit as their causes: those births, lifespans, and enjoyments caused by merit have happiness as their fruit; those caused by demerit have suffering as their fruit. Just as this suffering is of a contrary nature, so too, even at the time of sensual pleasure, there exists for the yogi a suffering that is of a contrary nature. (2.14)

How can there be suffering for the yogin at the time of sensory pleasure? As was stated previously, he will explain the perception of pleasure within suffering; that [suffering] is now being produced and established. However, this specific point has not yet been established therein. Because suffering is the result of karma, it is appropriate to establish it through a different sequence, and because there is much to be said on the matter. Furthermore, due to the sufferings of transformation (*pariṇāma*), affliction (*tāpa*), and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and due to the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person.

Transformation (*pariṇati*) is *pariṇāma*; heating (*tāpti*) is *tāpa*; and conditioning (*saṃskṛti*) is *saṃskāra*. "Heating and conditioning" (*tāpa-saṃskārau*) refers to heating and conditioning; "transformation, heating, and conditioning" (*pariṇāma-tāpa-saṃskārāḥ*) refers to those very things. These are themselves sufferings and the causes of suffering; by means of these...

Everything is indeed suffering due to the causes of the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Why is all this suffering? It is because the afflictions (*kleśas*) are suffering by reason of being the cause of suffering; actions (*karman*) are so because their fruits are pleasure and pain; and birth, lifespan, and experiences are so because they are the basis, the limiting conditions, and the objects for the afflictions and the rest, and thus are causes of suffering—therefore, all of this is indeed suffering.

[159,18] Is this so for everyone? No, he says: "for the discerning one" (*vivekinaḥ*). One who possesses the discernment (*viveka*) that distinguishes between the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth is the discerning one. The meaning is: for him who has direct knowledge (*abhijña*) of the afflictions, karma, and their maturation (*vipāka*), and who perceives the specific causes that establish the state of all-as-pain (*sarva-duḥkhatva*)—namely, because [the world] consists of transformation (*pariṇāma*), suffering (*tāpa*), and latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and because its constituent qualities (*guṇa*) and fluctuations (*vṛtti*) are mutually antagonistic—it is not so for another who does not perceive it in this way.

But for him, suffering is merely the state of being heated. Even while perceiving that "I am being heated" as if it were his own self, and even while remaining doubtful in that regard, he distinguishes at least this much: "This is my suffering. For if he were to distinguish even this much of a difference, then he would consider even the means of suffering to be merely the "means of suffering. And thus, thinking "all this is suffering," he would endure it; in that case, he too would be a person of discernment.

Therefore, although those lacking discernment perceive only suffering at the time of its manifestation, they nevertheless do not consider all of its causes and so forth to be suffering. For the discerning person, however, who perceives the cause of the suffering of transformation, everything is indeed suffering.

In that regard, he first explains the suffering inherent in change (*pariṇāma-duḥkhatā*): "This [experience] of everyone is permeated by passion. By the word "everyone," he demonstrates that this is perceivable through non-erroneous direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), as it is well-known to all living beings. The experience of pleasure depends on both sentient and insentient factors, being contingent upon means such as sons, cattle, gold, and so forth. At the time of experiencing pleasure, passion is a mental activity (*manovyāpāra*); for it is one characterized by that [passion] who experiences pleasure. Since every such activity is accompanied by afflictions (*kleśa*), it is a cause of merit and demerit (*dharmā-dharma*). And the latent disposition (*āśaya*) of karma is preceded by that [activity].

That which has begun to bear fruit is experienced at the time of enjoyment, while another is accumulated; therefore, it is established that the latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions, and as long as that root exists, there is its maturation.

Likewise, at a time of pleasure, perceiving the means of suffering which are contrary to that pleasure, one feels aversion; and likewise, with a mind preoccupied with the protection of the enjoyment of pleasure, one becomes deluded. Thus, there exists a latent disposition toward action (*karmāśaya*) produced by the prior operations of aversion and delusion. Alternatively, since aversion and delusion themselves take the form of such operations, the result is produced by them alone.

Likewise, whatever enjoyment of pleasure there may be, that enjoyment cannot occur without harming or injuring living beings. Since enjoyment itself is the cause of injury, it is intended here as the injurer; thus, there is a common subject for the two actions. Furthermore, another person also thinks, "He will enjoy what belongs to me alone. In that case too, since wealth is endowed with the capacity for all kinds of enjoyment, when it is being taken, there will certainly be suffering for others. How much more so when it is taken by actually causing them pain?

And therefore, even when an act of violence is committed, there exists a physical intention (*karma-āśaya*) consisting of the body, because the activity that takes that [intention] as its material cause is accomplished by means of the body.

[160,27] Thus, during a single period of enjoyment, the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is accumulated in many ways through the causes of greed, anger, and delusion. And so, because it is characterized by passion, hatred, and delusion, the experience of pleasure—which is itself characterized by a manifold latent deposit of karma—becomes painful as it undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*); this is called "suffering due to transformation" (*pariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). For one who possesses discernment and perceives things in this way, there is indeed suffering even at the time of experiencing pleasure, just as for one who eats curd-rice while knowing it to be mixed with poison.

Furthermore, all pleasure is indeed suffering because it is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), since the experience of sensual pleasure consists of a cognition of non-discrimination. This is what is meant by the statement: "And sensual pleasure is said to be ignorance. Where was this stated? Right here, by means of synonymous terminology, in the following commentary (*bhāṣya*): "When there is a state as if non-discrimination has occurred between two things that are absolutely distinct and absolutely unmixed, enjoyment is imagined; but when their own true natures are attained, there is only isolation (*kaivalya*) for them—how then could there be enjoyment?"

Or rather, as the author of the Sūtra stated later on: "Experience is non-distinction from the conditions. And ignorance, as it undergoes transformation, produces all that is harmful. Consequently, because it is the seed of suffering, even the pleasure derived from sense objects is indeed suffering; just as food, though more delicious, is [suffering] when eaten because it is the cause of disease.

In order to elucidate this very point—that sensory pleasure is ignorance—the author presents an example established in the Tantras: "Those things which are enjoyed by the senses are called enjoyments (*bhoga*), such as sound and so forth. The satisfaction that arises toward those objects is the pacification or cessation of the senses. What is the use of these fluctuations, which are caused by meaningless exertion? That state of remaining undisturbed is true happiness."

But that lack of peace and that which surrounds one due to craving arising from the desire for greed and so forth—that is suffering. Thus it has been said: "There is no suffering equal to craving; there is no happiness equal to the absence of craving."

[161,22] But surely, does not freedom from craving arise precisely through enjoyment at the conclusion of that enjoyment? And that enjoyment will be pleasant. To this he says: "And it is not possible to bring about freedom from craving for the senses through the repeated practice of enjoyment. Why? To this he says: "Because, through the repeated practice of enjoyment, the passions of the senses increase. And thus it has been said: "Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desired objects;
Like a fire with black antelope skin as fuel, it only increases all the more. [161,26–27]

The skill and proficiency of the sense organs increase in accordance with the practice of enjoyment. Even though the proficiency of the sense organs is preceded by that of the mind, nevertheless, the proficiency of the sense organs themselves is indeed observed in those who subsist on alms and the like. Therefore, the practice of enjoyment is not the means to happiness; rather, the cessation of the practice of enjoyment alone is happiness.

Indeed, this person—who, seeking pleasure, has settled upon, become bound to, engaged in, or pursued sense objects—is like one who, fearing a mild venomous scorpion, is bitten by a sharp-toothed viper; just as such a person, having developed fear of the mild venomous scorpion, is seized by the sharp-toothed viper and encounters a far greater suffering.

In the same way, this person—having turned away from that which appears to be the highest suffering but is in fact the great bliss of transformation—being terrified by the notion that it is suffering, sinks into a vast, shoreless mire of suffering. This is the point.

The suffering inherent in change (*pariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) is contrary even to pleasure for the yogin, even during a state of pleasure; for that yogin experiences pleasure only with a mind full of revulsion, because of the superior force of karma whose fruition is specifically determined as pleasure. Therefore, everything is suffering for the discerning one.

Now, the suffering of change (*pariṇāmaduḥkhatā*) is explained: even the enjoyment of pleasure, as it undergoes transformation, becomes painful when its subsequent connection is perceived—like the consumption of sweet curd-rice smeared with poison. Furthermore, by its very nature, it is of the form of ignorance (*avidyā*), even though it possesses the scent of favorable sensation (*anukūlavedanā*). In this context, however, the suffering of change is suffering by its very nature, because its essence consists of the cycle of attachment (*ratikulātmaka*).

How is it that for everyone, the experience of suffering—which is permeated by hatred, followed by hatred, dependent upon intentional and unintentional means, and reliant on instruments such as enemies and thorns—constitutes the fruition of unwholesome karma (*adharma*) exactly as before; and furthermore, as new [karma] continues to accumulate, there exists therein a latent disposition (*āśaya*) born of hatred.

Tormented by that suffering and longing for the means of happiness such as sandalwood and the like, one moves and exerts oneself through body, speech, and mind; and that movement results either in the benefit of others or in the infliction of pain upon others. Thereupon—

One accumulates merit and demerit through the benefit or injury done to others. And this latent deposit of karma, known as merit and demerit, produced by the benefit or injury to others, arises from greed and delusion. This, then, is the "suffering inherent in pain," which is long-lasting and widespread. For the discerning person who perceives it thus, everything—by virtue of its basis, its objects, and its causes—is nothing but suffering.

[163,16] Now, the suffering produced by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the experience of pleasure and pain is discussed. What, then, is the nature of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*)? From the experience of pleasure, there is an accumulation of pleasant impressions; from the experience of pain, there is also an accumulation of painful impressions. Since pleasure and pain are permeated by attachment and aversion, the accumulations of their impressions are likewise permeated by attachment and aversion. Thus, when the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma—consisting of birth, lifespan, and experience—is being undergone, they result in pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, the latent predisposition (*saṃskārāśaya*) for the experience of pleasure and pain is such that, just as the experience of pleasure and pain occurs in uninterrupted succession, so too do the predispositions for those experiences arise continuously, permeated by attachment and aversion. And these two are the "suffering of predispositions" (*saṃskāraduḥkha*), which has predispositions as its cause; such is the nature of that suffering of predispositions. For one who does not remember does not take up the means for action in order to experience [the result]. And it has been established that memory has predispositions as its cause.

Even though there is no suffering in the conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*) by way of its own nature, nevertheless, for the discerning person who knows that the conditioned formation is a cause of suffering, it constitutes suffering by its mere existence, like poison that has been swallowed. Thus, through these causes—transformation, affliction, and latent impressions—all is indeed suffering; because it is of a contrary nature, this beginningless stream of suffering agitates the yogi alone.

[164,9] But surely, since the other [the beloved] is also of a disagreeable nature, why does it not cause him distress? It does not distress the other because his mind has been made callous by the scars of discrimination against the impurities of extreme affliction and the like; thus, its disagreeable nature is not manifested. For there is one who receives upon his head even a blow from a lover’s foot, which is like the strike of a hammer, or who holds the urine and excrement of his son against his chest.

This [joy], surging like a great ocean of bliss, does not even know itself all that well; for that [bliss] is not of a nature opposed to it. Indeed, because the other is the perceiver, it causes passion alone to increase all the more.

[164,15] But surely, since the yogin also possesses an object of perception (*nimitta*) identical to that [of others], why does it agitate him? It indeed agitates him. Why? Because he is like the surface of an eyeball; the meaning is that this is due to his clarity and dispassion. Therefore, the object of perception is not always the same for him, because he is a knower (*vidvān*). For a knower does not have a mind scarred by the lack of discernment (*aviveka*) caused by the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. Nor is there "knower-ship" apart from the removal of that mind-scarred state. Therefore, because he is like the surface of an eyeball, it agitates only the knower and not the other.

In this regard, he explains the difference between the wise and the ignorant by means of two examples: just as even a woolen thread, though extremely soft to the touch, causes pain when placed upon the surface of the eye because of the extreme sensitivity of the eye's surface, so too does suffering distress the yogin whose wisdom is most discerning and whose heart is stainless.

That very same woolen thread, when cast upon other limbs, does not cause pain even with its most harsh touch; likewise, it does not afflict the other recipient with suffering, because his mind has been calloused by afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like—he is indeed comparable to a limb or part of the body that is more hardened than others.

Regarding this, he says: "In this way, these sufferings afflict only the yogin who is like an eyeless bowl, and not the other practitioner. Showing that for the other practitioner, however, they have the nature of being like other parts of the body, he says "but the other," concluding the sentence with the words "the torments follow after."

[165,5] Suffering, which has been brought forth by its own causes—namely, volitional and non-volitional factors that serve as the instruments for the attainment of suffering—and which has been presented to the *puruṣa* through the medium of the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhi*), thereby becoming his object of experience (*karman*); this suffering he abandons when discarding one body, and having abandoned it elsewhere, he again takes up another aggregate of suffering characterized by a body and so forth, being as if permeated on all sides by the fluctuations of the mind (*vitti*) consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is variegated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

What is the specific characteristic of the other, the practitioner? It is one who follows the notions of "I-making" (*ahaṅkāra*) and "mine-making" (*mamakāra*) that are to be abandoned. "I-making" is the erroneous conception regarding the body, the instruments [of action], their attributes, and their activities, qualities, and fruits. "Mine-making," however, is the notion of "mine" with respect to those external things, whether sentient or insentient. Because these two are erroneous and because they are the seeds for all afflictions, karma, and its maturation, they must be abandoned; for without them, passion and the like, as well as the results of karma, do not manifest.

Therefore, those two must be abandoned; for he is one whose nature it is to follow after the notions of "I" and "mine," which are themselves to be abandoned—thus, he is "one who follows after the abandonable egoism and possessiveness."

[165,15] Whatever has arisen is like other limbs and parts; they have as their objective cause (nimitta) both the external and the internal.
