Those for whom the elements (bhūta) are external, and the effect and the cause are internal, and both the external and internal are their objective cause, are those who have both external and internal objective causes.

The three joints consist precisely in the external and other objective causes; or, the state of being past, future, and present constitutes the three joints. And it will be stated that "suffering to be abandoned is that which is yet to come," or else that their nature consists of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and maturation (*vipāka*); or else that they consist of the sufferings of transformation (*pariṇāma*), pain (*tāpa*), and conditioning (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, those three-jointed torments flow along and adhere to [the mind].

[165,22] Thus, having seen himself as one who practices such non-discrimination and is being carried away by the stream of beginningless suffering, and seeing himself submerged in the stream of suffering as well as the multitude of living beings in the same state, the yogi takes refuge in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which brings about the destruction of all suffering.

[165,25] But is it not the case that one has already attained right vision (*samyagdarśana*) precisely because of being a yogin? It is said in reply: the status of a yogin arises solely from the practice of the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), even in the absence of right vision. Therefore, [the author] demonstrates that yoga is a means to right vision. Seeing both yoga and the fruit of yoga as nothing but suffering, one resorts exclusively to right vision as one's refuge. And so he will say later: "From detachment toward that [fruit] also, upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (*kaivalya*)."

For this reason as well, everything is suffering for the discerning person; and why? Because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*. But one might ask: for what purpose is the grammatical separation made in the *sūtra*, since it would have been sufficient to say "by transformation, pain, latent impressions, and the conflict of the functions of the *guṇas"? This is not a fault, because the experience of pleasure and pain, along with their latent impressions, are well-known to all people.

They have been specified as "the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions. This separate treatment is intended for those who are proficient in the knowledge that discriminates their causes and who possess the excellence of discrimination to understand that the functions of the *guṇas* are mutually antagonistic; however, they are arranged in a single aphorism because they share the commonality of being the cause of all suffering.

The qualities (*guṇas*) are *sattva* and the others; their activities are the "activities of the qualities" (*guṇavṛttis*). Due to the opposition among these, there is an "opposition of the activities of the qualities. Furthermore, those qualities are established in the forms of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth. Because they undergo a non-differentiated transformation through the relationship of primary and subordinate, they possess contradictory activities. Thus, when the activity of one arises, it is suppressed by the activity of another.

In this way, for all three [guṇas], there is at every moment a mutual suppression of their functions and a manifestation of their functions through one another. Among the guṇas whose nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, the acquisition of the function of any one is not unaccompanied by the others. Therefore, this is established: when *rajas*, whose nature is pain, arises, then because its function is itself of the nature of pain, it cannot be said that "it is not pain."

Since *rajas* indeed follows along with both *sattva* and *tamas*, these two also possess the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*). Because even the activity and cessation of *sattva* and *tamas* are consequent upon the operation of *rajas*, everything is nothing but suffering.

This he explains as follows: through their functions characterized by manifestation, activity, and stability, the *guṇas* are dependent upon one another for mutual assistance, even while they are mutually antagonistic.

Through the relationship of mutual assistance between one another, like oil, a wick, and fire, they initiate only a threefold cognition—tranquil (sāttvika), terrible (rājasa), and deluded (tāmasa). Because they follow one another as constituent parts, when a tranquil sāttvika cognition arises, it is immediately suppressed by a terrible rājasa cognition that seeks to emerge and is accompanied by tamas.

And when a terrible *rājasa* cognition arises, followed by other qualities, it is immediately suppressed by a rising cognition—either a deluded *tāmasa* one accompanied by *sattva*, or a *sāttvika* one accompanied by *tamas*. Likewise, a *tāmasa* cognition is alternately suppressed by the other two cognitions; and similarly, the *sāttvika* by the other two. Thus, the *guṇas* function through the process of mutual emergence and suppression.

Why? Because the fruit is the functioning of the qualities; since the qualities, which have the nature of the qualities, are established within the form of the mind, the mind is said to be subject to rapid transformation. In which tantra is this stated?

[167,13] Why, then, are the *guṇas* mutually opposed? Because multiple excellences (*atiśaya*) cannot coexist in a single place. Just as in a room there cannot be both darkness and light—each possessing its own excellence—so too, it is impossible for the *guṇas*, which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion and whose functions are illumination, activity, and restraint, to possess excellence simultaneously, whether by way of their form, such as pleasure and so forth, or by way of their function, characterized by cognition and so on.

Since universals (*sāmānya*) are non-contradictory and exist in unmanifest forms, their coexistence with manifest particularities (*atiśaya*) is logical. However, specific intensities of form (*rūpātiśaya*) and intensities of function (*vṛttyatiśaya*) are mutually contradictory. It is said that universals do indeed coexist with these intensities. Thus, when there is an intensity of the nature of pleasure (*sukha*), there is no intensity of the nature of pain (*duḥkha*) or of delusion (*moha*). Likewise, when one intensity is present, another intensity is not. Similarly, when there is an intensity in the function of knowledge (*jñāna*), there is no intensity in the function of the cause of greed (*lobha*).
Likewise, when there is an intensity in the function of any one [attribute], there is no intensity in the function of any other.

[167,22] Thus, these qualities (guṇas) have as their conditions pleasure, pain, and delusion, which are acquired through mutual dependence. Through the support of *rajas* and *tamas*, pleasure is acquired by *sattva*. Through the support of *sattva* and *tamas*, pain is acquired by *rajas*. Through the support of *sattva* and *rajas*, delusion is acquired by *tamas*. Consequently, all [qualities] become the causes of all effects.

If this is so, one might ask: "What is the distinction between this being a *sāttvika* condition, this a *tāmasa*, and this a *rājasa*? To this he says: "The distinction among these is produced by the state of being primary or subordinate. Through the status of being principal (*pradhāna*) or secondary (*upasarjana*), they receive their respective designations. For example, although all are composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), they are designated as "earthy," "fiery," or "watery."

Since there is thus a conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, therefore everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person. The phrase "due to the conflict of the functions of the *guṇas*" is intended for the sake of supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*).

As for the expression "by means of the sufferings of transformation, pain, and latent impressions" (*pariṇāma-tāpa-saṃskāra-duḥkhaiḥ*), it is formulated with separate case-endings in order to demonstrate that everything is suffering even for one who is free from craving for objects seen or heard; for detachment is not brought about for one who does not perceive the nature of suffering therein.
But this [is stated] because of the "opposition of the functions of the qualities" (*guṇavṛttivirodhāt*);

that is to say, since suffering is demonstrated by the mutually opposing functions of the qualities, detachment from them—which possess the characteristics of both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*)—is thereby cultivated. Furthermore, in this context as well, it is established that everything possesses the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest, insofar as all things exist through the relationship of primary and subordinate factors among the qualities. And having done so, the phrase "because of the opposition of the functions of the qualities" is recited separately even in the Sūtra.

Because it possesses the nature of suffering consisting of transformation, pain, and mental conditioning, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the seed for the origination of this great mass of suffering characterized by the primary and secondary qualities (*guṇas*). And its cause of non-existence is right vision (*samyagdarśana*), because it is the antidote. This is because knowledge (*vidyā*) relies upon reality as its object, whereas ignorance relies upon unreality; thus, knowledge alone is the cause of the non-existence of ignorance. Just as the perception of a single moon, which has a real object, sublates the perception of many moons, which has an unreal object.

[168,19] It has been established that everything is suffering, together with the source of suffering, characterized by afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and maturation (*vipāka*). By means of this suffering, one who is afflicted and discerning is the subject and the qualified person for this treatise on right vision (*samyagdarśana*); no other, because of being merely an experiencer of suffering. Wishing to demonstrate this by way of an illustration, he says: "Just as the science of medicine (*cikitsāśāstra*) consists of four divisions—disease, the cause of disease, health, and the medicine—so too, for one who possesses disease and its cause and desires to turn away from them, there is the treatise of medicine and health."
The object of the purpose.

In this same way, this treatise also consists of fourfold divisions, just as cyclic existence (saṃsāra), the cause of cyclic existence, liberation (mokṣa), and the cause of liberation. Among these, cyclic existence, which abounds in suffering, is that which is to be abandoned; the conjunction of the primordial matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa) is the cause of what is to be abandoned; the absolute cessation of that conjunction is abandonment; and the means of abandonment is right vision (samyagdarśana). These are the four divisions.

Just as the science of medicine is arranged to demonstrate the essential nature of four topics—the disease, the cause of the disease, health, and the medicine which serves its purpose—and for that very reason the disease and so forth are its four arrangements (vyūha), thus this treatise is "fourfold" (caturvyūha).

Saṃsāra is full of suffering and is to be abandoned; its cause is ignorance, and the cause of this conditioned saṃsāra is the conjunction of Pradhāna and Puruṣa. The abandonment of this conditioned saṃsāra is the purpose of the treatise on right vision, as is right vision itself. Thus, these four are its "arrangements" (vyūha), and so the treatise is called "fourfold-arrangement" (caturvyūha). Alternatively, it is called "fourfold-arrangement" because its arrangement regarding these subjects is fourfold.

Regarding that, as for the "nature of the knower": one might object that this should have been understood from the aphorism defining the knower, which states that "the seer is pure seeing. This is not a fault; for the author, desiring to explain the purpose of the commencement of the treatise, has established that the entire aggregate beginning with afflictions and ending in suffering is the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this treatise. It is for the sake of the discriminating person regarding that [subject matter] that the subsequent aphorisms are begun. And this was demonstrated in the first aphorism.

The very purpose of this treatise as it is being commenced is right vision (samyagdarśana). And since that [vision] has reached its proper occasion following the description of the suffering of saṃsāra, it must now be set forth; thus it is said: "In that regard, the nature of the abandoner... and so on.

The person (*puruṣa*) is neither something to be abandoned (*heya*) nor something to be accepted (*upādeya*). Why is this so? Because apart from what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, no real entity (*vastu*) is observed. The intention is this: just as in the world pleasure and its cause are to be accepted, while pain and its cause are to be abandoned, so too this person, being a real entity, ought to possess one or the other of these two qualities. What follows if this is the case? It follows that if there were abandonment of this person, it would entail the consequence of the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).

If this [self] possesses the quality of being abandonable, then it must be abandoned. But what would result from its abandonment? There would be the undesirable consequence of the doctrine of the annihilation of the self (*ātmocchedavāda*). What fault would there be in that? We shall demonstrate the fault in the *Kaivalyapāda*.

Furthermore, because this other [entity] does not exist, the abandonment [of suffering] is untenable. If it is argued that the self itself is the abandoner of the self, no; for there is a contradiction in an action being directed toward oneself, and because there is no distinction [between agent and object]. If the abandoner-self were different from the self that is to be abandoned, then there would be the consequence of infinite regress, since whatever is an abandoner must itself be something to be abandoned. Moreover, the simultaneous existence of two abandoners is impossible. Furthermore, if they occur at different times, the relationship of the abandoned and the abandoner is untenable.

Furthermore, if one accepts that the abandoner (*hātṛ*) is itself subject to abandonment, then because that abandoner would be non-enduring, the connection with the object to be abandoned (*heya*) would be untenable. Moreover, if the abandoner is non-enduring, it follows that the effort of the abandoner toward abandonment is futile, since the abandoner would realize its own state of being abandoned by itself. Furthermore, the fruit of abandonment would be unattainable; for the fruit of liberation is not simply the destruction of the bound self's own nature. Indeed, liberation is its fruit. Nor does even a dying person—whose moment of consciousness is about to perish—desire the destruction of his own nature.

Since destruction has already been attained, if the Creator were thus unstable, he would not desire the loss of his own nature, for that loss has already occurred through the attainment of its object.

We shall explain how the experiencer is eternal in the *Draṣṭṛ-sūtra* and in the *Kaivalyapāda*. Therefore, the Puruṣa is eternal and does not possess the quality of being something to be abandoned (*heya*). Transmigration, however, which consists of the manifest principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), is full of suffering and is to be abandoned. The meaning is that the Puruṣa does not possess qualities identical to those [of transmigration]. For if it possessed identical qualities, the consequence would be the doctrine of its annihilation.

[170,13] Let it be, then, that it is the appropriated, just as a substance that is a cause of pleasure is for the sake of pleasure. This is not so. Why? Because if there were appropriation of this, it would entail the consequence of a theory of causality (*hetuvāda*). If its connection with the fruit of the appropriation of substances and so forth were to be appropriated, then its appropriation would be without a cause, because there is no other appropriator. For a cloth is not appropriated by the cloth itself; rather, one thing has another as its object of appropriation. If another appropriator were possible, it would entail an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), such that that [appropriator] too would be appropriated by another, and that too by another.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of [the self] being for the sake of another. For one thing is taken up by another cause; when the *pradhāna*, characterized by *sattva* and so forth, is taken up, the *puruṣa* is accepted as its cause, just as clay is the cause when a lump of clay is taken up for the sake of a jar. If that *puruṣa* were the causal agent for the taking up of the *pradhāna*, it too would have to be taken up like the *pradhāna*, and thus it would possess the properties of *sattva* and so forth, because it is something to be taken up, just like a lump of clay. Consequently, the taking up of this *pradhāna* for the sake of an effect would result in being without a cause.

Now, if it is argued that [the world] exists for the sake of Īśvara or for the mutual benefit of puruṣas, then a collection of defects such as being an object of enjoyment, insentience, and subject to transformation would necessarily follow. Therefore, it is stated that the puruṣa is neither eternal nor does it possess the qualities of the pradhāna; furthermore, if it were a material cause (upādāna), it would entail the consequence of causal determinism (hetuvāda).

Thus it has been said: "But the cause is not a person. And if that [cause] were to take up [the effect], the activity of the Pradhāna would be without a cause and thus causeless. Furthermore, it is not possible for it to cognize its own purpose, because such self-interest is not observed in the case of light and other such things.

[171,11] In the rejection of both—that is, in the rejection of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—there follows the consequence of the doctrine of eternalism (*śāśvatavāda*), which is the consequence of asserting the permanence of the self (*ātman*). Even if the primary cause (*pradhāna*) and that which is to be accepted were eternal, nevertheless, in its nature as transformation (*vikāra*), it is indeed non-eternal. Furthermore, there are such defects as having a manifold nature, impurity, being ignorance (*avidyā*), and being for the sake of another.

If the *puruṣas* were likewise [identical] with the *pradhāna*, there would follow the consequence of no liberation; for bondage and liberation, as well as their causes—knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—would not differ in essence, and consequently, there would be no distinction between the bound and the liberated. Therefore, the doctrine of eternalism, which rejects both what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, is indeed the right vision (samyagdarśana). 2.15.

Just as a medical treatise and its purpose, which is health, cannot exist as a fourfold system without the fourfold set beginning with disease—which is distinct from the patient—likewise, this treatise on right vision and its fruit, which is liberation through abandonment, cannot exist as a fourfold system without the fourfold set beginning with that which is to be abandoned—which is distinct from the nature of the abandoner. Therefore, by means of the exposition of the fourfold set beginning with that which is to be abandoned, this treatise is described as being "fourfold."

How is future suffering to be abandoned? Past suffering has already passed; the suffering characterized by births past, having been transcended from the present birth, has been exhausted and carried away through its own experience, and thus it does not belong to the category of what is to be abandoned, because it has already ceased of its own accord.

Furthermore, that suffering characterized by the present birth, which has mounted upon the experience of its own moment and is established as having its own present moment distinguished by experience—that suffering, being of the nature of what is currently being experienced, does not become something to be abandoned in another moment. Since it is itself devoid of experience, it does not require another moment for its abandonment.

Therefore, it is precisely that future suffering—characterized by the pain of rebirth occurring immediately after death—which, like an eye-ball, afflicts the yogin; thus, it is that alone which is to be abandoned, and it is said to be relinquished through right vision (*samyagdarśana*). One must strive solely for the non-existence of future birth, not for the cessation of present suffering.

For if one were to strive for a present birth, right vision would be useless because it could not be applied due to lack of efficacy; this is because the present suffering has already set its fruit in motion, like a released arrow. However, since future [suffering] has not yet begun, the cessation of the seed is possible, and thus right vision becomes purposeful. For that [future suffering] is indeed the proper object of right vision. (2.16)

It has been stated that this treatise is said to consist of four sections (*caturvyūha*); thus, one section among the four, namely "suffering to be abandoned in the future," has been explained. Now, the second section—the cause or reason for that suffering—is being pointed out.

[172,15] Is it not the case that the cause of suffering has already been specified, and thus it was concluded at the end in the same way: "Ignorance is the seed for the arising of this entire great mass of suffering"? True, it is so; however, previously only the nature of suffering and the nature of its cause were specified. And the cause of suffering is not specified merely by its nature alone. Rather, the conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned.
The seer is the Puruṣa, whose characteristics will be described hereafter, who is the experiencer of the intellect (buddhi).
"Experiencer" means one whose nature it is to experience. Of what? Of the intellect. The intellect is the object of perception; it is the internal organ in the form of cognitive modifications.

But surely, objects such as sound and the rest are also directly perceived; to this he replies: all phenomena, including sound and the rest, are mounted upon the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*). Mounted upon the *sattva* of the intellect, they are perceived only as the forms of intellectual cognitions, not in themselves. If they were perceptible in their own right, the *puruṣa* would possess objects that are both known and unknown; however, it is established by reasoning that for the *puruṣa*, objects are always known. Therefore, all phenomena are perceived only when mounted upon the intellect.

This very object of perception is like a magnet; just as a magnet assists even iron by means of its functional activity, so too does it assist the Person (puruṣa) by means of the two-fold purpose of the Person—characterized as experience and liberation—and thus, like a magnet, it belongs to its own master, the self whose nature is pure consciousness (cittatva).

How is it "its own"? To this he says: "having become the object of action" (*karmaviṣayatvam āpannam*). Action itself is the object; thus, "the object of action" means precisely the attainment of the state of being an object. It has become the object of that which has the nature of seeing (*dṛśirūpa*), meaning it has attained the state of being visible (*dṛśyatām āpanna*). How, having come into being, does it attain the state of being an object of action? To specify this, he says: "having acquired its self-nature through another's form" (*anyasvarūpeṇa pratilabdhātmakam*).

[173,13] That which has acquired its own nature through a different form— namely, the forms of another person or self, and primordial form— and which has acquired specific forms and the specific intrinsic natures of sounds and so forth belonging to a person, becomes "one's own" (sva) for the purpose of liberation when it attains the state of being an object (karmatām āpanna) by virtue of being visible in the form of a person. Likewise, that which has acquired its own nature through the forms of sound and so forth becomes "one's own" for the purpose of experience when it attains the state of being an object by virtue of being visible.

[173,17] Now, how can that which is independent possess ownership? For nothing that is independent, while acting by itself, depends upon anything else. Even that which consists of the human goal produced as a consequence of its own activity arises from its very nature; it does not act through the command of a person. Therefore, it is argued that it is not logical for that which is independent to have ownership. To this he replies: although it is independent, because it acts for the sake of another by being the agent of the two types of human goals, it is dependent; and therefore, it is indeed "one's own" (sva).

"Of those two, the power of seeing and the power of being seen"—having begun with "the seer and the seen," the conclusion is stated as "the power of seeing and the power of being seen. This is formulated to demonstrate that this connection is beginningless, having raised the objection that the conjunction of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*) must have a beginning because it occurs immediately after the arising of the intellect. The conjunction of the power of seeing and the power of being seen is beginningless. Because the substrata are eternal, a permanent relationship is established; thus, the conjunction characterized by the state of being the seer and the seen between those two powers is also beginningless, being produced by purpose—that is, impelled by the aim of the person (*puruṣārtha*). This is the meaning.

And this being so, even though [the connection] is beginningless, the cessation of conjunction is possible upon the cessation of its purpose. However, for those engaged in action, the essential-nature conjunction exists by mere presence and is not produced by a purpose; thus, it is eternal. But the conjunction with merely adventitious attributes (*dharma*) is non-eternal because those attributes are non-eternal. That conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), however, is the cause of that which is to be abandoned; the meaning is that it is the cause of suffering.

And thus it is said in the *Tantra*: "Because of the avoidance of the cause of their conjunction"—that is, because of the avoidance of that ignorance (*avidyā*) which is the cause of the conjunction between those two, namely the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*puruṣa*). How is there avoidance? Through knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, through right vision (*samyagdarśana*), by means of its counteragent, [ignorance] is brought to an end. Therefore, from the avoidance of the cause of their conjunction, there arises an absolute remedy for suffering, one that exists for all time. What is this? It is right vision.

To explain how this is so, he provides a well-known example: just as the sole of the foot is susceptible to being pierced because it is soft and tender, and the thorn is capable of piercing because its nature is harsh, it is established by implication that their conjunction is a specific cause of suffering. In that regard, the avoidance of the pain caused by the thorn consists in not placing the foot upon the thorn.

He who knows this pair—the duality of the pierced and the piercer, or the duality of the two ways of avoidance—initiates one of those methods of avoidance in this world. By initiating [the remedy] there at every moment, he does not experience the pain born of piercing, such as that produced by the piercing of a thorn.

[174,19] Likewise here too, the Puruṣa, by way of the principle of *sattva*, [perceives] *pradhāna* as being like a thorn; their specific conjunction is independent of the objects of perception which lack any distinction [from themselves]. Having realized through right vision (*samyagdarśana*) the absence of any further purpose, and because the Puruṣa is immutable, and because the karma that initiates the body—like standing upon a thorn—is necessarily to be experienced, [the Puruṣa remains detached].

Having understood that sound and other objects arise unbidden as results [of past karma], their enjoyment occurs through a being that is separated from right vision (samyagdarśana). Perceiving the avoidance in this way, one does not undergo the suffering of saṃsāra, just as one avoids the pain of being pierced by a thorn.
Why is this so? Because of the capacity for perceiving a triad;

that is, because of the capacity for perceiving the triad consisting of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), the person (*puruṣa*), and their conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For the capacity of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is observed in this way: in the case of the foot, the thorn, and their conjunction, whereas for one who lacks such knowledge, the fact that these three do not constitute a perceived triad is seen to be the very cause of suffering.

[175,10] Desiring to explain this point, he says: "In this context, of the tormenting *rajas*. Although *pradhāna* is the primary tormentor, comparable to a thorn, nevertheless, because *rajas* is of the nature of suffering, it is stated that the tormenting power of *pradhāna* occurs precisely through the medium of *rajas*; thus, it is said, "of the tormenting *rajas*. Of that *rajas*, *sattva* alone is the object to be tormented (*tapyam*). Why? Because, like the action of cutting, the action of tormenting resides in the object.

For the action of heating occurs with respect to the object (karman), not with respect to the person who possesses the senses and is the subject of the passion that causes the heat; this is because the result of the heating has the person as its locus.

For an axe does not function upon itself or in that which is other than itself; rather, the act of cutting and its fruit reside only in the object to be cut, such as wood. In the same way, the suffering of the Puruṣa, while residing in the *sattva* through its activity, has passion (*rajas*) as its fruit; just as the axe acts upon the wood, the *sattva* of the Puruṣa functions only within the field of the visible.

For this reason as well, the action of heating does not reside in the person (puruṣa), because the seer is unchanging. For heating, too, is a modification of the object; just as the result of cutting is the bifurcation of the object being cut, so it is here. It cannot reside in the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is inactive and unchanging. And his state of being unchanging will be established by the fact that his objects are always known.

[175,23] If this is so, then the claim that "the *pradhāna* acts for the sake of the *puruṣa* because the *puruṣa* does not experience suffering" is untenable; for this has already been answered by the argument regarding the conformity of their functions (*vṛttisārūpya*). This very point is stated here as well: "Because its object has been shown. Since the *puruṣa* is unchanging and immutable, its object is said to be "shown. Therefore, when the object of seeing is the *sattva*, the *puruṣa* experiences suffering, conforming to and following its form. This conformity to its form occurs in the intellect (*bauddha*) through the proximity of that seeing.

The appearance of the intellect (pratyaya) as having the form of the Seer is like the appearance of a crystal as having the form of lac when in proximity to lac-dye; in the same way, it is metaphorically said that "the Puruṣa also suffers. (2.17)

The nature of the object of perception (*dṛśya*) is now stated. But was it not said in the previous sūtra, "of the perceiver and the perceived"? In that case, the nature of the perceiver (*draṣṭṛ*), which follows in the sequence of proximity, ought to have been explained first. This is not a fault, because the realization of the nature of the perceiver is preceded by the comprehension of the nature of the object of perception. For since the object of perception exists for the sake of a perceiver distinct from itself, the existence of a distinct perceiver is established. Precisely because of its primacy, the perceiver was placed first in the previous sūtra; however, in defining its characteristics, the logical order of meaning is intended here.

The "object of perception" (*dṛśya*) consists of the elements and the sense organs, and its nature is illumination, activity, and inertia; it exists for the sake of experience and liberation. Illumination, activity, and inertia are "illumination-activity-inertia. Because illumination is the most important, it is placed first. Since there is no fixed rule when many qualities are listed, there is no fixed rule regarding the order of the words "inertia" and "activity"; thus, the word "activity" is placed first. That which has these very qualities is "that whose nature is illumination, activity, and inertia. [Objection: How can *sattva* have the nature of illumination and activity? For it is *rajas* that has that nature. And how can *tamas* have the nature of inertia? For it is *sattva* that has that nature.

[176,18] But is it not the case that the very nature [of the thing] is its manifestation and its persistence? No; because the word *śīla* (habitual disposition) cannot apply to mere nature. For one who has the nature of playing the mṛdaṅga drum is not called a *mārdaṅgika* (drummer); rather, he is said to be one whose habitual disposition is the playing of the mṛdaṅga. Indeed, the word *śīla* is never employed with respect to anything devoid of activity.

[176,21] But surely stability (*sthiti*) and illumination (*prakāśa*) are also the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of *sattva* and *tamas*. Therefore, it follows by this very fact that the word "nature" (*śīla*) would apply to the intrinsic nature itself. It is replied: the word "nature" is not employed everywhere in reference to the intrinsic nature alone. Here too, regarding *rajas*, which has suffering as its intrinsic nature, the designation "nature" (*śīla*) is applied by connecting it with activity, as in "the nature of activity. Stability and illumination are also intended here as being of the form of functional operation (*vyāpāra*).

[176,25] Now, it might be argued that activity (*kriyā*) is indeed the very nature (*svarūpa*) of *rajas*. This is not so, because the equilibrium (*sāmya*) of the *guṇas* is admitted in the state of *pradhāna*. If activity were the nature of *rajas*, then *pradhāna* would also possess activity during the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*. For it is only in the state of manifestation (*kāryāvasthā*) that activity is admitted, not at the time of *pradhāna*. Therefore, the term "characteristic" (*śīla*) is used not with the intention of referring to an essential nature, but rather to something eternal.

In that regard, although *sattva* and *tamas* are by nature inactive (*akriyāśīla*), they possess activity solely through the activity of *rajas*, because of their constant conjunction with *rajas*, which is active by nature; this applies even to *sattva* and *tamas* in their functions of stability and illumination. Thus, by metaphorical attribution of that activity, *sattva* is designated as "active by nature" (*prakāśaśīla*) and *tamas* as "stable by nature" (*sthitiśīla*). Since the acquisition of their own essence for both stability and illumination is preceded by the activity of *rajas*, and since they manifest only when in motion, these dispositions of activity are attributed to *sattva* and *tamas*.

In this regard, that which has the nature of illumination is *sattva*; that which has the nature of activity and the nature of engagement is *rajas*; and that which has the nature of stability, the nature of obstruction, and the nature of restriction is *tamas*. These are the *guṇas*, whose distinctions are mutually colored—that is, those *guṇas* whose distinct divisions are colored by one another.

Just as it is said here that *sattva* is characterized by luminosity, so too, although *sattva* is capable of illuminating everything, its luminosity is restricted by its being colored (*uparaktatva*) by *rajas*. Likewise, the manifestation of activity in *rajas* occurs through its coloring by *sattva*, while its activity is restricted by its coloring by *tamas*. Similarly, the manifestation of stability in *tamas* occurs through its coloring by *sattva*, while its nature of stability is due to its coloring by *rajas*; yet stability itself arises from its own nature.

The activity of rajas occurs spontaneously, and the illumination of sattva likewise occurs spontaneously; in this same manner, the mutual coloring of sattva and the other guṇas should be understood in all other effects as well.

They possess the nature of conjunction and disjunction. Both conjunction and disjunction constitute "conjunction-disjunction"; those which have these as their properties are "possessors of the nature of conjunction and disjunction. When some effect is being initiated, they join with one another through the relationship of subordinate and principal factors. Likewise, when another property arises that is incompatible with the effect already initiated, they become mutually separated.

Those whose forms are acquired through mutual dependence: those forms, beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the post (*stamba*), have their forms acquired through mutual dependence; those by whom the characteristics of dharma and adharma are thus acquired are "those whose forms are acquired through mutual dependence."

Although they are distinct from one another and, in the ultimate sense, mutually different, their distribution of powers is undifferentiated; yet, there exists a distinction in their capacity for being oriented toward the commencement of effects that are entirely excluded [from one another].

This is what is meant: when a single effect is to be initiated, the constituent causes possess mutually interpenetrating powers at the time of that initiation, such that the distinction between their respective powers cannot be perceived as separate.

[178,9] Those which follow the distinctions of power (śakti-prabheda) among things of the same class and things of different classes—namely, for those of the nature of *sattva*, there is *sattva* as their common class; for those of the nature of *rajas*, there is *rajas* as their common class; and for those of the nature of *tamas*, there is *tamas*. Yet, in relation to one another, they possess different classes. "Those which follow the distinctions of power among things of the same class and things of different classes" means those whose nature is to conform to the specific variations of power belonging to both homogeneous and heterogeneous entities. For it is not possible for an undertaking of action to begin—whether in the realm of *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*—without conforming to the specific variations of power of these three.

[178,15] If this is so, then because each [cause] falls within the differentiation of all capacities, their predominance would be equal at the commencement of every single effect; therefore, he says: "At the time of predominance, the presence of all [causes] is demonstrated. When one [cause] acts as the predominant factor in initiating its own effect, the presence of the others at that time is likewise demonstrated in a subordinate (upasarjana) manner. Thus, they are said to have their presence demonstrated at the time of predominance. For it is not the case that all [causes] possess predominance simultaneously;
for if there were equality of predominance, they would be merely "predominant" [in name], and would not possess the status of being initiators of an effect.

Now, if it is asked: "How, moreover, is the existence of the others understood through the predominance of one when they initiate the effect? To this it is said: by way of being subordinate (*guṇatva*) and being auxiliary (*upasarjanabhāva*), and by means of mere activity (*vyāpāramātra*) characterized by the predominant factor; that is, by means of mere activity subsumed within the predominant factor. For an activity subsumed within the predominant factor would not be possible if the other two were absent due to their auxiliary status. Thus, their existence is inferred by means of the activity of the predominant factor.

[179,9] Those whose capacities are directed toward the performance of the human purpose (*puruṣārtha-itikartavyatā-prayukta-sāmarthyāḥ*): the human purpose consists of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*); the "performance" (*itikartavyatā*) of that purpose is the capacity directed toward the undertaking of an action in such a way that the object is accomplished. Those whose capacities are thus directed toward the performance of the human purpose are called "those whose capacities are directed toward the performance of the human purpose."
They are "benefactors by mere proximity" because they benefit the Person (puruṣa) merely by the presence of their form as objects of transformation. They are like magnets.

Following the entire mode of existence characterized by stability belonging to any one of them, without [the intervention of] cognition, they come to be designated by the term "Pradhāna. There is no other thing called Pradhāna apart from the three *guṇas* themselves; it is those very *guṇas* in a state of equilibrium that receive the singular designation "Pradhāna. When they undergo disequilibrium, they become subject to the designations of "transformations" (*vikāra*) and possess a mode of activity (*vṛtti*).

This is called the "visible" (dṛśya). This visible consists of the elements, the sense organs, and the self; that is, it consists of the elements and it consists of the sense organs. To the question of how it consists of those, he says: "by way of being the elements."

By means of earth and the other elements, both subtle and gross—that is, by means of the subtle form of the *tanmātras* and the gross form of the specific objects (*viśeṣas*)—the elemental state is indeed twofold: consisting of the *tanmātras* and consisting of the specific objects. It undergoes transformation, attaining both gross and subtle states. By means of the sense organs—that is, by means of the forms of the senses such as hearing, both subtle and gross—it undergoes transformation; [it transforms] into the subtle form of the *ahaṃkāra* and into the gross form of the senses such as hearing.

But that object of perception is not without purpose, for one observes that activity occurs everywhere only when a purpose is seen. Furthermore, one engages with an object only after having accepted its purpose. What, then, is the purpose of engaging with the object of perception? He says: "For the object of perception exists for the sake of the isolation of the portions [of the guṇas], just as fire and other things exist for the sake of the realization [of their nature] by the Puruṣa."

[180,9] He says that there are two states: enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). In this regard, the determination of the essential nature of desirable and undesirable qualities—which has reached a state of non-discrimination—is as follows: the determination of the essential nature, the comprehension of the essential nature, and the ascertainment of the essential nature of desirable qualities characterized by the touch of aloeswood, sandalwood, and so forth; and of undesirable qualities characterized by the touch of swords, thorns, and so forth, which are of a contrary nature. Its qualification is "having reached a state of non-discrimination," meaning it has attained a state of non-distinction from the cognition of the Puruṣa, such that one does not [discriminate] "this is the Puruṣa" and "this is the *sattva*."
Because the cognition has assumed a form through the appropriation of consciousness, that state of the cognition is designated as the experience of the Puruṣa.

Therefore, having distinguished the cognizer from the object of experience—that is, from the nature of enjoyment—by means of discriminative discernment, the ascertainment of the nature of that which is of the form of pure seeing is called *apavarga* (liberation). This is because, even after the cessation of mental fluctuations, there is no difference from the nature of the experiencer as it is being ascertained; for then he is established forever in his own nature. "Conformity with the fluctuations" is the distinction in other states.

[180,19] Apart from these two—enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*)—there is no other third view. As long as there is ignorance (*avidyā*), so long do the desirable and undesirable exist; thus, this is indeed enjoyment. Since the *puruṣa* is by nature neither to be rejected nor accepted, how can there be enjoyment when it is definitively determined? Therefore, the cognition that definitively determines the *puruṣa* is the counter-cognition (*pratipakṣa-pratyaya*) to the cognition characterized by ignorance which takes the form of enjoyment. For this reason, it is impossible to conceive of a third philosophical system distinct from these two views.

And so it has been said: "Indeed, one who possesses such right vision (*samyagdarśin*) perceives that while the three *guṇas*—possessing the characteristics already described—are the agents that bring about the cessation of all activity, the Puruṣa is the fourth, distinct from the nature of the *guṇas*, a non-agent who is their witness. Like a bystander witnessing the proceedings of a legal assembly, he observes all states of being brought forward by the *guṇas* characterized as internal organs; because their objects have been revealed, these manifested states are merely derivative (*gauṇa*)."

Seeing and perceiving things as fully established in the form of Buddhist concepts, he does not suspect that there could be any right view other than "I am not" and "this is not mine"; rather, he considers that there is simply no other right view at all.

To that extent, enjoyment and liberation are produced by the intellect (*buddhi*) and brought about by the intellect; they exist only within the intellect. It is observed that what is produced by one may reside in another, as for example, the dyeing of cloth performed by a washerman. How then can these two be attributed to the *puruṣa*? They are attributed to the *puruṣa* because they exist only in the intellect. Why is this so? Because he is the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) of their respective fruits, and because he perceives both correct and false cognitions.

He concludes the meaning explained by means of the illustration, "just as victory or defeat": bondage is precisely the intellect’s failure to complete its purpose. As long as the intellect thinks that enjoyment and liberation remain to be accomplished, so long is there bondage. Liberation is the final determination regarding that purpose. This final determination of the purpose by that very intellect is the completion of what was to be done. When the Self is perceived as distinct from the intellect and as the Puruṣa unrelated to bondage and liberation, [the intellect realizes] "there is nothing further to be done for this"; that final determination regarding what was to be done is the liberation of the intellect.

By this it should be understood that the acts of grasping, retaining, cognizing, deliberating, rejecting, speaking, ascertaining according to rule, and adhering are superimposed as existing upon the *puruṣa*. Since there is no difference in their being merely modifications (*pratyaya*), these qualities of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) exist only in the intellect, are produced by the intellect, and are superimposed as existing upon the *puruṣa* in such ways as "the *puruṣa* grasps" and "the *puruṣa* retains. Thus they are superimposed upon the *puruṣa*.

The apprehension (*grahaṇa*) of sounds and so forth by means of the auditory and other faculties is "perception" (*upādāna*). The non-forgetting of what has been perceived is "retention" (*dhāraṇā*). The determination of the general and specific characteristics of what has been retained is "cognition" (*vijñāna*). The mental deliberation (*ūha*) arising from a desire to further investigate the specific details regarding that which has already been cognized is "reflection" (*ūha*). The exclusion (*vyudāsana*) of contradictory properties (*dharma*) concerning what has been reflected upon is "negation" (*apoha*). Engagement with objects is "action" (*kriyā*). A particular state of the mind directed toward a sentence is "speech" (*vacana*).

Whatever principle is appropriate for a given object, and whatever its logical justification may be, the ascertainment of it exactly as it is constitutes "ascertainment according to principle" (*yathānyāyāvadhāraṇam*). Furthermore, the application of the mind toward that [ascertainment] again and again, in order to prevent wavering from correct cognition, is "adherence" (*abhiniveśa*). These factors, beginning with "grasping" (*grahaṇa*), have their existence superimposed upon the Person (*puruṣa*); for he is the enjoyer of their fruit—that is, the experiencer of the fruit of grasping and the rest. (2.18)

In order to determine the distinctions in the essential nature of the perceptible qualities (*guṇas*) as they have been described, and in order to determine the distinctions among their states of reality (*tattva-avasthā*), this aphorism is commenced: "The stages of the *guṇas* are the specific (*viśeṣa*), the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*), the mere mark (*liṅgamātra*), and the unmarked (*aliṅga*). The specific (*viśeṣa*), the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*), the mere mark (*liṅgamātra*), and the unmarked (*aliṅga*)—the object called *pradhāna* (the primary cause) is so termed because it does not mark (*na liṅgati*) anything, nor does it come from anywhere. Thus, by the rule *pacād yañ sarvadhātubhyaḥ*, the suffix *yañ* is applied in its etymological sense (*yaugika*), and it takes the gender of the word it denotes.

Alternatively, "aliṅga" means that for which no *liṅga*—that is, no mark, cognition, or determination—exists by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the object called *pradhāna*; this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

And those *viśeṣas* and so forth "fulfill" (*piparti*) the intention of the *puruṣa* by bestowing experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), or they "complete" (*piparti*) their own transformations; thus, from the root *pṛ*, the suffix *vanip* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule "it is seen after other roots as well. This being the case, that which ends in *n* when not denoting the agent is neuter; however, that which ends in *n* when denoting the agent possesses all genders, as in *berudṛśvā* and *merudṛśvanī*. Consequently, the *viśeṣas* and so forth are "joints" (*parvāṇaḥ*). To whom do they belong? They are the joints of the qualities (*guṇa-parvāṇaḥ*).
For some, this very reading is: "The stages of the qualities (guṇaparvāṇi) consist of the specific, the non-specific, the subtle elements (liṅgamātra), and the unmanifest (aliṅga)."

In this context, ether, air, fire, water, and earth are the gross elements (*bhūta*). Ether is originated from the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Air is originated by the subtle element of touch, which is characterized by both sound and touch. Fire is originated by the subtle element of form, which is characterized by the triad of sound, touch, and form. Water is originated by the subtle element of taste, which is characterized by the tetrad of sound, touch, form, and taste. Earth is originated by the subtle element of smell, which is characterized by the pentad of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

But is space not eternal, because there is no difference between it prior to production and at the time of its destruction? For in the case of each thing such as earth that possesses production, a difference is observed prior to its production and after its destruction. Likewise, if space were produced, there would have to be a difference prior to its production and after its destruction; yet no such difference exists. Therefore, space is unproduced.

If it is argued that the distinction lies in the absence of the granting of space, we say no; for there is nothing else besides that which possesses form, and thus the two are equal even in their eternity. Furthermore, space is eternal because it lacks the characteristics of the impermanent, owing to its all-pervasiveness, like the self and other such entities.

No—because it contradicts scripture (*āgama*). For there is a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "From this very Self, space (*ākāśa*) was produced. There is also a contradiction with traditional law (*smṛti*). If it is argued that the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) applies because it provides room [for other elements], we say no; for then the same metaphorical application would follow even for air and the other elements, since they are part of the same syntactical unity: "From space, air was produced."

[183,17] Furthermore, by asserting that "because there is no distinction prior to its production, it is not impermanent," you have effectively stated that "the absence of distinction constitutes permanence. This being the case, since even the self (*ātman*) and other entities lack distinctions such as bondage, liberation, or perception, it would follow as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the Vaiśeṣika existent itself is impermanent. Likewise, it would follow that atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth are also impermanent.

If it is argued that what is intended is the presence and absence of specific qualities before and after the very moment of origination—no, for that would entail the undesirable consequence of accepting the origination of space (*ākāśa*). If it is argued that even by one who asserts the origination of space, no such distinction can be stated—no, for there exists the distinction of being or not being a means to achieve the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, the reason "because of being all-pervading" (*sarvagatatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

[184,1] Space, consciousness, and minds are non-pervasive, impermanent, and exist for the sake of others rather than for their own sake, like a jar and other such objects. Furthermore, they possess the quality of origination because they are distinct from *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*, like a jar and other such objects. Thus, space possesses origination and is impermanent because it is an object of the external senses, like a jar and other such objects; because it is an element (*bhūta*), like earth; because it possesses qualities such as sound produced by conjunction with impermanent substances, like earth and the other elements; and because it causes irritation that can be removed by medical treatment, like wind. And so too is the sky.
An aggravation that cannot be remedied by treatment has become well known among physicians; by this, the similarity with the non-eternal is explained.

And these elements are the "particulars" (viśeṣa) of the "non-particulars" (aviśeṣa), which are the subtle elements (tanmātra) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. They are called "particulars" because they possess many particular qualities such as being calm, terrible, or delusive; and they are called "non-particulars"—that is, the subtle elements—because they lack such qualities as being calm and so forth.

Likewise, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are sense organs (*buddhīndriya*) because they exist for the purpose of the cognition of objects such as sound; they are inferred solely by means of the cognitions of their respective objects. The organs of action (*karmendriya*)—speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—are the effectors of actions such as speaking, and they are likewise inferred from those very actions. If it is argued that the organs of action, such as speech and so forth, are not established, we say no, because they are well-known from scripture (*śruti*). For, with reference to the organs, all the Vedas state: "Speech is the single unifying ground" (*vāg ekāyanam*), and so on.

Furthermore, in all instances of the Smṛtis, they possess the nature of sense organs (*indriyatva*) because they involve engagement in and withdrawal from the objects of injunctions and prohibitions, just like the ear and other senses. This is established by such [Smṛti rules] as "one should not be fickle with speech" and "one should not be fickle with hands or feet," which demonstrate engagement in and withdrawal from the objects of injunctions and prohibitions.

Likewise, the organs such as speech and the rest possess skillfulness, just like the eyes and other senses. Furthermore, the capacity of the sense organs is indeed accepted as existing in all limbs, since the functioning of the instruments [of action] is observed there. For snakes and the like, whose speech, anus, and so forth are present, and for those who are mute or impotent, the organ of generation is located precisely in the mouth. The eleventh is the mind (*manas*), which has all things as its object—namely, objects of the past, future, and present—as well as the objects of both the cognitive and active organs.

These eleven organs belong to that which is characterized by *asmitā*. *Asmitā* is the state of "I-am-ness," the notion "I am. That of which this is the characteristic is "characterized by *asmitā*"; for it is by the notion of *asmitā* that the sixth principle, called the *aviśeṣa*, namely *ahaṅkāra* (ego), is characterized or indicated. These are the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*) of that *aviśeṣa*. This sixteenfold transformation into the specific consists of the qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the rest, which abide in the form of the non-specific; among these, earth is predominant in *sattva* because it is the object of perception.

Even though these [elements] are non-existent [in their own right], there is a distinction among them based on what is subordinate and what is predominant. (185,12) The organs of action, because they are luminous, abound in *sattva*; however, the five cognitive organs, with the mind as the sixth, abound in *sattva* due to the predominance of illumination. The organs of hearing and the others abound in *rajas* due to the predominance of activity.

There are six non-distinctions (*aviśeṣas*). They are as follows: "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*) and "mere touch" (*sparśamātra*); here, even though there are two characteristics, the designation is made by means of the predominant one. Likewise, "mere form" (*rūpamātra*); here, even though there are three characteristics, the designation is made by means of the predominant one. Similarly, in the case of the latter two as well, the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding distinctions such as "peaceful" (*śānta*), "terrible" (*ghora*), and so forth. The divisions of one, two, three, four, and five characteristics are as follows: the division of the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*) has the single characteristic of the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*).

The specific variety of the subtle element of touch is characterized by sound and touch; in this manner, it should be understood that each subsequent [subtle element] possesses one additional quality. And the sixth non-specific [principle] is the mere "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātra); with respect to the subtle elements such as sound and the rest, it is the sixth non-specific [principle] among the eleven organs.

These are the first manifestation of the unmanifest *pradhāna*—which consists of mere existence, mere being, mere mark, and mere form—as the sprouting of a seed. Of the Self, which is the Great (*mahat*) in its substantial form due to its greatness relative to all specific and non-specific qualities, there are six transformations of the non-specific; these very six non-specific transformations are the modifications of *sattva* and the other *guṇas* when they abide in the form of the Great.

That which is supreme, subtle, beyond the specific elements, the mere indicative mark (*liṅgamātra*), the Great Principle (*mahattattva*)—in that, which consists of pure existence, having abided in the Great, having abided in the Great which is the nature of the cause, these [elements] experience the culmination of their growth, ending with the specific elements such as earth.

Being withdrawn and dissolved, the specific manifestations (*viśeṣa*) become indistinguishable and return toward the unmanifest (*avyakta*), abiding in that very Great Self (*mahat-ātman*) which consists of pure existence (*sattāmātra*) and pure mark (*liṅgamātra*). Of what nature is it? It is devoid of both existence and non-existence (*niḥsattāsattva*), being free from the qualities of specific and non-specific characteristics. It is "devoid of existence" (*niḥsat*) because it is non-existent (*asat*) in the sense of being slightly transformed from the unmanifest; it is "devoid of non-existence" (*niḥasad*) because it is existent (*sat*) as something more subtle than the non-specific principles; thus, the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) is called "existent and non-existent" (*sad-asat*).
The Unmanifest, however, is devoid of those qualities and is therefore called "devoid of existence and non-existence" (*niḥsad-asad*).

This is the transformation into the mere unmanifested mark (*aliṅga-mātra*) of those qualities (*guṇa*), such as *sattva* and the others, in which state the undifferentiated ones (*aviśeṣa*) reach their peak of increase and their dissolution. That which is devoid of being and non-being and is unmanifested is the transformation into the unmanifested mark (*aliṅga-pariṇāma*) of those very same qualities. Furthermore, there is no other subtle transformation of the qualities beyond this; for it has been explained that "having the subtle as its object culminates in the unmanifested."

Precisely because it is without marks (*aliṅga*), the purpose of the Puruṣa (*puruṣārtha*) is not the cause for the state of being without marks. The meaning is that the purpose of the Puruṣa is not the cause for the state of being without marks, nor is the state of being without marks impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa. He explains this as follows: "In the initial state of being without marks, the purpose of the Puruṣa is not the cause.

Why, then, is that state not impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa? To this he says: "Because in this state, the purpose of the Puruṣa does not exist as a cause; moreover, even that purpose of the Puruṣa itself—like the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest—is imperceptible even to the Lords (*īśvara*s)."

Since this is so, it is therefore explained as eternal. For whatever is impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa is seen to be non-eternal, such as the earth and other elements. And this state of the Pradhāna is not impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa; thus, it is explained as eternal.

However, regarding the three specific states—consisting of the subtle elements (*viśeṣa*), the non-specific elements (*aviśeṣa*), and the mere marks (*liṅgamātra*)—the state of the Great One (*mahat*) and the others at the beginning is impelled by the purpose of the Puruṣa. That purpose, that *puruṣārtha*, is the motive, the cause, and the reason; thus, the three states beginning with the Great One are explained as being impermanent.

The *guṇas*, however, follow after all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) and follow after all modifications (*sarvavikāra*). Just as a serpent follows after particularities such as height, crawling, and coiling, so too the *guṇas* follow after the principles (*tattva*) such as the *viśeṣas* and follow after the notions of individual objects (*piṇḍapratyaya*); they neither dissolve nor are they produced. Just as a serpent does not dissolve when its coiled state dissolves, nor is it produced when that state is produced, so it is with the *guṇas* as well. And just as clay does not dissolve nor is it produced when jars, pots, and the like dissolve or are produced.

The qualities (guṇas) appear as if they possess the properties of arising and perishing—subject to appearance and disappearance—as if undergoing the transition of past and future through their manifestations, which are themselves characterized by the three marks and consist of the persistence of the qualities while having those qualities as their material cause; yet, in their own essential nature, they neither perish nor are they born.

He provides an illustration for this very point: "Devadatta becomes poor; why? Because his cows die. The resolution is the same: his poverty results precisely from the death of the cows, not from the loss of his own essential nature. The application is equal and the reasoning is identical to the illustration. Just as Devadatta becomes poor, so too the richness of the *guṇas* consists in their increase through the manifestations (*vyakti*)—beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth—which follow upon the *guṇas* and are produced by the diversity of their mutual conflict; [this richness exists] until their dissolution.
And for those who are poor, there is neither decrease nor increase in their essential nature; thus, the meditative absorption is equal.

Since everything is an effect of the Pradhāna, why do the specific manifestations (*viśeṣas*) or the non-specific ones (*aviśeṣas*) not arise immediately? To this he says: the unmanifest (*aliṅga*) is proximate to the manifest (*liṅga*), just as the root of a tree is proximate to the seed; when combined within the seed, it is the root itself that first differentiates, and not the subsequent stages of the tree.

Thus, in that primary [principle], that mark is first perceived as being mixed and dissolved; it becomes manifest, but the subsequent specificities do not [appear] because they are remote. He says this very thing: "because there is no overstepping of the sequence," meaning because the sequence is not transgressed. For in the world, there is no overstepping of the sequence for anything that is arising.

Likewise, the six non-specific (aviśeṣa) principles previously mentioned are distinguished from one another because they are closely related and intermingled within the mere-liṅga (liṅgamātra). Why is this so? He says: "Because of the fixed order of transformation. Thus, among those non-specific principles, the elements and the senses are distinguished: within the subtle elements (tanmātras), the elements are distinguished as being intermingled; and within the mere-I-am-ness (asmitāmātra), the senses together with the mind are distinguished.

And so it was stated previously: there is no other reality beyond the specific elements (viśeṣa), such as space and the rest; the meaning is that there is no transformation into another reality distinct from the specific elements. This very point is expressed by saying that for the specific elements there is no other reality. For "reality" (tattva) indeed means that which is common to all living beings and persists until the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). There is nothing else arising from earth and the other elements that possesses such a characteristic.

However, the transformations of the dharma, the characteristic, and the state do indeed occur; the specific details of these transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state will be explained in the third chapter (pāda). 2.19.

The nature of the object of perception has been explained and determined. Now, this [sūtra] is commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the perceiver, for whose sake the object is perceived: "The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he beholds the mental modifications. The seer is the *puruṣa*, the apprehender of the object of perception whose nature has been explained. His definition is as follows: "He is pure consciousness alone," even though he is pure.

And [the phrase] "observing the conditions" (pratyayānupaśya) has been explained again; that is, the seer's abiding in its own nature and the conformity of the fluctuations with the object in other cases—those two very points are what is being established here.

"We shall establish that the person is the experiencer of the intellect (*buddhi*)," and this is now established here. "Seeing" (*dṛśi*) means vision, apprehension; that which consists of nothing but that is "pure seeing" (*dṛśimātra*). Because it is thus, it is pure. Even though it is pure, it is the observer of the mental state (*pratyaya*) of the intellect, precisely because it is pure seeing. Therefore, by observing that [intellect], it becomes of its same nature. When the activity (*vṛtti*) is in proximity to seeing, the appearance of the nature of seeing belongs to the seer; this is the conformity of the seer with the activity.

Since this [Self], which exists as pure seeing alone and is immutable by nature, perceives the cognitions born of the intellect (*buddhi*), therefore its establishment in its own essential nature is proven.

"Observing the conditions" (pratyayānupaśya) refers to this inference of their existence. How so? Because it is observed that visible objects such as jars are seen by means of something else distinct from their own nature, and because the illuminators of those objects, such as light, are themselves seen as distinct [from the objects they illuminate], it is understood—on the grounds of their being visible—that even the conditions which illuminate all objects must be seen as distinct from their own nature, just like the jars and the light that illuminates them.

And because one perceives only the cognition belonging to the Buddha, and perceives that [cognition] alone, never failing to perceive the cognition whose object is itself, therefore it is "pure seeing" (*dṛśimātra*). The inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding any other property (*dharmāntara*). By this, the notion that "the seer is the seeing" is excluded, as well as the notion of having a common substratum with fire and so forth, since the seer is nothing other than the act of seeing itself.

This is what is meant by "pure seeing" (*dṛśimātra*): the power of seeing itself is "seeing," and that very power is the "power of seeing. Nor is there any other possessor of the power of seeing; that very power is "seeing. In this context, he explains the meaning of the word "mere" (*mātra*): it means "unqualified by anything else. That is to say, it is unqualified by any particularities such as will (*icchā*) and so forth, nor by qualities (*guṇa*) or the attributes of qualities (*guṇadharma*).

That person has the nature of being a direct experiencer (*pratisaṃvedin*) of the intellect; thus he is an "experiencer. The meaning is that his essential nature is the perception of the conditions of the intellect. How is it understood that the person is an experiencer of the intellect, pure, and mere seeing? He says: "He is neither identical with the intellect nor entirely different from it. This means he does not possess the same characteristics, nor is he absolutely distinct. By stating he is "not identical," he expresses his state of being mere seeing and purity;
by stating he is "not entirely different," he expresses his conformity with the modifications (*vṛtti-sārūpya*).

Furthermore, how is it said that there is no similarity? First of all, it is not similar. Why? What is the reason? Regarding the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), he says, for the purpose of showing its difference [from the Puruṣa]: "The intellect is subject to transformation because its objects are both known and unknown. But what is this object of the intellect which is both known and unknown? That external form into which the intellect has transformed is the known; that form into which it has not transformed is the unknown.

If it were not to undergo transformation, or if, while not undergoing transformation, it were to manifest an object, then the state of being a cognizer would belong to the intellect (buddhi) at all times. Therefore, the fact that its objects are both known and unknown demonstrates its capacity for transformation. The intellect is subject to transformation because its objects are both known and unknown, like a lamp, the eye, and so forth.

The Puruṣa is of a different nature from that [Buddhi], having objects that are always known. For the object belonging to the Puruṣa is indeed always already known; therefore, the fact that the Puruṣa has objects that are always known constitutes its immutability.

He elucidates this: one might suspect that the state of being an object of knowledge for the Puruṣa is not always established; therefore, he asks, "Why?"—what is the reason? He says, "For indeed" (*na hi*), where the word *hi* serves to indicate what is well-known. Now, that which is called "intellect" (*buddhi*)—namely, the cognition belonging to the intellect (*bauddha-pratyaya*)—would be an object for the Puruṣa, whether it be unperceived or perceived. And yet, the cognition belonging to the intellect is always indeed perceived. Precisely because of that non-deviation [of the intellect from perception].

The distinctness of the Puruṣa is established. Therefore, the Puruṣa has objects that are always known. From this, its unchangeability (apariṇāmitva) is proven. "The Puruṣa is unchanging" is the proposition (pratijñā). "Because it has objects that are always known" is the reason (hetu). Intellect (buddhi) and so forth serve as the example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).

[190,21] But surely, it is the person (puruṣa) who perceives the object as determined by the intellect (buddhi), and for the person, every object of the intellect—whether known or unknown—is the same. This state of having objects both known and unknown exists because the person apprehends the object as determined by the intellect. Therefore, the person too must be subject to transformation (pariṇāmin), just like the intellect, because its objects are both known and unknown.

This is not a fault, because the object of the Puruṣa is the intellect (buddhi) alone. For it is the intellect itself, assuming the form of external objects, that is the object of the Puruṣa, and not the object in its own isolated nature. Therefore, the Puruṣa is eternal and does not possess objects that are sometimes known and sometimes unknown; whereas the intellect is always known. Thus, there is no transformation (pariṇāmitva) in the Puruṣa.

[190,27] But surely someone has said that "the person (puruṣa) perceives the object determined by the intellect (buddhi). How then can it be said that "therefore, even by them [the Sāṃkhyas], the non-transformative nature (apariṇāmitva) of the person is not accepted"? By the phrase "the object determined by the intellect," this is what is meant: he perceives the form of the intellect; he perceives the object which has assumed the form of the determination of the intellect. Otherwise, all the attributes of the intellect—such as being transformative, being for the sake of another, and acting through combination—would necessarily follow for him as well.

If it is argued that perception is impossible if there is no transformation, we say no; for perception itself is the very nature of the Puruṣa. One who imagines that the Puruṣa undergoes transformation should be asked this: what is accomplished by such transformation?
If he should say, "It is seeing," he should be answered: "Seeing is indeed the very nature of the person; therefore, transformation is purposeless."

If he should reply, "The perception of the person is not enjoyment; rather, it is modification itself that constitutes enjoyment," he should be told further: "Even so, because of its possession of modification, impermanence follows as a consequence, just as in the case of the body and so forth."

Furthermore, if it should be argued that a modification within its own self is not the cause of impermanence, but rather that modification occurring as a transition to another state is indeed the cause of impermanence, he should be answered as follows: because the state of modification itself constitutes a different state; for the modification of an entity that was previously unmodified is what constitutes a different state.

Furthermore, even if the existence of objects is admitted, it is impossible to establish a rule that there must necessarily be modification [of the self]. Nor is it the case that diamonds, lapis lazuli, and the like—which undergo modification within themselves—are not impermanent. Furthermore, there is no reason for a restrictive rule that only a vision produced by modification has a visible object as its domain, while eternal vision does not. If it is argued that perception itself is modification and not something produced by modification, then it would follow that the body and other such things, which possess modification, would also be perceptions.

Therefore, it is established that the *puruṣa* is indeed pure consciousness (*dṛśimātra*) and eternally unchanging, because its objects are always known. Although its essential nature is that of the final perception, this designation—“he sees,” “he will see,” or “he saw”—is caused by the presence or absence of the cognitions of the perceivable objects, just like the designation of the sun’s illumination. For example, although the sun is simply the illuminator, the designations “the sun illuminates,” “it will illuminate,” or “it illuminated” are caused by the presence or absence of the objects to be illuminated. Purity and so forth are the reasons by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), while the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth are the examples.

For this reason as well, it is dissimilar: because it determines all objects—that is, because it determines the entire range of objects such as the gross and the subtle—the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of the three *guṇas*, like the auditory organ and the others. "The witness of the *guṇas*" is the reason for its being a witness. "The *puruṣa* is devoid of the three *guṇas*" is the proposition (*pratijñā*). By way of contrast (*vaidharmya*), that which is not the intellect and so forth serves as the example; and because it is devoid of the three *guṇas*, it is dissimilar.

[192,16] "In that case, let it be that [the Self] is indeed dissimilar. And consequently, because of this absolute dissimilarity, the experience of objects would be impossible. To this it is replied: It is not absolutely dissimilar. Why? What is the reason here? The intention is that there is no reason to establish absolute dissimilarity for the pure [Self], which is by nature dissimilar from the intellect (buddhi), on account of an impure mental state (bauddha-pratyaya).

[192,19] This is because the status of being the witness of the intellect and its objects is established. For even though he is pure, he observes the mental modification (*bauddha-pratyaya*); and that observation of the mental modification has already been proven. The meaning of "he observes" is that when there is a transformation into the form of the object, he perceives the mental modification.
