Even while observing it, he is not of the nature of that [modification], nor is he composed of the three *guṇas*. Nevertheless, he appears as if identical with it, as if having the character of the determinations of the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded.

Therefore, [the Puruṣa] is eternal and not absolutely dissimilar [to the intellect], because of the conformity of its activity. In this regard, what was stated—that we shall demonstrate that the Puruṣa is the experiencer of the intellect—has now been demonstrated; likewise, that conformity has been shown. Thus it is said in the *Tantra*: "The power of the enjoyer is unchanging, its nature being as previously explained—the power of vision—and it does not undergo transfer into the mental modification (*pratyaya*), which is an object of the intellect and subject to transformation."

As if reflected because it is the object of the conditions, as if following its movement—that is, following the movement of this intellect—it perceives because it is the seer. The mental modification (bauddha-pratyaya), at the very moment it arises, becomes the object of the power of vision. The power of the enjoyer (bhoktṛ-śakti), perceiving by following that [modification], attains the form of the apprehension of consciousness; and by means of that mental modification through which the form of the apprehension of consciousness—the form of the apprehension by the Puruṣa—has been attained, [the power of the enjoyer] attains that form.

Like a red-hot iron ball that has taken on the form of fire, because it is the object of the act of seeing, the modification of consciousness (buddhi-vṛtti) is merely a semblance; being non-different from the modification of consciousness—merely through its conformity with it—the modification of the knower (jña-vṛtti) is designated as "the knower" itself, or simply as "perception," which is the modification itself. 2.20.

The very purpose of that [purusha] is the nature of the object of vision; by that term, the seer—the pure one who consists of mere seeing—is restated as having attained his true self. "For the sake of that" means for its purpose, having that as its objective; the meaning is: for the sake of being the object of the act of seeing. This occurs in the form of experience (*bhoga*) and in the form of liberation (*apavarga*). To the question "What is this?", he says: "The nature of the object of vision," that is, the nature of *pradhāna*, its own form, which is the attainment of its own form.

[193,19] But surely, since it was intended to explain the state of the fourfold arrangement (*caturvyūhatva*), why is this irrelevant matter being stated? This is not a fault, because the purpose of the ultimate cessation of suffering (*ātyantikaduḥkhanivṛtti*) is the subject at hand. How so? Because it is stated that the absolute cessation of suffering is achieved through the determination that the object of perception exists for the sake of another.

It is said: if the acquisition of the nature of the object-of-sight were for the sake of that [Puruṣa], then, when all objects for his sake have ceased, there would be an absolute detachment from the object-of-sight because his purpose has been fulfilled and there is no further task to be done; for there is no motive for its recurrence, since what has already been accomplished does not require to be accomplished again. If, on the other hand, the acquisition of the nature of the object-of-sight were for its own sake, then it would proceed again and again due to the persistence of its own interest, and consequently, there would be no final cessation. Therefore, it is determined that the object-of-sight exists solely for the sake of the Puruṣa.

The absence of an intrinsic purpose for the object of perception—which acquires its own nature through being perceived—is established because it is an object of enjoyment, like rice and the like; this is due to its insentience and its functioning through combination. Thus it is said: "The object of perception has become the domain of the action of the Puruṣa, whose nature is seeing. The word "iti" (thus) signifies a reason. For that very purpose does the object of perception acquire its self, meaning it acquires its essential form. The acquisition of its own nature by the Pradhāna is solely for the sake of the Puruṣa, because it falls under the action of seeing, just like rice and the like.

[194,12] He now declares the purpose of the Sūtra: Furthermore, because that purpose is fixed, once the Spirit (puruṣa)—having acquired its own nature and having obtained the support of consciousness—has accomplished the ends of experience and liberation, it is no longer seen by the Spirit; for there remains nothing further to be done apart from experience and liberation. ||2.21||

He establishes the connection with the Sūtra: for that person for whom the object of perception has already fulfilled its purpose, it would no longer undergo the state of being an object of sight; thus, there would be a loss of its own nature (*svarūpa*). And because of this loss of its own nature, its destruction would follow. Yet, it does not perish in its entirety. Why? What is the reason?

Because the primary natures (*pradhāna*) are manifold for each individual soul (*puruṣa*), it is thought that [the nature] has indeed perished only with respect to that one whose purpose has been accomplished.

[194,19] Even though it has perished with respect to one whose purpose has been accomplished, it has not perished because it is common to others. With respect to that one person whose purpose has been fulfilled—meaning for whom its function has been completed by effecting experience and liberation—it has "perished" because it no longer functions in the form of effects and instruments; yet, since there is no distinction between existence and non-existence [for the unmanifest], it is said to have "perished. The explanation of this is: "even though it has reached destruction. It is "not perished" because it is common to other persons. With respect to those for whom its purpose is not yet accomplished, it has not perished.

How is it that it is not lost? He says: with respect to virtuous persons, it has attained its destruction by bestowing enjoyment and liberation; for those virtuous persons, its effort has been accomplished. With respect to non-virtuous persons, its purpose remains unfulfilled because enjoyment and liberation—which were to be performed—have not been performed. For the sight of those non-virtuous ones, it indeed attains the state of being an object, becoming the "seen" (dṛśya) for that very sight.

Because it manifests as a person and is the emanation of the Person, it is called "the form of the Self. Furthermore, because it is common [to all], the Pradhāna is indeed one, like the earth and other elements. And because the effects and instruments are not distinct, the plurality of Puruṣas is established. Moreover, the distinction between Puruṣas is proven by the diversity of pleasure and pain.

And for this reason, because the powers of seeing and the capacity for vision are eternal, their conjunction is explained as being beginningless. Thus it has been stated in the *Tantra*: "Because of the beginningless conjunction of the substrata (the *dharmiṇas*), there is a beginningless conjunction of the qualities (*guṇas*) and the Puruṣas; and because the attributes (*dharmas*)—from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the final effects—are not distinct from their substrata, there is likewise a beginningless conjunction of these attributes with the Puruṣas. (2.22)

The object of sight has been determined, and the seer has also been determined. It has also been stated that the conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heya*). That conjunction must now be ascertained as to its nature; therefore, this aphorism was composed for the purpose of determining the essential nature of conjunction: "Conjunction is the cause of the perception of the essential natures of the powers of the owner and the owned. This means it is the cause—the instrumental reason—for the perception of the essential natures of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), which are the powers of the owned and the owner, respectively.

That in whose presence the essential nature of those two is perceived—just as in the case of the mouth and a mirror—is the cause of the perception of their essential natures; the meaning is that this conjunction is to be inferred from the effects consisting of the essential natures of the seer and the seen.

And the proof here is that the perception of the essential natures of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*) is preceded by their conjunction, because it is a perception of the essential natures of an object and its subject, like the perception of the essential natures of an eye and a mirror. Whatever perception of pleasure and pain is under dispute is preceded by a conjunction with the causes of pleasure and pain, because it is a perception of pleasure and pain, like the perception of pleasure and pain from sandalwood and a thorn.

Regarding this, it is said: the Puruṣa, the master, is conjoined with his own object of perception through his own intellect for the purpose of seeing—that is, for the purpose of perceiving experience and liberation. The meaning is that the conjunction is indeed prompted by the act of seeing.

Therefore, from that conjunction, the perception of the object of sight (*dṛśya*) as mediated by the faculty of seeing (*darśana*)—which is non-distinct [from the self]—is experience (*bhoga*). But that which is the distinct perception of the seer’s own nature (*svarūpa*) is liberation (*apavarga*). Since the conjunction is impelled by these two effects of seeing, the conjunction terminates with the effect of seeing; thus it is said that, like the conjunction of the person (*puruṣa*), seeing is the cause of disjunction. It is further stated that the vision of the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the person is the cause of the disjunction of the primary matter (*pradhāna*) and the person, because the purpose of the effect is fulfilled through such vision.

The vision of the true nature of transmigratory existence and the cause of transmigratory existence brings about the cessation of the cause of the union with suffering and the sufferer, because its object is the true nature of the sufferer and the cause of suffering, just like the vision of the true nature of a disease and the cause of a disease.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of the conjunction between the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*), because it is the cause of the conjunction that brings about suffering, just like the false knowledge that causes the conjunction between a disease and its cause. The conjunction of the seer and the seen is preceded by false knowledge, because it is a cause of suffering, like the conjunction between a sick person and the cause of their illness. Since the vision (*darśana*) has as its object the true nature of the sufferer and the cause of suffering, it is the opposite of non-vision (*adarśana*), which has an object contrary to that; thus, non-vision is said to be the cause of the conjunction, and ignorance is its cause. Furthermore, this is because the conjunction is the cause of suffering.

Since it is non-perception alone that brings about cessation and perception performs no other function, therefore perception is not the cause of liberation here. It is precisely through the absence of non-perception that there is an absence of bondage—the cause of suffering which is the effect of non-perception; that is liberation. Furthermore, liberation is not something to be produced apart from the absence of bondage. Consequently, the eternality of liberation is established.

When vision exists—that is, when vision whose objects are the seer and the seen exists—there is the destruction of non-vision regarding those same objects. This is because vision and non-vision are contradictory in a single locus, like darkness and the mass of rays from the sun. Therefore, vision is said to be the cause of isolation (*kaivalya*); "undisturbed discriminative discernment is the means of liberation."

[196,26] And what is this so-called "non-seeing"? Is it not already stated that it is simply ignorance (*avidyā*)? And that has been explained as being like a non-friend or a non-cow's footprint, by way of its opposition to knowledge (*vidyā*). True, it is so; however, the conceptual distinctions found in the treatises will now be demonstrated in order to determine our own preferred position. For, by effecting the refutation of entities imagined by others, the firmness of the entity established according to one’s own preference is brought to even greater strength.

The phrase "What is this? should be connected with all the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that are about to be explained. This is a specific inquiry regarding what was asked in general terms: "What is the application (*adhikāra*) of the qualities (*guṇas*)? *Adhikāra* means application; it is the activity (*pravṛtti*) of the qualities.

[197,12] But surely, how can there be a suspicion of non-perception regarding the domain of the *guṇas*? It is said: through the medium of the object (*artha*), there is indeed non-perception of the domain. For as long as the activity of the *guṇas* continues, so long is there bondage; and it is established that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of bondage. Even through the medium of words, when there is indeed non-perception other than perception, then there is suspicion, for the domain of the *guṇas* is indeed other than perception.

Or rather, is it the non-arising of the mind (*citta*) which is of the nature of seeing, self-abiding, and has already manifested its objects? Here, however, the doubt is raised by taking "non-seeing" (*adarśana*) as having the first member of the compound as the predominant factor: the non-arising of the mind is the absence of seeing prior to its arising. To the question, "What is meant by 'non-arising'? he says: the doubt regarding its own object of sight occurs precisely through the medium of an external object. For one who lacks a purpose must necessarily have a purpose to fulfill.

[197,20] What is the purposefulness of the *guṇas*? That purposefulness of the *guṇas* which consists in experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) is called "non-perception" (*adarśana*). Here, however, the doubt arises precisely through the medium of the purpose: for when something has a purpose, that purpose must necessarily be accomplished.

What, then, is the defect in these positions? It is said: if the subject matter were the non-perception of qualities, it would follow that knowledge is purposeless; for in this position, knowledge would not be the adversary of non-perception. Since there would be no contradiction between knowledge and its form, liberation would consequently be impossible, because activity would continue to occur again and again due to the continued presence of a motive.

Even in the position that it is the non-perception of the possession of qualities (*guṇārthavattā*), this same fault applies. Likewise, even in the position of the non-arising of the mind (*cittānutpāda*), this same fault applies. For non-arising is the absence of perception; and since that is a non-entity (*avastu*), its cessation through knowledge is untenable. Indeed, when there is an absence, the application of an antidote is entirely purposeless.

[198,8] Now, regarding the statement "ignorance has ceased along with one's own mind": here, someone who perceives a distinction between ignorance and non-perception in some respect engages in conceptualization. How so? For that which is not ceased is indeed perception, because it is being perceived. But that which is ceased—having dissolved along with the mind into its own cause—is the seed for the arising of one's own mind, the cause of its production; the conceit is that this is "non-perception" because it is not perceived.

Consequently, since it would follow that the state of non-cessation is itself a state of perception, this position would indeed be flawed. However, if there is non-perception in both the states of cessation and non-cessation, then the desired conclusion is established; thus, there is no fault. [Objection: Is it not the case that when the formative forces of stability (*sthitisaṃskāra*) have perished, the formative forces of motion (*gatisaṃskāra*) become manifest? [Reply: This does not connect with the question, "What is this non-perception?"

How, then, is the connection explained? In that regard, it has been stated that ignorance (*avidyā*), co-arising with one's own mind, is the seed for the arising of the mind. From this, the following point is established by implication: the mind ceases within its own cause and arises again. Consequently, this is also established by implication: the cause of the mind also functions through both persistence and movement. Therefore, he asks in order to clarify this very point.

The *sthiti-saṃskāra* is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) that causes the equilibrium of the *guṇas* to remain stable; its exhaustion is the exhaustion of the *sthiti-saṃskāra*. The *gati-saṃskāra* is the latent impression whose purpose is movement—that is, the activity of the *guṇas* in the form of the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth; its manifestation is what is meant by "its appearance."

If it functions by both persistence and motion, what fault would there be? He demonstrates this with an example: regarding that which was stated, if the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) were to function through persistence alone, it would not be *pradhāna* because of its failure to produce transformations—that is, due to its lack of transformation into the forms of the *mahat* and so forth.
For it is called *pradhāna* because it "produces" (*pradhatte*) transformations; therefore, if it did not produce transformations, it would not be *pradhāna*.

Likewise, if it existed only through motion (*gati*), it would exist eternally only in the form of modification; because its modifications would be eternal, it would not produce further modifications. Consequently, by losing its status as a cause, it would cease to be the *pradhāna*. Alternatively, "functioning in both ways" means that the *pradhāna* which exists through both motion and stability (*sthiti*) is "functioning in both ways. It is only in this manner that it acquires the conventional designation of *pradhāna*, the conventional designation of being the primary cause, and the conventional designation of causality. Otherwise, there is no such thing as the *pradhāna*-status of the *pradhāna*. This applies even to other causes.

The same investigation, having an identical scope, applies to the Puruṣa, Īśvara, atoms, and other such entities imagined by others; this very principle is now being examined in its present context. Some maintain that "non-perception" is simply the power of perception itself. Others hold that the power of perception in its unmanifest state—like a seed in its unmanifested state as a sprout—is what constitutes non-perception. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "The purpose of Pradhāna is the manifestation of the Self; manifestation is perception, which is the state of being made known; non-perception is the opposite of that."

In this view, since that very same thing which is unmanifest in nature exists as a latent power (*śakti*) and is thus "non-perception" (*adarśana*), while that very same thing when manifest is "perception" (*darśana*), it is impossible for non-perception to cease through perception, because a contradiction within its own self is untenable.
Similarly, immediately after the manifestation of vision, the Puruṣa—though his nature is vision—is capable of all cognition because he is essentially consciousness;

yet prior to activity, that is, prior to the primary activity of Pradhāna, he does not see. Likewise, the object of vision, Pradhāna, though capable of performing all causal operations, is not seen at that time prior to activity, even though it exists in the ultimate sense. Thus, some maintain that the non-perception of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa is their inherent property.

In this case as well, the prior state of both is non-perception, and their subsequent state is perception; thus the aforementioned fault remains exactly as it was. Even though the object of perception is essentially identical with and inseparable from the Puruṣa, it is not perceived by the Puruṣa in its own form independent of the cognition of the Puruṣa. Or, if it is perceived by the Puruṣa as qualified by the form of the Puruṣa, then non-perception exists as a property of the Puruṣa in dependence upon the cognition of the Puruṣa. This he clarifies:

Although it is not of the nature of the Puruṣa, the object of vision (dṛśya) depends upon the condition of being seen; that condition is ignorance (ajñāna). Depending on that, because it is perceived either as having the form of the Puruṣa or through confusion with it, the cognition of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), though not of the nature of the Puruṣa, appears as if it were identical to the Puruṣa due to its dependence on the Puruṣa. This being so, there is no fault, for this [appearance] is merely a property of the object of vision.

This presentation is for the purpose of demonstrating all the positions of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Some maintain that "seeing" is knowledge, and that very knowledge is "non-seeing. This conceptual construction is based on accepting the predominance of the meaning of the final member in a compound (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*). The fault of this has already been explained in the *Avidyāsūtra*.

These are the conceptual constructions found in the treatises and the conceptual constructions belonging to other philosophical systems. In this regard, the intention is that although there is a great abundance of such conceptual constructions, the goal is not established by mere abundance alone. However, for one who holds that the cause is the conjunction of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), non-perception (*adarśana*) is not logical, because it contradicts perception. This has already been explained, so no further effort is made here. (2.23)

[200,17] For all *puruṣas*, there is no distinction in their conjunction with the *guṇas*. The conjunction with the *guṇas* is undifferentiated and common to all; nevertheless, the conjunction of each individual *puruṣa* with his own intellect (*buddhi*) is specific to that individual, being directed toward objects not shared by others. That which constitutes this unique conjunction of one's own intellect is precisely *adarśana* (non-perception). Its cause is *avidyā* (ignorance). The meaning is that *avidyā*, which consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of erroneous cognition, is the cause—the instrumental reason—for that conjunction which serves as the means for perceiving the essential natures of the powers of the "owner" (*svāmin*, i.e., the *puruṣa*) and the "owned" (*sva*, i.e., the *prakṛti*).

[200,22] But has it not been stated that "error is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) which is not established in the nature of that [object]"? Likewise, it has been stated that "ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. In this regard, how can it be called the "residual impression (*vāsanā*) of erroneous cognition"? This is not a fault; because the residual impression is the effect of ignorance, it is itself called ignorance.

Even when the causes have dissolved, even while the state of equilibrium persists, the latent impression of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsanā*) becomes the cause for the repeated activity of *pradhāna*. It is not the reverse; because [the effect] does not exist prior to the arising of the intellect (*buddhi*), this very impression is declared to be the cause of the conjunction between *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*.

He explains that very point: "One who is permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of erroneous cognition does not reach the culmination of the task—that is, the attainment of the goal. He states what the culmination of the task is: "the discernment of the Puruṣa" (*puruṣakhyāti*). The intellect (*buddhi*) does not attain that state. For the functional capacity of the intellect culminates in the discernment of the Puruṣa. As long as it possesses its office—that is, as long as it has tasks to perform—it revolves again and again under the influence of the latent impressions of erroneous cognition.

That intellect, culminating in the discernment of the Puruṣa, reaches its final goal. He clarifies this further: "Having fulfilled its office and being freed from the bonds of non-vision (adarśana)—since karma and its maturation are rooted in non-vision, non-vision itself is the bond—upon the cessation of non-vision, the bonds cease; and because of the absence of the cause of bondage, namely the absence of non-vision, it does not return again."

[201.23] Here, someone raises an objection by means of the story of a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*). A *paṇḍaka* is a hermaphrodite. It is said that he was addressed by his foolish wife: "Noble son, why am I not pregnant? Why is it that I am not with child? He said to her, "I shall produce a child for you when I am dead. Likewise, this [cognition], while existing, does not bring about the cessation of the mind; what hope is there that it will do so once it has perished?

This is the intention of the author: if ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of the conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), and knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cause of its cessation, then when that knowledge is present, ignorance—which is its opposite—is removed. However, even after the arising of knowledge, there is no cessation of the mind (*citta*).

In this regard, just as there is no cessation of the mind when knowledge exists, so too it will not cease even when knowledge is lost; for now, [the mind] is like the birth of offspring from a eunuch or a corpse. For this very reason, ignorance (*avidyā*) also is not the cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

[202,11] Here, one who is a teacher-like authority (ācāryadeśīya) states a rebuttal. The use of the term "teacher-like authority" is for the purpose of demonstrating the lack of substance in the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). I shall state the response by way of refutation alone.

[202,13] Is it not the case that liberation is simply the cessation of the intellect (*buddhi*)? How does the cessation of the intellect occur through the absence of non-perception (*adarśana*) as its cause? That non-perception, which is the cause of bondage, ceases through perception; the cessation of that [non-perception] is itself liberation. Why this confusion regarding an irrelevant point?

It has been established in detail that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of the conjunction between *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*, which is the cause of suffering. Therefore, since the cessation of non-perception is logically established through perception, he considers the prima facie argument to be without substance.

[202,17] But has it not been stated that the intellect (*buddhi*) is not withdrawn immediately after knowledge (*vidyā*)? It is replied: By means of knowledge, ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed withdrawn; there should be no confusion regarding this point. However, when that [ignorance] has been withdrawn, the withdrawal of the intellect also necessarily occurs, because there is no other cause for the conjunction with the intellect apart from ignorance. Consequently, the withdrawal of the intellect itself is liberation (*mokṣa*).

As for the claim that cognition does not cease immediately after knowledge [arises], that is without foundation. Why? Because we observe many varieties of relationships between causes and their effects; for example, [objects] such as a chariot have carpenters and the like as their causes.

Palaces and the like do not cease to exist simply because their causes—the carpenters and others—have ceased their activity; for even when a tree is broken, it is not seen immediately after the breaking, but rather due to its specific state. Likewise, the mind also, like an arrow released from a bow, continues to exist for some time through perception, depending on the momentum of its previously initiated *saṃskāras* until those *saṃskāras* are exhausted. Thus says the Śruti: "For him, there is delay only so long [as he is not liberated]. (2.24)

Four arrangements (*vyūha*) have been introduced. Among them, it was stated that "suffering is to be abandoned" and "future suffering is to be abandoned"; the meaning is that one arrangement, corresponding to the state of disease, has been explained. Furthermore, the cause of what is to be abandoned, together with its objective cause (*nimitta*), namely that which is called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), has been mentioned. The second arrangement, corresponding to the cause of the disease, has been described as the conjunction of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*) as its objective cause. This restatement of what has already been said is for the purpose of removing any doubt regarding that subject by means of an explanation supported by reasoning.

[203,17] Hereafter, abandonment—which stands in the place of health and is the purpose of the treatise on liberation—must be explained. Furthermore, the enumeration of what is about to be discussed is for the sake of concentrating the intellect of the listeners. "In the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of union; that is abandonment, which is the isolation of the seer."

The word "that" (tat) refers back to the previously mentioned ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of the absence of that non-perception—namely, ignorance—there is an absence of the conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), which is the cause of suffering; this means the absolute cessation of bondage. This abandonment is like the state of health. That is the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Seer; that very abandonment, the absolute cessation of bondage, is the isolation of the Seer, the Person. Its explanation is: the state of non-mixture for the Person, meaning non-conjunction with the qualities (*guṇas*) once again.

Having explained the meaning of the individual words, he now demonstrates the meaning of the sentence: "The cessation of suffering upon the removal of its cause is 'abandonment' (hāna). Then the Puruṣa is established in its own nature," as it has been said; or rather, "the power of consciousness is established in its own nature."

[204,10] But surely, if karma with indefinite fruition exists, how can there be cessation? And how could the body be produced again by means of that karma with indefinite fruition? No, for this has already been answered: it was stated that through right vision (*samyagdarśana*), the seed of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is burnt, and thus karma ceases to be productive, using the illustration of rice grains whose husks have been removed and whose seeds have been burnt. Therefore, for the wise man, there is no commencement of a body due to the absence of the cause. //2.25//

The third arrangement, which corresponds to the state of health and is called "abandonment," has been explained. Now, desiring to explain the fourth arrangement, which corresponds to the medicine, he says: "What is the means for attaining abandonment?"

[204,17] But how can there be a means for attaining abandonment (*hāna*), given that this abandonment is not something to be attained because it is a non-entity? For abandonment is simply the cessation of bondage. This is not a fault. Since the cessation of ignorance is to be accomplished through effort—just like the breaking of shackles—it is figuratively said that abandonment, although a non-entity, is "attained" when right vision (*samyak-dṛṣṭi*) has arisen and ignorance has ceased.

The means of liberation is the unfluctuating discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). What, then, is this discriminative discernment? He says: it is the cognition of the distinctness between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, meaning the thorough understanding of the similarities and differences between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*. However, that discriminative discernment does not become stable—meaning it is not capable of performing its function—as long as false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) has not been removed, because it is subject to fluctuation.
And so it has been said: Just as gold that has not been refined does not shine, so too does the consciousness of one whose impurities have not been removed fail to manifest clearly.
Likewise, for one seized by the crocodile of sensual desire, even his knowledge is no raft. Thus it is said.

But when false knowledge has its seed-nature burnt away—having become incapable of initiating its effects, namely the production of bondage, precisely because its seed-nature is burnt—then, for that *sattva* whose dust of afflictions has been shaken off (where "afflictions" refers to the very dust), which is unstained by the impurities of passion and the like, and which abides in the supreme state known as mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*) and abides in pure clarity of knowledge, there arises a flow of discriminative cognition. It reiterates this: through the continuous states of discriminative knowledge, it becomes stainless.

This discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), being of such a nature, becomes unshakeable. When discriminative discernment is thus unshakeable, then false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) undergoes the state of having its seed burnt, because of their mutual opposition. Furthermore, there is no recurrence of false knowledge precisely because its seed has been burnt. And so it has been said: "Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so too, once the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been burnt by knowledge, the self (*ātman*) is not born again. (MBh 12.204.16; cited twice!)
And that such discriminative discernment is the path to liberation, the means for its attainment; this is the meaning. [2.26]
In order to manifest the evidence for his own experience regarding the arising of right vision in one who has already produced right vision, he says: "His wisdom is sevenfold on the final stage.
The word "his" refers to one in whom discernment has arisen—that is, one in whom right vision has been produced.

"Recollection" (pratyāmnāya) means reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa). "Sevenfold" refers to the removal of the impurity of the veil of affliction; for impurity itself is the restriction [to worldly existence], consisting of the afflictions (kleśas) and actions (karmans), which is precisely that "impurity. From its removal, there occurs the non-arising of other cognitions regarding the intellect (vitti), and the non-arising of contrary cognitions such as "mine" and "I. The explanation of this term "sevenfold" is that wisdom (prajñā) becomes sevenfold in kind for the discerning intellect.

He describes those seven aspects in sequence: "All suffering that is to be abandoned has been thoroughly understood as something to be abandoned through reasoned arguments; there is no further aspect of suffering for him to be thoroughly understood."

[205,28] By the use of the plural form "the causes of what is to be abandoned have been exhausted" (*kṣīṇā heyahetavaḥ*), both afflictions (*kleśa*) and karmas are denoted. Furthermore, not even the slightest residue of these afflictions and karmas is to be imagined, because their seeds have been burnt by the fire of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). By this also, the state of being the "final stage" (*prāntabhūmitva*) is expressed. And thus:

For one for whom the correct conditions have arisen, there is nothing further to be endured because the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted. Furthermore, the conviction that "I have accomplished what was to be done" arises as a condition characterized by the ripening of right view (*samyagdarśana*). Just as a person afflicted by disease, upon the destruction of the causes of that disease, has the conviction "I am now free from disease; no further medicine is required," even so this second type of wisdom (*prajñā*) has been described.

The direct realization of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is "abandonment" (*hāna*). Because it is proximate to abandonment and because its nature is equivalent to abandonment, the meditative absorption of cessation itself is designated as "abandonment. That [cessation] has been directly realized, brought into the range of experience. This is understood as the final consummation of isolation (*kaivalya*), such that it is known: "Isolation has been accomplished; there is nothing further to be done. This third variety of the wisdom of the highest stage (*prāntabhūmiprajñā*) has thus been explained.

The means for the removal of suffering (*hānopāya*), which consists of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), has been cultivated and thoroughly practiced. When the wisdom of the discerning one arises as a certainty that right vision (*samyagdarśana*) has appeared exactly as it is, this is the fourth variety of wisdom. Thus, this fourfold [wisdom] is "liberation from duty" (*kāryavimukti*); the meaning is that this four-aspected wisdom constitutes the fulfillment of the purpose of the *puruṣa*.

Alternatively, *kāryavimukti* is the liberation or cessation of the effect; that liberation of the effect is fourfold—thus ends the sentence. It is connected with the following term, *prajñā*. How so? The mind (*citta*) joined with wisdom (*prajñā*), that is, joined with the discernment of the distinction (*vivekakhyāti*), is the "wisdom-mind" (*prajñācitta*); its liberation is its dissolution (*pralaya*), which is the "liberation of the wisdom-mind. That is threefold. And thus he will say later: "Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the reversion of the constituents (*guṇas*) once they have ceased to serve the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣa*)."

In this regard, liberation as the cessation of the effects is fourfold. The emptiness of the *puruṣārtha* (the purpose of the self) was explained previously; now, the cessation of the qualities of the intellect (*buddhi*) is explained. The re-absorption (*pratiprasava*) of those qualities of the intellect—such as *sattva* and the rest—which have fulfilled their office and are empty of *puruṣārtha*, constitutes the triad of liberation of wisdom and liberation of mind. Just as the qualities of the intellect, having performed their functions and ceased their duties, abide in the form of the intellect and are oriented toward dissolution.

Like stones fallen from the peak of a mountain, they become unstable due to the absence of any further function; thus, along with that intellect (*buddhi*), they are on the verge of dissolution into their own cause, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Alternatively, together with their effect—the state of the intellect—or rather with their own cause, the ego-sense, they attain the state of unmanifestness (*avyaktabhāva*) even as their cause approaches the Wise One (*puruṣa*). Thus it is said that "they set together with it. This is the first liberation of consciousness from the mind.

And for these [evolutes], once they have been dissolved, there is no further production with respect to the Puruṣa, because of the absence of any purpose. For the fourfold effect has been fully released. This is the second liberation: liberation of wisdom and mind.

In this state—the state of the dissolution of qualities whose purposes have been fulfilled—one has transcended the connection with the qualities; that is, one has transcended the relationship characterized by the seer and the seen. Being a light consisting solely of its own nature, it is a light that is nothing but the very nature of pure consciousness. This is the Puruṣa, solitary and pure; thus, this is the third liberation: liberation from the mind through wisdom.

Observing this state of evenness, which is a "limit-state" (prāntabhūmi)—meaning a state or condition that has reached the limit of all afflictions—a person who perceives wisdom as having become the ripening of the mark of right vision is designated as "skilled" (kuśala); "skilled" is the conventional term for him. Even during the process of re-absorption or dissolution of the mind, he remains liberated and is still called "skilled" by virtue of his prior state.
Why is he skilled? It is said: "Because he has transcended the qualities (guṇas). For one who has transcended the qualities is indeed skilled. (2.27)

The discriminative discernment is established; discriminative discernment has been attained, culminating in the fruit of the sevenfold wisdom of the final stages, and serving as the means for liberation. Since there is no accomplishment without a means of achievement, this [treatise] is commenced for the purpose of establishing the means for the attainment of discriminative discernment: "From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the illumination of knowledge up to discriminative discernment."

It is not intended to be restricted that discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) arises solely from the practice of the limbs of yoga; rather, it is for this very reason that it is established that discriminative discernment is accomplished through such means as service to the teacher and the practice of dharma. What, then, is the restriction? It is that it does not occur at all without some means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). However, the practice of the limbs of yoga is not the *only* means; rather, it is simply that the accomplishment of discriminative discernment certainly occurs through the practice of the limbs of yoga.
Thus it has been stated by the teachers: "Yoga is conducive to the knowledge of reality."

The limbs of yoga are about to be described; their practice is "the practice of the limbs of yoga. From that comes the destruction of impurity known as the afflictions (*kleśa*). Upon their destruction, there is "radiance," meaning excellence. To the question of what its limit is, he says: "It continues until discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*)," which is the supplement to the text.

The commentator himself explains more clearly the limbs of yoga that are about to be described. Through their practice, there occurs the destruction—that is, the elimination—of the five-fold error which consists of impurity; upon its destruction, there is the manifestation, or the illumination, of right vision. He explains how this comes about: "In whatever measure the means are practiced, in that same measure impurity undergoes attenuation. And thus Manu has declared: (208.22)

"One should burn away defects by means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and sins by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*); one should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and the qualities that obstruct [the self] by means of meditation (*dhyāna*). (YS 2.34) Just as impurity is diminished, so too does the radiance of knowledge increase in accordance with the sequence of that diminution, like the sun at the end of the winter season. This very increase reaches its culmination; what is its limit? He says: "Until discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*). (YS 2.27)

The explanation of this is that [the practice] continues until the knowledge of the discrimination between the nature of the qualities (guṇa) and the Puruṣa; purity indeed culminates in the discriminative discernment of the difference between the Sattva and the Puruṣa.
The practice of the limbs of yoga leads to the destruction of impurity and to discriminative discernment.

Regarding "the cause of attainment," there are exactly two types of causes: one that serves as the basis for the purification of phenomena, and the other which is the cause of both; it does not exist otherwise. In this context, following the discussion on causes, he explains the causes well-known in the treatises. He states that how many such causes there are in the treatise: there are exactly nine. He expresses them in a verse: "Arising, duration, manifestation, transformation, dependence, attainment, separation, difference, and support—these are remembered as the ninefold causes."

Thus, in order to distinguish that, examples will be introduced. Among these, the mind is the cause of the arising [of consciousness], for knowledge is the function of the mind, just as waves are the function of water.

The cause of the persistence of the mind is the purpose of the Puruṣa; for the mind persists by virtue of having experience and liberation as its purpose, just as food is the cause of the persistence of the body.
Light is the cause for the manifestation of form; at that time, there is cognition of form. For indeed, when form is not manifested by light, there is no awareness of it.

The cause of the modification of the mind is another object. For it is by the proximity of another object that the mind undergoes modification, just as fire is the cause of cooking. Just as fire is the cause of that modification known as cooking, which consists in the state of being cooked.

The cognition of smoke is the causal condition (*pratyaya-kāraṇa*) for the cognition of fire; the meaning is that it is the cause of the cognition which is the result-bearing means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In the previous case, however, by the phrase "of the cognition," the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the cognition was intended.

The practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause for the attainment of discriminative discernment, just as merit is the cause of pleasure; it is likewise the cause for the separation from impurity, just as an axe is the cause for that which is to be cut.

The cause of alteration is, for example, a goldsmith with respect to gold. For having broken up the gold, he makes another object, such as a *vardhamānaka*; likewise, having broken up that *vardhamānaka*, he makes yet another kind of ornament. Thus it is called "another."

[210,14] Thus, for a single cognition of "woman," ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of delusion (*mūḍhatva*); aversion (*dveṣa*) is the cause of that same cognition of a woman being painful (*duḥkhatva*); likewise, passion (*rāga*) is the cause of its being pleasurable (*sukhatva*). Similarly, for that very same cognition, when it is neutral—being devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—the cause is knowledge (*jñāna*) endowed with discernment (*viveka*). In this way, a single cognition of a woman is divided into many forms, like gold, through distinctions such as delusion, pain, pleasure, and neutrality.

[210,18] It is the cause of support. Support (*dhṛti*) is the act of supporting; the body is the cause of that for the sense-faculties. For the sense-faculties do not obtain support without reaching the body. If these sense-faculties are thus the cause of support for that body, it is because the body is supported by means of the activity of the sense-faculties.

Likewise, the great elements, such as space and the rest, are the cause of the support of bodies; for bodies, beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass, are indeed originated from the great elements. And these [elements], by way of being mutual benefactors and beneficiaries, are the cause of support.

[210,24] Likewise, for all categories of beings—those of animals, humans, and gods—the cause of sustenance is mutual dependence. Why? Because they exist for one another's sake. The animal realm serves as the cause of sustenance for both the human and divine realms by providing assistance through being used as mounts, milked, offered as oblations, and so forth.

Likewise, the human state is the cause of sustenance for the divine and the animal realms through sacrifices, protection, and so forth; similarly, the divine state is the cause of sustenance for the other two through cold, heat, rain, and the like.
In this way, even the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas) serve as causes for stability through their mutual assistance;

indeed, the entire world is sustained by their reciprocal dependence. Thus, he negates any other cause by stating that there are only nine causes. These should be applied, as far as the occurrence of a purpose permits, even to other unmentioned categories of objects according to whatever purpose arises. However, the practice of the limbs of yoga attains causality in two ways, as has already been explained. (2.28)

[211,13] What, then, are those limbs of yoga whose practice obtains a twofold causality? In this regard, the limbs of yoga are determined as eight: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). These are the eight limbs.

But is it not the case that in other treatises on yoga, the six limbs consist precisely of posture (*āsana*) and so forth? For instance, it is said: "Yoga is said to have six limbs," and so on. Furthermore, it is only posture and the others that directly assist meditative absorption (*samādhi*), whereas restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*) do not.

This is not a fault, because the qualification for yoga is established for one who possesses both restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*). For there is no qualification for yoga for those who act according to their whims; as the Śruti declares: "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct, nor one who is not tranquil. Likewise, in the Atharvaveda: "Those whose austerity and celibacy exist, in whom truth is firmly established," and so forth. Similarly, in the Gītā: "Abiding in the vow of a student" (BhG 6.14). Therefore, restraint and observance are also constituent parts [of yoga].

Regarding *yama* and *niyama*, the mention of *yama* first is for the purpose of demonstrating its preeminence; for the preeminence of *yama* is established everywhere. For the qualified yogi who is endowed with *yama* and *niyama*, the practice of the subsequent limbs—beginning with posture (*āsana*)—is attained once each preceding one has reached the state of stability. Indeed, it is not possible to ascend to a higher step without first having ascended the first.
As it is said elsewhere: "The various rules for standing and sitting, or even the specific prescriptions for yoga—all those which give rise to distraction are not the causes of yoga."

The abandonment of all defects and meditative absorption (*samādhi*): these two constitute the cause of yoga through definitive determination. Whether other factors exist or not—let them be or not let them be—it is because of the preeminence of that meditative absorption and the abandonment of all defects that they are praised; it is not for the purpose of negating the other limbs such as posture (*āsana*). We shall explain the practice and the essential nature of these restraints (*yama*) and so forth in their proper order, for it is impossible to practice them without first understanding their essential nature. (2.29)

Among those [observances], such as the *yamas* and others, the *yamas* are explained first: non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), truthfulness (*satya*), non-stealing (*asteya*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and non-possessiveness (*aparigraha*) are the *yamas*. Among these, non-violence is the absence of malice toward all beings in every way, with one's whole self, and by every means; it is the absence of malice toward all beings, both stationary and moving, as well as their non-affliction.

[212,25] It is shown that among the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), non-violence (ahiṃsā) is the primary one, and it must be practiced with body, speech, and mind by means of every faculty. Furthermore, the subsequent restraints, such as truthfulness and the rest, have non-violence as their root; they are for the purpose of non-violence, they serve the aim of non-violence, and because they are intent upon its accomplishment, they are taught as being intent upon the accomplishment of non-violence itself. What is meant by this? He says: they are adopted for the sake of making non-violence pure; they are adopted for the sake of establishing the purity of non-violence.

For it has been said: "Indeed, this brahmin, insofar as he undertakes many vows, to that same extent, by desisting from those things caused by negligence which are the source of violence, the root of violence, and the occasion for violence, he practices that very non-violence which is pure in form."

Because of the undertaking of various vows such as those concerning truth, and because of the undertaking of other non-contradictory vows, for one who has desisted from the causes of violence and whose impulse toward the causes of violence has ceased, non-violence arises in its purest form due to the absence of causes—just as, for example, when one practices the vow of begging for alms and the like, there occurs the cessation of the causes of violence such as agriculture.

Truth is speech and thought in accordance with what has been seen, what has been inferred, and what has been heard; that is truth. This is what is meant: when a comprehension of an object as it truly is has arisen through unerring means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the application of speech and thought in exactly that same manner in order to communicate that comprehension to another is truth.

This very point is stated: speech is uttered for the sake of transferring one's own understanding to another. Even though that speech conveys its intended meaning, it may nevertheless be deceptive. For example, when something true is employed for the purpose of deceiving another, it appears as false in certain instances depending on place, time, and other factors—just as when it was said to Yudhiṣṭhira, "Aśvatthāman is killed," while he was actually an elephant.
Or, one who is deluded might speak what is false while thinking it to be true;

or, the speech may be barren of realization, being insufficient for the listener's comprehension, such as a doubtful statement whose specific context and so forth are not grasped; or, it may consist of harsh words, such as "goats and sheep," and the like.

Therefore, speech that is free from such defects as these, which accompanies a straightforward mind and is directed toward the benefit of all beings, attains the state of truth. It does not attain the state of truth if it is directed toward the injury of beings, even if it is supported by the power of the facts.

And even if it were thus stated in the manner described above so as to be faultless, if it were intended solely for the purpose of harming living beings, it would not be truth; for that which has the destruction of living beings as its objective does not attain the status of truth, even if it is free from the three faults such as deception and the like—it would simply be evil.

He says this very thing: by that mere semblance of merit, that reflection of merit, which resembles the words of Satyakauśika, one would encounter bitter darkness. Therefore, having examined all things, one should speak the truth which is beneficial to all.

And it has been said: "One should speak the truth; one should speak what is pleasant; one should not speak an unpleasant truth; nor should one speak a pleasant falsehood. This is the eternal dharma. (214.15) Theft (*steya*) is the appropriation of another's property without the authority of the scriptures, motivated by desire. Since theft is impossible for those who are free from desire, the prohibition of that very theft is stated; that non-theft, which consists of the absence of desire, is called *asteya*.

Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the organ of generation for a person whose senses are guarded, whose senses are well-guarded, and who is devoid of the mental, verbal, and physical activities directed toward unchaste conduct.

The non-acceptance, non-appropriation, and non-possession of sense objects—resulting from seeing the defects in their acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and injury—is what is meant; it is not, however, non-acceptance due to incapacity. These are the *yamas*. (2.30)

[214,22] Since other dharmas are practiced with restrictions of genus, place, time, and so forth, the same contingency would apply here as well; therefore, to preclude that, he says: "But these... These, namely non-violence and the others, known by the name of the Great Vows (mahāvrata), are to be practiced by those who have renounced (saṃnyāsin). Of what nature are they such that they bear the name "Great Vows"? They are defined as: "The Great Vow is universal, being unconditioned by genus, place, time, or occasion. It is both great and a vow, hence a "Great Vow" (mahāvrata). Its greatness consists in its universality.

[214,26] But how is it that these [virtues] are not delimited by genus (*jāti*) and so forth? To demonstrate this lack of delimitation, he illustrates non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) by way of its exclusion: in that regard, non-violence delimited by genus belongs to a fisherman only with respect to fish and not elsewhere; for his violence is restricted to the genus of fish. And since that [violence] is delimited by the genus of fish and does not pervade all fish-grounds, it is indeed not universal.

That very non-violence, when restricted by place—such as "I shall not kill at a sacred site like Prayāga"—is not universal, because non-violence at sacred sites does not extend to places other than those sacred sites.

And that very [time], being delimited by time—as in "not on the fourteenth day" or "not on an auspicious day"—does not encompass any time other than the fourteenth day and so forth; thus, it too is not universal (*asārvabhaumī*).

Even for that same fisherman who has ceased [his activity] with respect to all three—birth, place, and time—there exists a restriction of duty delimited by a convention (*samaya*), such as: "I shall kill for the sake of gods and Brahmins, and not otherwise. Thus he remains on the ground of the convention of *śrāddha* and so forth, abstaining from eating; yet even that is not universal. And just as for a Kṣatriya, violence is restricted only to battle and not elsewhere—this is an illustration of that which is delimited by convention.

Furthermore, those restraints (*yama*)—non-violence and the rest—which are not limited by species, place, time, or circumstance, must be observed in every way. On all levels, regarding all species and so forth, in all objects, and toward all living beings, they must be practiced entirely without deviation. Being distinguished in this manner, these universal restraints are called the "Great Vow" (*mahāvrata*). (2.31)

Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (*niyamas*). Among these, purity consists of that produced by earth and so forth; by the word "and so forth," water is included. It also includes the consumption of pure substances such as clarified butter, milk, and the like. By the word "and," seeing and hearing pure things are also included. This is external purity.
[215,29] Internal *ahuna* is said to be the washing away of the impurities of the mind, such as desire, anger, and so forth, by means of the waters of cultivating their antidotes.

Contentment is the lack of desire for further means beyond those already at hand, arising from confidence in the available means; it is the conviction that "enough" even when there is no satisfaction with what is merely present, due to confidence in the available cause of consolation.

[216,12] Austerity (*tapas*) is the endurance of dualities (*dvandva*). And the dualities are hunger and thirst; hunger is the desire to eat. Hunger and thirst constitute austerity when they are caused by eating and drinking in small quantities. Cold and heat constitute austerity when they are not countered at all, or are only slightly countered. Regarding standing and sitting: "One should stand during the day and sit during the night"—this is the established tradition of the *Smṛti*. There are also the "silence like a log" (*kāṣṭha-mauna*) and the "non-silence like a log" (*akāṣṭha-mauna*). "Silence like a log" is devoid of the use of hands and other such gestures. "Non-silence like a log" involves the use of hands and other gestures, but is devoid of speech and the like.

[216,18] "The vows of these yogins are according to what is appropriate and possible. He says "according to what is appropriate" for the purpose of prohibiting practices contrary to [the rules of] *homa* and other such rites. What are those [vows], such as the *kṛcchra* and so forth? The *kṛcchra* includes the *prājāpatya* and others: eating in the morning for three days, in the evening for three days, and food obtained unasked for three days; fasting for three days. The *cāndrāyaṇa* includes the *yavamadhya*, *pipīlikāmadhya*, and so on, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*) which states: "One should reduce the morsel by one each [day]," and so forth.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass, followed by a fast for one night—this is the *sāntapana-kṛcchra*, which is called *amṛta*.

These same substances, practiced three times over, constitute the *mahāsāntapana*. The inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including the *parāka* and other such penances. "Self-study" (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), the study of the Upaniṣads and so forth, or the recitation of the *praṇava*. "Realization of the inwardly directed consciousness" (*pratyakcetanādhigama*) is also the absence of obstacles. (2.32)

In this regard, when there is obstruction by *vitarkas*—which are thoughts contrary to the *yamas* and *niyamas*—one should cultivate their opposites in the manner that will be described. For if these *vitarkas* are not cultivated as opposites, they would cause the yogin to incline toward violence and other such acts.

When such thoughts as violence and the like arise in this practitioner of the divine life (*brāhmaṇa*), one must consider what kind of thoughts those are—whether they be thoughts of non-violence and so forth, or thoughts of violence and so forth. In that regard, the thought concerning non-violence is: "I shall kill the one who harms me. Similarly, regarding truthfulness, the contrary conviction is the thought: "I shall speak untruth. Likewise, the thought concerning non-stealing is: "I shall take this person's property for myself. Similarly, the thought concerning celibacy is: "I shall have sexual intercourse with his wife."
Likewise, there is the discursive thought of one who has no possessions, thinking, "I shall become the owner of possessions."

The word "of this" (*asya*) is used in all cases, such as killing and so forth, for the purpose of demonstrating its accompaniment. Regarding stealing: "I shall take this substance as my own" is the act of establishing a connection between oneself and the property of another. Regarding possessiveness: "I am the owner of this" refers to regarding oneself as the owner of substances belonging to others, as is the case with princes, kings, ministers, and the like.
Thus, being afflicted by the blazing fever of discursive thought that carries one away from the right path, one should cultivate their antidotes.

How should one cultivate this? One should reflect: "While being cooked in the terrible embers of saṃsāra, I have accepted the yoga-dharma which grants fearlessness to all beings. Indeed, if I were to abandon thoughts of violence and the like, yet take them up again, I would be equal to one who lives the life of a dog. One whose conduct is like that of a dog is a "dog-liver" (*śvavṛtta*); or, one whose conduct is like a dog is a "dog-liver. One should cultivate the thought: "I would be equal to such a person."

Just as a dog licks what has been vomited, so too is the act of taking back what has been abandoned; this is the intended meaning. One should reflect: "I am equal to such a person; how could I become like that? This is not proper. Thus one should meditate.

This and other such [faults] should also be applied to other sūtras and to the sūtra on the rules of restraint (*niyama*). Regarding purity (*śauca*) and the others, one should understand that there are specific discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) for each, such as "I will not practice purity," and so forth. In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), however, only the restraints (*yama*) are demonstrated; this is because they must necessarily be performed, and because of the gravity of the fault incurred by their non-performance, for the sake of showing great respect for them. (2.33)

The intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), classification (*bheda*), cause of origin (*prabhavahetu*), and fruit (*phala*) of discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) are demonstrated by the Sūtra itself. Their intrinsic nature is that discursive thoughts are violence and so forth. Their classification is that they are performed, caused to be performed, or approved. Their cause of origin is that they are preceded by greed, anger, and delusion. Their state as weak, middling, or intense refers to the mildness, mediocrity, or intensity of the fault. That their fruit is an endless succession of suffering and ignorance indicates the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣabhāvana*).
Alternatively, the fruit is explained by that very same [statement].

In this regard, violence alone is cited as an illustration for the sake of demonstrating all [unwholesome actions]. It is threefold: committed, caused to be committed, and consented to. "Committed" means by one's own activity; "caused to be committed" means by the activity of one who is employed; "consented to" means by the activity of others, having mentally approved it.

Furthermore, each one is threefold. How so? Through greed, one kills a deer for its meat, skin, or bone; through anger, thinking, "This person has done me harm"; and through delusion, thinking, "This will be my merit. Thus, there are these nine divisions. Each of these is again divided into three: how so? Greed, anger, and delusion are again threefold—weak, middling, and intense. Each one...

Furthermore, it becomes threefold: weak-weak, medium-weak, and strong-weak; likewise, weak-medium, medium-medium, and strong-medium; likewise, weak-strong, medium-strong, and strong-strong. Thus, violence consists of eighty-one varieties.

Furthermore, although that [violence] consists of eighty-one varieties, it is nonetheless incalculable due to the distinctions among its applications (*niyoga*), conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), and aggregations (*samudaya*). For instance, as has been stated regarding the distinction of application: one person, having been commanded, enjoins another, such as a king; and he too, being enjoined, enjoins yet another, and so on. All those who are thus enjoined commit violence either through aggregation or through conceptualization. Likewise, even the original commander, acting in conjunction with and in coordination with those to be enjoined, carries out the act of violence.

This is because the various classes of living beings, such as executioners and those to be executed, are innumerable. The same should be applied to falsehood and the other [non-virtues] as well; the distinctions of being committed, caused to be committed, or approved should likewise be applied.

Indeed, these discursive thoughts have suffering and ignorance as their infinite fruit. Suffering and ignorance—these two are the infinite fruit for those [thoughts]; thus they are called "those whose fruit is infinite suffering and ignorance. Suffering is their infinite fruit, and ignorance is also their infinite fruit. Therefore, one should not even overlook these discursive thoughts with the mind; rather, one should cultivate their antidote.

In this regard, three types of suffering for the victim are set forth by way of their distinctions in order to demonstrate the distinction in their results. Thus, the perpetrator first robs the victim of his vitality (*vīrya*) through such means as staring at him with a murderous form, threatening him, and so forth; having robbed him of his vitality, he causes him pain by striking him with weapons and the like; thereafter, he deprives him even of life—that is, he separates him from his vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Due to the expenditure of that [victim's] vigor by this slayer, his implements—whether animate or inanimate, such as cattle or fields—become depleted of their vigor.

Because the infliction of suffering through the falling of weapons and the like constitutes a specific form of violence, one experiences suffering among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth.

Likewise, because of the taking of life, even while remaining at every moment on the verge of death on the path between birth and death, though he may wish for death at every moment, he somehow manages to breathe out only with great difficulty, because the ripening of suffering is certain and must necessarily be experienced.

And if, by some means, through the acquisition of merit, there should be only a very small amount of harm resulting from the acquisition of abundant merit, then even though one has attained happiness due to that abundance of merit, one might still have a short life because of the fault of the harm committed during the process of implanting [the seeds].

In this manner, what has been said regarding violence should be applied as appropriate to falsehood and the other [unwholesome actions] as well. Thus, one should contemplate the undesirable maturation that follows upon thoughts such as violence, just as it does in the case of actual action; one should not direct the mind toward such thoughts. (2.34)

The discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) to be abandoned through the cultivation of their opposites (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*) are those whose nature is no longer productive and which have become non-productive; that is, when they do not arise in the mind of the practitioner, having been cut off at the root, then the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) produced by that—consisting in the stability of the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*)—arises as an indicator of *siddhi*, making known the accomplishment of the fruits such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). Thus, the fruit of yogic accomplishment is indeed established.

Furthermore, another kind of sovereignty arising as a secondary consequence is mentioned for the sake of praising the limbs of yoga. How is it that even each one of the [limbs] beginning with non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), when established, is observed through direct perception to possess such a sign of stability—one that is not equaled even by the fruits of dharma such as sacrifices? How much more so, then, is this the case for their collective power to bring about the perfections of yoga (*yogasiddhi*)? He demonstrates this as follows: "When non-violence is established—that is, when there is stability in non-violence—and when [non-violent] thoughts arise, hostility ceases in his presence."
Even among those such as snakes and mongooses who are eternally intent on mutual hostility, there occurs an abandonment of enmity in the presence of one who does not harm. (2.35)

When there is firm establishment in truth, there is stability in truth; that is, the attainment and arrival of the fruits of actions such as sacrifice occurs through the words of one who speaks the truth—this is the implied sense. For example, when it was asked, "How can even a non-virtuous person become virtuous?", he became virtuous by virtue of that speech. Just as the Brahmin Kuṇḍadhāra, when addressed by the gods with the words, "May his mind delight in dharma," became virtuous.
Thus, when told, "Attain heaven," one attains heaven; just as Triśaṅku, being told by Viśvāmitra, "Attain heaven," attained heaven. What more need be said? His word becomes unfailing. (2.36)

When one is established in non-stealing and free from craving, what happens to him? He receives the service of divine attendants; jewels from all directions wait upon him and reveal themselves to him. (2.37)

[222,16] When established in the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there is the attainment of vigor (*vīrya*). From the attainment of the holy life, one brings forth qualities without obstruction; because of being unobstructed, one brings about the self. One becomes possessed of unimpeded vigor in all activities directed toward wholesome goals. The meaning is that one is not bound by any kind of resistance.

Furthermore, one becomes capable of instilling knowledge in disciples who are disciplined or in virtuous persons who are worthy, just as the Blessed Lord Vyāsa was born with [all] that is to be known (*saṃjñeya*). 2.38.

[222.21] For those who abide in non-appropriation, there is the awakening to the "how" of birth. This is their awakening to the mode of existence of birth: "What indeed is this [birth] of mine? What is its essence? How indeed is it known? By what manner is it so? What shall we become after the time of death? Or shall we not exist? If we shall exist, what shall we be? How shall we be? In this way, for them, regarding the prior, posterior, and middle limits [of existence], there is no appropriation.

The desire to know the Self regarding the past, future, and present is the precursor to right vision; it manifests in its own true form. Because of the absence of attachment to external possessions, the contemplation of one’s own Self proceeds effortlessly. It does not arise even with effort for others whose thirst is extended by the fever of possessiveness. (2.39)

The perfections (*siddhi*) have been described in relation to the restraints (*yama*); now we shall speak of them in relation to the observances (*niyama*). From purity (*śauca*) comes self-disgust with one's own body and non-association with others. By means of self-disgust with one's own body, one who undertakes purity becomes a renunciant (*yati*) who perceives the defects of the body, perceives the loathsomeness of the physical frame, and is free from attachment to the body. Furthermore, there is non-association with others. One who contemplates the true nature of the body and desires to abandon even his own body—seeing no purity in the body despite washing it with earth, water, and so forth—how could he ever associate with the utterly impure bodies of others? (2.40)

Furthermore, there is this other result: purity of being (*sattva-śuddhi*), cheerfulness (*saumanasya*), one-pointedness (*ekāgrya*), mastery over the senses (*indriya-jaya*), and fitness for the vision of the Self (*ātma-darśana-yogyatva*) come to him. Through the stabilization of each preceding quality, the succeeding one manifests. How so? From purity comes purity of being; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery over the senses; and from that, the fitness of the *buddhi-sattva* for the vision of the Self. Therefore, all of this is attained through the stabilization of purity. Thus, this is indeed the perfection of purity. (2.41)
From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness; when the thoughts of discontent do not arise, it is unsurpassed—there exists nothing else superior to this.
And so it has been said:

"Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, whatever worldly pleasure there is, and whatever great divine pleasure—pertaining to the gods and so forth—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving" (MBh 12.168.36 / 12.171.051 / 12.268.6 / 13.134.057d). [2.42]

The perfection of the sense of touch results from the exhaustion of impurity through austerity. There is generally the conceit that "austerity, while being performed, destroys the veil of impurity; how much more so when it has been completed! [224,20]

[224,22] Because that obscuration has not been abandoned, there is the accomplishment of the body, such as *aṇimā* and so forth. The body born of connection with parents and so on—the seed-born (*bīja*) and the one produced from the womb and so forth—all of this will be destroyed by asceticism (*tapas*). Consequently, there is the accomplishment of the body characterized by *aṇimā* and the other powers.

Likewise, the impurity of the senses, which consists of the obscuration caused by unrighteousness (*adharma*) and other factors arising from contact with sense objects and the like, is washed away by the stream of the river of austerity (*tapas*). Similarly, there is the perfection of the senses, beginning with hearing from a distance. (2.43)

From the practice of private recitation comes communion with one's chosen deity. The gods, seers, and perfected beings who are favored appear to one whose habit is the practice of recitation, and they assist him in his tasks, such as providing instruction and the like. (2.44)

Success in concentration comes from devotion to Īśvara. For one who has surrendered all states of being to Īśvara, concentration is perfected. Through this perfection of concentration, he knows everything desired as it truly is; likewise, his wisdom knows things as they really are across different places and times. (2.45)

The restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), together with their accomplishments (siddhi), have been explained. Now we shall describe the postures (āsana) and the others. Among these, the posture is that which is steady and comfortable. A posture is one that is both steady and comfortable. That posture in which steadiness of mind and limbs arises for one who is steady, and by which no discomfort occurs, should be practiced. For example, the names well-known in other treatises, such as the lotus-posture (padmāsana) and so forth, are demonstrated.

In that regard, in a clean place such as a temple, a mountain cave, or a riverbank, near fire or water, free from living creatures, devoid of thorns, and pure— one who is himself pure, having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) correctly, having paid homage to the Supreme Lord, the sole benefactor of the entire world, and having prostrated before the other Lords of Yoga and one's own gurus, should sit upon a seat made of *caula*, *jinaka*, or *kuśa* grass— preferably one that causes no discomfort— and facing either east or north, he should settle firmly in his posture (*āsana*).
Therein, that which is called the *padmāsana* (lotus posture) consists of drawing back the left foot and placing it upon the right, and likewise placing the right foot upon the left.

Pressing the chin firmly against the neck, with his gaze fixed on the tip of the nose like that of a sleeping deer, with the lips closed together like those of a water-snake, not touching the tips of the teeth with the teeth, with the chin and chest held at a distance of about a fist's breadth, with the tip of the tongue placed between the shining gaps of the teeth, and having placed his hands either in the *kacchapaka* (tortoise) position or the *brahmāñjali* (sacred gesture) upon the palms— having thus established himself once in this posture,
and then repeatedly becoming free from effort regarding the specific arrangement of the limbs and the body— that was the *padmāsana*.
And all this is the same for other seats as well; there is only some slight distinction.
