Likewise, having placed the right foot upon the left and having laid the right hand upon the left hand, that posture by which one sits is the *bhadrāsana*; the rest is the same.
Likewise, the *vīrāsana* (heroic posture) consists of having one leg drawn up and the other knee placed upon the ground; the specific details mentioned here apply everywhere.

Grasping the right big toe with the left thigh and calf so that it is drawn inward, and likewise grasping the left big toe with the right thigh and calf so that it is drawn inward, and sitting in such a way that the two heels do not press upon the testicles—that is the *svastika* posture.
Stretching out the two feet so that the ankles are level, the big toes are level, and the knees are level, one should sit like a staff; that is the *daṇḍāsana*.
Nor [should it be] shaped like a yogapaṭṭa, nor supported by a pillar, nor provided with a support.
The cross-legged posture is a reclining position with the arms extended down to the knees.

The Krauñcaniṣadana, Hastiniṣadana, and Uṣṭraniṣadana should be understood precisely according to their resemblance to the shapes of the sitting postures of a curlew, an elephant, and a camel, respectively.
With his straight shanks placed upon the ground, he stood perfectly balanced.
Stability and ease: by another way of considering it, stability and ease are also to be personally envisioned; that posture by which effortlessness arises is also called "stability and ease."

"According to one's ease" (*yathāsukham*) means that posture in whatever form it may be which results in comfort for him; by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), other postures taught by the teacher are also to be understood. (2.46)

Now, the means for mastering the postures (*āsana*) is established: through relaxation of effort (*prayatna-śaithilya*) and infinite meditative absorption (*anantya-samāpatti*). The ellipsis of the sentence is "it comes to be. The supplement is that the posture becomes firmly accomplished. It is perfected by the cessation of effort—that is, by the non-performance of effort after the binding of the posture—by which the limbs do not tremble. By this cessation of effort; for it is by effort that one causes the limbs to shake. The meaning is that by this one becomes one whose posture is unshakable.

Or, it has attained infinity. The universe is infinite; infinity is the state of being infinite. Having attained that—that is, having pervaded it—the mind, abiding in the state of the universal, effects and stabilizes the seat. ||2.47||

From that comes non-overpowering by the pairs of opposites; from that, due to the stabilization of the seat. This is the incidental result: that one is not overcome by the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. (2.48)

Furthermore, there arises proficiency in breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth. How so? When that [posture] is present, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). When the seat is firm, the drawing in of the external air is inhalation (*śvāsa*). Just as water is drawn up through a tube due to continuity, so too, due to continuity, the external air connected with the downward-moving wind (*apāna-vāyu*) is drawn in through the tubes of the nostrils; that drawing in is inhalation. Likewise, the expulsion of the abdominal air is exhalation (*praśvāsa*).

For the abdominal air is indeed connected with the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa). Its expulsion outward is exhalation (praśvāsa). The cessation of the movement of these two is what is meant; therefore he says: "Prāṇāyāma is the absence of both. (2.49)

That [retention of breath], however, is threefold: external, internal, and stationary. It is observed to be long or subtle according to place, time, and number. It consists of external function, internal function, and stationary function. That in which there is an absence of movement preceded by exhalation is the external function (*bāhyavṛtti*). That whose function is directed toward the inward entry of the external air is the external function; therefore, it is called "external. Others call this "filling" (*pūraka*).

[228,11] That in which there is an absence of pleasure preceded by exhalation is "internal-functioning" (*ābhyantaravṛtti*). That whose function consists in the expulsion of internal air toward the outside is "internal-functioning. Therefore, it is internal; they call that *recaka* (exhalation).

The third, however, is the state of being like a pillar (stambhavṛtti). In that state, there is the absence of both; that is, the absence of inhalation and exhalation. That [state] arises from a single effort. Just as water poured upon a heated stone undergoes contraction on all sides, so too do the functions of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and the rest undergo contraction through a single effort. Thus it is said: "There is no simultaneous movement of the two."

All three of these are also observed in terms of their spatial extent (*deśa*), such that one can say, "this is its extent. For example, when the breath moves externally and is drawn inward for rinsing (*ācamana*), its spatial pervasion extends from the tip of the nose down to the big toe. Likewise, when the breath moving internally is expelled outward, its spatial pervasion extends from the big toe up to the tip of the nose. When it moves in a state of stillness (*stambha*), it pervades the space from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head. Alternatively, even when moving externally, there is indeed a spatial pervasion in a sequence starting from a span (*vitasti*) and so forth.
They are perceived by time through the determination of the measure of moments, such that one realizes: "This many moments have been passed by means of breath control."

Likewise, it is observed by means of numbers: the first *uddhāta* is observed as occurring after this many past inhalations and exhalations. Just as the cessation of winds agitated by suppression occurs once they have surged up to the crown of the head, that is the first *uddhāta*; that alone is the mild (*mṛdu*) stage.

Furthermore, when the wind that has been once uplifted and restrained is observed by means of as many past exhalations, this second stage of the element of increase is called "moderate breath control" (madhya-prāṇāyāma).
Likewise, the third [exhalation] is observed through this many inhalations and exhalations; that same triple exhalation is called "intense."
Likewise, due to the attainment of length and shortness by the winds, it also becomes subtle. 2.50.

The fourth [type of breath control] is that which projects both external and internal objects. The external objects are the big toe and so forth. For the external air, when drawn inward, pervades and projects into the internal regions. The internal objects are the earth and so forth. And that [air], being expelled outward, pervades and projects the earth and other elements as perceived through space, time, and number. That is the fourth breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), which projects both external and internal objects.

[229,18] That which is observed with respect to external objects by way of place, time, and number—being drawn in and pervading—is likewise observed with respect to internal objects, and it pervades and draws in those observed by way of place, time, and number. This fourth breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is that which draws in both external and internal objects.

By means of place, time, and number, it is observed, projected, and pervaded with respect to external objects; likewise, it is observed, projected, and pervaded by place, time, and number with respect to internal objects. In both ways, it is long and subtle. Through the projection of both external and internal objects, it attains length and subtlety in both respects.

What is meant by this? He says: "Preceded by that" means preceded by the projection of both objects. Through the mastery of the stages (*bhūmi*), by the sequence of mastering the wind that functions in both, there is the absence of movement in both—the external and internal courses—of the two, namely *prāṇa* and *apāna*; this is the fourth [state].

Fearing that there might be no distinction between the third and fourth [types of breath control] because both involve the commonality of the cessation of movement, he says: "The third is the absence of movement initiated all at once, not attended to by its objects, observed in terms of place, time, and number, and being long and subtle. The fourth, however, is the absence of movement occurring either gradually or after the inhalation and exhalation have reached their limit through the determination of their objects; this is the distinction between the third and the fourth. (2.51)

[230,17] Thereupon, the obscuration of light (*prakāśāvaraṇa*) is destroyed. That by which light is obscured is the "obscuration of light," namely *karma*. For the yogin who practices breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), that by which discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) is obscured is the "knowledge-obscuring *karma*. As it is said in another treatise: "Having veiled the *sattva*, which is luminous by nature, with a great delusive net (*indrajāla*) consisting of intense delusion (*mahāmoha*), it employs that very same *sattva* in what ought not to be done."

When that very being is covered by the great illusion of perverted cognition, it is then employed in all kinds of improper actions by the karma of obscuration. Through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), this karma—which obscures its light and binds one to saṃsāra—becomes weak; not only does it become weak, but it is also diminished at every moment.

And thus it is said that something else also results from the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma): the mind’s fitness for the concentrations (dhāraṇās) which will be described hereafter. This follows from the statement, "Either from breath control itself, or by means of exhalation and retention of the breath," for it is stated that through these two, the attainment of stability of the mind is achieved. (2.53)

[231,15] Now, wishing to describe a particular kind of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), he begins with a question: for others, withdrawal is merely the drawing back of the senses from their own objects; here, however, it is stated to be distinguished: withdrawal is that wherein, in the absence of contact with their own objects, the senses seem to follow the very nature of the mind.

In the absence of the conjunction of the sense organs—such as the ear and the rest—with their respective objects, such as sound and the rest, for meditators who have withdrawn their minds from their own objects due to perceiving the defects in those objects, it is as if the mind conforms to its own essential nature. When the mind of a yogin assumes a particular form, that is called "conforming to the essential nature of the mind. What is meant by this is that when the mind is restrained, the senses are likewise restrained along with it; they do not require any other means for the sake of mastery.

They cease precisely through the cessation of the mind. This is expressed by the syllables heard in the phrase "the king of the bees. The meaning is "the king of the bees": when the king of the bees flies up, the bees fly up after him; when he settles down, they settle down after him. In the same way, the senses are restrained when the mind is restrained; this is *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal). 2.54.

[231.26] Then, from the steadiness of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the supreme mastery over the senses arises. The word "iti" signifies completion. Among those forms of mastery, those through which supreme mastery is born from the steadiness of withdrawal are now described: [232.11] "Victory over the senses with respect to sound and the other objects; furthermore, non-addiction, non-occurrence again and again, or non-attachment," so some say. He explains the term *vyasana*: attachment is *vyasana*. How? It is called *vyasana* because it "scatters" (*vyasyati*) or casts the practitioner away from the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).

Alternatively, "non-opposition" refers to the non-apprehension of opposed things such as sound and so forth, which constitutes mastery. Its explanation is as follows: it is logical that there is a connection with sound and so forth, authorized by the treatise, according to one's own will; others consider that regarding those things which are not opposed, one proceeds or does not proceed according to one's desire.

[232,17] Some maintain that in the absence of passion and hatred, there is a state empty of pleasure and pain, devoid of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted, and characterized by mastery over the cognitions of sound and so forth. However, the distinction in the Middle Way is that even the mere presence of passion and hatred is not excluded.

[232,21] But this is the supreme among all the aforementioned forms of mastery over the senses: that when the senses have their mental activity restrained within a particular [object], they do not require any further means for the sake of conquest, as was previously described regarding the other forms of mastery over the senses. In this case, however, the yogis do not depend upon any further effort-induced means for its attainment. ||2.55||

Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in the *Śrīpātañjalayogaśāstrasūtrabhāṣyavivaraṇa*, the work of the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavat, a disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda and a teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order.

The five external means (*bahiraṅga-sādhana*) for yoga characterized by conscious awareness (*samprajñāta-yoga*) have been stated. Now, the three internal means (*antaraṅga-sādhana*)—namely, fixation (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—are being described for that very same yoga. Indeed, this chapter has been concluded solely through the explanation of the external means, precisely because of the distinction between the external and internal. Furthermore, these three means are mentioned separately because they function in combination (*saṃhatyakāritva*). This is done by demonstrating the internal means which arise immediately following the exposition of the external means.

The connection between the chapters (pādas) has been explained. Furthermore, since the various manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ) are primarily demonstrated in this chapter, it is commenced as a separate unit; for we have already stated that this is precisely the reason for its designation by a specific name.

Retention (*dhāraṇā*) must now be explained. Following withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), retention—which has been brought forward in its proper sequence—should be defined. Retention is the binding of the mind to a location (*deśabandhaś cittasya dhāraṇā*). "Binding to a location" means being fixed upon a location. To what [is it bound]? To the mind.

And he himself explains everything: the "navel-wheel" (*nābhicakra*) refers to the region of the navel being like a wheel; because all the constituent parts (*vāyu*/*avayava*) are arranged there in the form of a wheel, it is called the "navel-wheel. The heart is shaped like a lotus. Regarding the "light in the head": the aperture of the channel at the crown of the head is designated as "light" (*jyotis*) because of its luminosity. The mind is bound to such internal locations as the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, and so forth, as well as to external objects such as the moon, the sun, and others.

The operation of that mind in an unwavering form with respect to such objects as these is called concentration (dhāraṇā). "By mere operation" means that it proceeds by means of the cognition of that specific place alone, being devoid of distraction. (3.1)

In this context, *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) is the one-pointedness of the mental process (*pratyayaikatānatā*). It occurs in that location which is the object of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), such as the navel-center (*nābhicakra*) and so forth; it is the one-pointedness of the mental process whose objective support (*ālambana*) is the object of meditation—the place or whatever else is being meditated upon. This consists of a continuous flow of similar cognitions, a stream of identical mental states that is not touched by nor intermingled with other dissimilar mental processes. That is *dhyāna*.

Retention (*dhāraṇā*), however, is the state of the mind remaining fixed on that very same object of meditation (*dhyeya*), even when it is touched by other cognitions consisting of conceptual constructions regarding that object. Just as for one who is fixing their gaze on the sun, there is indeed retention even during the cognitions of its circularity, its intense rays, and so forth, because the mind remains there by way of mere mental fluctuation (*vṛtti*). Meditation (*dhyāna*), moreover, is not like that; for meditation is simply a continuous flow of a single cognition untouched by other cognitions of a different kind. (3.2)

That very state, appearing as the mere object while being, as it were, empty of its own nature, is *samādhi*. That same *dhyāna*, which consists of a flow of identical cognitions, having abandoned—as it were—its own continuity of a single cognition, appears as the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), manifesting as if it were the object itself. It is "as if empty" of its own nature consisting of cognition, that is, of the nature of grasping. Just as a crystal substance, when reflecting the appearance of an adjacent object, is as if empty of its own nature;
when this occurs due to the mind's absorption into the intrinsic nature of the object of meditation, then that very *dhyāna* is called *samādhi*.

[234,28] But has it not been stated previously that "yoga is samādhi" as the primary factor (*aṅgin*)? Here, however, samādhi is described as a member (*aṅga*) of yoga. What, then, is the distinction here between the member and the possessor of the member? It is said: in the statement "yoga is samādhi," a specific state of mental stability (*cittasthiti*) is intended. Here, however, the distinction is that for the continuum of cognitions (*pratyayasantāna*), the state of having the form of the object of meditation (*dhyeyākāratva*)—due to its penetration by the nature of the object of meditation—is the member. ||3.3||

This triad of dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi, when fully accomplished together in a single place and with a single object, is called *saṃyama*. Thus it is said: "The three means having a single object are called *saṃyama*.

For this reason—that wherever *saṃyama* is mentioned for the sake of conquering what is to be conquered, this triad should be understood as being present there—this technical term (*paribhāṣā*) "saṃyama" is applied to this triad in this treatise.

And he will say: "From *saṃyama* on the three transformations, there is knowledge of the past and the future; and from *saṃyama* on the gross form, the essential nature, the subtle, the inherence, and the purposefulness, there is mastery over the elements" (YS 3.16). [3.4]

From the mastery of that, there is the light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*). From the mastery—that is, the stabilization—of that *saṃyama*, there arises for the wisdom of *samādhi* a light comparable to the light of a lamp, which is capable of manifesting the desired object. To the extent that *saṃyama* becomes firmly established, to that same extent the wisdom of *samādhi* becomes firmly established. By means of this light of the wisdom of *samādhi*, which is capable of illuminating objects that are obstructed or remote, yogins perceive their intended object as if it were held in the palm of their hand. (3.5)

[235,28] Its application to the stages: the application—that is, the practice—of that mastery (saṃyama) must be performed with respect to the stages, both external and internal, which consist of the objects of meditation to be described, such as the three transformations and so forth.

[236,7] For one who seeks the direct purpose of conquering those stages, there is the application of that *saṃyama*—of the stage already conquered—to the stage immediately following the stage where *saṃyama* was attained by the yogin; that is, after the conquest of the preceding stage, *saṃyama* must be applied to the next stage.

For example, regarding earth and the other elements, which possess gross nature, subtle constituent parts, and functional utility across their respective stages (*bhūmi*), one should first apply *saṃyama* to the gross stage; immediately after conquering that, one should apply *saṃyama* to the immediately subsequent stage, which is the essential nature itself. One should not bypass the immediately following essential nature and instead apply *saṃyama* to the subtle stages and so forth.
Why is this so? Because, O Ajita, one does not obtain mastery in the higher stages—the final stages—by skipping over the immediately adjacent lower stage.

[236,15] Furthermore, if one were to apply self-restraint (*saṃyama*) to the peripheral stages (*prāntabhūmi*) without first conquering the immediately preceding stage, one does not obtain that very self-restraint. Consequently, the fault lies precisely in that non-attainment. And because of that non-attainment, and because of the absence of self-restraint, how could there be [the light of wisdom] in that peripheral stage which is the object of self-restraint? This is the meaning. It is the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*). Because of the absence of the causal sign (*nimitta*); for indeed, when the conjunction of oil, wick, and flame is absent, there is no light from a lamp.

For a yogin who has mastered the higher stages—that is, one who has mastered the stages beginning with the Self and so forth—it is not appropriate to practice *saṃyama* on lower stages such as the knowledge of another's mind (*paracittajñāna*) and the like. Why? Because that object, the Self and so forth, has been realized in a different way, being superior to the higher stage, and thus stands in contrast to the lower stages of the knowledge of another's mind and so forth; for it is not mixed with the knowledge of another's mind and the like, since its nature is discernment attained through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For in that case, if one who has mastered the restraint of the higher stages were to take another's mind as an object, the yogi’s own mind would also become confused in its mental aspect; thus, it is not logical, because in that state the object—such as the self—is realized precisely through its distinctness [from the subject].

The explanation of others regarding the meaning of the knowledge of others' minds and so forth is incorrect, because it has been understood otherwise; for by means of attaining the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of higher stages such as the self (*ātman*), one has already attained the meaning of the lower stages, such as the knowledge of others' minds.

In this position, one would have to say that restraint regarding the lower stages is useless; it would not be the case that it is "not appropriate. To say it is "not appropriate" appears, as it were, incorrect.

"How will one understand that 'this is the stage immediately following this stage' and 'this is what must be conquered next'? To this he says: "In this regard, yoga itself is the preceptor; yoga is the attainment of mastery over the previous stages; by that very means, the immediate succession is understood."

[237,18] How, indeed, has it been said that "yoga is to be known through yoga"? By means of yoga consisting in the attainment of previous *saṃyama*, the object of the subsequent yoga is to be discerned. And that yoga is *saṃyama*; it proceeds and is distinguished precisely from yoga—that is, precisely from the attainment of previous *saṃyama*.

Just as for one born blind who wishes to ascend a flight of stairs, the knowledge of the next step is produced by the condition of the tactile sensation of the foot upon reaching the first step; in the same way, yoga proceeds from yoga.
Since this is so, therefore the yogi who knows thus, being vigilant and disciplined through yoga, delights for a long time in the yogas that bear the fruit of mastery over yoga. ||2.6||

The triad is internal compared to the former. The triad of retention (*dhāraṇā*), meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), and concentration (*samādhi*) is internal to the five preceding means, such as restraint (*yama*) and so forth, for the sake of cognitive yoga (*samprajñāta-yoga*). In this context, the mention of "internal" is for the purpose of indicating that these three should be practiced with diligence even when the preceding means have not been fully perfected.

For even without the accomplishment of the fivefold means such as *yama* and the rest, yoga is brought about through the attainment of the triad beginning with *dhāraṇā*, solely by virtue of the penetration of impressions (*saṃskāra*) established in previous births—just as in the cases of those dissolved in the body (*videha*) or in primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*). Yoga is not possible for anyone without the triad beginning with *dhāraṇā*, because that triad consists of the continuous flow and unification of their operations, and because yoga has the form of the perfection of the mind (*cittasampatti*).

But when there is the perfection of knowledge and dispassion (*vairāgya*), then nothing else, such as concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and so forth, is required. And thus it is heard in tradition that for Maṅki, Piṅgala, and others, all success was attained through dispassion alone. Likewise, it has been stated previously in two verses beginning with "The rules for places and postures" (3.7).

That too is external for the seedless [yoga], yet even that which is internal for the seeded yoga becomes external for the seedless yoga. Why? Because it exists even in its absence. Since the seedless yoga exists even in the absence of those three internal means of the seeded [yoga], it is considered external with respect to all the specific distinctions of the Puruṣa.
Some, having seen [the truth] very clearly, are detached from the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as if from birth itself.

For them, through the cultivation of the means of cessation and supreme dispassion, seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*) will indeed arise; for they have no need for the observation of *dhāraṇā* and the rest. And so it has been said: "The yoga of one whose mind is concentrated has been explained; but how may one whose mind is emerged (*vyutthita*) also be joined with yoga?"—it is for this reason that the following is undertaken. Likewise: "For those who are dissolved into the body-less [beings] or into primordial nature (*prakṛti*), [concentration] is conditioned by existence (*bhava-pratyaya*). (3.8)

[238.25] Now, regarding the moments of the mind of cessation (*nirodhacittakṣaṇa*): the mind associated with cessation that is in the process of ceasing is that which ceases during those moments; these are the "moments of the mind of cessation. The meaning is: "at those times of cessation. The use of the plural number in "in the moments" (*kṣaṇeṣu*) is for the purpose of demonstrating its occurrence across the past, future, and present.

Regarding cessation (*nirodha*), the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is indeed that wherein the mind, following the nature of cessation, ceases. The activity of the *guṇas* is mobile, and the mind is subordinate to the activity of the *guṇas*; thus, the transformation of that mind as it ceases from its external activities is an inevitable occurrence. For a mind that does not undergo transformation, cessation is not possible through immutability (*kauṭasthya*) like that of the *puruṣa*. Therefore, he asks: "What then is the nature of that transformation of cessation?"

The transformation of cessation is the sequence of the mind at the moment of cessation, characterized by the suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation. "Emergence" refers to the various arisings or fluctuations of the mind in the form of objective conditions (*pratyaya*). The latent impression produced thereby is a quality (*dharma*) of the mind, which is its substratum (*dharmin*); it is not itself of the nature of an objective condition.

Likewise, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of cessation and birth is of a nature that lacks causal conditions; it is a property of the mind alone. And since that latent impression of emergence (*vyutthāna-saṃskāra*) is of a nature that lacks causal conditions, it is not ceased when causal conditions cease; it is not overcome when the causal conditions for emergence cease.

And from the cessation of the conditions, the formation born of cessation arises. Regarding those two—the formations of emergence and cessation—there occurs their suppression and manifestation within the mind, which is the substratum (*dharmin*) of these formations.

Do these two—the disappearance and appearance—occur without restriction? No. How then? The latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence (*vyutthāna*) diminish, attaining a state of incapacity for their own effects; the latent impressions of cessation (*nirodha*) are established. These two—the suppression and manifestation—do not exist as attributes (*dharma*) of the mind at every moment of cessation; rather, it is the mind’s following after those two, suppression and manifestation, that constitutes the transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*) of the mind.

This is what is being stated: for a single momentary state of mind, this transformation of formations (*saṃskārānyathātva*) occurs through the overcoming of the formations of emergence and the manifestation of the formations of cessation; it is called the "transformation of cessation" because, even though there is a connection with the formations of emergence which are waning, the cessation that is manifesting possesses superior strength.

[240,12] Then, it has been explained that the mind being ceased from external conditions is "that which has residual impressions" (*saṃskāraśeṣa*); another [state] is "that which has residual impressions preceded by the practice of the condition of cessation" (*virāmapratyayābhyāsapūrva*).
What is meant by this? He says: because transformation culminates in cessation, and because it culminates in the absence of conditions, it is called the "transformation of cessation."
[240,16] Even though the causal conditions exist during the state of conscious awareness (*samprajñāta*), they are not intended to be expressed;

rather, it is only the moment-to-moment transformation of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that is intended to be expressed. Just as when the mind has ceased its activity on the stages, meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—though present—is not intended to be expressed because only the cessation itself is intended to be expressed, so too in the state with seed (*sabīja*), only the mere transformation of the latent impressions is intended to be expressed, and not the causal conditions, nor the absorption, nor one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*). ||3.9||

For one who follows the transformation of that mind toward cessation, there arises a state of peaceful flow from the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). This peaceful flow depends upon the proficiency of the formative forces of cessation; proficiency is firmness, and depending upon that firmness, the mind becomes serene and flows peacefully.

Regarding how long that state of tranquil flow lasts, he says: beginning from that *saṃskāra*—the *saṃskāra* of cessation—as long as the *saṃskāra* of the nature of emergence does not overcome the *saṃskāra* of the nature of cessation, so long does his state of tranquil flow continue. [The term] "emergence" (*vyutthāna*) is so called because its nature is to emerge, since it is produced by emerging; that which has this [nature] is the *saṃskāra* by which the *saṃskāra* of the nature of cessation is not overcome. [This continues] "due to the arising of the *saṃskāra* of cessation. (3.10)

The transformation of the mind into concentration (*samādhi*) consists in the disappearance of its capacity for all objects and the emergence of one-pointedness. "Capacity for all objects" is a property of the mind, characterized by its manifold fitness for the purposes of both enjoyment and liberation; as he will state: "The mind, colored by the seer and the seen, has all things as its object. "One-pointedness" is also a property of the mind; it is the equilibrium of the subsided and the arisen mental modifications in a mind being concentrated. This results in the disappearance—that is, the concealment—of the mind's capacity for all objects.
For nothing that already exists will perish; rather, there is the arising of one-pointedness, which means its manifestation. That which does not exist does not come into being.

The mind is that which underlies both that destruction and that emergence as its substrate. The term "concomitance" (*anvaya*), taken from the preceding sūtra, is also applied here. The mind, being invariably accompanied by the destruction of the capacity for all objects and the emergence of one-pointedness, undergoes transformation through the predominance of concentration (*samādhi*). This concomitance of the mind with the destruction of the capacity for all objects and the emergence of one-pointedness is the transformation into concentration.
And the predominance of concentration has been explained in the context of the stage of one-pointedness: "But that which exists in a one-pointed mind illumines the true object."

He says this very thing: this mind, because of the experience and the scriptural authority regarding those two qualities—omniscience and one-pointedness—which are its own nature and not distinct from it during the arising and passing away of objects, becomes concentrated. This is the transformation of the mind into concentration due to the predominance of concentration. (3.11)

Furthermore, at the time of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the transformation of the mind into one-pointedness consists of two equal cognitions, one subsided and the other arisen. For the concentrated mind whose external fluctuations have ceased, the preceding cognition has subsided—that is, it has become latent—while the succeeding cognition, similar to it, has arisen—that is, it has manifested. The concentrated mind, distinguished by its state of integration, is the state of concentration; this concentrated mind follows after both the subsided and the arisen cognitions.

Furthermore, in that very same way, just as the initial condition was calm and the subsequent one arose resembling it and was also calm, and then another arose which was calm, and yet another arose which was calm—thus, until the failure of concentration, the concentration continues to waver by means of the formative forces of emergence.

This indeed is the transformation into one-pointedness, which is the continuous succession of similar and dissimilar cognitions arising and passing away every moment within the mind, the subject of these attributes.
In this regard, from the cessation of external activity until the mind remains as a mere residue of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), that is the transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*).

Likewise, from the cessation of external conditions until the cessation of all conditions without exception, and even after the cessation of all conditions without exception, because there is no arising of one-pointedness [of mind], there is the transformation of meditative concentration (samādhi).

Likewise, at the very moment of transformation through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because both the subsided and the arisen states occur simultaneously and in equilibrium, there is the transformation into one-pointedness (*ekāgratā-pariṇāma*). Since each subsequent transformation is inseparable from the preceding transformation, all three transformations have thus been explained in their proper sequence.

What is the purpose of this exposition on transformation? It is said: it is for the sake of cultivating dispassion toward the fact that the functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile, secondary, entirely subject to the nature of transformation, and unstable. Likewise, this exposition is also for the sake of attaining knowledge of the past and the future through *saṃyama* upon the three kinds of transformation. (3.12)

By this, the transformations of dharma, characteristic, and state in the elements and the sense organs have been explained—by this aforementioned transformation of the mind, distinguished by its forms as dharma, characteristic, and state. In the elements—the gross elements such as earth and so forth—and in the sense organs—the ears and so forth, which do not undergo transformation into other principles—it should be understood that the transformation of dharma, the transformation of characteristic, and the transformation of state have been described.

By means of the transformation of the mind, which is perceived through its instability, an extension is made [to the elements and the senses]; for the transformation of the elements and the senses—which possesses three modes of transformation—is as difficult to discern as the transformation of the mind.

But has it not been stated that the transformations of the mind consist of cessation, concentration, and one-pointedness, and not the transformations of characteristics, marks, and states? Why, then, is there an extension of these [terms] here? To show that these have indeed been mentioned, he says: "In that regard, the suppression and manifestation of the two qualities (dharmas)—emergence and cessation—constitute the transformation of qualities (dharmapariṇāma) within the mind, which is the substratum (dharmin)."

For it is from this very statement regarding the differentiation of dharmas that we have spoken of the differentiation of dharmas; and because of the statement regarding the suppression and manifestation of those two—the emergence and cessation of dharmas—we have indeed also spoken of the transformation of characteristics and the transformation of states.

How is a dharma overcome when it passes from the characteristic of the present into the characteristic of the past? And that which passes from the characteristic of the future into the characteristic of the present manifests. Because of this statement regarding its overcoming and manifestation, the transformation of state is said to be weak in form at every moment; thus he says: "The transformation of characteristics is called immutable."

That cessation, having abandoned the future characteristic of the time-period, does not transcend its nature as a phenomenon (*dharmatva*) nor its nature as the phenomenon of cessation, because it does not originate as a non-existent effect. For if a non-existent effect were to originate, the existence of three time-periods for a single entity would be untenable; moreover, there would be an absence of that which possesses the three characteristics and is delimited by the three times.

Therefore it is said: while not transgressing its very nature (*dharmatva*), it has entered the present characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*); in which present characteristic its manifestation occurs by way of its own essence—this is the second time-period (*adhvan*) of this cessation, viewed from the perspective of the future path.

But when emergence (*vyutthāna*) ascends to the present characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), then cessation (*nirodha*) will reach the third time-period (*adhvan*), the past characteristic; thus, that third time-period will indeed exist. It might be argued: "When the present characteristic is attained, cessation does not possess the three time-periods. To this he says: "And it is not devoid of the past and future characteristics. Why? Because by means of those very [characteristics], it is itself future, present, and past.

[244,15] Likewise, emergence possesses three characteristics associated with the three time periods—the past, future, and present. Having abandoned the present characteristic, yet not having transcended its nature as a dharma (*dharmatva*), as previously explained, it enters the past characteristic when the dharma that was ceasing has reached the state of having ceased, while still remaining within the temporal sequence.

Having observed the present first time-period of this emergence, the second [time-period] is the second. But in the second sequence, it is precisely the third time-period that becomes the second; yet it is not devoid of the characteristics of the future and the present.

Furthermore, upon emerging from cessation, the conditioned factor (*saṃskāra*) that was being realized through the process of cessation leaves behind its future characteristic (*anāgata-lakṣaṇa*) and, without transcending its essential nature (*dharmatva*), enters into the present characteristic (*vartamāna-lakṣaṇa*). In this state, when its own form (*svarūpa*) is manifested, there occurs its activity—the capacity for producing its own effect. This is its activity when its own form is manifested; this constitutes its second temporal period (*adhvan*) when viewed from the perspective of the future. And yet, it is not devoid of the characteristics of the past and the future.

Just as the mind is not joined with the two states of emergence and cessation, so too is cessation, and so too is emergence; this is the transformation of characteristics belonging to the mind and its states of emergence and cessation.

In this way, the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) is observed. How so? At the moments of cessation, while cessation is occurring, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of cessation become powerful; by virtue of the power of these formative forces, there is also the power of cessation. Consequently, the formative forces of emergence (*vyutthāna*) are weak, and from that very fact, there is also the weakness of emergence. Likewise, at the moment of emergence, there is the predominance of the formative forces of emergence and the weakness of the formative forces of cessation. Thus, for those phenomena (*dharma*) which are joined with states that are respectively firm and weak at every moment, there is the transformation of state.
In that regard, he shows by what form there is the transformation of what, [stating]: "of the substratum (dharmin) by means of its attributes (dharmas)."

Transformation [is as follows]: Just as the mind, which is the substratum (*dharmin*), undergoes transformation through states such as cessation and emergence; and just as the factors (*dharmas*) belonging to the three times undergo transformation through their characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*); and just as mental factors such as cessation undergo transformation through characteristics such as the future and so forth; and just as even these characteristics undergo transformation through their stages (*avasthās*); and just as characteristics such as the present undergo transformation through stages such as strength or weakness—thus, by means of these transformations of factors, characteristics, and stages, the world remains non-empty in its defining characteristic and non-empty in its form, consisting of the activity of the *guṇas*.

The functioning of the *guṇas* is mobile. This very nature of the *guṇas*, which is the cause of their activity and the cause of all operations, has been described as belonging to the *guṇas*, namely *sattva* and the others. By means of this threefold transformation—of property (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*)—which is well-known in the case of the mind, one should understand that there is likewise a threefold transformation in the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*), due to the distinction between the property and the possessor of the property (*dharmidharmin*).

[246,10] From the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), however, there is only one transformation (pariṇāma). How so? Because a property (dharma) is merely the very nature of the substratum (dharmi). Indeed, there is no such thing as a "property" existing separately apart from the substratum; nor is that which is called a "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) conceived as something separate by abandoning the property; nor does there exist a distinctness of states (avasthā) apart from the characteristic. Therefore, this is simply the modification of the substratum itself, which is elaborated in three ways through the medium of properties and through the distinction of those properties.

[246,14] But how is it that this is merely a modification of the substrate (*dharmivikriyā*), and not an absolute origination and destruction of what was previously non-existent? To this he says: In that regard, for a dharma such as a jar existing within its substrate called "clay" throughout the time-periods of past, future, and present, there is only a change of state (*bhāvānyathātva*) which constitutes a change of condition (*pratyayānyathātva*). Thus, one speaks of a "past jar," a "present [jar]," or a "future [jar]"—all while the dharma remains within the substrate itself. This is simply the change consisting in the manifestation and disappearance of that very dharma; it is not a change in substance (*dravyānyathātva*). That same substance of clay is the substrate, and it possesses different forms (*rūpāntara*).

He demonstrates the illustration: just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into something else, such as earrings and so forth, there is a change in its state (*bhāvānyathātva*), consisting of a difference in configuration (*saṃsthāna*) such as a swastika or earrings; yet there is no change in the substance (*dravya*) of the gold.

Another says: "One who conceives of the undertaking of non-existent effects holds that the substratum (*dharmin*) is distinct from and superior to its attributes (*dharma*), and that the attributes do not exist [independently], yet will combine as something else and different. However, there is no single substratum that persists through past, future, and present attributes without being distinct from those attributes."

If the persisting entity (anvayī dharmin) were not distinct from its properties, but rather non-different from them—failing to transcend its prior reality, that is, its own essential nature as each preceding substance—and yet were to persist by following through the distinctions of prior and posterior states, as well as the distinctions of past and other states, then this fault would follow: that persisting entity you intend would undergo transformation even while remaining immutable, or it would exist without undergoing any modification at all.

To this, he replies: "There is no fault here. Why? Because we do not accept an absolute [position], and because we do not accept that the substratum (*dharmin*) is either absolutely immutable or subject to total destruction. If the substratum were absolutely immutable like the Self (*ātman*), then, since the qualities (*dharma*) are non-different from that substratum, it would follow that they too are immutable;

thus there would be a fault. However, absolute immutability is not accepted for the qualities as substrata. For he will state that the qualities possess a permanence characterized by transformation (*pariṇāminityatva*)."

Alternatively, it is because one does not admit an absolute difference between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin). For if there were an absolute non-difference of the substrata from the recurring properties, the substrata would attain immutability (kauṭasthya). Or, if there were an absolute difference of the properties, they would undergo absolute destruction. However, neither absolute difference nor absolute non-difference is admitted; therefore, the fault of immutability does not apply.

How is it that there is no immutability? He says: "This world departs from manifestation, yet it is not immutable. Why? Because permanence is denied. For permanence is indeed denied precisely because of its being an effect. If it is argued that it is utterly destroyed, he says: "Even when it has departed, it exists," because destruction is denied. Since the cause is permanent and the effect is non-different from it, utter destruction is strictly denied.

And therefore, as for what is said by some—that this is an example of a contradictory pseudo-reason (*viruddha-hetvābhāsa*)—how so? In the argument, "In what way does this modification depart from its manifestation, because of the negation of permanence; yet even though it has departed, it exists, because of the proof of destruction," the reason "because of the negation of permanence" contradicts the established tenet that "even though the modification has departed, it still exists."

How is it that manifestation (*vyakti*) is the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*), while disappearance (*apāya*) is its falling away (*pracyuti*)? If there were a modification (*vikāra*) that had fallen away from the acquisition of self-nature, then the negation of permanence (*nityatva*) would not be tenable. However, that which is the continued existence of a modification even after it has departed from manifestation—that indeed is permanence.

The negation of permanence consists in the falling away from the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) by means of modification. That which falls away from its acquisition of self-nature is impermanent. That which exists does not fall away from its acquisition of self-nature. Existence and falling away from the acquisition of self-nature are two contradictory properties that cannot coexist simultaneously. Thus, this reason, by relying upon the very tenet it is intended to establish, contradicts that very tenet; therefore, it is a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*).

This is not a fault, because it is accepted that things possess both manifest and unmanifest properties. For just as a jar, though existing in a house, is not perceived there, yet one cannot on that account assert that it does not exist—it is manifested by means of light; so too this triple world, while existing merged within its cause, is made manifest for the sake of the *puruṣa*'s purpose through the nature of its qualities (*guṇa*), which were previously unmanifest.

In the same way, when the formative forces of motion (*gati-saṃskāra*) have ceased and the formative forces of stability (*sthiti-saṃskāra*) are manifested, that which was being conjoined with respect to its cause departs from manifestation. Just as a jar or similar object, though existing when the light of a lamp is obscured, recedes from manifestation due to the lack of support, so too here the properties (*dharma*) such as the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest—which belong to the three times and possess the nature of conjunction and disjunction—recede from manifestation; however, the substrata (*dharmin*) such as the *sattva* and the other *guṇas* do not.

Consequently, the three worlds—beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and ending with the primal pillar (*stamba*)—which constitute the nature of the qualities (*dharma*) of sentient beings and so forth, exist as having the property of being unmanifest. It is said that this very triad of worlds "departs from manifestation" because, despite existing as a collection of extremely subtle qualities that have been utterly suppressed, it is not perceived in the form of manifest, gross qualities. However, there is no departure from the essential nature of the substrate (*dharmin*). Thus, because it is eternal by virtue of its nature as a substrate, it is said that even when it has departed [from manifestation], it still exists.

Thus, since the single substratum (*dharmin*) consists both of the form of manifestation (*vyakti-rūpa*) and the form of potentiality (*śakti-rūpa*), its impermanence exists in the form of manifestation and its permanence in the form of potentiality; how, then, could there be this contradiction? For Devadatta, though always perceived through activities such as moving, does not cease to exist when those movements and so forth come to rest; rather, it is the movement itself that becomes concealed. Therefore, it is like a jar or similar object remaining in an unmanifest state.

An individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is also a substratum (*dharmin*) when considered in relation to its own other properties (*dharmas*). And that [manifestation] is accepted as eternal in its form as a substratum, but non-eternal in its form as a property. Thus, since the distinction between property and substratum among modifications (*vikāra*) is not fixed, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is indeed admitted.

In this regard, the reason "because its permanence is denied" does not contradict the statement "it departs from manifestation. Nor is there a contradiction with the statement "even though it has departed, it exists," because the two refer to different objects. Furthermore, the reason "because its destruction is denied" does not contradict the statement "even though it has departed, it exists," just as Devadatta, although he has departed from the outside, still exists.

Thus, failing to understand the intention of the opponent, this attempt to establish it as an example of contradiction brings to light a situation comparable to the story of the blind man’s mirror. For instance, it appears just like a certain blind man who, without recognizing his own lack of power to see, purchases a mirror for his own use.

Furthermore, even if you were to assert both permanence and impermanence by superimposing them upon a single individual or a single capacity with the desire to prove your thesis, even so, this would not constitute a case of contradictory exemplification (*viruddha-udāharaṇa*), because it would result in proving the opposite. How so? When it is said, "Even that which has departed exists," this is stated as a negation of permanence. By the phrase "because of the negation of permanence," what is actually meant is "because of impermanence. The existence of even that which has departed is called permanence.

The opposite of permanence is impermanence. And the impermanence of the subject (pakṣa), which is itself impermanent, cannot serve as a reason that, by proving its opposite, would contradict permanence; for a reason does not incur the status of being contradictory unless it proves what is undesirable.

Furthermore, even if you were to argue that the negation of permanence consists in "falling away from the acquisition of self-nature" (*ātmalābhāt pracyutiḥ*), even so, there is no difference in meaning; there is merely a difference in words. "Falling away from the acquisition of self-nature" and "impermanence" have one and the same meaning.

Furthermore, even if you were to rely on the argument that "there is no proof for permanence," nevertheless, because this word "due to the negation of permanence" does not express the meaning "because there is no proof for permanence in a single piece of mother-of-pearl."

Alternatively, even if one were to respond by superimposing the term "designator" (vācaka), the resolution remains exactly the same: that there is neither permanence nor impermanence, nor any other form, [given the distinctions between capacity and manifestation, or property and property-bearer].
By this, the objection regarding contradiction—namely, that "the individual exists even when departed [from its universal], because destruction is denied"—is refuted.

This being the case, how can there be existence for that which is devoid of manifestation and not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), given that it does not exist because it is not perceived, like a flower in the sky?

To this it is replied: the reason [adduced], "non-apprehension," is unestablished, because [the effect] is apprehended through both inference and scripture. This manifest [effect] exists even prior to its production, since it arises from that [cause]; for if it were non-existent, it would not arise, just like the horn of a donkey.

Furthermore, if that which is non-existent were to become existent, and that which is existent were to become non-existent, then no one would find confidence anywhere. Moreover, if non-existence were due to non-perception, then by what means could the existence of the liberated self, the soul, and the cause [of the world]—which are not perceived before their manifestation and after their cessation—be denied? Thus, there is the scriptural authority: "The being of the non-existent does not exist; the non-being of the existent does not exist" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.16). Furthermore, non-perception through direct observation is not the cause of non-existence.

Now, if it is argued that the modification belongs to the manifestation itself and yet exists, why is it not perceived? To this he says: "Its subtlety is due to its association with the immediate cause; therefore there is non-perception, not because of non-existence."

[250,13] Now, the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is stated as follows: "The characteristic-transformation is a property (*dharma*), just as a jar or the like [is a property] of clay. When a property exists within the time-periods (*adhvan*) such as the past and so forth, it is a "past" property. What is meant by this? It means that it is endowed with the characteristic of the past, yet it has not fallen into non-existence; furthermore, it is not dissociated from the other two [characteristics], namely the future and the present.

Because the cause, the clay, exists in the present, it is logical that the jar—which is conjoined with it—is also characterized by the present mark, even though it is not yet manifest there. Likewise, although the future jar will come to be as the very clay existing in the future, it is inseparable from the mark of the future; similarly, while existing in the present, it is endowed with the mark of the present and is inseparable from the marks of the past and the future.

Likewise, the future [entity], endowed with the characteristic of the future, is not separated from the characteristics of the present and the past; because the past and future characteristics constitute its very substance, just as they do for a jar, it remains inseparable from the past characteristic even though it is remote.

How can a phenomenon endowed with a single characteristic be inseparable from the other two characteristics? To illustrate this inseparability, he says: just as a man who is attached to one woman is not thereby detached from the rest; for in the case of the remaining women, his passion is characterized by the past and the future. This is because it has been established that what exists does not perish and what does not exist does not arise.

In this regard, concerning the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*), the fault of the confusion of time periods (*adhvasaṃkara*) is raised against all phenomena (*dharma*), because every phenomenon would be endowed with all characteristics. For how could that which will exist be present, and how could it be past? Consequently, there would be the presence of the present and future within the past; the presence of the past and future within the present; and the presence of the past and present within the future. In this way, there is a mutual confusion of the time periods.

The following response to that is stated: It has not been proven that the properties—namely, the lump of clay, the jar, and the shards—belong to the subject called "clay," nor that they are non-different from other properties. Furthermore, even if their status as properties and their mutual difference were established, one must still state how a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is thereby proven.

How is this so? Just as in the state of a lump of clay, a jar is endowed with the characteristic of the future; it is neither present nor past. Even so, by considering its nature as clay and its future existence, it is not even dissociated from the past and the present.

Likewise, that which is endowed with the characteristic of the present is neither past nor future; even when considered in its form as a substratum (*dharmī*), it is devoid of the two characteristics of the past and the future—namely, those characterized by perishing and arising.

The same should be applied to the lump of clay, the potsherds, and so forth. Therefore, he says: "It is not the case that this dharma has only one characteristic at the present time; rather, it possesses three characteristics in the manner already described. Consequently, the time-periods (adhvan) do not become confused."

For in this way, the mind is not of the nature of passion (*rāga*); thus, when the mind is not characterized by passion, and when it is established that passion and other states are distinct from its nature and from one another, there is no confusion between them. Why? Because at the time of anger, passion does not manifest. Indeed, at the time of anger, passion does not manifest as it does in its own proper time. For at the time of anger, passion is either past or future; likewise, anger is also [past or future] at the time of passion.
If there were only the single characteristic of the present moment, then [passion] would not exist at the time of anger.

Furthermore, since there is a contradiction in three characteristics functioning simultaneously within a single characteristic, such a possibility does not exist. However, it would be possible for the characteristics to occur sequentially, just as there is a sequential occurrence of their respective manifestors, such as the manifestor of a jar or other objects.

And it has been stated that excellence of form (*rūpātiśaya*) and excellence of function (*vṛttyatiśaya*) are mutually exclusive. In a jar endowed with the excellence of function and its present form, the excellence of forms such as the state of a lump (*piṇḍa*) and so forth cannot occur due to contradiction. For this very reason, past and future forms coexist with these excellences, because they do not contradict them by virtue of being inherent in the general substrate (*dharmisāmānya*).

Therefore, there is no confusion between the time periods (*adhvan*). Just as when passion (*rāga*) itself is active in a certain instance, it does not mean that passion is absent elsewhere in the other three [time periods]; rather, even though it is past or future, it exists then by virtue of being generally endowed with the nature of mind. The same applies to the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

[252,24] But surely, since the lump and the shards are past and future, and because they do not exist during the state of the jar, the substratum (dharmin) called "clay" must also be past and future. Thus, considering that the lump and the shards are absent from the substratum, one might suspect that the three time-periods (adhvan) are untenable for the properties (dharma), such as the lump and the shards. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The substratum does not belong to the three times. For the substratum called "clay" is neither past nor future by virtue of the lump and the shards being past and future, because the cognition of "clay" persists throughout all its states. What then? It is the properties [that belong to the three times].

The lump and so forth belong to the three times, for at the time of the jar, neither the lump nor the shards are perceived; therefore, one should not suspect that the connection with the three times does not apply to phenomena.

Those phenomena, such as a lump of clay and so forth, which are characterized and marked by the three times, undergo various states—such as being firm or weak—and are designated as "different" through their change of state, as in the case of saying "this is a new jar" or "it is old. This is due to a difference in condition (*avasthāntara*), not due to a difference in substance (*dravyāntara*) beyond the clay itself.

Just as a single line, when in the place of hundreds, becomes one hundred through two zeros in the third place; and that same line, when in the place of tens, becomes ten through one zero in the second place; and that same line remains one in the first place.

Or, for example, even though there is oneness, a woman is called both "mother" and "daughter," and she is also called "sister" in relation to another. Thus, in this way, the differences in words, cognitions, and so forth, arise solely from different states (*avasthāntara*), not from a difference between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmī*). Therefore, the argument put forward by others—that the difference in cause and effect is caused by a distinction such as time, which is characterized by words and cognitions—is rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by this.

Regarding this third [type of] transformation, that of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), some have stated the fault of the consequence of immutability (*kauṭasthya-prasaṅga*). How does the consequence of immutability follow? The time-periods (*adhvan*), such as the present and so forth, are established by their own respective functions. How so? When the property (*dharma*)—the jar—does not perform its own function while in the state of a lump of clay, it is then "future. When it performs it, it is then "present. When, having performed it, it has ceased, it is then "past."

In that case, that very same property (dharma)—whether past, present, or future—is established as being essentially identical with the substratum (dharmin) while mounted upon its own specific activity; it does not exist as a distinct form. Consequently, because the substrata and their qualities are eternal, and because [the properties] are non-different from that eternity, it follows that the states of the properties and characteristics would attain immutability (kauṭasthya); thus, this is stated as a fault.

This is not a fault. Why? Because even though the *guṇas* are eternal, due to the variety of their mutual friction (*vimarda*), and because of the diversity of their emergence and suppression (*udbhavābhibhava*), it is not admitted that the *guṇas* are absolutely immutable like the *puruṣa*.

This is because their transformation (*pariṇāma*) is accepted. Furthermore, although they are in a state of incessant transformation, there is no attainment of the status of a different substance apart from their mutual friction; thus, there is no immutability.

How is there a variety of transformations? He says: Just as a configuration such as the body and so forth is something that has a beginning, possesses a cause, is a mere attribute (dharma-mātra), is identical with its cause, non-distinct from it, perishable, and subject to disappearance upon the emergence of another attribute—for whom is this configuration? He says: for sound and other [qualities] which are imperishable. Likewise, the subtle principle (liṅga) called the Great One (mahat) has a beginning, possesses a cause, is a mere attribute, is perishable, and is identical with the imperishable qualities (guṇas).

In that [unmanifest], which consists merely of the principles beginning with the Great One (mahat), there is the notion of modification; however, there is no perishability due to the diversity caused by the mutual suppression of the guṇas, for the guṇas are eternal in their own nature.

In this regard, there is an illustration: even a deceased entity, assuming the form of a lump and then attaining another form, such as a jar, undergoes transformation according to its nature (*dharmatā*).

[255,12] [The form of a jar, having abandoned the characteristic of the future, attains the characteristic of the present; thus it transforms by way of its characteristic. 255,14 Likewise, a jar, experiencing newness and antiquity at every moment, attains transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*). Thus, for the substratum (*dharmin*) such as clay, the "state" (*avasthā*) is another property (*dharmāntara*), such as the lump and so forth. The substratum has existed in the form of states such as the lump or the shards.

[255,17] Therefore, transformation is in fact one alone, though it is presented through its various distinctions. This same principle should be applied to other objects as well—such as clay, and likewise to the body, the senses, and so forth. These transformations of quality (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*) do not transcend the essential nature of the substrate (*dharmī*); thus, there is only one transformation of the substrate that encompasses all the specific variations consisting of the transformations of quality, characteristic, and state. Why? Because transformation is defined as the emergence of a new quality upon the cessation of a previous quality within a persisting substance; therefore, the substrate itself is nothing but transformation. It can be said:
To practice. 3.13.

[255.23] But what is this substrate (*dharmin*) in which, while it remains constant, there occurs the emergence of one property (*dharma*) upon the cessation of another property, such that this is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*)? In this regard, the substrate is that which conforms to properties that are subsided (*śānta*), arisen (*udita*), or unmanifested (*avyapadeśya*). That which has the nature of conforming to subsided, arisen, and unmanifested properties is the "concomitant" (*anvayin*); it is designated as the substrate because its essence remains undifferentiated even when its states are differentiated. A "property" (*dharma*) is defined as a capacity delimited by potentiality; for example, the capacity of the substrate gold to assume the state of being a necklace, an earring, and so forth—this very capacity is the property.

And although that [potentiality] is unmanifest, its existence is inferred from the diversity in the production of effects within the substratum (*dharmin*). For example, a lump of *kaṅka* clay produces effects such as earrings at another place and at another time; by observing this diversity in the production of those effects, one understands that the [clay] has the capacity to produce other and yet other varieties. Thus, the existence of that [potentiality] is inferred from the diversity in the production of effects within that substratum. By the statement "one substratum has various and distinct attributes," he expresses the non-identity of the attributes of a single substratum.

In that regard, that which is perceived is the present; experiencing its own function, such as the fetching of water and so forth, it is distinguished from other phenomena that are either quiescent or inexpressible.

But when one is endowed with the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) in its general form, then, because it is merely the essential nature of the substratum and because it constitutes the very self of the substratum's essential nature, what is this [distinction], and by what is it differentiated in particular? The meaning is that differentiation belongs only to those forms that have mounted upon functional activity (*vyāpāra*), and not to those whose nature is observed as following from the collection of causes.

[256,22] But what, then, are those factors that are quiescent (*śānta*), arisen (*udita*), or indeterminable (*avyapadeśya*)? Indeed, those factors (*dharma*) belonging to a substratum (*dharmī*) which, having performed their function, have passed away are quiescent. Those still possessing their function are arisen; they are immediate successors (*samanantara*) to the future characteristic. Likewise, the past moments are immediate successors to the present. For what reason are they not immediate successors to the past? Because they exist—that is, because there is no state of prior and posterior [between the past and the present]. That which occurs after another is its subsequent immediate successor.

And the other [the future] is prior in relation to that [the present]. Therefore, since there is no posteriority here [in the past], this [past] is not itself prior; thus, due to the absence of priority and posteriority, there are no states immediately following the past. Just as there is priority and posteriority between the future and the present, it is not so for the past. Consequently, the past has no immediate successor (*samanantara*).

As for this reading, "that which is future becomes the immediate antecedent of the present," it has no connection with the subject under discussion. Therefore, the correct reading is: "That which is future becomes the immediate antecedent of the past," because this alone is logically consistent with the meaning.

How is this so? When the formative force of emergence (*vyutthāna-saṃskāra*) is first overcome by the formative force of cessation (*nirodha-saṃskāra*), then that formative force of emergence, having abandoned the present time-period (*adhvan*) and entered the past time-period, becomes present once again while being future. Thus, although it was not immediately contiguous (*asamanantara*) [to the past] while still in the future, it becomes immediately contiguous to the past; for there is no difference in the mere essential nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*) of phenomena (*dharma*) across the two characteristics of the past and the future.

[257,19] Now, as for those that are "indescribable" (*avyapadeśya*), in order to demonstrate what is meant by "indescribable," he says: "everything has everything as its essence. How so? It has been stated therein: the transformational diversity (*pāriṇāmika*) of taste and so forth, consisting of various forms, is observed in stationary objects (*sthāvara*) derived from water and earth. For example, just as a single taste assumes a variety of forms—such as sweetness or pungency—in sugarcane, ginger, and other plants; likewise, color takes on diverse forms such as white, black, and so on. The same applies to smell and the other qualities.

Likewise, there is a manifold diversity of juices and other constituents among mobile beings derived from immobile ones; that is, when immobile things are consumed by mobile beings, they undergo a universal differentiation into juices, blood, and so forth. Similarly, there is a manifold diversity of juices and other constituents among immobile things derived from mobile ones, as is well known from the science of botany (Vṛkṣāyurveda) regarding trees and plants.

Thus, among the stationary things there are the stationary, and among the moving things there are the moving; in this way, through the non-interruption of the species and the non-destruction of beings and so forth, everything has everything as its essence. Even the three worlds exist upon the tip of a finger. Likewise, there are hundreds of passages from the Śrutis and Smṛtis, such as "Brahmā created [the world] from his thumb" and "from the pores of his skin," and so on.

If everything were of the nature of everything, then everything would be perceived everywhere; and as for the objection that "grief born from the separation of loved ones should not arise," he recites the answer: "Because of the restriction by place, time, form, and cause. The "restriction" (apabandha) of place and so forth means their binding (avabandha); therefore, there is no simultaneous manifestation of all things in their entirety.

For some embodied beings, in a particular place and at a particular time, and in a particular manner, there is a manifestation [of these qualities] due to the observation of causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, as in the case of Rāhu and others. By this very fact, the occurrence of grief and other states caused by the loss of what is esteemed is also explained. Therefore, because they exceed the scope of numerical enumeration in each individual case, these qualities cannot be fully specified.

[238,18] That which persists through those properties—whether quiescent, emergent, or indeterminable, and whether manifest or unmanifest—which consists of both the general and the particular, and which takes the form of "existence" (sattva) and so forth, as well as "sound" (śabda) and so forth, is the persisting substratum (anvayī dharmī). However, for that proponent for whom this external and internal world is merely a collection of properties (dharmamātra) devoid of persistence, or for whom it is mere consciousness (jñānamātra), there can be no experience. This is because, since these properties are momentary and perish, it is impossible for them—whether past, future, or present, or simultaneous—to enter into a relationship such as that of the enjoyer and the enjoyed. Thus, experience is non-existent.

[238,23] He demonstrates the absence of a connection: why? Because another consciousness would be the non-agent of an action performed by a different consciousness; how then could it be designated as the experiencer? Furthermore, a connection with the fruit is logical only when the agent is directed toward that fruit; it is contradictory to say that one is the agent while another is connected with the fruit.

And there would be an absence of memory; that is, an absence of memory regarding objects such as what has been done or what was to be done. For one person does not remember what was seen by another; indeed, Vasumitra does not remember what was seen by Caitra. And because there is recognition of an object, [in the form] "this is that very same thing," [it follows that the self exists].

We recognize [the underlying entity]; therefore, the persisting substratum (dharmī) remains constant, while its "alteration through properties" (dharmānyathātva)—meaning its alteration by means of its attributes—is accepted and understood. However, there is no alteration in its own essential nature (svarūpa). Just as we recognize that gold alone persists even though it follows through various distinctions such as necklaces and the like, so too here. Therefore, this is not merely a collection of properties (dharmamātra) devoid of any underlying continuity. ||3.14||
[260,10] Now, the cause for the distinction between transformations is stated:

for only when transformation is established can the practitioner apply restraint (*saṃyama*) toward the three types of transformation. Because, by means of some indicative mark (*liṅga*), the cognition of the past and so forth can be produced, but not otherwise; thus, the difference in sequence is the cause for the difference in transformation. For a single substrate (*dharmin*), such as the mind (*citta*) and so forth, there is only one transformation.

Since it would follow that attributes (dharma) and so forth are distinct from the substratum (dharmin), this reason—namely, "the difference in sequence"—is stated for the purpose of establishing a difference in transformation. Sequence means immediate succession; its "difference" is its distinction [from other sequences].

For three sequences are observed that possess mutually distinct characteristics: through the sequence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and states (*avasthā*), there is a sequence of factors (*dharma*) that is distinct; through the sequence of factors and states, there is a sequence of characteristics that is distinct; and through the sequence of factors and characteristics, there is a sequence of states that is distinct.
