That distinctness of theirs, which is established as having ascended the well-known path, is the cause of distinctness and the inferential indicator of the transformations (*pariṇāma*) that constitute sequential effects.

For example, clay is the substratum (*dharmin*), which is analyzed through properties such as powder and so forth— properties that arise at non-simultaneous times and proceed sequentially. In every instance where "clay" is mentioned,
it demonstrates that the substratum called "clay" follows after properties such as powder, lump, jar, shards, and fragments, whose mutual differences are perceived.

[259.22] Immediately following the powder is the lump; immediately following the lump is the jar; immediately following the jar are the shards; immediately following the shards are the fragments. Thus, the sequence consists of the very phenomena themselves—clay as powder, clay as a lump, clay as a jar, clay as shards, and clay as fragments. This is the sequence of distinct phenomena (*dharmāntara*), not a sequence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) nor of states (*avasthā*). Just as whatever phenomenon is the immediate successor (*samanantara*) of another phenomenon, that is its sequence.

How is it that "the lump gives rise to the jar"? The meaning is that the clay, which exists in the form of a lump, becomes a jar. This is expressed as "the lump gives rise to the jar" by resorting to non-difference; however, the lump does not itself undergo a transformation into another property.
Rather, through the dissolution of the property of being a lump, a property called "jar"—which is its opposite—arises immediately thereafter.

The transformation of phenomena (*dharmapariṇāma*) is twofold: transformation into that which is similar (*tulyapariṇāma*) and transformation into that which is dissimilar (*atulyapariṇāma*). For example, when a lump [of clay] gives rise to a jar, the substratum (*dharmin*) called "clay" transforms through properties (*dharma*) such as those of the jar; this is transformation into a dissimilar property (*atulyadharmapariṇāma*). Furthermore, from the moment of the jar's birth until its reduction to shards, the clay transforms precisely in the form of the jar; this is transformation into a similar property (*tulyadharmapariṇāma*).

[260,14] Now the sequence of the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāmakrama*) is explained: the sequence of the transformation of characteristics is the present state of a jar arising from its future characteristic; likewise, when a contradictory property arises for the lump [of clay], there is the sequence of the past state arising from the present. There is no sequence for the past. For a dharma, the characteristic that immediately follows the present characteristic is the sequence of characteristics; however, there is no characteristic immediately following the past characteristic.

Why? Because immediate succession (samanantaratva) exists only when there is a relation of prior and posterior; however, that [relation] does not exist for the past. Therefore, sequence belongs only to the two characteristics of the future and the present. The purpose for establishing the absence of sequence in the past will be explained in the context of the sūtra: "From mastery over moment and its sequence" (Yoga Sūtra 3.52).

Likewise, there is a sequence of transformation of states: in the case of a new jar, at its end, in the state of finality, antiquity is observed. And that [antiquity], being inferred through a sequence following a succession of moments, occurs by means of the gradual wearing away of its novel state at every moment.

Antiquity (purāṇatā) comes into being; and it reaches its highest manifestation at the end [of an object's existence]. In the middle, however, it is not perceived due to its subtlety. Therefore, although the process exists during the intermediate state, it is not observed. It is inferred by the sign of its manifestation at the final time—that very process by which this antiquity has reached its highest manifestation. For indeed, as soon as a jar is fully produced, its antiquity, though arising every moment, is not grasped.

And thus he will say: "Sequence is that which consists of the succession of moments and is discernible through its final limit by means of transformation. Therefore, because the sequence of states is distinct from the sequence of the characteristics of dharmas, this third transformation is distinguished from the transformations of dharma and characteristic.

These aforementioned successions obtain their own specific forms only when there is a distinction between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). However, when the attribute and the substratum are intended to be non-distinct, no such distinction of succession is obtained therein. Even an attribute becomes a substratum with respect to another attribute; indeed, apart from the qualities (*guṇas*), the status of being a substratum and an attribute is not established. Furthermore, even for the Great One (*mahat*) and the rest, there is the status of being a substratum with respect to the Undifferentiated (*aviśeṣa*); for the Undifferentiated, with respect to the Particulars (*viśeṣa*); and for the Particulars, with respect to the "tranquil" (*śānta*) and "arisen" (*udita*) states.
But when, from the perspective of ultimate reality, a property is expressed by means of a metaphorical identification with the substratum, then this sequence appears precisely as a unity.

In that regard, with respect to the duality of the mind, there are two kinds of phenomena: those perceived and those unperceived, as well as those apprehended and those unapprehended. To the question "Which are they?", he says: therein, those consisting of conditions—such as attachment, aversion, and delusion—are perceived; those which exist merely as entities (*vastumātra*) by their own nature and are capable of producing effects are unperceived. And these, by virtue of the existence of their activity within their own objects, are exactly seven.

How are they understood? They are understood through inference as having their mere existence established by the presence of an effect as a logical mark (*liṅga*); however, they are not perceived in their own essential form (*svarūpa*) by those who are not omniscient. For that reason, they are spoken of individually.

[262,13] Cessation, qualities, and formations. "Cessation" has been explained. "Qualities" refers to both *dharma* and *adharma*. "Formations" (*saṃskāra*) are of the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). "Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) has its characteristic already stated. Now, "life" (*jīvana*): with respect to *dharma* and the other qualities, the activity of all the instruments characterized as vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs by means of a certain mental quality; that is called "life. It is the desired operation, power, or capacity—the qualities of the mind. Being devoid of perception, they are imperceptible. Thus, these seven mental qualities beginning with cessation are said to be unperceived. (3.15)

These three transformations—consisting of the form of the essential nature (*dharma*), the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the state (*avasthā*)—are presented as the object of *saṃyama* for the yogin who has acquired all the means of practice, who has fully mastered the restraints (*yama*) and other practices through concentrated meditation, and whose *saṃyama* is most firmly established, in order to attain knowledge of any desired object, whether past, future, or present. All three together constitute a single object of *saṃyama*.

[262,22] Through *saṃyama* on the three transformations, there is knowledge of the past and the future. *Saṃyama* must first be applied to the three transformations until the light of the wisdom of *samādhi* arises. And whatever object that [wisdom] is directed toward, it brings that object into direct perception exactly as it is. When *saṃyama* is performed upon subtle, obstructed, past, future, or remote objects with the intention of attaining them, then that object comes under the mastery of the yogin.

Through *saṃyama* upon the moments of existence (*dharmakṣaṇa*), the states (*avasthā*), and the transformations (*pariṇāma*), knowledge of the past and future arises for the yogin. The triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* performed upon a single object is called *saṃyama*. By means of that *saṃyama*, the threefold transformation being directly realized brings about knowledge of the past and future regarding those transformations.

Because all objects are subject to transformation and because they possess past and other temporal states, through *saṃyama* upon the three types of transformation pertaining to all objects associated with the three times, everything becomes directly perceived. Likewise, dispassion arises in one who beholds the universe as unstable, characterized by transformation at every moment. (3.16)

[263,17] This other field of mastery is now introduced for the purpose of understanding all words and their meanings: through the mutual superimposition of word, meaning, and cognition, there arises a confusion; by practicing *saṃyama* on their distinction, knowledge of the sounds of all beings is attained. In this regard, what is the word, what is the meaning, or what is the cognition? What is the cause of their confusion, and how is their distinction to be made?

In this regard, it is first investigated whether sound (*śabda*) is that which is uttered by speech and perceived by the ear, or whether it is something distinct from speech; or whether speech itself is it, or something separate from it. First of all, speech is not sound. Why? Because speech is meaningful only with respect to phonemes (*varṇa*). "Speech" (*vāk*) is the sense organ connected to the eight locations [of articulation], whose function is exhausted merely in the manifestation of phonemes; it does not exert any activity toward the manifestation of meaning or the manifestation of sound.

Likewise, the auditory organ (*śrotra*) perceives neither the sound itself nor the object that is sound. Why? Because its domain consists solely of the transformation of the resonance (*dhvani*). "Resonance" (*dhvani*) is the universal (*sāmānya*) which takes the form of both articulated letters (*varṇa*) and non-articulated sounds (*avarṇa*). Its particular transformation consists of the nature of articulated letters such as 'a' and so forth, as well as the nature of the cries of crows and other animals; it is manifested by the dulling of the sense organs. Thus, the auditory organ, which terminates in the manifestation of nothing more than this transformation of resonance, does not operate upon either the external object or the word-meaning.

But is it not the case that sound is precisely that which is apprehended by the auditory organ? No; because it is that which causes the cognition of meaning. That which causes the cognition of meaning is "word" (śabda). What, then, is this? It is the *pada*.

Furthermore, that [word] is apprehended by a cognition which synthesizes the sounds (*nāda*); for when the various sounds, which are the objects of the sense of hearing, arise and each deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the cognizer, the cognition that is produced by the final sound is the "cognition synthesizing the sounds. This arises in the mind of the cognizer, which has acquired impressions through the sequence of the initial sounds. By means of that single cognition, the word is apprehended.
And that word, because it is perceptible, does not depend on any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like color and other such sensory objects.

[264,13] But surely the Blessed Upavarṣa has said: "The phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the *visarjanīya* [constitute the word 'go']. That is not so, because they lack expressive power (*avācakatva*). Why? Because a collection (*samudāya*) is impossible. And the impossibility of a collection follows from the impossibility of their occurring at a single time. For at the time of the utterance of the phoneme *ga*, the phonemes *au* and the *visarjanīya* do not exist; nor do the phonemes *ga* and the *visarjanīya* exist at the time of the utterance of the phoneme *au*; nor do the other two coexist at the moment the *visarjanīya* is produced. Thus, due to the impossibility of a collection of phonemes, there is a lack of expressive power.

Just as phonemes do not exist simultaneously at one and the same time, so too the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the memories produced by them lack the capacity to signify because they do not occur at the same time. Furthermore, since the purpose of a formative impression is the application of memory, and memory functions only with respect to an object already experienced, while the cognition [of meaning] is something new.

Furthermore, if it were admitted that linguistic formations (*saṃskāra*) are expressive, then the comprehension of meaning would arise from words; one would declare a sequential state of being by means of a verb, because "the dharma has the word as its root," and thus that which is not based on words would be disregarded—thereby denying what is well-established.

Furthermore, even if one were to metaphorically designate memory (*smṛti*) and mental impression (*saṃskāra*) as "sound" (*śabda*) because they arise when phonemes (*varṇa*) exist, this so-called "arising when that exists" would not necessarily apply only to those [phonemes]. It could occur wherever there is existence or non-existence. Moreover, that [designation] would only be possible once the sound-nature of phonemes has been established. However, in cases such as a mirage (*marīci*), due to self-conceit and lack of discrimination, one forms a cognition of something as being what it is not; therefore, this is not a cause for determining the reality of an object in all instances.

Moreover, since the comprehension of meaning occurs only when the activity of speech and hearing is present, and because there is no deviation from that, it follows that sound-ness (*śabdatva*) exists in the state of being produced by that [activity]. Therefore, the final phoneme is not expressive, because it is a phoneme, like the first phoneme. Likewise, the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the memory of those [phonemes] are not expressive, because they are impressions of memory, like the impressions of the memory of the first phoneme.

If it is argued that the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, is the expressive unit (*vācaka*), this is not so. Why? Because it would follow that the meaning is cognized from the mere utterance of the final phoneme alone. For every listener possesses impressions deposited by the phonemes *ga*, *k*, and so on, uttered on previous days; thus, the meaning would be understood there from the mere utterance of the final phoneme. If it is further argued that the utterance of the initial phoneme is for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*), this is not the case; since the preceding phonemes do not exist simultaneously with the final phoneme, there can be no assistance (*sāhāyaka*), and therefore a restriction is impossible.

[265,10] If it is argued that even for you, since phonemes (*varṇa*) manifest the word (*pada*), there is the very same fault—that preceding phonemes must be uttered for the sake of restriction—and therefore, rather than postulating that phonemes manifest the word, it is more logical that phonemes themselves are the signifiers (*vācaka*), we reply: no, because it is accepted that phonemes merely deposit their own impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the intellect. For it is in the intellect, which has been built up by a succession of impressions from phonemes that perish as soon as they are uttered, that the word appears.
This alone is what constitutes the manifestation of the word by the phonemes; it does not operate directly toward the word like a lamp.

It is not more plausible that, through the medium of a single cognition, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) should abide in a single substratum and stand in a relationship of mutual assistance, as is the case with the perception of desirable or undesirable objects, memory, desire, aversion, and so forth. For never can a connection be established between the final phoneme and the preceding phonemes, nor with their respective memories or mental continuities.

[265,18] Now, if it is argued that the letters themselves possess the capacity to denote meaning precisely because they produce a cognition accumulated through a succession of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) brought about by their fixed order and phonetic form, this is not so, because it abandons what has already been accepted. For if the cognition—distinguished by the multiple impressions of the letters—has as its object either the meaning or the word, then the theory that "the comprehension of the word-meaning [arises from the letters]" would be contradicted.

Therefore, one must accept that there is a word distinct from the individual phonemes, which is the object of a single cognition. Consequently, it is not the final phoneme—whether accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding phonemes, or the memory of them, or the impressions themselves—that is the expressive agent; for it depends upon the assistance of those impressions, just like the cognition itself.

This being the case, how is it that there is no operation of the phonemes (*varṇa*) with respect to the object or the word? To this he says: because phonemes cannot occur at a single moment. And speech cannot occur at a single time because it proceeds sequentially. Therefore, their natures are mutually independent; since there is an absence of any connection whatsoever, they do not assist one another.

Having failed to touch the word, having failed to establish anything as an operation upon the word, and having failed to designate it, whether they appear or disappear, individually or collectively, they do not even grasp the nature of the word with a mere sidelong glance. Since each one individually lacks the nature of a word due to the impossibility of simultaneous existence, they lack the nature of a word even as a collective entity; how much more so when they exist individually, being meaningless?

Furthermore, each individual phoneme (*varṇa*) is accumulated with the capacities for all denotations. It is "accumulated" with those capacities that manifest all those denotative words (*abhidhāna*) by which it is expressed—just as the hub of a wheel is the center of its spokes. For example, the letter *ga* is accumulated with the capacity to illuminate all words such as *kavarga*, *agni*, *gagana*, and so forth.

[266,18] Because it stands in a relation of contrast (*pratiyogitva*) with other phonemes that act as its auxiliaries (*sahakārin*): just as the word *gauḥ* depends upon the auxiliaries *ga*, *au*, and the visarga, while being the contrastive counterpart (*pratiyogī*) to the vowel *i* in the word *agni*. Therefore, due to its connection with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of different phonemes, each word attains, as it were, a manifold form (*vaiśvarūpya*). Furthermore, the subsequent phoneme is established by the preceding one for the manifestation of a specific word-particularity; the preceding phoneme is established by the subsequent one; and the middle one is established by both the preceding and the subsequent.
In this way, many phonemes, following a sequence—that is, conforming to a specific order and succession—[constitute a word].

[266,23] By means of a conventional sign regarding meaning (*arthasaṅketa*), these [words] are delimited by that convention (*saṃketa*)—that is, the agreement (*samaya*)—in the sense that "these [words] follow this sequence with respect to this meaning. Thus, they are delimited by that conventional sign of meaning.

A word (*pada*) is designated by means of the convention of phonemes (*varṇa*). For a word is that which possesses a function inseparable from its phonemes and depends upon a conventional agreement regarding a specific sequence of phonemes; indeed, its convention is nothing other than the convention of the phonemes themselves.

These phonemes, being thus [limited] and divested of the capacity for all denotations, are excluded from other capacities for denoting other words because they are intent upon the function of manifesting a specific word that conveys a particular object possessing a dewlap and so forth; having ceased from those other capacities, and being under the influence of their mutual assignment to distinct functions, the letters *ga*, *au*, and the visarga—whose powers to illuminate other indifferent words have receded—illuminate the object possessing a dewlap and so forth by manifesting the word.

Therefore, the connection of these phonemes—which are delimited by conventional signs for meaning, which are expressed according to the path of logic, whose sequence of sounds is assisted [by mental effort], which are joined with a specific order, and which arise through a particular sequence—this single manifestation in the intellect (*buddhi-nirbhāsa*), this manifestation of the intellect, is the word (*pada*); it is the ground (*bhūmi*) or, as it were, the foundation, serving as the designator (*vācaka*) of the designated object (*vācya*), whereas the phonemes themselves are not. However, it is conventionally designated by means of the phonemes.

That word is a single entity; whereas any object possessing parts, such as a jar, is observed to be the object of multiple cognitions, the word is not like that. It is the object of a single cognition, as is directly perceived by everyone in the world. Furthermore, because phonemes are manifold and arise at non-simultaneous times, they do not attain the status of being the object of a single cognition. For one who seeks to refute this—this [word] which is grasped by a single cognition through inference—his proposition would contradict direct perception.

Thus, projected by a single effort, and having been brought about by the ripening of the cognition whose cause is the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by the sequence of phonemes, it suddenly flashes forth in the final cognition as undivided, devoid of parts, and for that very reason, non-sequential and not consisting of phonemes; it is established by the operation of the final phoneme-cognition and manifested solely through the apprehension of the final phoneme, which is assisted by the succession of operations of the preceding phonemes.

[267,16] When speakers express [meaning] through phonemes with the desire to convey their understanding to another, and when listeners hear them, it is apprehended as an established fact through worldly cognition, which conforms to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless linguistic usage and functions through mutual consensus. Furthermore, it revolves within the circle of the beginningless wheel of saṃsāra.

The comprehension of meaning arises from the word alone; this is the prior linguistic usage, which is perceived as established by the worldly intellect permeated by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus, for those whose purpose consists merely in engaging in linguistic usage that proceeds with a blurred form—just as they have no dispute regarding the self (*ātman*), so too they have no dispute regarding the word (*pada*).

Therefore, the word (*pada*) is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), because, while being apprehended by a single cognition, it is expressive, like a lamp; and because it is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, like a lamp and like a cognition. The phonemes are not the word, because they are employed sequentially by a single agent and because they function as instruments, like an axe, wood, and so forth.

Regarding this, someone says: "Neither the phonemes (*varṇa*) nor the sounds (*dhvani*) manifest the *sphoṭa* of words and sentences by way of being manifestors, just as the light of a lamp and so forth [manifest objects]."

"Because it exists, like a jar," and so forth—such proofs are indeed formulated according to one's preference regarding an object imagined apart from worldly convention. In accordance with worldly usage, the *sphoṭa* is not the designator of meaning, because it is distinct from the phonemes, like a jar. There is no contradiction with what is perceived, because the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished.
But for one who denies the phonemes because they arise immediately after the cognition of them, there would be a contradiction with what is perceived, just like the denial of the moon in the sky.

Or rather, this cognition of an object arising from color is produced immediately after the cognition of that [color]; for it arises from that, just as the cognition of fire arises from incense and the like.

"Or, like a lamp, the letter *ga* and others are the indicators of the word *go* and so forth, because they are invariably perceived and because they are indicated prior to that [perception]. Thus [it is said].

To this it is replied: "Neither the phonemes (varṇas) nor the sounds (dhvanis) manifest the sphoṭa of either the word or the sentence"—this statement would have no room for intelligent people if the word or the sentence were not already established in its own right. For if there were no word or sentence distinct from the phonemes, how could there be scope for such a claim that they do not manifest the sphoṭa of the word or the sentence? And this being the case, by one who denies the sphoṭa in respect of the word and the sentence while they remain unseen, the word and the sentence themselves must necessarily be admitted.

Furthermore, even if it were stated according to the opponent's own intention, there would still be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For the opponent does not admit any *sphoṭa* other than words and sentences, which could then be refuted; indeed, for him, the word and the sentence themselves are the *sphoṭa*.

Furthermore, if it should be argued that "it is the phonemes, arranged in a specific sequence and delimiting a meaning, that are negated as being the word and the sentence," that too is not tenable, because of an inherent contradiction.

Furthermore, if one were to say that it is the word or sentence distinct from the phonemes that is being negated, even so, by negating its manifestation while referring to that which is distinct, the admission of a word or sentence distinct [from the phonemes] follows as a consequence.

Furthermore, even if this is a refutation of the words and sentences postulated by others, the reason "because they are manifestors" (*vyañjakatvāt*) remains unestablished (*asiddha*). How so? There are three possible alternatives: do the phonemes manifest a word that is distinct from themselves, or one that is non-distinct from themselves, or do they manifest a meaning? If they manifest something distinct, then the reason would be unestablished with respect to its own nature (*svato 'siddhaḥ*).

[269,5] Furthermore, even if it were non-distinct [from the object], it would still be unestablished for the opponent. Moreover, because it is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*), manifestation belongs only to that which is distinct, not to that which is non-distinct, as in the case of a lamp and the like. Indeed, a manifestor such as a lamp is employed for the purpose of manifesting another thing, not for the sake of manifesting its own self. If it were employed for the sake of manifesting its own self, then it would be manifested even by one who is blind from birth.

Now, if it were established that the manifestor is distinct [from the phonemes], they would have to be manifestors either of the word-base (*pāda*) or of the meaning. In that case, just as carrying a palanquin and so forth—which requires many agents—cannot be accomplished by any single one of them, so too the communication of the meaning of the phonemes cannot be accomplished by any single one of them, because it is something to be achieved by many; this has already been demonstrated.

Nor can it be said that phonemes are produced by imparting some degree of refinement (*saṃskāra*) to the object to be manifested, according to the analogy of the well-digger; for the denotatum is the object of a single cognition.

And just as, according to the system of the Sugata, a consciousness that is perishing is incapable of imparting a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) to a consciousness about to arise—because there is no persisting substratum whatsoever—so too, due to the absence of mutual connection among phonemes produced at non-simultaneous times, it is impossible for each preceding phoneme, as it perishes, to provide strength to each succeeding phoneme as it is about to arise. Therefore, phonemes are not the manifesters of meaning.

[269,19] By process of elimination, it is an established principle that phonemes alone are the manifesters of the word as something distinct. For us, however, while the mental substratum (dharmin) remains stable, when the series of latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by each preceding phoneme reaches its full maturation, at the moment of the arising of the final phoneme, there suddenly flashes forth a cognition whose nature is the manifestation of a single, partless cognition grasped by a single act of awareness; thus, the fault of the incapacity to deposit latent impressions does not follow.

Furthermore, even if phonemes manifest their own cognition, that cognition is manifested as being the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the apprehension of meaning; however, the phonemes do not function as instruments with respect to the result. This is because they are exhausted in producing a cognition that does not itself constitute an instrument. For it is the cognition alone that is the operation directed toward the result. That which has an operation directed toward the result is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that is the word (*śabda*).

Consequently, because they are mediated by the cognition that serves as the cause for the comprehension of meaning, the phonemes do not possess the status of being expressive (*vācaka*). However, it is not denied that the phonemes indirectly convey the word (*pada*).
Therefore, this verse should be read as follows: "Either the phonemes or the sounds manifest their own distinct meaning through their nature as manifestors, just like lamps, light, and so forth."

In the same way, it is indeed admitted that even things such as jars (*ghaṭa*) are merely the presentation of something other [than themselves]. For jars and the like, by their mere perception, certainly present either the cognition of their suitability for cooking, carrying, holding, and so forth, or some other [cognition]. Likewise, since they exist, it is accepted that phonemes (*varṇa*), through a traditional sequence, present a word (*pada*) distinct from themselves—just like jars and the like; thus, this case is also equal [to the previous one].

"Because it exists, like a jar," and so forth—such proofs are employed according to one's preference regarding an object imagined apart from worldly convention; for they function within the context of worldly discourse.

[270,10] Whether it be a universal (*jāti*) or a cognition (*buddhi*), let it arise from whatever source; that which brings about the comprehension of meaning from something distinct from the phonemes—which are uttered and then perish—is *sphoṭa*. And this must necessarily be accepted as the cause, because the effect cannot be produced by the phonemes. Thus, for one who asserts, "The *sphoṭa* is the designator of the meaning because it is distinct from the phonemes," there would be a contradiction with their own tenets.
Furthermore, the claim "because it is distinct from the phonemes" is unestablished for one of the two parties, since its distinction from them is not established in itself.

Furthermore, by one who accepts the fourfold class of words consisting of nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles, something other than the phonemes (*varṇa*) must be accepted as the manifester of the word-class (*padajāti*). The phonemes are not capable of manifesting the word-class; for phonemes manifest only the phoneme-class (*varṇajāti*). Nor is it possible for a class of a whole (*avayavin*) to be manifested by its parts when those parts have different times of birth and destruction. Even if the parts were stable, the hands, feet, and so forth do not manifest "bodiness" apart from the body; how much less so when they are unstable?

Furthermore, in cases such as *kiṃ cāśvaḥ*, *ayātam ayātam akṣaḥ*, and *tena mama vāyur vāyuḥ*, where the phonetic forms are identical, the same single phoneme cannot manifest both the nature of a noun and the nature of a verb, which belong to mutually contradictory categories.

Alternatively, if the phonemes *a*, *ś*, *v*, *a*, and the visarga—which manifest the name and genus "horse"—were distinct from those that manifest the genus of verbs, then it would be logical for distinct things to manifest distinct genera; however, since they are one and the same, this is not possible.

Even if it were to be postulated that "this is a noun" or "this is a verb" based on factors such as meaning, context, or the proximity of other words, nevertheless, a single phoneme could not—through meaning, context, and so forth—bring about the manifestation of the universals (jāti) of "noun" or "verb. For a single Brāhmaṇa does not manifest both the universal of being a Brāhmaṇa and the universal of being a Kṣatriya.

Therefore, many distinct *a*-sounds, as well as *śa*-sounds, *va*-sounds, and so forth, must be admitted. In this way, even words such as "cow" (*go*) are indeed distinct. Thus, the universals "cow-word-ness" (*go-śabdatva*) and "horse-word-ness" (*aśva-śabdatva*) are established. Likewise, the universals "mat-ness" (*matva*), "āt-ness" (*ātva*), and "amīt-ness" (*amītva*) are established. This being the case, the phonemes (*varṇa*) such as *a* manifest only the universals such as *ātva*, and not the specific classes of nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*) such as "horse" and so forth.

Therefore, one must accept that the word (*pada*) exists as something distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), serving as the manifestor of the universal of wordhood (*padatva-sāmānya*). This being the case, this verse should be read as follows: "But he who would deny the *sphoṭa* immediately after the cognition of the phonemes, his denial would be as futile as denying the moon by saying there is no moon; for this cognition of the non-phoneme arises immediately after the knowledge of those [phonemes]. [The opponent objects: "This cognition of the non-phoneme (*avarṇadhī*) arises from the phonemes, since it occurs immediately after the knowledge of them."
Because it is mediated by the cognition of the instrument (*karaṇabuddhi*), its status as arising immediately after is unestablished.

If it is argued that it arises through a succession, then you are proving what is already established. Smoke also lacks causality with respect to the cognition of fire, because the cognition of smoke is the cause [of the cognition of fire]. It has already been stated that just as smoke and so forth possess a causal function through a succession, phonemes and so forth are also accepted as providing assistance through a succession.

Therefore, this verse should be read as follows: "This cognition of meaning does not arise from phonemes, since it occurs immediately after the cognition of them; whatever is such [i.e., arises immediately after another cognition] does not arise from that [directly], just as the cognition of fire [does not arise directly] from smoke."

Furthermore, unlike a lamp, the phonemes *ga* and *au* do not assemble to manifest the object possessing a dewlap and so forth; for there is observed a deviation in these two because they do not persist at the time of the manifestation of the object. This same lack of persistence is inferred even in the case of the visarga (*ḥ*), due to its non-abiding nature. Phonemes do not remain for as long as it takes for the object to be manifested, whereas a lamp, by persisting for the duration of the manifestation of the object, attains the status of being its cause.

Therefore, this verse should also be recited as follows: "Or, like a lamp, the letter *ga* and others are not the denoters of 'cow' (*go*) and so forth, because they are invariably perceived [as distinct from the word-meaning] and because they are established as preceding it."

And there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this: letters are not denoters of meaning, nor are they a direct means of valid cognition with respect to meaning, because they depend upon convention (*saṅketa*), like numerical figures or images of deities. Just as the figures for "hundred" and so forth, and images of Viṣṇu, depend upon convention and merely illuminate the traditional teaching (*āgama*), they do not become a means of valid cognition with respect to the actual objects such as "Viṣṇu" or "hundred."

That which does not depend upon convention (*saṅketa*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as a sentence or a distinct class of objects like a lamp; letters (*varṇa*) are not like that, and thus their lack of validity follows, just like [the case of] images. Furthermore, we have already stated that letters manifest a sphoṭa—which is distinct from themselves and conveys the meaning—because they do not directly depend on convention, unlike images of deities such as Aṅka or Viṣṇu, which do so. The sphoṭa, however, does not directly depend on that convention.
Therefore, who is able to refute the *sphoṭa*, which has been reinforced by the power brought forth through a retinue of many arguments?

This being the case, the commentary on that term is now stated: its analysis is based on conventional cognition (*saṅketabuddhi*). For conventional cognition has a form distinct from word, object, and knowledge; therefore, the analysis of the term must be made from the standpoint of that cognition.

He demonstrates the nature of convention (*saṅketa*): that a synthesis (*anusaṃhāra*) of this many phonemes (*varṇa*) of such a kind is the designator (*vācaka*) of this meaning. For example: "This mark is one hundred," "one thousand," or "this is an image of Viṣṇu."

The convention (*saṃketa*), however, consists of the mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) between the word and its object; it is of the nature of memory and is not of the nature of error. Just as in the cognition "This is Viṣṇu" regarding an image, or "This very one is the four-armed [Viṣṇu]," so too in the cognition "Both this and that," the cognitions of the image of Viṣṇu have forms mutually superimposed upon one another.

[272.21] Likewise, that which is this word is this object, and that which is this object is this word; and that which is the cognition is the object and the word. In this way, convention (*saṃketa*) consists of the nature of mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*). Thus, these—word, object, and cognition—are conflated through mutual superimposition. For example: "cow" as the word, "cow" as the object, and "cow" as the cognition.

He who knows the distinction between these—words, objects, and cognitions—is omniscient. Why? Because such knowledge of their distinction is impossible [for anyone else]. For those who are not omniscient are not able to comprehend them through such a distinction.
Furthermore, every word possesses the power of a sentence; when "tree" is uttered, "is" is understood, for a word-meaning does not deviate from existence (*sattā*).

For what purpose is this stated? Here, the means for knowing the cries of all beings (*sarvabhūtarutajñānopāya*) is intended to be explained. Furthermore, the cry of all beings has as its object only the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), not the meaning of individual words (*padārtha*). This is because isolated words, like phonemes (*varṇa*), are devoid of meaning and lack conventional usage. Just as phonemes [are meaningless] in relation to other phonemes...

Just as words possess the purpose of illuminating their own meanings, so too do words serve as the means for establishing a sentence by depending upon one another. This being the case, the authority belongs to the sentence alone, because no meaning is cognized through the employment of isolated words.

Furthermore, a word alone is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), because there is no definitive determination [of meaning] by that alone, just as with individual phonemes. Nor is a word a signifier (*vācaka*), because it depends upon convention (*saṅketa*), like the numerals for "one hundred" and so forth. Nouns and verbs alone are not signifiers, because they are never used in isolation, just like prefixes (*upasarga*). Even where a word is intended to be used in isolation, there is necessarily some word such as "is standing" or "Devadatta" revolving in the mind; thus, the non-usage of words in isolation is not established. "Devadatta... [L104v1]

In expressions such as *pralambate*, *paryāgacchati*, and *abhyagacchati*, the prefixes (*upasarga*) and governing particles (*karmapravacanīya*) have no independent meaning whatsoever. Likewise, in cases such as *abhimānāyate*, *sumanāyate*, and *durmanāyate*, it is established that the prefixes function merely as indicators (*dyotaka*). Similarly, in instances like *pratiṣṭhate* and *adhīte*, the prefixes likewise possess only an indicative function and not a denotative one (*vācaka*). Furthermore, there is no action (*kriyā*) without an instrument (*sādhana*); when only an object (*karman*) is employed, some instrument—whether a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*)—is necessarily understood.

Furthermore, because the relationship between roots and suffixes is unstable and subject to excess, they lack expressive power due to deviation. For example, for some, the root *daridrāti* is taught as denoting mere wealth (*dravya*). However, the word *daridra*, which functions like a particle or prefix, recurs in forms such as *drāti*, *nidrāti*, and *daridrāti*. In that case, it must be stated what the root is: is it *drā* (the state of being sleepy), or is it *daridra*?
For some, however, only *daridra* is recited, while the word *drā* is also transmitted separately.

[273,27] Thus, some recite it as containing only the letter *sa*, and they apply the augment *kā* before the suffix *vī*. Others, however, having recited it together with the *kā*, effect the elision of the *kā* before the suffixes *avi* and *vī*. In that case, it must be stated what the base (*prakṛti*) is; it is not clearly known.
Whether the limit is the base or the limit is the suffix, it is impossible to distinguish the meanings of the base and the suffix.

In some cases, even a prefix (*upasarga*) has attained the status of being a part of the base (*prakṛti*), as in examples such as *asaṃgrāmayata* (he did not fight) and *śūra* (hero). Likewise, in forms such as *tateḥ* (of the act of stretching), *nāsyāpatyam iḥ* (his offspring is "iḥ"), *iyān* (so much), and *adhunā* (now), who could state the portion of the meaning of the base when the base itself is absent? Similarly, in *agnicit* (fire-piling), *sopasut* (with pressed Soma), *bhidā* (cleaving), *chidā* (cutting), *atha u kati* (and how many?), *amā* (at home), *paca* (cook), *paṭha* (read), and so forth, who could state the meaning of the suffix when the suffix is absent?

Regarding such cases where the deviation is observed in both the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya), who would be able to imagine that they possess meaning? In this instance, let it be so, but not elsewhere; thus, one cannot adopt the "half-old woman" approach (ardhajaratīya). In expressions such as *uddālakapuṣpabhañjikā* ("the gathering of Uddālaka flowers") and *puṣpapracāyikā* ("the picking of flowers"), what is the meaning of the preceding and following members? Since there is no syntactic connection (*pratyanvaya*) even in words like *prajña* ("wise"), what meaning could belong to what?

In cases such as *ṛṣabha*, *vṛṣabha*, *vṛṣa*; *udaka*, *udakumbha*, *kṣīroda*; *yāva*, *yāvaka*; and *kūpa*, *sūpa*, *yūpa*, and so forth, it must be stated which [element] has which meaning. In examples such as *dadhy-aśāna* ("eat curd") and *madhv-atra* ("honey here"), what is the limit, and which word is the expressive unit?

Therefore, since phonemes (*varṇa*), bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and words (*pada*) are observed to deviate from their meanings everywhere, they must serve as the means for reaching the indivisible sentence (*vākya*) whose deviation is never observed. These [elements] are to be analyzed by being extracted from the sentence—which is without joints or connections, indivisible, and which produces a variety of effects through the sounds of false phonemes and words.

And these [phonemes], which do not constitute parts of the sentence, appear like parts of the sentence because they are the means; yet, being non-existent until the fruit [is attained], they are false—just like the digits for a hundred and so forth—and are employed specifically during the conjunction of the articulatory organs for the purpose of manifesting the unuttered sentence. As they are discarded, through their manifold variety of differences such as time and the completion of their own sequence, they cause the self of the sentence to appear as if it were sequential, as if it were being produced, as if it were being accomplished, and as if it were very long.
They cause it to assume a state of temporal duration, as if possessing divisions, and a state of manifold forms.

This being so, as for what is said—namely, "Having extracted the donkey's horn from the rabbit's horn, what is that?"—this is false. Just as the water of a mirage, though false, is extracted from the reality of the parched desert; and just as a man is extracted from a post, and a post from a man, and silver from mother-of-pearl; and just as the water of a mirage and so forth are the causes for the cognition of things such as the parched desert as they actually are, so too are phonemes, words, bases, and suffixes.
They are extracted both as the cause for the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence consisting of real entities and for that comprehension itself.

In some cases, that which is already attained through its meaning is abstracted away, as for example, the water of a mirage. In other cases, however, it is intended for the sake of a specific purpose, such as when the digit "one hundred" is abstracted from a number like one hundred, or as written characters—which, depending on convention, consist of established symbols—are abstracted from phonemes such as the letter 'a'. And yet, all of these serve as means for conveying the reality of things as they are; nor, by that much, is their falsity denied. The same applies to words and so forth.

For those who, by means of conventions regarding roots, suffixes, words, and phonemes—which are themselves like the false letters of a script and are but secondary means—themselves construct various methods for understanding the meaning of sentences according to their own conventions and employ them in practice, yet consider these to be true; surely such a person, wishing to see the moon in the sky, perceives even the cloud that serves as the means for seeing the moon as being the moon itself.

Just as the sentence alone is the truth, so too is the meaning of the sentence alone the truth; neither isolated words nor isolated word-meanings attain the status of truth. Every entity consists of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). For there is no particular apart from the universal, nor is there a universal apart from the particular. When "cow" is uttered, "it exists" is understood. Therefore, even when a single word is employed, the meaning of the sentence—wherein the meanings of other words are implicitly included—is what is perceived, not the isolated word-meaning.

This being the case, word-meanings convey this [sentence-meaning] individually when there is doubt, because a definitive determination arises from their totality, like a crow perched on the top of a post. This is unproven for us, for that which is called a "post" is not the sentence-meaning.

It is well known as a distinct category (*pṛthak-padārtha*). For if [the word] "existent" (*sat*) were applied to a tree, a post, a head, or a crow—such that one says "being a tree," "being a post," "being a head," or "being a crow on the head of a post"—then, due to the requirement of implicit other words being understood within the compound, there would be no cognition at all of a "crow standing on a post. Even when those [other words] are present, because the cognition of "existent" arises, a cognition of another entity "existent" (*sat-padārtha-antara*) necessarily follows.

Therefore, since even each individual word has a sentence-meaning that is essentially doubtful, how could word-meanings—being individually non-existent—convey the sentence-meaning? Consequently, this verse should be read as follows: "But the sentence conveys this [meaning] when there is doubt regarding each part, because a definitive determination arises when they are combined, like the crow atop the post."

Thus it is expressed by means of a sentence; therefore, the meaning of the sentence is not apprehended as a separate form by others. Furthermore, because one understands that "it exists" at the end, and because of the word "tree," the state of being a tree is established.

As for the claim that "tree-ness" is not expressed by the word *palāśa*, this is indeed true; for the meaning of the sentence "tree" is not denoted by the sentence "palāśa," because their objects are distinct. For [the former] is different...

The meaning of the word *palāśa* is "there is a *palāśa*" or "it stands"; it is distinct from the meaning of the word *vṛkṣa*. Furthermore, when the existence of phonemes (*varṇa*) as partless entities is admitted individually, how could a sentence—which is composed of words consisting of partless phonemes—be conceived as having parts? For it is not possible for something with parts to be produced by actions, space, and so forth. If, on the other hand, the possession of parts were admitted, the same fault would necessarily follow there as well.

"If there were existence of words and phonemes, their distinction would be like that of atoms; and from that, there would be the non-existence of everything. This is a scare tactic for children (*bālavibhīṣikā*). (ŚV Vākya-k. 150) Since we accept that atoms are merely properties such as existence (*sattva*), we shall explain clearly by setting this aside: this is a scare tactic for the elderly (*vṛddhavibhīṣikā*).

[276,12] Now, if it is asked: "Since even when a single word is employed, other word-meanings are included, what is the purpose of employing multiple words?"—it is a restatement for the sake of restriction (*niyamārtha*). For although it follows from the meaning that the means (*sādhana*) exist because the agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and object (*karman*)—namely Caitra, fire, and rice—are expressed by the verbal action, there is a restriction: "Caitra alone is the agent," "by fire alone as the instrument," and "only rice as the object."

Moreover, there is a restatement even without the purpose of restriction. And a single word is observed to function for the sake of the sentence-meaning; for example, "The Vedic scholar (śrotriyaḥ) studies the meters (chandaḥ). In this collection of action and its means, the single word "Vedic scholar," which expresses the agent, functions within the phrase "studies the meters. Likewise, the verbal form "lives" implies specific actions and their means.

In the sentences "He studies the *chandas* (Veda)" and "He sustains his vital breaths," as well as in the expression "The learned man lives" (*śrotriyo jīvati*), there is the manifestation of the word-meanings. In every respect, since the power of the sentence resides in all the words, it is said that all words indeed possess the meanings of the other words [with which they are combined].

Therefore, in some cases the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is implied by the verb itself, and in other cases the action (*kriyā*) is expressed by the noun alone. Consequently, their distinction is difficult to discern. Thus, having separated the word from the sentence, that which expresses the action—such as "he lives" (*jīvati*)—or that which expresses the grammatical factor (*kāraka*)—such as "Vedic scholar" (*śrotriyaḥ*) or "Kṣatriya" (*kṣatriyaḥ*)—must be analyzed.

Otherwise, if it were not analyzed by being separated from the sentence, then in cases such as *bhavaty aśvo ’jāyaḥ*, where the identity is not determined due to the similarity between noun and verb, how could it be analyzed as either an action (*kriyā*) or a particle (*karmapravacanīya*)? [In this case,] *bhavati* is the form of the pronoun *nidadhi* (from the root *dhā*) with the suffix *śatṛ* in the locative case; whereas in *bījād aṅkuraḥ*, *bhavati* is a verb.

"Aśvaś carati" ("The horse moves") is an expression denoting a genus (*jāti*). "Aśvas tvaṃ grāmam" ("O horse, go to the village") is the usage of the second person singular imperative of the root *śvi*. "Ajāpayaḥ pīyatām" ("Let goat's milk be drunk") is a nominal word (*nāmapada*). "Ajāpayas tvaṃ rājānam" ("O goat-milk, go to the king") is the form of the second person singular imperative of the causative (*ṇijanta*) of the root *jap*.
Having demonstrated the confusion among those words, meanings, and cognitions, their distinction is now established:

"The palace whitens" (*śvetate prāsādaḥ*) has the sense of an action (*kriyārtha*); "The palace is white" (*śvetaḥ prāsādaḥ*) has the sense of a factor of action (*kārakārtha*). Because an entity possesses both the nature of an action and a factor of action, it is expressed both by means of the sense of an action and by means of the sense of a factor of action, as in "it whitens" and "white."

Just as a word consists of action and its factors—such that "that which is white is the act of whitening" and "that which is the act of whitening is white"—so too there is a single word distinct from action and its factors; likewise, the object denoted by it consists of action and its factors; likewise, the cognition regarding it consists of action and its factors; likewise, the object consists of the word and the cognition, and the cognition also consists of the word and the object. Why? Because of the connection expressed as "this is that":
whatever is the object, that is the word; whatever is the word, that is the object; and whatever is the cognition, that is the same.

The cognition that "this object and this word are one" is a conceptual cognition (pratyaya) consisting of memory; this is convention (saṅketa). Thus, the distinction [between object and word] must be made through the form of their commingling.

How so? That object which is white—such as a palace or the like possessing the quality of whiteness—is the objective support (*ālambana*) for both the word and the cognition, serving as their denotatum (*vācya*) and their object (*viṣaya*). For that object, while undergoing transformation through its own states such as newness or oldness, is neither accompanied by the word nor accompanied by the cognition; this is because it exists even in the absence of the word and the cognition. Likewise, the cognition is neither accompanied by the word nor accompanied by the object, because it exists even in the absence of the other.

Likewise, sound also [is distinct], because there is a deviation between the sound and the cognition of the object; thus, there is a distinction such that the object is one way, the sound is another way, and the cognition is yet another way.

And so, through *saṃyama* on this distinction—specifically, through *saṃyama* on the distinction that "this is the meaning" and "this is the cognition," as manifested by these phonemes which have been conventionally designated as sentences—the yogin attains knowledge of the cries of all beings, by means of directly perceiving, in their own forms, the words, the word-meanings, and the cognitions that have been previously distinguished. (3.17)

[278,18] Through the direct realization of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there arises knowledge of previous births. Indeed, these formative forces are twofold: those designated as latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are perceived, and those that are unperceived, which are the causes of memory and the afflictions (*kleśa*). The perceived ones—both of these—are mental phenomena (*vittadharma*) produced by the experience of the maturation (*vipāka*) of afflictions and karma; they consist of merit and demerit (*dharmādharma-rūpa*), have merit and demerit as their cause, were constructed in a previous existence, and were brought to completion in a birth immediately preceding the one past.

The properties of transformation, decay, cessation, power, and vitality have been previously explained; they are imperceptible. When *saṃyama* is practiced upon these two types of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it becomes capable of bringing about the direct perception of those impressions.

And because they are produced as qualified by the experience of place, time, and cause, even at the time of direct realization, they appear as perceived precisely as qualified by those specific qualifiers such as place and so forth. Therefore, there is no direct realization of them without the experience of place, time, and cause.

Thus, from the direct perception of *saṃskāras*, knowledge of previous births arises for the yogin. In the case of other living beings as well, when he desires to know their birth, knowledge of their previous births arises through *saṃyama* upon their *saṃskāras*—that is, from the direct perception of those *saṃskāras*.

In this regard, in order to illustrate the fruit of the direct realization of the *saṃskāras*, this narrative is introduced: as the Blessed One Jaigīṣavya was observing the transformation of births throughout ten great cosmic cycles (*mahāsarga*) due to his direct realization of the *saṃskāras*, there arose in him knowledge born of discernment, which has dispassion as its cause.

Then the Blessed One Āvaṭya, the holder of the lineage, said to him: "Since you possess an unassailable intelligence due to your spiritual fitness throughout ten great cosmic cycles, and since you have observed the suffering of going to the realms of hell and animals, what have you found to be greater—pleasure or pain—as you were born again and again among gods and humans?"

Having approached the Blessed One, Jaigīṣavya said: "O Lord, because of my spiritual fitness throughout ten great cycles of creation, and because my wisdom and mental essence remain unsubdued, I have observed that even as I was born again and again among gods and humans, whatever I experienced—all of it was suffering; thus I perceive it as nothing but suffering."

The Blessed One Āvaṭya said: "This supreme mastery over the *pradhāna* belonging to the Venerable Jaigīṣavya, and this unsurpassed happiness of contentment—why has even this been placed within the category of suffering? The Blessed One Jaigīṣavya replied: "In comparison with the pleasure of sense-objects, this unsurpassed happiness of contentment and the happiness of mastery over the *pradhāna* have been described as such; however, in comparison with the happiness of *kaivalya*, they are indeed nothing but suffering."

This quality belongs to the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*), and it consists of the three *guṇas*. Furthermore, since a cognition consisting of the three *guṇas* is placed on the side of what is to be abandoned, [the author] asks: "In relation to what, then, do these two become pleasure? He replies: "The thread of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is of the nature of pain. However, that which consists in the cessation of the suffering of the stream of craving is pleasure—serene, unafflicted, and favorable to all. This has been described as the pleasure of the company of loved ones and the pleasure of mastery over *pradhāna*. (3.18)
[280,25] Knowledge of another's mind arises from mastery over the mental processes of others.
Through mastery over another's mental process, there is direct perception of that process; upon that direct perception, knowledge of the other person's mind, which is connected to it, occurs. (3.19)

In this regard, one might suspect that because the yogi directly realizes another's cognition, he would consequently experience suffering when that other suffers and happiness when that other is happy; anticipating this, it is said: "And that [realization] does not have an objective support (*sālambana*), because [the other's object] has not become an object for him. The yogi knows the other's cognition as 'affectionate,' but he does not know, 'The other's cognition is affectionate toward such-and-such an object. For the yogi does not know the specific object—whether of the nature of pleasure or pain—of the other's cognition, by virtue of which the other would become happy or unhappy."

[281,18] But surely, if one does not perceive the object, how can one perceive that "one is attached to that"? It is said in response: one perceives the generality that "there is attachment toward that," but one does not apprehend a specific pleasure that has become the object of the cognition of the happy person. Rather, it is merely the cognition of another that becomes the object of the yogi’s mind. 3.20.

[281.22] Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, the power of its being perceived is obstructed; when there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility occurs. The "form of the body" (*kāyarūpa*) is the form belonging to the yogin’s own body. By means of *saṃyama* upon that form, he obstructs—that is, he suppresses—the power of that form which is perceivable by the eyes of others. Consequently, the light of the eyes of others does not come into contact with the form of the yogin’s body, and from that, invisibility results. By this, the invisibility of sound and the other sense objects is also explained.

When there is restraint (saṃyama) upon that power of perception which belongs to the word "yogi," that power of the word's perception becomes established. Consequently, another person does not hear the word "yogi. The same should be understood regarding touch and the other sense objects as well. 3.21.

Through the withdrawal of that karma which is either departing or non-urgent, or through the signs of death (*ariṣṭa*), there arises knowledge of the future limit (*aparāntajñāna*). Karma that ripens as lifespan is of two kinds. How so? That which takes up a sign as its cause and has its fruit brought about quickly is called "urgent" (*sopakrama*); whereas that which flows slowly and will yield its fruit after a long time is "non-urgent" (*nirupakrama*).

Just as a wet cloth, when spread out and expanded, would dry in a shorter time—that is, more quickly—so too, action accompanied by effort exhausts itself by swiftly bringing about its maturation as a lifespan.
Just as that same cloth, when folded up and not spread out, would dry only after a long time, so too does life proceed slowly when there is no exertion.

Or just as a fire, when applied to dry undergrowth and joined with a favorable wind, would burn it down in the shortest time when directed from all sides, so too will karma that is accompanied by effort exhaust the lifespan in the shortest time.
Just as that same fire, when placed gradually upon a heap of grass, would burn it only after a long time, so too is karma without momentum.

This aforementioned karma is of two kinds: that which determines a single birth (*ekabhavika*) and that which determines the lifespan (*āyuṣkara*). Through restraint (*saṃyama*) regarding this [lifespan-determining karma], there arises knowledge of the future limit (*aparāntajñāna*), that is, knowledge of one's own death (*prāyaṇa*). Likewise, through restraint regarding the two kinds of karma belonging to others, there also arises knowledge of the death of others. And the purpose of knowing the time of death is the preparation for what must be performed by the person (*puruṣa*).

[283,19] Or, there is knowledge of death derived from omens (*ariṣṭa*). Omens are of three kinds: internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, an example of the internal is as follows: one does not hear the sound within one's own body when the ears are covered, or one does not see light when the eyes are pressed.

Likewise, the *ādhibhautika* [dream] is when one sees the messengers of Yama (*yamapuruṣa*), or perceives deceased ancestors as having arrived unexpectedly. The *ādhidaivika* [dream] is when one suddenly sees perfected beings (*siddha*) and so forth, or perceives and acts upon everything in a distorted manner. In this regard, the common worldly expression is "it was an ill omen" (*ariṣṭa*). For it is said: "I had a distorted vision; it was an ill omen. (3.22)

[284,16] The powers regarding loving-kindness and the others. There are three meditative cultivations: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*). In that regard, by cultivating loving-kindness toward beings who are happy, one attains the power of loving-kindness. By cultivating compassion toward those who are suffering, one attains the power of compassion. By cultivating sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit and virtue, one attains the power of sympathetic joy.

From cultivation—that is, from the cultivation of friendliness (*maitrī*) and so forth—whatever concentration (*samādhi*) arises is *saṃyama* whose object is the cultivation of friendliness and the rest. From that *saṃyama* directed toward friendliness and the others, powers of unfailing vigor arise for the yogin.

But toward those of evil character, his attitude is one of equanimity and not cultivation. Consequently, due to the absence of cultivation, there is no concentration (*samādhi*) within that equanimity; therefore, strength does not arise from equanimity, because of the lack of restraint (*saṃyama*) therein. (3.23)

Regarding powers, there are those such as the strength of an elephant and so forth. By means of these powers, which have friendliness and other qualities as their objective supports, the powerful yogi, having practiced *saṃyama* upon the powers of elephants and the like, becomes possessed of the power of an elephant and so forth. (3.24)

[3.25] By directing the light through the outgoing [form of concentration], there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote. That which was described as the luminous outgoing [concentration]—its illumination is "light" (*āloka*). Having directed (*vinyasya*) that light toward an object, whether subtle, concealed, or remote, and having established it there, the yogi perceives it.

[287,21] Knowledge of the worlds through *saṃyama* on the sun. Having performed *saṃyama* on the sun, one should perceive the entire array of worlds directly. The commentary, however, has its meaning already explained, as it is well-known from all the Purāṇas. ||3.26||

[YS 3.27] Knowledge of the arrangement of the stars through *saṃyama* on the moon. Having understood the layout of the worlds through *saṃyama* on the sun, one should thereafter perform *saṃyama* on the moon and discern the arrangement of the stars. Through *saṃyama* on the sun, only the layout of the worlds is known—how the worlds, rivers, oceans, and mountains are spread out; but it is not known how the stars are thus arranged or connected to one another. However, from *saṃyama* on the moon, there arises the comprehension of the specific modes of the arrangement of the stars.

[287,28] Regarding the Pole Star (dhruva), there is knowledge of the motion of those [stars]. Therefore, having immediately thereafter applied *saṃyama* upon the Pole Star, one should discern the motion of the stars: "By this method they move; by this they are distinguished"; "At this time, this planet is in opposition with that planet"; "It has such a hand-position" (*ittha-hasta-maya*); "Its rising is thus"—through these means, one should discern the auspicious and inauspicious [effects] for living beings, and so forth.

[288,19] Likewise, having applied restraint toward other celestial palaces above, one should understand all such things as: "those celestial palaces are of such types and have proceeded in such a manner," and so forth. 3.28.

[288.21] Knowledge of the bodily arrangement [is attained] at the navel-center. Having performed *saṃyama* upon the navel-center, one should discern the bodily arrangement. It should be known that the three humors—wind, bile, and phlegm—are of such magnitude and have such a basis, and so forth.

Likewise, the seven elements (dhātus) exist in both external and internal states. (Taste) is the skin, which is external to all; then, internal to that, is blood; then flesh; then bone; then fat; then marrow; and finally, semen is the most internal of all. Thus, each preceding one among these is external—this is their arrangement. In the same way, one should understand the configuration of the channels (nāḍīs). 3.29.

[288,27] In the cavity of the throat, there is the cessation of hunger and thirst. A thread is seen beneath the tongue on the upturned surface of the tongue; below the thread is the throat, and below that is the cavity. By restraining the mind there, hunger and thirst do not afflict one. (3.30)

In the *karmāṇḍī*, which is the channel named Kūrma located beneath the well in the chest, one who practices restraint attains a firm footing; he attains stability of mind. Just as a snake or a lizard becomes exceedingly steady by means of its chest through concentration (*dhāraṇā*). (3.31)

[YS 3.32] There is the vision of perfected beings in the light at the crown of the head. Because there is another aperture in the skull which is luminous, it is called "light" (*jyotis*). By practicing *saṃyama* upon that, there occurs the vision of perfected beings who move in the space between heaven and earth. 3.32.

Or, everything [is known] through intuitive insight (*prātibha*). For the yogi who practices *saṃyama* upon the Self or who directs his intense concentration toward Īśvara, there arises spontaneously an intuitive, illuminating mental knowledge; this is the precursor to the knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja*), whose characteristics will be described later. Just as the morning light, slightly emerging and turning red at sunrise, is the precursor to the sun about to rise, so too do yogis know everything through the arising of intuitive knowledge. (3.33)

[290,12] <bh> There is the knowledge of the mind in the heart. That which is this small, lotus-like, downward-facing mass of flesh within this city of Brahman, the body—being like a house due to its connection with the hollows of the channels at the opening of the dwelling—it is the "house. Consciousness is the mind; through *saṃyama* upon that lotus, the abode of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) situated in the lake of the chest, there arises knowledge of the mind, which is the *sattva*. 3.34.

[YS 3.35] Experience (*bhoga*) is the non-distinction of the cognitive state (*pratyaya*) between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, which are absolutely unmixed. Through *saṃyama* upon one's own nature, as distinct from that which exists for another, there arises knowledge of the *puruṣa*. *Sattva* is the mind (*citta*), and the *puruṣa* is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Between these two, which are absolutely unmixed, absolutely dissimilar, and utterly separate, experience belongs to the *puruṣa* insofar as there is a conformity of modifications (*vṛtti-sārūpya*), which is the non-distinction of their cognitive states. From that which exists for another—the *sattva*—which appears as if mixed with the cognition of the *puruṣa*, by discerning it through *saṃyama* upon one's own nature, which consists of pure consciousness (*citimātra-svarūpa*), knowledge of the *puruṣa* comes to be.

What is that "being of the mind" (cittasattva) intended for the sake of another, by discerning which one practices *saṃyama* upon the *puruṣa* for its own sake? It is the being of the intellect (*buddhisattva*), whose nature is luminosity, which is a common substance and performs the functions of objects; it is bound together by the duty of accomplishing the purpose of the *puruṣa*. Having brought under control and reduced to subordination the *rajas* and *tamas* that are bound to this same being, it has been transformed for the yogin through the cognition of the distinction between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*.

And from that [Prakṛti], which is characterized by existence, transformative, consisting of the three guṇas, impermanent, impure, for the sake of another, and insentient, the Puruṣa is entirely dissimilar: he is pure, distinct, unchanging, for his own sake, eternal, and of the nature of pure consciousness alone.

The experience (*bhoga*) of the *puruṣa* is the non-distinction of the cognitive presentation (*pratyaya-aviśeṣa*) between those two, which are absolutely unmixed; this is because the object has been presented [to the *sattva*]. That is the cognitive presentation of experience. Furthermore, no experience other than the presentation of the presented object is possible, given that [the *sattva*] is unchanging. Because the *sattva* exists for the sake of another, the cognitive presentation of experience is not distinct from the object seen by the *puruṣa*.

But that which is distinct from that secondary cognition and from the cognizer—a specific, purely conscious, and separate spiritual cognition—is the self-referential cognition, for it is the Person (puruṣa) himself who appears as the cognition due to the impossibility of transformation [in the Person]. From that, a wisdom having the Person as its object arises by itself.
[291,15] But surely, if the Puruṣa is made an object of cognition, and if the Puruṣa is thereby perceived, it follows that the Puruṣa is for the sake of another (parārtha). This is not a fault.

For the Puruṣa is not seen by means of a cognition of the Puruṣa—that is, by a cognition whose object is the Puruṣa—which is essentially the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*) and is a property of the *sattva* of the intellect; this is because the intellect is insentient (*acetana*).

The Puruṣa alone perceives that cognition as having itself as its object and appearing as the Puruṣa; it is precisely by virtue of the cognition’s appearance as the Puruṣa that the cognition has the Puruṣa as its object. It is not that the cognition actually has the Puruṣa as its objective support. Just as a mirror transforms into the shape of a face when a face is near it, so too the mind, transformed into the form of the Puruṣa, appears as the Puruṣa and is apprehended by the Puruṣa.
And so it has been said: "By what means, my dear, could one know the knower? The meaning is that the person never becomes an object for anyone.

[291,24] But surely, just as the eye, being reflected back from the surface of a mirror, becomes the perceiver of the face, so too the Person (puruṣa), being reflected back from the sentient being (sattva) of the mind, should perceive its own self? No, because transformation is impossible for the Person. For neither the activity toward nor the withdrawal from the mind can be established for that which is unchanging.

Nor does the eye turn back to grasp the face, because the face is experienced as having the surface of the mirror as its locus; for one's own face does not reside within the locus of the mirror. Furthermore, it is because of the conformity to the mirror: just as a long face is seen in a sword-blade, yet one's own face is not long. If it were perceived by the eye turned back, then the conformity to the mirror would be illogical. (3.35)

[292,19] From that, intuition, hearing, sensation, vision, and taste arise. Then, from concentration upon one's own object, through intuition born of self-restraint, there arises mental knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, the distant, the past, and the future. From hearing, there is the hearing of celestial sounds. From sensation—that is, from the knowledge of touch—one knows the touch of the Siddhas and others. From vision—that is, from visual knowledge—one perceives celestial form.

From *āsvāda*, which is the sensory cognition of the tongue, there arises the perception of divine flavors. From *vārta*—that which exists in worldly activity (*vṛtti*), namely the knowledge of worldly transactions—he correctly attains the true nature of the principles of such transactional conduct. ||3.36||

[292,26] These are obstacles in concentration (*samādhi*) and accomplishments (*siddhi*) in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Those [powers] such as intuitive insight (*prātibha*) and so forth, when arising for one whose mind is concentrated on the *puruṣa*, are obstacles because they are contrary to the vision of the *puruṣa*. When arising for one whose mind has emerged from concentration, they are accomplishments. Although they arise from restraint (*saṃyama*) upon the *puruṣa*, nevertheless they do not arise for one who is dispassionate and whose mind is concentrated. 3.37.

[293,13] Entry into another's body occurs through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind. The meaning is this: the mind—which has become fluid like a struck bell, flickering with the brilliance of a mass of glowing coals, and is without a fixed support—is bound to the body by the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*); "bondage" refers to its state of remaining confined within the mere body.

The cause of that bondage is karma. The loosening of the cause—the slackening of the latent impressions of karma—occurs through the power of *samādhi*. Furthermore, the awareness of the movement of the mind arises precisely from *samādhi*. Because of the destruction of the bond of karma and because of the awareness of the movement of one's own mind, for these reasons the yogi rejoices, becomes deluded, or becomes greedy; and by virtue of perceiving the existence of his own mind’s movements in this way, the yogi draws the mind out of his own body and projects it into other bodies.

When his mind rises up, the senses rise up after it; therefore, due to the attainment of the activity of the senses, the activities of the vital breaths and so forth arise in other bodies. Just as bees fly up after the king-bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too the senses follow the mind during the entry into another body. (3.38)

From mastery over *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, as well as the power of upward departure (*utkrānti*). The function of all the sense organs is life-force (*jīvana*); that by which the body is sustained through the combined operation of any one of the eleven sense organs is life-force. Because that life-force must necessarily fulfill the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), its fivefold activity is set forth according to the distinctions of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*.
