In this context, *prāṇa* is the movement through the mouth and nose, with its function extending as far as the heart. *Samāna* is so called because it equalizes [the nutrients]; its function extends from the navel, reaching down to the region of the anus. *Apāna* is named for its removal of urine, feces, and so forth; it functions from the navel down to the feet. *Udāna* is so called because it leads the body upward; it begins at the soles of the feet and functions up to the crown of the head. *Vyāna* pervades the entire body.

Among these, the *prāṇa* is the most preeminent; through its conquest, there is the conquest of all the others, such as the *apāna* and so forth. The means for their conquest has been explained in detail in the *Hairaṇyagarbha*.

But here, because they are conquered by the conquest of the mind, no separate method for their conquest is stated; rather, they are indeed conquered through the conquest of *prāṇāyāma*. Therefore, it is not necessary to attend to a separate presentation of the means for their conquest; instead, only the result of the conquest of *udāna* is mentioned. From the conquest of *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and so forth—by "and so forth," one includes the edge of a sword and similar obstacles. Furthermore, at the time of death, there occurs the upward departure (*utkrānti*) [of the vital breath]. By mastering that upward departure occurring at the time of death through the conquest of *udāna*, one attains it with independence. (3.39)

[294,26] From the mastery of the *samāna* [breath], there is blazing. Having mastered the *samāna*, the yogi causes the fire to be kindled by means of the *samāna* wind; because the *udāna* and the fire share the same substratum, the yogi, acting as the causal agent for that act of kindling, first ignites the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*). 3.40.

Through *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, divine hearing arises. But what is this connection upon which *saṃyama* is practiced? He says: Space is the support of all ears; and since sounds have space as their substrate, space alone is their support. The connection between the ear and space is the absence of any obstruction between the ear and the sound to be perceived.

And so it has been said regarding those who possess hearing in the same location: "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) means that by which one hears; those whose hearings are in the same location are "those with hearing in the same location. For them, there occurs a single auditory perception for all. This is logical only when there exists a single entity that provides space and is of an unobstructed nature. And this is the mark for the existence of space (*ākāśa*).

Likewise, it is stated that space has the nature of non-obstruction. Why? Because, with the exception of space, one observes the obstruction of material things such as jars, which possess characteristics distinct from space. Therefore, that which possesses no obstruction even within gems, diamonds, and the like, is space. For this very reason, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of space is also well-known.

[295,24] He states the mark of the auditory organ: the auditory organ is inferred from the apprehension of sound. For, between a deaf person and one who is not deaf, one perceives sound while the other does not. That cause by which the apprehension of sound occurs for the non-deaf and its non-apprehension for the other is the auditory organ. Therefore, the auditory organ alone has sound as its object, because sound is not heard by the deaf. For the yogi who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the connection between the auditory organ and space (*ākāśa*), the divine auditory organ functions. 3.41.

From *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and from the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) on lightness like that of cotton, there arises the power of moving through space. Wherever there is a body, there is space; because space provides room for it, the body has a connection with that space characterized by inseparability. When the yogi has performed *saṃyama* upon that connection between the body and space—characterized by the attainment of mutual inseparability—he conquers that connection. Then, by attaining absorption in light things such as cotton, down to the level of atoms, having mastered that connection, he acquires lightness like that of cotton and other such objects.

Having mastered the connection between the body and space, one who has attained meditative absorption moves upon water with both feet for the sake of gaining mastery over lightness equal to that of cotton and the like. Thereafter, one moves upon the thread of the *ūrṇā*-hair at the navel; having there acquired a lightness equal to the thread of a cuckoo's down, one moves again upon rays of light. Thence, upon the wind; and thence, his movement in space becomes according to his will. (3.42)

[296,19] External non-conceptualized functioning is the "Great Bodiless" (*mahāvideha*); from that follows the destruction of the veil of light. That mental functioning which arises by its own power outside the body—in another location or toward a specific object—due to the force of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), is the retention (*dhāraṇā*) called "Great Bodiless. If this occurs as a mere mental functioning directed toward an external object while one is still established within the body, then it is said to be "conceptualized," because it is preceded by volitional intent (*saṅkalpa*) on the part of one remaining in the body.

However, that external functioning of the mind which, due to the power of concentration, arises from the loosening of the causes of bondage in the body, and which is independent of the body as if the mind had already gone outside—that indeed is called "unconstructed" (akalpita). Just as in the case of the constructed [meditation], the attainment of external functioning is limited by the body, so it is not in the case of the unconstructed; there is no observation of a limit defined by the body as a substratum.

Both of these are indeed Videha, because they are externally conceived. Among them, that which is designated as the "unconceived" (akalpita) Mahāvideha is established there by means of the "conceived" (kalpita). Because the unconceived is to be accomplished through the cultivation of conception, they accomplish it by means of the conceived—that Mahāvideha by which yogins enter into the bodies of others.

And then, from that state of great disembodiment (*mahāvideha*) resulting from *dhāraṇā*, there occurs the destruction of the threefold fruition of afflictions and karma—which constitutes the veil of the luminous *buddhisattva*—and which has its root in *rajas* and *tamas*. (3.43)

[YS 3.44] Through *saṃyama* on the gross form, the essential nature, the subtle, the inherence, and the capacity for purposeful action, mastery over the elements (*bhūtajaya*) is attained. The gross, the essential nature, the subtle, the inherence, and the capacity for purposeful action—thus each element is fivefold. Among these, the specific qualities of the earth element, beginning with sound, are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; they are called "specifics" (*viśeṣa*) because they are produced from the five-fold *tanmātras*.

Of the earth, together with its qualities such as form and so forth. First, regarding the earth, its qualities are form, weight, dryness, motion, stability, endurance, divisibility, patience, blackness, hardness, and the state of being enjoyed by all. Thus it is said. Likewise, the qualities belonging to water are moisture, luster, subtlety, softness, weight, protection, purity, cohesion, and so on. Similarly, the qualities belonging to fire are upward movement, purification, burning, cooking, lightness, and luminosity, and so forth.

Likewise, the aerial qualities include moving horizontally, purification, projection, impelling force, and so forth. Likewise, the ethereal qualities include omnipresence, non-obstruction, and non-resistance.

Thus, these particularities—sound and the rest—are defined in the treatise by the term "gross" (sthūla) along with their attributes such as form (ākāra), for the sake of conventional usage. Likewise, the four particularities beginning with taste, which are watery (āpya), are called gross together with their attributes such as subtlety (saukṣmya). Similarly, the three particularities beginning with color (rūpa), which are fiery (taijasa), are said to be gross along with their attributes such as upward movement (ūrdhvabhāktva). In the same way, the particularities of the aerial element (vāyavīya)—namely sound, touch, and horizontal movement—are gross. Likewise, the particularities of space (ākāśa), such as omnipresence (sarvagatatva), are gross. This, then, has been described as the first, gross form of the elements.

[298,11] Now, the second [category], its own nature (*svarūpa*), is being stated. And that is the universal (*sāmānya*): among the various earth-elements, that which is undifferentiated and pervasive is "earth" itself, namely solidity (*mūrti*). Likewise, among the watery elements such as taste and so forth, the pervasive universal is "water" itself, namely moisture (*sneha*). Similarly, among the fiery elements such as color-form and so forth, the pervasive universal is "fire" itself, namely heat (*uṣṇatva*). Likewise, among the airy elements such as touch, lateral movement, and so forth, the pervasive universal is "air" itself, namely motility (*praṇāmitva*).

Likewise, the second form is expressed by the term "essential nature" (*svarūpa*), namely that space (*ākāśa*) is simply that which has all-pervasive extension as its universal (*sāmānya*) inherent in sound and so forth.

Sound and the other [qualities] are the particularities (*viśeṣa*) of that universal form (*sāmānya-rūpa*). And thus it has been said: "Of these elements, earth and so forth, which are endowed with a single genus and permeated by the qualities such as *sattva*, only the specific properties such as sound are differentiated from their universals."

[297,19] Substance (*dravya*) is a collection (*samudāya*) of generalities (*sāmānya*) and particulars (*viśeṣa*). Why? Because a collection resides in two; "residing in two" means it exists in two modes: it has parts whose distinctions have subsided, meaning it is devoid of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttapratyaya*). For example: a body, a tree, a herd, or a forest.

A collection (*samūha*) that follows after parts whose distinctions have been grasped, or follows after parts whose distinctions have not been grasped, is designated by the word "both" (*ubhaya*). For example, in the phrase "both gods and humans," one part of the collection consists of the gods and the other part consists of the humans. By means of those very two parts—which follow their respective internal distinctions as they have been grasped—the collection is denoted as "both."

In the expression "a forest of trees" (*āmnāṇāṃ vanam*), both difference and non-difference are intended. By the term "of trees," there is the intention of difference; by the term "forest," there is the intention of non-difference. Through these two—difference and non-difference—the genitive case in "of trees" and the nominative case in "forest" are employed. Thus, one single collection is intended by those two.

Furthermore, that aggregate is of two kinds: one whose parts are separately established (*yutasiddhāvayava*) and one whose parts are not separately established (*ayutasiddhāvayava*). An aggregate whose parts are separately established—that is, whose parts are established independently—is a forest or a multitude (*saṅgha*). An aggregate whose parts are not separately established—that is, whose parts are not established independently—is a composite whole (*saṅghāta*), such as a body, a tree, or an atom.

Even atoms possess parts, because they are effects of existence and so forth, and because they are corporeal, just like jars and other such things. Patañjali states that a substance (*dravya*) is a collection that follows after its constituent parts which are inseparably established; this is what was described as having the nature of both the universal and the particular.

[299,21] Now, what is the subtle form (*sūkṣmarūpa*) of these? It is the *tanmātra*, which is the cause of the gross elements (*bhūta*). Because it is composed of many atoms (*paramāṇu*), a single part of that *tanmātra* is an atom. That too consists of both the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣātmā*), and is a composite (*samudāya*) followed by distinct parts that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*). Thus it is for all *tanmātras*. Consequently, the *tanmātras* are devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), and so are their constituent parts.

"Atoms"—this is the third subtle form of the elements, which is the object of *saṃyama*. And because it is composed of the *tanmātras*, space (*ākāśa*) possesses parts and is impermanent. Furthermore, it is not possible to perceive a substance called "space" apart from sound, because there is no difference between a property and that which possesses the property (*dharmadharmiṇoḥ*).

[300,5] But is it not the case that for hair and the like, blackness departs and whiteness arises? Thus, blackness and the rest possess the properties of disappearance and appearance; therefore they are qualities (*guṇa*). That which does not perish along with blackness and persists through whiteness is the substance (*dravya*). In the same way, even for space (*ākāśa*) and the like, their existence is distinct from their qualities, due to the difference between sound, cognition, and so forth.

[300,9] It is not so, because there is no illustrative example. Those very same afflictions (*kleśa*), whether black or white, transform through qualities such as being black or white; for it has been stated that "everything consists of everything. Indeed, nowhere can the essential nature of a substance be removed by means of something immutable. As for the claim that "whatever is perceived through both sight and touch is a substance," that too is not a fault, because it is apprehended by both sight and touch since it is a collection of color and touch that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*).

[300,15] But is it not the case that color (rūpa) is not grasped by touch, nor is tangibility (sparśa) grasped by sight? That which is grasped by both—such that one thinks, "That very thing which I see, I am touching"—is a substance (dravya). However, that which is grasped by the eye alone and by touch alone is a quality (guṇa).

[300,18] It is not so, because [the reason] is inconclusive with respect to a heap consisting of a mixture of different species, such as beans, sesame, and barley. Furthermore, the heap is perceived through both sight and touch. Moreover, sight and touch are perceivers of qualities alone, because they are external sense organs, like the ear. For there exists no universal (jāti) distinct from the quality, since it is not perceived as something separate.

Furthermore, even in the case of a jar and other such objects, it is only color and touch that are apprehended through sight and touch by means of mutual superimposition, as in the case of saying, "This color is foul-smelling" or "it is fragrant. Therefore, space (*ākāśa*) as well, being composed of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), cannot be cognized apart from sound; thus, it possesses parts and is impermanent.

[300,24] Now, the fourth form of the elements: manifestation (*khyāti*) characterized by stability is the *guṇas*. They follow the nature of their effects and conform to the properties of their effects; they are designated by the term "concomitance" (*anvaya*) because of their persistence. This is the fourth form of the elements, which is the object of *saṃyama* regarding the concomitance of the *guṇas*.

[301,12] Now, the fifth form of these is their purposefulness (*arthavattva*). Its explanation is that they have enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) as their purpose. And this [purposefulness] persists through the *guṇas*. In that regard, this persistence of the purpose of enjoyment and liberation within the *guṇas* is the fifth form of the elements (*bhūtas*), which is the object of *saṃyama* known as "purposefulness."

The *guṇas* are the invariable concomitants (*anvayin*) within the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the gross elements (*bhūtas*), and the modifications of those elements (*bhūtavikāras*). Thus, the subtle form of the *tanmātra* is followed through the gross elements and their modifications; likewise, the essential nature of the gross elements is followed through the gross modifications of the elements. Therefore, everything is purposeful. Because the *guṇas* exist for the sake of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), and because they are all-pervasive (*sarvānvayitva*), everything—including the modifications of the elements—is purposeful by virtue of serving that end.

Now, regarding those elements, beds, and the five gross forms—having first performed *saṃyama* on the gross, and immediately after the direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) resulting from mastery over them—one should perform *saṃyama* on their essential nature (*svarūpa*). Then, on the subtle.

Furthermore, through *saṃyama* applied respectively to the sequence beginning with "again" (*punar*), "in the lineage" (*anvaye*), and "in the meaningfulness" (*arthavattve*), there arises accordingly the vision and mastery of each respective [level], starting from the gross. Having mastered the essential forms of the elements (*bhūta-svarūpa*), the yogi becomes a conqueror of the elements. Through that mastery, the primary natures (*prakṛti*) of the elements become compliant with his will, just as cows follow their calves; that is, the elemental natures conform to his volition. (3.44)

[301,25] He now states the fruit of self-restraint (*saṃyama*): "From that, the manifestation of *aṇimā*, perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by its properties. Regarding this, he asks what *aṇimā* is and says: "It is *aṇu* (atomic). It is subtler than the subtlest and is unimpeded by anything. By means of that *aṇimā*, one enters into everything, even a diamond; likewise, one becomes invisible to all.

[301,29] *Laghimā* is lightness; one becomes lighter even than cotton and other such things, and by means of that, being without support, one is able to go everywhere. *Mahimā* is greatness; one becomes great and pervades even space (*ākāśa*). *Prāpti* is attainment; while remaining right here, one touches the moon even with the tip of a finger. *Prākāmya* is the state of having abundant desire; one becomes one whose desires are fulfilled according to wish, and there is no obstruction to one's power. Because of this freedom of will, one emerges from the earth as if from water.

[302,15] Mastery (*vaśitva*) is mastery over the entire world. Its explanation is as follows: he becomes the master of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), and others become subject to him. Sovereignty (*īśitva*) means that he rules over those primary elements—their manifestation, arrangement, and withdrawal; that is, their arising, persistence, and dissolution. The power of determining according to one's desire (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*) means that wherever there is a desire, there itself it reaches its conclusion and its end. Because of his true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), the nature of the primary elements remains exactly as he has willed.

Even though that yogi is capable, he does not effect a reversal of the nature of things; he does not make fire cold. Why? Because another, the previously established Supreme Lord (*parama-īśvara*), who has mastery over all desires, has already willed those things to be otherwise through His volition. For it is not so.

For one who desires to effect a reversal of objects, that reversal occurs toward an already established object even without hatred; because of the absence of impurity, it does not bring about a reversal of the object, for he is one who practices what is more auspicious. These eight powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), arise from mastery over the elements.

The perfection of the body will be described later. Regarding "non-affliction by their properties": the yogin is not afflicted by the properties of those elements. Earth, with its own property of solidity (*mūrti*), does not obstruct the yogin’s bodily movements and so forth; thus, he can even enter through solid rock. Water, though slippery, does not moisten the yogin, even if he remains in water for a thousand years. Fire does not burn him with its heat. Wind, though moving, does not carry him away.
Even though it is by nature unobstructed and its form is manifest, it becomes veiled and does not become manifest; it remains invisible even to the perfected ones (siddhas). ||3.45||

The perfection of the body consists of beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine solidity. He is beautiful, handsome, graceful, radiant, possessed of extraordinary strength, and has a body as firm as a diamond. (3.46)

[YS 3.47] Through *saṃyama* on grasping (*grahaṇa*), essential nature (*svarūpa*), egoism (*asmitā*), inherence (*anvaya*), and purposefulness (*arthavattva*), mastery over the senses is attained. All of this is explained by the previously mentioned sūtra (3.46). However, the distinction here is that egoism alone (*asmitāmātra*) is like the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) among the gross elements. An object, such as sound and so forth, consists of both the universal and the particular. The function of the senses toward these objects, which consists in the perception of the specific qualities of the object, is "grasping" (*grahaṇa*). Furthermore, the form of grasping does not occur in the mind merely with respect to the universal—that is, the mere appearance of the universals of sound and so forth.

How could a specific object of its own domain be determined by the sense organ if it were not first perceived? It could not be determined at all, given the difference between the determinative cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) of one with cataracts and that of one without cataracts. Therefore, there can be no mental determinative cognition regarding an object not first perceived by the sense organ. Consequently, one must first apply *saṃyama* to this function, which consists of the specific [perception].

[304,10] Now, as for the essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is the second form of the sense organs. The specific characteristic of the sense organs is the perception of the particularities of objects, which consist of both the universal and the particular within their luminous nature. Just as the specific characteristic of a lamp is its illumination taking on the particular forms of jars and so forth, while mere illumination is the universal; therefore, the sense organ is a substance (*dravya*) consisting of both the universal and the particular, which follows after the distinction of its inseparable parts.

Like a lamp. Just as the attribute of having a general form proceeds into gross objects and the like, so too the sense organ, whose nature is luminosity, proceeds into the function of grasping which consists of specific substances. Therefore, restraint should be practiced upon this second nature of the sense organs.

The third form of those faculties is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), characterized by the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*). Of that universal ego, the faculties are the particulars, following as inseparable constituent parts and inhering in the nature of grasping. In this regard, one should practice *saṃyama* upon the "I-am-ness."

The fourth form of the intellect consists of the *guṇas*, which are determinative by nature and characterized by the functions of illumination, activity, and inertia; it is of these that the sense organs, along with the ego, are transformations. In this regard, one should practice *saṃyama* upon the following of the *guṇas*.

The fifth form of matter is that which is inherent in the qualities (guṇas), namely their possession of purpose for the sake of the Spirit (puruṣa). Therefore, as before, there is both the purposiveness and the inherence of all things.

[304,24] Thus, there is restraint (*saṃyama*) upon these five forms of the sense-faculties (*indriya-rūpa*) in their respective order, without deviating from that sequence. Having achieved mastery over each of those five individually, one attains mastery over the five essential natures (*pañca-svarūpa*). From that mastery over the five essential natures, the yogin’s mastery over the sense-faculties and so forth arises for the sake of the results to be described hereafter. As for the statement "thereafter, there is complete control over the sense-faculties," that refers merely to sovereignty over the activity of grasping objects, characterized by the non-perception of objects [due to their dissolution]. (3.47)

[305,16] From that, there arises swiftness like the mind, the state of being without organs, and mastery over the primary matter (*pradhāna*). Following from that victory over the senses, there is the unsurpassed state of the body; "unsurpassed" (*anuttama*) means that there is nothing superior to it. "Swiftness like the mind" refers to the attainment of movement. "The state of being without organs" (*vikaraṇabhāva*) is the attainment of function by the sense organs—which are independent of the body—according to the desired location, the desired time, and the desired objects such as sound and so forth.

Mastery over all nature and its transformations—meaning mastery over the eight primary natures (*prakṛti*) and their modifications—is called "conquest of the primal matter" (*pradhānajaya*). These three accomplishments are termed the "Honey-like" (*madhupratīkā*). And these are attained through mastery over the five forms [of subtle elements]. (3.48)

[305,23] For one who consists solely in the discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience. This belongs to the *sattva* whose stains of *rajas* and *tamas* have been entirely shaken off, which abides in a supreme flow of stability within its own self-sustained clarity, which dwells in the supreme state known as "mastery," and which rests in the unsurpassed purity of knowledge consisting solely in the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*. He possesses sovereignty over all things; he has power over the entire range of objective entities.

The meaning is as follows: in their entirety—that is, in their complete nature consisting of both primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*), and in their essence consisting of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the qualities (*guṇa*)—the objects of perception, which are all the qualities, exist as the state of being transformed into causes such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, characterized by the determination of the qualities. Following after the properties that are respectively subsided (*śānta*), arisen (*udita*), or latent (*avyapadeśya*), they are obtained as the objects of perception and enjoyment for the Lord, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who is pure consciousness (*dṛśimātra*).

[306,19] Omniscience (*sarvajñātṛtva*) means the discriminative knowledge (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arising simultaneously and without succession regarding all constituent qualities (*guṇas*) which exist as being in states of quiescence, emergence, or indeterminacy. This is the perfection (*siddhi*) called "Free from Sorrow" (*viśokā*), characterized by mastery over everything and omniscience;
having attained this, the yogi dwells as a master, omniscient and with the bonds of affliction destroyed. (3.49)

From detachment even from that, when the seeds of defects are destroyed, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). When this occurs to the omniscient one who presides over all states of being—namely, the discriminative cognition of the *sattva* resulting from the destruction of afflictions and karma—in this manner: "And what kind of Puruṣa is he? He is contrary in nature to *sattva*, immutable, pure, and distinct from *sattva*. Thus it is.

Then, for one who becomes dispassionate because of the direct perception of all things by the Omniscient One, those seeds of affliction—which consist of the latencies of ignorance and are like burnt rice seeds, incapable of germination—perish along with the mind as its substratum, which has fulfilled its purpose and dissolved. When these have perished, the person no longer experiences this triple suffering characterized as internal and so forth.

Thus, when these *guṇas*—which have manifested in the mind in the form of afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), and their maturation (*vipāka*), and have thereby fulfilled their purpose—are withdrawn at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), there occurs for the *puruṣa* an absolute separation from the *guṇas*, which is isolation (*kaivalya*). At that time, the *puruṣa* is simply the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) established in its own nature. In this context, by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even from that state," it is indicated that even for one who has not attained the powers of yoga (*yogaiśvarya*), isolation results from right vision (*samyagdarśana*). 3.50.

[307,17] Upon being invited by those who dwell in celestial realms, one should avoid attachment and pride, for otherwise an undesirable consequence would follow. "Those who dwell in realms" (*sthāninaḥ*) are the gods such as Indra and others who inhabit heaven and the like. "Being invited by them" refers to such words as, "O, O, please stay here. When that occurs, attachment and pride arise in one who remembers his own inferiority; these two must not be performed. If attachment and pride were to occur, an undesirable result would ensue.

[307,21] Indeed, there are these four types of yogins: the beginner (*prāthamakalpika*), the one who has reached the stage of honey (*madhubhūmika*), the one whose light of wisdom has arisen (*prajñājyotis*), and the one who has transcended what is to be cultivated (*atikrāntabhāvanīya*). He explains them in order: therein, the first is the "one whose light has arisen" (*pravṛttajyotis*), who is a practitioner (*abhyāsī*) habituated to practice, and for whom some form of activity—such as that of the *jyotiṣmatī* and other stages—has begun to arise.

The second [type of yogin] possesses truth-bearing wisdom (*ṛtambharaprajña*). The third has conquered the elements and the sense organs. He, however, having cultivated all things to be cultivated, having realized them, and having mastered them, has performed the binding of protection. For protection must be established for what has been acquired; he is one who possesses the means for the realization of what is to be cultivated and the accomplishment of what is to be done. "Means for the accomplishment of what is to be done" (*kartavyatāsādhanāni*) refers to the practices such as cultivation (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*), and he is one who possesses these.

But for the fourth [type of yogin], who has transcended that which is to be cultivated, there remains only one purpose: the relinquishment of the mind (*cittapratisarga*) itself, which is the dissolution of the mind (*cittapralaya*). His wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding the final stage (*prāntabhūmi*) is of seven kinds. In this regard, when a Brahmin who has directly realized the second stage, the "Honeyed" (*madhumatī*) stage—the stage of truth-bearing wisdom (*ṛtaṃbharaprajñā*)—the gods who dwell in those realms perceive his purity of being and invite him to their abodes. The commentary beginning with "O! and so forth has its meaning well known. (3.51)

[309,9] Through *saṃyama* on the moment (*kṣaṇa*) and its sequence (*tatkrama*), knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arises. He explains the moment and the sequence himself in detail: therein, that substance which is the limit of reduction, beyond which no further reduction can be made, is the atom (*paramāṇu*). Likewise, when time—conceived by the common intellect as characterized by days and nights—is reduced, that limit of reduction, beyond which it is impossible to reduce it further, out of a desire to grasp the smallest unit, is the moment (*kṣaṇa*); it is a real entity (*vastubhūta*).

Alternatively, the time during which an atom, having moved, leaves its former location and reaches the subsequent one—that is a *kṣaṇa*. The meaning is that in every respect, this subtle moment exists.

Regarding that moment which occurs as the interruption of a stream: its "stream" is a continuous succession (*prabandha*), and its "non-interruption" is its continuity (*nairantarya*). That moment which has the nature of occurring as such a non-interruption of the stream—that continuity of the moment is what constitutes the "sequence" (*krama*) of the moment. Furthermore, there is no real aggregation (*vastusamāhāra*) of those two—the moment and its sequence—because the sequence of moments is not a real entity and because the moment itself is a single unit; thus, there is no aggregate or collection of the two.

[309,20] But surely, if there were no such thing as a moment (*kṣaṇa*) or its succession (*krama*), how could months, years, and so forth proceed? To address this, he says: "From the synthesis of cognition" (*buddhisamāhārāt*), that is, from the synthesis of moments and their succession as constructed by cognition; and because this arises from the cognition that binds together the connection with various locations and so forth, there are the *muhūrta*, day-and-night, and so on. Consequently, this distinction exists only within the mind.

For one whose mind flows with a serene and uniform cognition and whose consciousness is established on a stage of one-pointedness, there is an equality between a single moment and a thousand yugas, even while time is experienced; this is not so for one whose mind has emerged from meditative absorption. Likewise, even in a dream, what is mentally constructed as a thousand *yojanas* is traversed in a mere *ghaṭikā*, whereas it would take many years to travel that same distance in waking life. Therefore, the accumulation of time is produced solely by the diversity of the intellect.

However, for one who holds that time is distinct from action, eternal, and all-pervasive, even such qualities as "slowness" and "quickness" do not serve as valid evidence for the separate existence of time, because they are exhausted within the mere action itself. For an action of fixed duration is the very definition of an action whose transformation has not yet been fully perceived, as in the expressions: "he sleeps until the milking of the cows is finished" or "he studies until the cooking of the rice is done. And that very thing is time.
Indeed, it is not possible for that which is eternal, all-pervasive, and immutable to delimit other entities like a *prastha* measure does, because it lacks any relational connection with them.

If it is argued that time, being possessed of activity (*kriyāvat*), is the delimiter like a *prastha* measure and so forth, then because that [time] also possesses activity, and because that which possesses activity must be delimited by another delimiter possessing activity, there would have to be yet another time as its delimiter; this leads to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, due to its possession of activity, it would also follow that time is impermanent.

If it is argued that time itself should be delimited by its own activity, then other things would also be delimited by their own activities; thus, the conceptualization of time as a distinct entity is pointless. In that case, let action alone be time.
Furthermore, if time were a delimiter merely by virtue of its existence, then it would follow that this applies to all things as well, since there is no difference in their mere existence.

If it is argued that this same dilemma applies even to the position that time is action (*kriyā*), we say no; for action is universally established, and since its capacity to delimit is proven in such cases as "I have sat until the milking of the cows," it is action itself that is obtained as the delimiter, not some other entity called time.

Furthermore, the cognitions of "long" and "quick" are produced by the slowness or proficiency of effort, and are not based on a distinct time-entity. Thus he says: "Indeed, this time, consisting of years and so forth, is devoid of objective reality (*vastu-śūnya*); it is a mental construction (*buddhi-nirmāṇa*) to be fashioned by the intellect."

[310,24] That which conforms to verbal properties follows along with conceptual constructions of words such as "moment" (*truṭi*), "twinkling" (*nimeṣa*), "day and night" (*ahorātra*), and so forth. To worldly people whose vision is distracted by the phenomenal world, it appears as if it were the very nature of the object itself. But the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the actual form of the thing; it is real, inferred through the alteration of that substance, and it is based upon succession. And succession consists in the immediate sequence of moments, serving as the cause for the cognition that perceives no distinction within the flow of moments.

Yogins who know time call that moment "time. Yet two moments do not exist simultaneously such that their combination could be conceived, because two co-nascent moments cannot occur within a single substratum (*dharmin*). Indeed, when Caitra is born, he is born in a single moment; two moments do not exist together therein. Nor can there be a sequence between two [simultaneous] things, because two co-existent moments are impossible.

The sequence (*krama*) is that immediate succession (*ānantarya*) of a future moment following from a preceding one; for example, the immediate succession of a jar that arises after a lump of clay is its sequence. Indeed, a jar produced from a lump of clay situated on one wheel does not exist in the sequence of a lump of clay situated on another wheel. Therefore, there is only a single present moment. The preceding and succeeding moments—the past and the future—do not exist, because the preceding and succeeding are merely the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substratum (*dharmin*).
And the substratum (dharmin) is indeed mounted upon the present moment alone; therefore, there is no eternal collection of that—namely, a collection of moments and their sequence.

As for those moments that have occurred or will occur—the past and future moments—they are the substrata (*dharmin*) which are to be explained as existing through transformation (*pariṇāma*), in dependence upon the transformation of the substratum. Thus, by means of that single moment, the entire world undergoes transformation; indeed, all these phenomena (*dharma*) and all entities are mounted upon that very moment—that is, they are mounted upon the present moment.

As for what was stated—that there is no succession for a past moment—the purpose of that is the negation of succession and non-succession. For if there were a succession of moments, it would follow that the succession of moments possesses substantial reality (*vastutva*). Indeed, through the mastery over these two—the moment and its succession—there arises the direct realization of them, and from that, knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*). Since all objects are indeed marked by the moment and its succession, one discriminates and knows them all without exception. (3.52)

Regarding that knowledge born of seclusion (*vivekaja*), what is its object of cognition? Its specific object is now proposed: because difference is determined through genus (*jāti*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and location (*deśa*), there is a comprehension of two things as distinct from one another. When two things are identical in their location and characteristics, the difference in genus is the cause of the distinction between objects—that is, the cause of the determination of their mutual difference—as in the case of "this is a cow" and "this is a mare."

Where there is no difference in genus and there is only one single genus, then, despite the equality of genus, the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) serves as the differentiator of distinctness, as in the cases: "the brindled cow" (*kālākṣī gauḥ*) and "the healthy cow" (*svastimatī gauḥ*).

Where there is neither difference in genus nor difference in characteristic, there the difference in location is the cause for determining their distinctness. For example, when two *āmalaka* fruits possess similarity in genus and characteristic, the difference in location is what makes them distinct, such that one is designated as "this is the eastern *āmalaka*" and the other as "this is the northern one."

But when a previously existing *āmalaka* fruit moves toward a northern location for a knower whose mind is distracted by something else and whose consciousness is agitated, while the subsequent fruit remains in the eastern location, then—since they occupy the same space—the distinction between "this is the former" and "this is the latter" would be impossible for two identical things. Since the object of knowledge exists and is of a single nature, there must be an indubitable knowledge of its true reality; therefore, this was said: "From that, realization arises from discriminative knowledge. That is to say, realization arises from the knowledge born of discrimination, which is produced by *saṃyama* upon the moment and its sequence.

How, then, is the region characterized by and concomitant with the eastern *āmalaka* fruit distinct from the region characterized by and concomitant with the northern *āmalaka* fruit? Those two *āmalaka* fruits, being characterized by and concomitant with the "eastern" and "northern" [directions], are distinct from the experience of the characteristics of their own respective regions and serve as the marks of their own regions. That moment which is distinct from the experience of those [fruits], and which is marked by the experience of the characteristics of its own region, is the experience of the characteristics of another region; this [distinction] is the cause for their difference.
By this analogy, because the atom— which possesses a distinct characteristic and a dissimilar nature—

directly perceives the characteristic of the location of the preceding atom, and because it directly perceives the characteristic coexisting with the location of the preceding atom, when the subsequent atom moves away from that location and occupies the previous location, the moment of the subsequent atom is distinct from its experience of that [previous] location. Due to this difference in moments, for the Lord or the yogin, there arises a cognition of their alteration (*anyathātva*), which constitutes the delimitation of their distinction.

On this point, others explain as follows: those ultimate particularities (*viśeṣa*) residing in atoms which are eternal, they themselves produce the cognition of difference (*anyatā-pratyaya*). What, then, is the use of mastery over their moments and their sequence? Just as the particularities residing in jars and other objects produce the cognition of difference, so too the particularities residing in atoms should produce the cognition of their existence and the cognition of their own presence. They also produce the cognition of the distinction between their substrates.

To this it is replied: the cause of difference has already been stated as the distinction of location, the distinction of form, obstruction, and genus, specifically in the case of gross objects; however, this does not apply to atoms because they undergo transformation at every moment. For such a determination of difference could only occur if there were final, stable particularities; it is not possible, however, in the case of things that are in a state of incessant transformation.

When the preceding atom transforms into the form of the succeeding atom, and the succeeding atom [transforms] into the form of the preceding atom, then—since there is no ultimate distinction remaining therein—the discernment of their difference is impossible. In that case, comprehension can only arise from the discriminative knowledge produced by *saṃyama* upon the moment and its sequence. For it has been stated that atoms are impermanent; therefore, the differentiation of moments is accessible only to the intellect of a yogin.

Thus, he demonstrates the established proof of the impermanence of atoms by means of presenting the opinion of another teacher; therefore, it was said: "Vārṣagaṇya maintains that there is no distinctness of fundamental genus (*mūlajāti*) because of the absence of differences in form, obstruction, and genus."

Just as the plurality of *pradhānas*—one for each individual soul—is contrary to reason because there is no distinction of form, spatial separation, or genus, and thus the distinctness of *pradhānas* is untenable, being like the objects of experience for a single person; so too, if atoms were the ultimate cause, their distinctness cannot be postulated. Consequently, it follows that there is a single root-cause. For the diversity of atoms has not been stated to be eternal; and since atoms possess form and other qualities due to their corporeality, they must be non-eternal, just like jars and the like. (3.53)

The "star-like" [knowledge] has all things as its object, yet has no object in any way, and is non-sequential; this is knowledge born of discernment (*vivekaja*). It is the knowledge that has reached its ultimate limit among the divine seers (*devarṣi*), the celestial musicians (*gandharva*), and others. It is called "star-like" because it is born of discernment; the meaning is that it arises from one's own intuitive flash (*svapratibhottha*) and is not derived from instruction (*anaupadeśika*). It cannot be taught by another, nor can it be correctly grasped through verbal instruction. This is because it has all entities as its object; there is nothing whatsoever that remains outside its scope.

[315,16] And he knows everything—past, future, and present—in every way, through all its modes, all its particularities, and in every respect and by every means; it is grasped simultaneously, mounted upon a single moment. In a single moment he apprehends everything in every way, not sequentially like those who hold that things arise from non-existence and so forth.

This very knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*), when fully perfected, is a portion of that [highest state]; it is precisely this portion of knowledge that is both yoga and a lamp. Or, it is the lamp of yoga, hence "yoga-lamp. Beginning from the stage called *madhumatī* until the complete attainment of this knowledge born of discrimination—that is, all knowledges extending up to the perfection of discriminative knowledge, which are endowed with qualities such as mental swiftness (*manojava*)—are portions of this very [state]. (3.54)

[315.23] It might be argued that for one who possesses the sovereignty of knowledge (*jñānaiśvarya*), isolation (*kaivalya*) follows immediately after that dispassion (*vairāgya*). To this, he says: "For one who has attained discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*)—or even for one who has not—there is isolation upon the cessation of external perception. How so? "Isolation occurs when there is an equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*."

When the sattva of the intellect (buddhisattva) becomes free from smoke and dust, devoid of the stain of darkness, consists solely of the cognition of the distinctness of the Puruṣa, is endowed with the power of the cognition of that distinctness alone, has its seeds of affliction burnt away, and has the form of the latent impressions of the conditions of ignorance ceased, then it attains, as it were, a state of similarity in purity to the Puruṣa.

[316,11] Even though the three qualities (*triguṇa*) are distinct from the Puruṣa, and the Puruṣa is likewise distinct from them, nevertheless, because it has been transformed by the cognition of their difference, it is said to have attained a state resembling purity. At this stage, isolation (*kaivalya*) occurs for one who possesses discriminative knowledge—whether that be the Lord or one who is not the Lord, or anyone else. This is because the cessation of ignorance alone is the cause for both; for one whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, there is no further dependence on knowledge.

Since one who possesses right vision considers everything to consist of the three guṇas, and since a cognition consisting of the three guṇas is to be abandoned, he never has any regard for cognitions such as the "honeyed" (madhumatī) and so forth.

As for that which was mentioned regarding the knowledge born of yoga and sovereignty, that was introduced as an incidental topic following the path of the purification of the sattva-constituent, which leads to right vision (*samyagdarśana*). In the ultimate sense, however, non-vision (*adarśana*) ceases through knowledge. When that has ceased, the aforementioned afflictions (*kleśa*), such as egoism (*asmitā*) and the rest, no longer exist, because they have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their field. And due to the absence of afflictions, there is an absence of the fruition of karma; for it has been established that the latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) is rooted in the afflictions, and that its fruition occurs only when the root exists.

Therefore, this treatise is solely for the purpose of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), not for the sake of knowledge, sovereignty, or supernatural powers (*vibhūti*). In this state, the *guṇas* have fulfilled their office; they no longer persist as objects of perception for the *puruṣa*. That is the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *puruṣa*. Then the *puruṣa* becomes a light consisting of its own nature alone—stainless and solitary. The word "iti" marks the end [of the section]. Thus ends [the work] composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, a disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda and a teacher of the Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order.
In the Vivaraṇa on the Bhāṣya to the Patañjala-yoga-sūtras, the third chapter, the Vibhūti-pāda.

In the first quarter, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is primarily indicated; in the second, its means of accomplishment are explained; and in the third, there is a sequential presentation of the knowledge and sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) resulting from the practice of the limbs of yoga for the sake of right vision (*samyagdarśana*). And all of that is established through the exposition of Jaigīṣavya as being "of the nature of suffering" (*duḥkha*).

It has been stated that the destruction of suffering is the absolute cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Likewise, it was just explained that through detachment from those [afflictions], when the seeds of the defects are destroyed, there is isolation (*kaivalya*); and furthermore, for one who has attained discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) or even one who has not yet attained it, isolation occurs when the purity of the *sattva* and the *puruṣa* becomes equal. Since that isolation must be established by means of its opposite, this summary of the *Kaivalyapāda* is now undertaken.

Likewise, the various modes of awakening the latent impressions (vāsanā) accumulated over many previous births must be demonstrated solely for the sake of liberation (kaivalya). Similarly, another type of perfection (siddhi) not mentioned previously is introduced here for the purpose of praising the attainment of samādhi that is conducive to liberation. For the praise of one thing is achieved by disparaging something else of a similar class. In this regard, the fact that this serves as a means of praise will be revealed by what is to be said later: "The karma born of meditation is neither black nor white and leaves no residue; it is of three kinds for the yogi, but otherwise for others."

Perfections (*siddhi*) arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Those arising from birth are, for example, the attainment of perfection in other bodies such as the heavens through yoga and so forth; or the attainment of perfection in former bodies through elixirs (*rasāyana*) in the abodes of the *asuras*, by consuming soma, *āmalaka*, and the like, without discarding the previous body. Through mantras being recited, there is the power of traveling through the sky and so forth. Through austerity, there is the perfection of will (*saṃkalpasiddhi*), such as being able to assume any form at will and going wherever one desires, and so on. Perfections born of meditative concentration have already been explained previously. (4.1)

In this regard, "attainment" (*siddhi*) refers to the excellence of the body and its instruments. As for attainment through birth, there is no doubt that one who has fallen away from a previously acquired body and its instruments will take up another body. However, regarding one whose body has not fallen away, when undergoing transformation into another birth, the question arises: is that very same body and its instruments the material cause, or is it something else? In that case, the transformation of the body and the sense organs—which have already undergone transformation into another birth—into yet another birth occurs through the influx of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Upon the cessation of the previous transformation, for those very factors that were performing their prior functions, the arising of a subsequent transformation occurs through the incorporation of new constituent parts. Why? Because it is impossible for a large-sized effect to arise from a small-sized material cause (*upādāna*). Indeed, a plate weighing eighty *palas* cannot be produced from a lump of gold weighing only ten *palas*. The primary natures (*prakṛti*) of the body and the sense organs sustain their respective transformations—the body or the sense organ—by depending on causes such as merit (*dharma*), which are not yet fully manifest; by the use of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one should understand that they also depend upon demerit (*adharma*) as a cause.

It has been stated that depending upon the signs (*nimitta*) such as merit (*dharma*), the primary natures (*prakṛti*) favor their respective transformations. Regarding this, it is asked: what is the sign for the primary natures, and does it serve as their motive or not? To this he says: "The sign is not the motive for the primary natures; rather, from it comes the breaking of the veil, like a farmer. Indeed, the sign consisting of merit and so forth is not the motive for the primary natures. Why?
Because a cause is not set in motion toward the production of an effect by means of an effect, such as merit and so forth, which serves as the sign.

How, then, does the breaking of the obstruction arise from that sign of the Dharma and so forth? It is like a farmer: just as a farmer, wishing to flood another field from a field already full of water, does not remove the water with his hand, but rather breaks the barrier to it; once that is broken, the water itself flows to flood the other field.

In the same way, Dharma destroys Adharma, which is the veil of the *prakṛtis*; and Adharma also destroys Dharma, which is the veil. When that [veil] is destroyed, the *prakṛtis* themselves spontaneously overflow and fill their respective transformations (*vikāra*).

Or, for example, just as that very same farmer is not able to force the watery or earthy juices to enter the roots of the grain in that very field; rather, he removes the mung beans, *tinduka* fruits, *gavīśruka*, *śyāmāka*, and so forth from those roots of the grain. Once they have been removed, the juices naturally penetrate the roots of the grain themselves.

In the same way, dharma is the cause for the cessation of adharma, and adharma is likewise the cause for the cessation of dharma, because purity and impurity are absolutely contradictory. However, dharma does not serve as a cause for the activity of primordial nature (prakṛti). Now, when a yogi creates many bodies, do they possess a single mind or multiple minds? Regarding the perfection of samādhi, a certain unstated distinction is now stated: "The creative minds arise from the mere state of 'I-am-ness' (asmitāmātra)."

Taking the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) as the cause of the mind, the yogi creates emanated minds—minds that are not of the nature [of the original], not the mind of Īśvara, and which are new. The mention of "mind" is merely an illustration; the sense-faculties likewise arise from the mere state of "I-am-ness" (*asmitāmātra*). Consequently, they become possessed of mind and possessed of instruments.

Furthermore, in the absence of the mind and the sense faculties, the body would be like that of a corpse and thus useless. If, however, there were only a single mind, the distinction between primary and subordinate factors, as well as the differentiation of their activities, would not be possible. In this regard, although there is only one field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) due to his omnipresence, the undertaking of many bodies is logically established. Nevertheless, for the sake of the various distinctions in activity—both principal and subordinate—the diversity of instruments (*karaṇa*) must be admitted.

[320,25] Some, however, maintain that even the *kṣetrajñas* (knowers of the field) are different for each distinct body. Others raise the objection here regarding the "attainment of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Still others offer the resolution that the *kṣetrajñas* possess karma acquired in accordance with their respective states. 4.4.

If it is thus that many minds proceed preceded by the intention of a single mind, it is said in response: although there is a diversity of activities among all those minds, there is one motivating mind that produces, within another body, a representative form pertaining to the specific place destined for the fruit.

And that [emanated mind] conforms to the mind of the yogin. Furthermore, other emanated minds, though distinct and engaged in various activities, conform to the leading mind of that [yogin]. Consequently, their engagement, withdrawal, dependence, and so forth—such distinctions in activity—are logically established, just as there are distinctions in the natural activities of Rāhu. Thus, activity preceded by the intention of a single mind is made possible. (4.5)

Among those, that which is born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is free from latent dispositions (*anāśaya*). The transformation-mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) is of five kinds, produced through the power of birth, herbs, mantras, asceticism, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Among these, that very mind which is born of meditative absorption is indeed free from latent dispositions; it is devoid of the latent tendencies of afflictions and karma (*kleśakarmāśaya*). For such a mind, there is no latent disposition—that is, no activity of passion and so forth—and therefore there is no connection with merit or demerit for the yogin, because his afflictions have been exhausted. For it has been said: "The latent tendency of karma has its root in the afflictions."

And because of the absence of that [ignorance], the latent deposit of karma (karmāśaya) is untenable. However, for others who have already established birth and so forth, the latent deposit of karma certainly exists because their afflictions (kleśa) have not been extinguished. 4.6.

Why is it that only the yogin possesses this intention regarding karma, while others do not? Because for the yogin, karma is neither white nor black, whereas for others it is of three kinds. This aphorism concerns the commonality between those who have attained perfection and those who have not.

[322,10] But is it not the case that the preceding sūtra also has a general scope? No; for its purpose is to praise the accomplishment of meditative concentration (samādhi). If it had a general scope, the praise of the accomplishment of meditative concentration would be inappropriate. However, since it has a specific scope by means of enumerating the accomplishments, the praise of the accomplishment of meditative concentration is justified through the proclamation of the defects of the fourfold accomplishment of birth and so forth, which belong to the same class.

Furthermore, since the negation of the purpose of liberation for those who seek to establish the origin and so forth of the world follows by implication, the preceding sūtra has a specific subject matter; this [present] sūtra, however, has a general subject matter, as it is introduced as the reason for the preceding sūtra.

[322,16] This class of action is indeed fourfold. That which belongs to the wicked—those of evil mind who transgress the path of the scriptures—is purely black (*kṛṣṇā*) and most impure. That which is accomplished by external means, such as the performance of sacrifices involving one's wife, sons, cattle, and priests, is white-black (*śukla-kṛṣṇā*). What is this? It is that wherein there is an accumulation of the latent deposits of karma (*karmāśaya*) through the gateways of harming or favoring others; because it is produced with a great abundance of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is both black and white.

[322,20] Is it not the case that, because it is understood from the scriptural treatises on rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, that [action] is only white and not black? To this it is replied: No, because of the inconclusiveness of optional (kāmya) rites. For those very rites are the causes of both benefit and harm. If it is argued that they are indeed beneficial because their results, such as heaven, are desired, we say no; for since even the violation of another's wife is desired, it would follow by your logic that it too is beneficial.

If it is argued that [the case of killing] is not the same because, in the case of approaching another's wife and so forth, there is the occurrence of admitted faults and because it is prohibited, whereas in the case of engaging in the fire of passion there is no such thing—[we reply] no, for it is the same in that case as well. Because of the prohibition against being "one whose self is desire," there is also union with the undesired; and since birth and death, which consist of admitted faults, are necessarily occurring, they are indeed the cause of both the desired and the undesired. And that union with the undesired is determined to arise from harming others and the like, because the prohibition of those acts is logically established.

For it is certainly impossible to enjoy the fruits such as heaven without both birth and death. If that [heavenly fruit] exists, then since it is of the nature of suffering, it follows that sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma possess a dual nature. If it is argued that it is only other types of karma that are prohibited as causes for initiating birth and death, we say no; because [the result] occurs only when that [karma] is present, for when that [prohibited karma] exists, birth and death necessarily follow.

Furthermore, according to your position, the eternal [Self] would always act, and birth and death would not occur; for these two belong only to that which acts, not to that which does not act. Therefore, it is understood that the eternal lacks causality. Moreover, regarding the action by which one will undertake birth and death in heaven and so forth—if that action belongs to another life, then there would be the consequence of no liberation, because the fruit of what was performed in a previous birth must necessarily be experienced even during the non-performance of optional or prohibited rites.

If it is argued that the obligatory rites (*nitya*) are for the purpose of exhausting the karma of previous births, that is not so, because such a restriction is untenable. It cannot be established that only those prior karmas which have undesirable fruits have already begun to produce their effects, while those with desirable fruits have not; for as long as there remain unseen fruits (*adṛṣṭaphala*), liberation is impossible even for one who performs only the obligatory rites, since they still initiate new births.

[323,9] Therefore, it is established that even desired things possess a dual causality, because external means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and ritual actions (*karman*) consist of both affliction and favor. Furthermore, the cessation of previously performed desired rituals such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and others cannot logically occur through the eternal [Brahman], because there is no contradiction between them. And there is no contradiction because both are of the nature of purity (*śuddhi*), and because this is established by the Tantras.

Furthermore, if one were to argue that "actions initiated over many lifetimes produce each individual birth, and no uninitiated effect remains," even so, since the karma of previous births has reached exhaustion by yielding its fruit in the present life, it follows that only the new, desirable actions performed in the current life initiate the cycle of birth and death with heaven as their fruit— thus, they take on the nature of being white or black.

And from that, observing both the suffering of birth and death and the pleasure designated as heaven, we shall infer that its cause is twofold in nature. Thus, when this is established, we shall infer that even in the case of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice and others, the performance of violence—which is prohibited—though for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), is nonetheless of the nature of pain (*duḥkharūpa*). For even when violence is for the sake of the ritual, it remains undesirable (*aniṣṭabhūtā*) and thus results in pain.

Regarding what was stated—that the scripture which is without distinction is like the "head" and constitutes the rebuttal—therein, the argument that "it is like the head" is unestablished as a formal illustration (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhatva*) of that kind. However, as for the statement "the scripture which is without distinction," the relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakatva*) is logically tenable due to the contradiction regarding the essential nature of the *homa* sacrifice. But since there is no such contradiction in the case of violence (*hiṃsā*), both [scriptures] can serve as valid reasons (*hetu*), just as eating serves as the cause for both pleasure and the maintenance of the body.

And just as bathing at a sacred ford has the visible purpose of refreshment, so too violence, without abandoning its nature of having undesirable results, does not indeed fail to bring about a sacrifice of great fruit.

[323,26] Now, if it is argued that even those rites accomplished by external means are eternal and purely "white" (śukla) simply because they lack connection with desire (*kāma*), this is not so; for there is no distinction between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*) rites insofar as they possess defects. Just as the optional rites are considered defective due to their connection with desire—as in the case of one who desires [results]—so too, the fact of possessing the defect of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of desire and the like, is common to both; thus, even the obligatory rites possess a dual nature. Furthermore, the state of being possessed of ignorance is inevitable for one engaged in the obligatory rites, since causes necessitating expiation (*prāyaścitta*) necessarily arise.

Moreover, all action belongs only to the ignorant, because action does not arise for the wise man. For a wise person does not regard any fruit as distinct from abiding in his own true nature (*svarūpa*). And abiding in the mere true nature proceeds through the cessation of all activity. Thus, the undertaking of action is not possible for the wise man; for one who has set out upon a land route does not employ a boat or other means intended for embarking upon a waterway.

[324,15] But surely, if this were so, there would be no distinction between obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites? To this it is replied: there is no fault, because the purpose of obligatory rites is merely the cessation of mere action (*karma-mātra-nivṛtti*), which is the fruit desired by one who has turned away from optional rites. For when one has desisted from optional rites, his actions—performed for the most part by a pure agent free from desire—possess an exceedingly pure fruit; and due to the abundance of their purity, they serve the purpose of purification (*saṃskāra*). Moreover, the very cessation of desire is itself a great fruit.

Furthermore, for one who performs obligatory rites (*nitya*), there arises a reflection in the form of right vision (*samyagdarśana*) such as: "What is the purpose? What shall I do? Or what is its fruit? And what are the defects in its performance? Thus, there is a distinction regarding the obligatory rite. However, both types of action alike share the nature of being composed of white and black elements, because they are accomplished by external means and thus involve injury to others. Therefore, it is said:

The class of white action belongs to those who possess austerity and self-study. For that, being dependent solely upon the mind, requires no external means; it does not depend on external instruments and does not come about by causing pain to others.

[324,26] It is neither white nor black for renunciants whose afflictions are exhausted and who possess their final bodies. For these, who have only one body remaining, it is not white because of renunciation, and not black because of the non-performance of actions and the non-undertaking of external means. Nor is it a mixture of white and black, due to the two causes of external renunciation and non-undertaking. And so it has been said: "The threefold fruit of action—unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to renunciants. [325,8]

But for other beings—those perfected through birth, herbs, mantras, or austerity, as well as others—the threefold karma (white, black, and mixed) is as before, just as in the second chapter where it was stated that "the root is affliction" and so forth. (4.7)

Since isolation (*kaivalya*) is the subject under discussion, its obstacles—the afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), and latent dispositions (*vāsanā*)—must be explained. Furthermore, the activity, the counteragent, the cessation, and the detailed explanation of those afflictions have already been provided. In the same way, for actions and latent dispositions as well, their activity, state, counteragent, and cessation must be described; therefore, the subsequent sūtras are commenced, because through their cessation isolation is established, and not otherwise.
Consequently, there is the manifestation only of those latent dispositions that are conducive to their fruition (*vipāka*).

Therefore, from that threefold karma—characterized as previously described, consisting of black, white, and mixed forms—which is ripening and serves as the cause, there arises the manifestation of those very latencies (*vāsanā*) which are concordant with its maturation; that is, the fruit which is the maturation of that very karma, and which corresponds to it, conforms to it, and is of the same nature.

This is what is meant: among the karmas that serve as the causes for maturation as gods, animals, or humans, whatever kind of maturation corresponds to a particular type of karma, the latencies (*vāsanā*) that are concordant with that maturation follow after that karmic maturation and arise accordingly; it is the manifestation of those [latencies] alone, because they have been conditioned by a karmic maturation similar to them. Just as a calf, seeing its mother, runs after her, there is no manifestation of other [latencies] that are not concordant with it.

For divine karma, while ripening and approaching the state of manifesting its fruit, cannot serve as the cause for the manifestation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of hell-beings, animals, or humans; this is because the relationship between a cause and its effect must be characterized by a specific and corresponding suitability. Rather, it is only those [karmic tendencies] that are compatible with the divine state that are manifested. The same reasoning and conclusion apply equally to the cases of hell-beings, animals, and humans.

When karma pertaining to the hells is ripening, impressions (*vāsanā*) corresponding to that karma manifest. Likewise, when karma pertaining to the animal realm is ripening, impressions conforming to its maturation are revealed. The same principle applies to the human realm as well. For it is not possible for the maturation of any particular karma to occur without depending on impressions similar to its own maturation.

Nor can there be a manifestation of impressions without other karmas—whose form corresponds to the karma that initiates the maturation producing those impressions—being oriented toward maturation. Such is the case with both karmas and impressions.
The state of being mutual cause and effect is not subject to contradiction. 4.8.

In this regard, there is no immediate succession for latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are most remote due to the intervention of many births, times, and places, with respect to a karma that is ripening—just as there is none among distant friends, kinsmen, and so forth. Furthermore, just as a proximate impression is more potent, a remote one does not approach with such potency. Therefore, for remote latent impressions, there is no immediate succession.

In the absence of that [latent impression], this fault would follow: just as the ripening of a cat [would occur] separated by a hundred kalpas, so too the divine ripening immediately preceding the future ripening of a cat [would occur]. In that case, because it is more proximate, the divine latent impression (vāsanā) would not function as the cause for the manifestation of the cat's ripening due to its opposition [to it]. Furthermore, if the latent impressions of the cat were not taken up because they are remote—being separated by a hundred kalpas—then the ripening of the karma that causes the cat's ripening would be impossible.
Consequently, it would follow that both karmas and latent impressions are rendered purposeless.

To this it is replied: there is indeed immediate succession even for those [impressions] separated by birth, place, and time, because memory and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) possess a single nature. For instance, the ripening of a scorpion's sting and the like, which are manifested by the manifesting agent—their own karma—even if they are separated by a hundred births, by a remote location, or by ten thousand eons, are nonetheless manifested by that very karma which acts as their manifesting agent.

[327,9] But has not the remoteness of time already been stated as being due precisely to the intervention of births? Why, then, is the mention of "time" (kāla) made again? It is said that for certain small creatures and others, many births occur even within a single day; since there is no remoteness of past time in those cases, the term "time" is employed.

Among those, the latencies (vāsanā) conditioned by the ripening of a cat, which were previously brought forth by their own manifesting conditions, arise again through the emergence of their own manifesting conditions; they are manifested immediately—that is, very quickly—by taking up the latencies conditioned by the ripening of a cat. Why is this so? Because even for these [latencies] that are separated [in time], a similar action serves as the manifesting cause (nimitta).

For the karma that is the cause for manifesting the maturation of an ox is not the occasion for manifesting the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of a cat, because they are dissimilar; indeed, a manifesting cause must be concordant with its effect. Upon seeing a moment of sourness and the like, the tongue salivates. Therefore, there is immediate succession (*ānantarya*) among the latent impressions, since their manifesting causes are identical. This being so, there is neither proximity nor distance among the latent impressions, because they reside in the same mental substratum (*cittāśraya*). Furthermore, this is another reason for their immediate succession: because memory (*smṛti*) and the formative impression (*saṃskāra*) are of one and the same nature.

Previously, a cause of immediate succession for the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—namely, an action (*karman*) of a similar kind that manifests it—was stated. Now, this other [cause] is being stated: as are the experiences, so are the formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*); as are the conditions (*pratyaya*), so are the latent impressions. And those predispositions consist of the nature of latent impressions; as are the latent impressions, so are the memories. Thus it has been said: "The cognition colored by the object of apprehension manifests in the appearance of both the apprehended and the apprehending," and so forth.

From latent impressions (saṃskāras) separated by birth, place, and time, memories arise; and from those memories, in turn, further latent impressions are produced. Thus, these memories and latent impressions are manifested through the force of the acquisition of activity by the store of karma (karmāśaya). It has also been established that the acquisition of activity by the store of karma likewise depends upon causes such as place and so forth.

And for this reason, even though they are separated by an interval, because the relationship between cause and effect is not interrupted, there is indeed immediate succession (*ānantarya*). As is the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), so is the memory (*smṛti*). Furthermore, because their manifesting agents are specifically determined, remoteness is not a cause [for the failure of memory]. Since a memory of a similar kind arises precisely from a mental impression even when it has been separated by a hundred eons, immediate succession is established. (4.9)

Now he demonstrates that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) bring about maturation (*vipāka*) because they are beginningless, and he establishes that the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are also beginningless and that each one undergoes entry into innumerable wombs for the sake of attaining detachment. Their beginninglessness is due to the permanence of the aspiration (*āśis*). Because the aspiration for those latent impressions is permanent, they are beginningless. This aspiration for a self—namely, "May death not come to me," or "May I have more"—is observed in everyone; yet it is not innate, nor does it proceed by its own inherent nature, even though it is deeply rooted.

Why is it that for one who has just been born, having not yet experienced the nature of birth and death, there occurs a fear of death caused by the recollection of aversion or caused by the recollection of suffering? It could not be so in any way; for the appropriation of a cause such as the recollection of suffering is not possible for that which is inherent (*svābhāvika*). Furthermore, an inherently existing entity does not depend upon a cause. Indeed, the heat of fire, being its inherent nature, would not be observed to require a cause for its own effect.
