Furthermore, memory with respect to an object—whether desired or undesired—is not observed to arise for anyone unless that object has been previously experienced. Likewise, when one does not recollect a previously experienced beloved, no longing for that object is seen; similarly, when one does not recollect a previously experienced unpleasant thing, neither hatred nor fear toward that object is observed in the world. Moreover, every being who is born in this life, having not experienced birth and death in this very lifetime, is seen immediately after birth to have a wish for self-preservation. Therefore, because of that wish for self-preservation, [it follows that there must be a prior experience].

The experience of death in a previous birth is inferred; from that, a birth prior to that, and again one prior to that. Thus, we infer the beginninglessness of the impressions of memory (*smṛti-saṃskāra*) and of the experiences of birth and death which are their causes.

In exactly the same way, it is established that each individual living being undergoes passage through many wombs. Thus, these latent impressions (*vāsanās*) are difficult to remove and cannot be abandoned. Why is this so? Because this mind, permeated by beginningless latent impressions, under the influence of objective signs and the influence of karma, acquires certain latent impressions produced by the ripening of actions belonging to the same class as those currently maturing; having acquired them, they serve for the experience of the person until its mandate is completed.

This mind is like a lamp in a jar or a palace; it expands and contracts, taking on the dimensions of the bodies of elephants, mosquitoes, and so forth, just as a lamp does within jars, palaces, and the like. Others have maintained this view. Regarding that, he has stated what is logical with the words "and likewise" (*tathā ca*). And thus, even if there were contraction and expansion, there would be no interval between death and the subsequent time of birth.

It is called *antarābhava* (intermediate existence) because it exists within this interval. They say that the body by which one wanders—that is, the wandering or transmigration—is the *ātivāhika* (conveying) body, and this is appropriate given that the mind is not all-pervasive (*avibhu*). The Teachers (*ācāryāḥ*) maintain that for this all-pervasive mind, its very activity (*vṛtti*) is what undergoes contraction and expansion. The mention of "the Teachers" is for the sake of honor, as their position is supported by reasoning. Since the mind is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), its stability and movement are possible even if the senses were all-pervasive; likewise, the state of having detached limbs (*vikaraṇabhāva*) and omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) of yogis are consistent with such all-pervasiveness.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) that is devoid of experience, because it is not perceived, like the horn of a hare. This is also because of the Vedic scripture which states: "For one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant. Likewise, the scriptural passage, "Now, he who worships these as infinite," demonstrates the pervasiveness of the instruments of perception.

And that capacity for contraction and expansion of the mental process (*vṛtti*) depends upon signs such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth. The sign is twofold: external and internal. The external consists of actions requiring physical means, such as the body, like praise, salutation, and so on. What, then, is the internal? He says: it is faith and so forth, which depend solely upon the mind alone.

And thus it has been said: "Those abodes of meditators such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest, which are activities of consciousness—when they are free from the assistance of external means, independent of external means, and produced by mind alone—they bring about the preeminent Dharma."

[330,25] Of these two signs—the external and the internal—the internal mental sign, produced by the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth, is more powerful. How so? By what are knowledge (*jñāna*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*) surpassed? By nothing at all; this is the meaning. For the collection of powers (*vibhūti*) enumerated in the third quarter [of the *Yoga-sūtra*] is to be accomplished through knowledge and dispassion. Who, other than the power of the mind, could turn the Daṇḍaka forest [into a desert]? And who could drink the ocean like Agastya?
Therefore, mental power alone is true power, not physical power. Hence, it is mental.

"Because the scripture says, 'They speak of it as supreme,' and likewise the Blessed One declared: 'O scorcher of the foe, a sacrifice of knowledge is superior to a sacrifice consisting of material substances; O Pārtha, all action in its entirety culminates in knowledge' (BhG 4.33). ||4.10||

[331,16] But how, then, is there the cessation of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? Because they have been established since beginningless time, their cessation does not seem possible. Furthermore, without their cessation, the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*) is not tenable; therefore, it is said: because these are comprised of cause, fruit, support, and object, in the absence of these, there is the absence of that [the latent impressions]. "Cause, fruit, support, and object" refers to *hetu*, *phala*, *āśraya*, and *ālambana*.

Because these [defilements] grasp and bind these [factors] such as the causes, in the absence of those [causes], or in the absence of those [defilements], there is an absence of the latent impressions (vāsanās). Therefore, the cessation of the latent impressions is logically established.

What is that cause? He says: First, for those whose minds have not been transformed by the Dharma, there is non-Dharma (*adharma*). From that non-Dharma comes suffering; from suffering arises aversion (*dveṣa*), which underlies suffering. Thus, precisely because of ignorance (*avidyā*), one practices what is prohibited and thereby incurs non-Dharma. From that comes suffering; from suffering arises aversion, which underlies suffering. Consequently, as before, there is an effort toward the acquisition of pleasure and the avoidance of pain. Through that effort, moving by means of speech and body, one either benefits or harms others.

Furthermore, from those [actions] arise merit and demerit through the favoring of others and the harming of others; from those two arise pleasure and pain; and from those two arise attachment and aversion, exactly as before. From that arises effort (*prayatna*).

Thus, this wheel of saṃsāra has six spokes and its revolution proceeds without interruption; and for this wheel, which turns at every moment, ignorance is the leader, like a young mare for a chariot wheel.

[332,11] That which is the root of all afflictions—this wheel with six spokes that has ignorance as its driver—is the cause of the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). For it is by means of this turning of the wheel that they are produced. However, in the absence of ignorance, the wheel of causes such as the *dharmas* also falls apart, like a wheel whose hub-fastening has been shattered. And through that disintegration, the latent predispositions that produce births through the turning of the wheel become incapable of their function.

As for the fruit, that object depending upon which something comes into existence is the fruit of that [cause]. That too is a subsumer of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), because in its absence there is no manifestation of the latent impressions; for the fruit such as pleasure and so forth is what deposits the latent impressions. Indeed, there is no production of what was previously non-existent, nor does that which is absolutely non-existent arise.

The mind (*manas*), possessing its office (*sādhikāra*) like a task to be performed, is not devoid of the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). It possesses its office because it consists of the knowledge of the nature of the person whose purpose has been accomplished and because ignorance (*avidyā*) has ceased; thus, it is the substratum (*āśraya*) of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For, depending upon that [mind], the wheel of causes revolves. Indeed, when the mind has completed its office and is devoid of the purpose of the person to be accomplished, the latent impressions, being without a substratum, cannot endure.

Whatever object has become manifest, or whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) it manifests, that [object] is its objective support (*ālambana*). In this way, all latent impressions are subsumed by these four: cause, fruit, basis, and objective support. In the absence of those causes and so forth, there is also the absence of the latent impressions that depend upon them, just as shade ceases when the umbrella is absent.

And the means for their absence has been explained in the second quarter [of this work]. Therefore, when right vision exists, the seat is not an obstacle to liberation; rather, liberation occurs precisely when ignorance ceases. 4.11.

But has it not been stated that "in the absence of these, there is the absence of that"? And if so, this would constitute an abandonment of the established tenet (*siddhānta*). For what is the tenet? It is that there is no possibility or arising of the non-existent, nor is there the destruction of the existent. If, on the other hand, the latent predispositions (*vāsanās*) do exist, then—being substantially real (*dravyatvena vastusatyaḥ*)—how could they ever cease? The meaning is that they simply will not cease. In that case, how can it be said that "in the absence of these, there is the absence of that"?

Or how can there be isolation (kaivalya) while the latent impressions (vāsanās), produced by causes, persist? To this, he recites the reply: "The past and the future exist in their own nature, because the factors of existence (dharmas) possess temporal paths."

It is indeed so. Alternatively, this commentary may be understood according to the established tenet (*siddhānta*) itself. How is it that in the absence of these, there is an absence of that? It is not said that there is an absolute non-existence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of causes and so forth. Why? Because "there is no arising of the non-existent, nor is there the destruction of the existent," how could the latent impressions—which exist as substantial entities (*dravyatva*) and real things (*vastutva*)—be brought to cessation? Or, if the latent impressions are merely conceptualized by words, they will not be absolutely eliminated; the meaning is that they continue to exist in the form of the past.
"Having a future manifestation" (*bhaviṣyadvyaktika*) means that for which there will be a manifestation; as, for example, the form of a jar in its state as a lump of clay.

That which has its means of accomplishment consisting of the performance of duties is "future. That which possesses a manifested existence is "past"; that whose manifestation—the attainment of the state of being an object of perception—has already occurred. For example, a broken jar is called "past. That which is unmanifested is "not yet come" (future); for its manifestation, a means must be employed. That whose manifestation has not yet passed is "present," as in the case of a jar engaged in its own activity.

[334,5] We maintain that these three—the characteristics of the past, future, and present—which exist as the nature of a dharma within a present substratum (dharmin), are the objects of knowledge for a valid cognition (pramāṇa) consisting of non-erroneous knowledge as determined by the entire world. Why? Because they are the objective domain for the arising of certain knowledge.

And if this entity did not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*), then this cognition devoid of an object would not have arisen; just as, for example, a rabbit's horn and the like do not serve as a cause for the arising of a determinate cognition. But that is not the case here, because it is the objective referent for the arising of a determinate cognition of an entity.

Alternatively, cognition regarding a past or future jar and so forth does not have a non-existent thing as its object. This is because, while being conceptualized by words, it arises in a determinate form, like cognition whose object is a present jar; and because it is non-erroneous; and because it is inferable from a logical mark (*liṅga*), like the cognition of fire from smoke; or because it arises immediately after the perception of a logical mark.

Alternatively, whatever past or future entity exists by way of its own nature must exist, because it is the object of a cognition that arises immediately after the perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*), just like a well-known inferable object. Therefore, the past and the future exist by way of their own nature.

Furthermore, for that proponent for whom the fruit of an action—whether it be sacrifice and the like, which partakes of enjoyment and leads to enjoyment, or meditative concentration and the like, which partakes of liberation and leads to liberation—is not to arise, his position results in a mere non-entity (*nirupākhya*), like a rabbit’s horn. For a rabbit’s horn is not described as being "about to come into existence. It is not so in this case;

rather, it is described by those of sharp intellect who are skilled in such matters that "heaven will come to be through sacrifice" and "liberation will come to be through meditative concentration and the like."

Therefore, because it is indefinable (*nirupākhya*), with reference to that—that is, with reference to the result—how could the wise, not perceiving for themselves that "this [act] should be performed by means of that result as its cause, and by this [act], that [result] will come to be," authorize what is wholesome or provide instruction? Furthermore, if one were to act based on mere perception, it would follow that there is no distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome; or else, the wise would be those who practice erroneously, while the unwholesome would be those who possess correct vision.

Furthermore, if it were from non-existence that knowledge arises, even those who are virtuous would not strive for the sake of the fruit; and because there is no distinction in non-existence, the restriction of causes could not be established. Or else, everything might arise from everything, and one would not take up a specific cause. If one were to take up a cause, then someone seeking oil would take up sand as well—what use are sesame seeds, which require so much effort to produce? Moreover, this [effect] would have arisen as something absolutely non-existent and unprecedented, yet such a thing is never observed.

Therefore, karma conducive to experience (*bhoga-bhāgīya*) or conducive to liberation (*apavarga-bhāgīya*) is the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) capable of bringing into the present that very fruit which already exists; it does not produce something previously non-existent.

For it is established that a causal factor, such as a pot, assists the specific qualities of its effect—such as curd, milk, ghee, or buttermilk—by manifesting their more intense states through the process of transformation, rather than producing the curd itself as something entirely new. It is the same with karma conducive to experience and so forth in this case.

Furthermore, the substratum (dharmin) possesses the nature of multiple properties (dharmas) and consists of multiple properties. For example, a lump of gold has as its nature properties such as the "presently arisen," the "past," and the "indeterminable" states of a necklace, an earring, and so forth. Of that substratum, the properties are established according to the distinction of time-periods (adhvan), that is, according to the distinction of characteristics such as the past and so on.

Just as a present entity, having attained a specific manifestation such as a bracelet or the like, exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) and in the form of an effect (*kāryarūpataḥ*) by virtue of being mounted upon its activity, so it is not with the past and the future. Rather, the future exists by way of its own manifest nature that is yet to be; and the past exists by way of its own experienced manifestation, which has already passed beyond perception.

However, since manifestation occurs only for the present time-period (*adhvan*) by way of its own nature, that manifestation does not belong to the past and future time-periods. Furthermore, at the time of one time-period, the other two time-periods cannot possibly be concomitant with the substrate (*dharmin*), because of contradiction. Thus, the avoidance of the confusion of the time-periods has been explained.

Furthermore, for one for whom past and future lack their own characteristic by way of intrinsic nature, the distinction of the time-periods (*adhvan*) of phenomena does not obtain. How so? For such a person, a jar that is yet to come or one that is past does not exist; nor indeed do shards or a lump of clay constitute a jar.

Consequently, even a jar existing in the present would have to be called "past" or "future," because the lump of clay and the potsherds are not jars, and the jar is absent from the clay; furthermore, the expressions "the jar will be" and "the jar was past" would have to be applied to the lump and the potsherds respectively. And in that case, for one who intends to speak thus, even a cow would be a horse, and a horse would also be a cow.

Now, if it should be argued that the prior non-existence and the posterior non-existence of a jar are designated as its "past" and "future" states respectively, then even so, for those who maintain the reality of things (*satyavādins*), it would be logical for the word denoting the entity—the jar—to designate its non-existence by saying "the jar is past" or "the jar is future."

Furthermore, no such restriction is logically tenable; for it is by means of the jar alone that one designates "the jar has passed away" or "the jar will come to be," but one does not designate the potter and so forth as "the potter and so forth have passed away" or "will come to be."

If it is argued that this is because only the jar is not perceived there, we say no; for then it would follow that the elephant-driver and others could also be designated [as absent] when they too are not perceived there. If it is argued that designation applies only to what was previously perceived, we say no; for then it would follow that the action of making a jar and so forth could also be so designated.

[336,26] Now, if it is argued that by that [non-existence] there is an absence of action and so forth in the jar, we say no; for a specific relation is untenable for non-existence. Indeed, neither a relation characterized as inherence (*samavāya*) nor one characterized as contact (*prāpti*) is possible between existence and non-existence, such that this would be the non-existence of the jar but not of action and the rest. Furthermore, if it were related to either of the two, it would follow that non-existence is a real entity (*vastu*). If it is then argued that it is indeed a real entity, then the future and past objects are already established.

[337,7] Now, if it is argued that by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra), the constituent parts in the state of the potsherds will be the "pot," and thus one could refer to them as "the pot has come into being" or "it is a pot" because of their relationship—just as one says "food is life"—then even here, just as the pot does not exist in the potter’s wheel, stick, string, and so forth, so too it does not exist in the lump of clay or the potsherds. And since there is no difference in the absence of the pot in these cases, the restriction that the designation "the pot is past" applies to the potsherds but not to the potter and so forth would be untenable.

Furthermore, even for existing means of accomplishment (sādhana) that produce things such as jars, a connection with the non-existent produced effects, such as jars, is not tenable. And in the absence of such a connection, there would be no activity of the causal factors (kāraka) with the intention of producing a jar.

If it is argued that the relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), which is non-separately established (*ayutasiddha*), is not denied for produced effects and their causes, we say no; for the states of being separately established or non-separately established are observed among entities existing at the same time. Nowhere, however, is either separate establishment or non-separate establishment observed between a non-entity and an entity.

Therefore, since a relationship is admitted even between that which is produced and that which produces, the effect must indeed exist; it exists both prior to and after its production because of its connection with other entities, as is well known in the case of a jar and the like. This is because it is yet to be perceived and has already been perceived, like a jar situated in a room; because it is to be reached by an agent with a specific aim, like an object in another location; and likewise, because it is to be attained through the activity of the agent.

Furthermore, ordinary people do not perceive or communicate a non-existent object—like a lotus in the sky—by means of the words "past" and "future"; thus, there would be no liberation. Therefore, the past and the future exist indeed by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*). It is not that the three time-periods come into being after having previously been non-existent; rather, it is simply the manifestation of those things that already exist.

Therefore, there is an absolute cessation of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in their manifested form; however, since they remain in the form of the *guṇas* yet are incapable of producing effects, there is no fault of the absence of isolation (*kaivalya*), nor is there any contradiction with the established doctrine. ||4.12||

In order to demonstrate in what manner past, future, and present phenomena exist, he says: "They are the natures of the qualities, manifest and subtle. Indeed, these phenomena belonging to the three times—those mounted upon the three paths of the past, future, and present—are, when present, mounted upon the characteristic of the present; they are of a manifest nature, having as their intrinsic being the state of becoming objects of cognition through the three means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The past and future subtle selves have not attained the state of being objects of worldly cognition; they consist of the six non-specific (aviśeṣa) forms and have the nature of the "I-am-ness" (asmitā) and so forth. From that [come] the manifest selves, the sixteen transformations, characterized as cause and effect.

All this—whether internal, consisting of cause and effect and manifest in nature; or that which is subtle and characterized by non-differentiation, such as the sense of "I" (asmitā) and so forth; or that which is liberation, the mere *liṅga* because of its subtlety and lack of differentiation—all this world is merely a particular arrangement of the qualities (*guṇa*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, whose natures are luminosity, activity, and inertia. In the ultimate sense, therefore, they have the qualities as their essence and the qualities as their inherent nature.

And thus is the instruction of the Śāstra: the supreme form of the *guṇas* is their own ultimate nature (*paramārtha-rūpa*), which consists of neither decrease nor increase for each one individually. And that does not come within the path of vision; it does not become an object of sight. But that which has entered the path of vision—characterized by a configuration produced by the absence of poison through the suppression of the *guṇas*—is like an illusion (*māyā*), yet it is not an illusion itself because of its lack of substance; it is "like an illusion" because it is utterly trifling and merely a partial transformation of the *guṇas* abiding in a state of equilibrium. (4.13)

When all qualities (*guṇas*), such as earth and the rest, exist [in every object], how can there be a single sound produced from a conch-shell or similar source? Likewise, how could there be the status of being the objective support for a single cognition, such as "the auditory faculty" and so forth? Indeed, this cannot be the case; for by reason of the presence of the three *guṇas*, the cognition would necessarily be "three. Similarly, each of the sense faculties would possess a triadic nature, and thus no fixed rule (*niyama*) regarding them would be possible.

For indeed, the restriction that the state of being the object of apprehension belongs to the sound alone, while the state of being the apprehender belongs to the auditory organ alone, is not tenable. The same should be applied to touch and the other [objects], as well as to the tactile organ and the others. Yet such a restriction is observed; therefore, the cause for this must be stated. He says: "Because of the unity of transformation, there is the reality of the entity."

The single transformation of those qualities (*guṇa*)—which have the nature of manifestation, activity, and stability; which consist of grasping; which are characterized by a predominance of *sattva*; which have the nature of a knower; and which abide in the state of self-sense (*asmitā*)—is the sense-organ of hearing, acting as an instrument. Just as a lamp is a single transformation of oil, wick, and fire despite their mutual opposition, so too should it be understood that each individual sense-organ, such as the skin and the rest, is a single transformation of those qualities when they are employed for the purpose of the person’s objective experience.

This should also be applied to the other elements. Of sound, touch, form, and taste—which belong to the same genus as moisture—there is a single transformation, namely a water atom consisting of parts of the *rasa-tanmātra*. The single transformation of those atoms is water.

[339,16] A single transformation of sound, touch, and form—which belong to the same genus as heat—is the atom of fire (*tejaḥ-paramāṇu*), consisting of parts that are mere form. A single transformation of those atoms is fire, which has water as its fuel and which kindles even pieces of wood.

Likewise, from sound and touch—which are of the same genus and are directed toward transformation—the single transformation is the wind-atom (*vāyu-paramāṇu*), which consists of parts of the subtle element of touch (*sparśa-tanmātra*). From those atoms, the single transformation is wind (*vāyu*) and the seven hosts of Maruts.

In the same way, space is the single transformation of the components of the sound-tanmātra, which are non-obstructive and of the same genus. Following the path thus described, one should apply and understand that, based on qualities such as viscidity, heat, and mobility, there is a commonality consisting in the commencement of a single modification. Therefore, because even many things undergo a single transformation, their having a single object and the restriction of the grasped and the grasper are both established.

But is it not the case that this object of a single cognition, such as sound and so forth, simply does not exist? All of this is merely the unfolding of consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it arises only when consciousness exists. How is it that it arises only when consciousness exists? He says: There is no object that exists apart from consciousness, nor is there anything perceived separately from consciousness or existing independently of it. Consciousness, however, is not perceived as separate from or existing independently of the object. Therefore, we maintain that the object does not exist apart from consciousness.

[340,11] There is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard: there is no graspable object apart from consciousness, because it is not perceived apart from consciousness, just like the nature of consciousness itself. Waking cognitions are empty of external objects, because they are cognitions, just like cognitions occurring at the time of dreaming. Or, waking objects are imagined by consciousness, because they are objects, just like dream-objects. Or, consciousness is non-different from its objects, because it is consciousness, just like dream-consciousness.
If this were so, what would be lost to us? Because of the dissociation of the Puruṣa from the visible, the isolation (kaivalya) under discussion would not be established.

Just as there is the non-existence of the pillar and so forth when they are being perceived, so too there is the non-existence of consciousness because it is being perceived. And in the absence of that [consciousness], due to the absence of a mark (liṅga), the non-existence of the perceiver would also follow. Thus, for whom could there be isolation (kaivalya), and with what object of perception could there be separation? Or with what [object] could contact (samprayoga) be asserted as bondage? And in the absence of bondage, the fruitfulness of engagement for the sake of worldly prosperity and the supreme good (abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa) would not be possible.

Furthermore, by asserting that there is no object apart from consciousness (*vijñāna*), one accepts that "consciousness" and "object" (*artha*) are one and the same entity, just as "fire" and "flame" (*anala*) are. This being the case, the distinction between consciousness as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the object as the grasped (*grāhya*) is merely a difference in terminology; the status of a single entity as both grasper and grasped is not actually denied. If that were so, it would follow that even the *puruṣa* (Self) possesses the nature of both grasper and grasped. Consequently, liberation would be impossible, and many other such faults would ensue.
They attain.

Therefore, by this direction and by the force of this fallacious reasoning, those who deny the intrinsic nature of things—claiming that an object is merely a mental construction like the objects of a dream, and not [an external reality]—[are refuted].

Having themselves accepted that "it exists in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ asti*) and that "it is thus," they have established the object through their own greatness. How then can they, having personally grasped and accepted that very object by the power of conceptual cognition—which is itself devoid of valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇātmaka*)—now deny what they have accepted? Having asserted "this is so," they now repudiate it by saying "this does not exist. Their words would thus be utterly unworthy of trust; for those who reject their own experience cannot possibly be considered as speakers whose extensive discourse deserves belief.

In this regard, the proposition that "the object does not exist apart from consciousness" contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). We perceive consciousness as the agent of cognition; we apprehend the object as having a broad base and other such forms. Furthermore, consciousness is the grasper and illuminator, while the object is that which is to be grasped and illuminated. Since object and cognition are perceived with distinct specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is not even a scent of non-distinction between them. Consequently, your reason—"because it is not perceived as distinct"—is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Nor does cognition itself possess a form such as a broad base and so forth; for it is impossible for a single cognition to be both the illuminated object and the illuminator, just as in the case of a solitary lamp.
Since two distinct lamps are never observed to stand in the relation of the illuminated and the illuminator, and since a single entity cannot reach its own self, the same applies to cognition.

Even dream-cognition is not without an objective basis (*anirālambana*), because its object is something that has been previously perceived. This contradicts both the thesis itself and common worldly experience. All cognition possesses an objective basis (*sālambana*) because it is cognition, just like the cognition of a faulty statement from an opponent or the cognition of the excellence of one's own statement. Consequently, reasons such as "because it is cognition" for proving that cognitions are without an objective basis are rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by such examples. (4.14)

And why is it unreasonable to say that an object does not exist? Because there is a distinction between the two paths due to the difference in minds despite the identity of the object: a single object, such as a son or the like, which serves as the focal point for many minds and becomes the domain of multiple minds, is common and shared. Indeed, that object is not dependent on a single mind; and because it lacks dependence on a single mind, it cannot be merely imagined by multiple minds either.

[342,14] However, it is established as independent of the mind, abiding in its own nature through its autonomy. How so? Even when the object is identical—that is, when an object such as a son is one—there is a multiplicity of cognitions, the subjects, due to the difference in minds regarding that single object such as a son.

How is there a differentiation of the mind? He says: It depends on the mental object (*dharma*). Even when the objective entity is the same, just as from a son alone there arises in the parents a cognition of pleasure, from that very same son and so forth, depending on what is not a mental object (*adharma*), there will arise for those who are harmful a cognition of suffering.

If something were imagined by the mind of someone else, the mind of others would not be affected by what was imagined by that other mind; this is not logical, because we do not observe anything occurring between things that are utterly unrelated. Furthermore, if the mind of one person were to be affected even by what was imagined by another, then everyone would perceive everything. But this is not observed. Therefore, an object is not imagined by the mind; thus, there is a distinct path for the object and the cognition, which are separate due to the difference between the grasped and the grasper. There is not even a scent of confusion between these two.

An object such as a cloth, which has become the objective support for a cognition of pleasure, is not imagined by that cognition, because it colors many minds that are contrary to one another—just like the merits, defects, and fallacies of the propositions of a proponent and an opponent. Furthermore, if the consciousnesses of the proponent, the opponent, and so forth were also mere consciousness (vijñaptimātra), there would be a total collapse of the conventional practice of proof and what is to be proven.

Now, if it is argued that those very forms of cognition possess distinctness apart from one's own consciousness, let it be so. That very entity is established as a different thing because it is the object of another cognition; there is merely a disagreement over terminology. However, the distinction between the subject and the object is not something to be proven. Therefore, these two are eternal, and there is not even a scent of confusion between them.

[343,14] Now, if it is argued that even though the object (*vastu*) is established in its own nature, its being the objective support for distinct cognitions such as pleasure and so forth is not logically consistent—here it is said:

Furthermore, the object consists of the three *guṇas* and is mobile; because the functioning of the *guṇas* depends upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, it becomes connected with the various forms of pleasure, pain, and so on by the cognitions (*vittis*), owing to its capacity for transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) and its possession of manifold powers.

Furthermore, a causal condition (*pratyaya*) that arises in conformity with the signs (*nimitta*) of phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth becomes a cause by means of each respective sign as its own nature (*ātman*). By way of its essence as *sattva*, an entity such as a son is a cause of pleasure in dependence upon the signs of merit (*dharma*) and so forth. By way of its essence as *rajas*, however, it is a cause of suffering in dependence upon the signs of demerit (*adharma*). By way of its essence as *tamas*, that very same entity is a cause of delusion in dependence upon ignorance (*avidyā*). And by way of its essence as mere existence (*sattāmātra*), that very same entity is a cause of the knowledge of equanimity in dependence upon right vision (*samyagdarśana*).

Some say: among these very Buddhists, certain others who accept external objects maintain that the object arises simultaneously with the cognition. Just as consciousness arises and perishes every moment while being empty of a permanent substratum (*dharmin*), so too is the object known by the cognition and perishes along with it, because it is an object of experience (*bhogyatva*), like pleasure and the like.

For example, just as the nature of pleasure, pain, and so forth—which are objects of experience—arises and perishes simultaneously with consciousness and is non-common (*asādhāraṇa*), so too an object such as a jar has an origin and destruction occurring at the same time as the consciousness, precisely because it is an object of experience.

They, too, like the Vijñānavādins, contradict the commonality [of objects] and their status as the objective supports for multiple minds such as pleasure and so forth; by asserting that the object does not exist in prior or subsequent moments—that is, in the preceding moments relative to the arising of one's own consciousness and in the succeeding moments—they deny the very nature of the object itself.

Therefore, the intrinsic nature of an object does not coexist with cognition, because it is recognized as "this is that very same thing. Unlike cognition, an object is not recognized as "this is that very same thing" throughout its arising and perishing; for one does not think, "This is my very same cognition from before. On the contrary, an object is recognized as "this is that very same thing. Even if the object and the cognition were to exist at the same time, there would still be a distinction between them.

Nor does recognition arise from similarity, because the apprehended object and the apprehending subject possess simultaneous arising and perishing. For a cognition of similarity occurs when, while one thing is established as being seen, another thing similar to it is perceived; likewise, there arises a subsequent desire, such as "I shall see something similar to that. Indeed, for one whose death is certain that very day, no longing to see an object arises on the following day, nor does he desire, "Someone like me shall look upon it. And this is not observed in reality; for a person strives for his own sake, and such a thing is not seen among those belonging to different continuums.

Therefore, a present object does not arise simultaneously with the present cognition, because it is an object of apprehension, like a past object. Or, a past object does not arise from the destruction simultaneous with the past cognition, because it is an object of apprehension, like a present object. Objects apprehended by past or future cognitions exist even now, because they are objects of apprehension, like objects apprehended by a present cognition. A present entity likewise exists in its very same state in preceding and succeeding moments.

If it is argued that [the argument] is inconclusive because of pleasure, pain, cognition, and so forth, we say no; for it has already been established that the past and the future exist by way of their own nature (*svarūpa*). This being the case, since pleasure and the rest also exist by way of their own nature, the example "like pleasure and the rest" is equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*).

If it is argued that, because of the specific nature of present form, the objects characterized as past and future do not exist—just like pleasure and so forth—then this is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For the state of old age does not exist within the very state of childhood. (4.15)

For this reason as well, the dependence of an object upon the mind is not tenable. An object must be either dependent on a single mind or dependent on multiple minds. Regarding its being dependent on a single mind, we say: an object is not dependent on a single mind; for if it were, what would that object be when that mind is absent, distracted, or ceased? It could not be dependent on a single mind. If it were the case that an object is dependent on a particular mind, then when that mind is distracted or otherwise occupied, or has ceased, [the object would likewise cease].

Or, when that valid cognition has perished, if the object is not grasped by it and has not become the domain of another [cognition], then—because it is dependent solely upon that single mind—that object would at that time lack a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) and its intrinsic nature would remain unapprehended. Since the valid cognition itself has ceased, what could that object be at that moment? It could be nothing at all; for since it is defined by the mind as its means of valid cognition, in the absence of that [mind], it cannot exist by virtue of it.

[345,10] But surely, just as that cognizing consciousness ceases, so too does that [object] cease precisely because of its momentariness; what, then, would there be to be designated in that regard? It is said: [there must be something to be designated], for otherwise conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) would be abolished and systematic determination (*niyama*) would be impossible. Conventional practice such as "This is fire, do not touch it," "Take this," or "Apply this ointment" would be lost, because the object would perish simultaneously with the single moment of the cognizing mind.

If it is argued that "a cognition produced in that same continuum might be absolutely similar [to the original experience] for the sake of conventional practice," even in this case, who could determine that it must be experienced by another [person] who is similar to that very continuum, and that it has become the object of another's means of valid cognition? For there is no cause for such a restriction.

Moreover, because it depends upon a single mind at the time of conventional usage, it is not logical for one cognition to have as its object and support that which is the object of another cognition. Furthermore, an entity does not depend upon many minds; therefore, how could we engage in such conventional transactions as, "Take this" or "Give this"?

Nor would those possessing such vision engage with one another through the giving of instructions by teacher to disciple and so forth. Therefore, things are neither eternal nor dependent upon a single mind; for when the cognizing mind perishes or is distracted, the nature of the thing remains undetermined.

Furthermore, from what could an object that is being connected with the mind arise? Its arising from anything whatsoever is not tenable; for we have already stated that it does not arise from its own continuum.

Furthermore, those parts of this entity that are not present—that is, those which have not become objects for a single cognition—would not belong to it. For if one part of the entity has become an object and is dependent upon the mind, while the other does not, then there would be no "back," and consequently, even the "belly" facing forward would not exist at all.

Furthermore, even if many minds were to arise simultaneously by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" logic (*kākatālīya*), and the object of those minds were to emerge at that same time, this has already been refuted by the very demonstration of the absence of a back and belly [in the simultaneous existence of multiple entities]. Nor can the ocean of worldly convention, which depends on beginningless time, be crossed by means of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" anecdote. Moreover, all the faults found in those who praise the view of consciousness (*vijñāna*) are exactly the same here as well.

Therefore he says: The object is independent and common to all persons; when it is present, the entire worldly transaction is made possible. Furthermore, minds are independent and function according to each individual person. From the connection between these two—the object and the mind—there arises perception, which is the experience (*bhoga*) of the person (*puruṣa*). Therefore, the person is the experiencer, the mind is the instrument, and the object is the field of action, having become the object of work. Thus, this is the distinct path for these three: the experiencer, the instrument, and the object. (4.16)

How is it that experience belongs to the person (*puruṣa*) due to the connection between the mind and its objects? He says: for one for whom an object does not exist apart from the mind, or for whom an object is dependent solely upon the mind, the status of that object as known or unknown is untenable; therefore, he says that an object is known or unknown depending on the coloring (*uparāga*) of the mind by that object.

The coloring of the mind by that object is its dependence upon it; that mind which possesses such dependence is "dependent on that coloring. The state of being so is "the state of dependence on that coloring. Because of this state of dependence on that coloring, the object is either known or unknown.

That object by which the mind is colored is known, and that by which it is not colored is unknown. Furthermore, this coloring depends upon a transformation of the mind; for the mind, undergoing transformation into an external form via the path of the sense faculties, becomes connected [to that object].

What, then, is the cause for the transformation of the mind? It is said that objects are like magnets; they are equal to magnets, while the single mind possesses the nature of iron. And because it has the nature of iron, it undergoes modification when an object is present. Objects, too, are like magnets, because they possess the capacity to induce a modification in the mind by their mere presence. Therefore, the objects, having come into contact with the mind—which has been transformed into their own form—color it.

That object by which the mind is colored is known; other objects, however, which do not color it, remain unknown. Therefore, because an entity possesses both known and unknown aspects as its nature, the mind undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*). Furthermore, for that proponent who maintains that the object is dependent solely upon the mind, or that the mind itself is the object, there would follow either omniscience regarding all objects or ignorance of all objects, because a mind that is not known would be non-existent.

And this [simultaneous perception of the known and the unknown] is not observed. Rather, we understand that the mind possesses objects both known and unknown. And since there is no possibility of attaining objects that remain in a stable state, and because otherwise a connection [between the object and its cognition] could not be conceived, this [state of having known and unknown objects] depends solely upon the transformation of the mind; thus, the mind is subject to change (pariṇāmin). 4.17.

However, for that master—the experiencer—whose mind, whether its objects are known or unknown, becomes the object in the form of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), there is no possibility of the mind being an object when its modifications have ceased.

Therefore, for that *puruṣa*, the mental modifications are always known. Since they are directly perceived by him, it cannot be established that their objects are ever unknown, because the *puruṣa* who is their master is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*).

Alternatively, the mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*) are accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because they are apprehended as objects of cognition independently of words or inferential marks (*liṅga*), just like a jar perceived directly. This is also because they possess a determinate form and because they are not objects of doubt. For if mental modifications were always imperceptible, some of them might occasionally be subject to doubt, just like external objects; however, none have ever been observed to fall within the path of doubt at any time.

Moreover, it sometimes happens that an object, having been known, is subsequently perceived as "known"; this would not be possible if the mental modification were not perceptible by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor can it be inferred there by way of its result, because the result is not determined.

Therefore, because doubt lacks an object and because the modifications of the mind are always perceived by their very nature as distinct from their objects, all mental modifications are always directly perceived. This is because they function as illuminators for the perceiver, as instruments, and as manifestors, just like a lamp and similar objects. Nor is there any inconclusiveness regarding this due to the eyes and other senses; for even in those cases, the objects are grasped through direct perception.

Just as jars and other things are perceived as distinguished by the light of a lamp or similar source, so too are sounds and other objects perceived as distinguished by the "light" of the auditory organ and the rest.

Nor can it be said that they are not perceived because they cannot be apprehended separately. For example, the rays of two lamps are mutually intermingled, such that one cannot say, "this ray belongs to this lamp" and "that ray belongs to that lamp. They are not distinguished, yet their lack of perceptibility does not follow from that alone. Likewise here, the eyes and so forth cannot be apprehended separately due to their intermingling with external light and other factors of a similar kind; yet their lack of perceptibility does not follow merely from that. For whoever...

If one denies the mental modifications that are being directly perceived, one would surely be denying even the Self itself; for all apprehension is dependent upon mental modification, just as the perception of form is dependent upon light. Therefore, it is said: "The mental modifications are always known to the Puruṣa."

And this state of being an ever-knowing subject belongs to the Lord, the Puruṣa, because he is unchanging. For that state is necessitated by his nature as a permanent perceiver. If the Lord, the Puruṣa, were to undergo transformation like the mind, then the mental modifications concerning those objects would be both known and unknown—just as the objects such as sound are known or unknown to the mind.

That collection of objects such as sound and so forth, which are either known or unknown, is to be understood as dependent upon the transformation of the transforming mind (*citta*). Likewise, even in the case of the sense organs, their state of having objects that are known or unknown is seen to be dependent solely upon transformation. However, among the various mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of the mind, there is no such thing as being known or unknown; rather, those mental modifications are eternally known. Therefore, the fact that the mind is always known in the form of its modifications leads one to infer the unchanging nature of the Lord, the Puruṣa.

"The Puruṣa is unchanging" is the proposition (*pratijñā*). "Because its objects are always known" is the reason (*hetu*). By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), the mind and the senses are the examples (*dṛṣṭāntaḥ*). However, since the subject under discussion is the perceiver who possesses objects, the example "like the liberated self" (*muktātmavat*) is not tenable for the purpose of negating the state of having objects always known; for the liberated one is devoid of objects. (4.18)

There might be the suspicion that the mind itself will appear as both its own form and the form of the object—that is, as the grasped and the grasper—since mental modifications are indeed self-cognized in their own forms, just as a lamp illuminates jars and other objects as well as itself. What, then, is the use of postulating a person (puruṣa) distinct from the mind who perceives the mental modifications?

To this it is replied: that [mind] does not have its own appearance as its object, because it is visible, just like the other sense organs such as the ear and so forth, and like objects such as sound and so forth. The sense organs do not have their own appearances as their objects, nor do sound and the rest have their own appearances as their objects, because they are visible. The same should be understood for the mind as well; it should be realized that the mind does not have its own appearance as its object because it is visible.

[349,22] But surely, like fire itself, it may possess both self-luminosity and the appearance of objects; just as jars and other things, being objects to be illuminated, require another light for the perception of their own form, so it is not with a lamp. Just as a lamp is both self-luminous and the appearance of objects, so too let the mind be thus because of its very nature as an illuminator—what need is there for a self? For people in the world do not take up another lamp for the sake of perceiving a lamp.

Furthermore, if they were to be apprehended, there would indeed be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, if consciousness were to be apprehended by something distinct from it, that [distinct thing] would have to be apprehended by another, and that by yet another; such a consequence would follow. Moreover, because consciousness has the nature of luminosity (*avabhāsa*), and the apprehender likewise has the form of luminosity, there can be no relationship of mutual assistance between them, just as in the case of two lamps. Therefore, even a conceptualized (*kalpita*) apprehender of consciousness is useless. Let it be, then, that cognition is self-luminous (*svābhāsa*) and also illuminates other things (*parābhāsa*).

To this it is replied: This attempt to refute the self by relying on a wretched example while ascending the path established by the consensus of the entire world is impossible. Why? Because fire is not the example. For fire does not illuminate its own nature as something unilluminated; if fire, being unilluminated, were to illuminate itself by itself like a jar or other objects, then the example would be appropriate. But that is not the case, for fire is never unilluminated.

[350,10] Furthermore, this is luminous. And that luminosity is observed in the conjunction of the illuminated and the illuminator. Conjunction does not exist in a mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), for conjunction belongs to two things. In the absence of conjunction, there can be no manifestation of an intrinsic nature.

As for the claim that fire does not require another illuminator—unlike a jar or similar objects—that is because it lacks the nature of something to be illuminated; it is not, however, because it possesses a nature to be illuminated like a jar. Nor does this imply it cannot be grasped by something distinct from itself; for it is indeed grasped by the eye, which is equally distinct from it.

Light is employed for the purpose of removing the darkness that obstructs an object of illumination, such as a jar; it is not so because the light itself possesses a non-luminous nature. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that fire does not require another light, saying that "between two lamps there is no mutual assistance. If, despite their difference, two lamps do not assist one another because they are not of a non-luminous nature, how much less would they do so when there is no difference at all?
In this case, it simply does not depend upon any other light.

However, the state of having a distinct object of apprehension (*vyatiriktagrāhyatva*) does not fail; for two lamps are seen together, just like a jar and other objects. By this, it is established that cognition has a distinct object of apprehension because it is visible, just like a lamp and so forth.

And just like a lamp and so forth, since cognition is luminous by nature (*prakāśasvarūpa*), its independence from any other instrument is also established. Thus, even the slightest scent of the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) does not exist.

As for the claim that because cognition is of the nature of illumination, its grasper is also of the nature of illumination, and thus there can be no relationship of mutual assistance between the two—like two lamps—it is not a fault; for the eye and the lamp, as well as the self and cognition, belong to different categories.

[350,26] But is it not the case that the mind (*citta*) is apprehended as the object by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), such that there is the relationship of subject and object within a single entity? This is not a fault, because the mind consists of the three *guṇas*. Therein, that mind which is dominated by *tamas* is perceived by another modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of *sattva*, just as the body is scratched by the hand. Even in that case, the perceiver—the subject—is indeed distinct, namely the *puruṣa*. By this, [the distinction is established] through the relationship of grasper and grasped between different classes (*jātyantara*), and because [the *puruṣa*] is partless (*niravayava*).
And we have already replied that the person himself must be both the object of apprehension and the apprehender.

Furthermore, if it is said that "the mind has its own appearance," it would follow that the mind is indeed ungraspable; such is the meaning of the word. For when it is stated that it "has its own appearance," the meaning is that it is not perceived or grasped by another. It is not, however, meant that it grasps itself. In the employment of such expressions, the word possesses a contrary meaning.

For example, the meaning of the word "unsupported" (*apratiṣṭha*) is that space is established in itself (*svātmapratiṣṭha*). Likewise, the expression "Devadatta is well" (*svastha*) means he is free from disease, not that he is established in his own self. In this regard, for one who declares the reason "because of being visible" (*dṛśyatvāt*) to be unestablished (*asiddha*), there would be contradiction with direct perception, contradiction with the world, and the collapse of conventional usage. Thus he says: the activity of sentient beings, that is, of living creatures, is observed because they experience the movements of their own cognitions.

Having perceived and observed one's own respective intellects functioning thus—"I am angry," "I am wealthy," "there is passion for me in that," or "there is anger for me in that"—the activity of those possessed of discernment (*viveka*) is observed for the sake of abandoning anger, greed, and so forth. Likewise, [they observe]: "my mind is serene," or "it is turbid," or "it is deluded. Therefore, it is not logical that this [intellect] does not grasp its own nature; for it is not reasonable to say that the intellect, having been heard to be fluctuating, is nonetheless unseen. (4.19)

Even granting this argument—that the mind may possess both its own appearance and the appearance of the object—the refutation remains: at the time of cognition, there is no determination of both. If it determines the object, then because it consists of multiple moments (*nānākṣaṇatvāt*), the determination of itself is not tenable. On the other hand, if it determines itself, then it is not directed toward the object; for in determining its own self, it likewise consists of multiple moments.

[352,11] Now, if it is argued that the determination of both [objects] is indeed a single [act of cognition], we say no, because cognition is partless (*niravayava*). For it is not logical that a mental state devoid of parts should possess the capacity to illuminate many things simultaneously, like a lamp. It is only through a distinction of parts that a lamp can have the property of illuminating many things; however, the existence of parts in cognition is not admitted by our opponents.

Furthermore, if one accepts that a single cognition determines both [self and other] in a single moment, there follows the undesirable consequence of a distinction between action and its agent. That which is the determination of both is the action; that which performs the determination is the agent. And for a proponent of momentariness (*kṣaṇavādin*), it is not logical for a single cognition in a single moment to determine both self and other. Why? Because it has been stated for the sake of establishing momentariness: "That which is the arising of an entity is itself the action, and that very thing is the agent"—this is the accepted position.

Furthermore, if there were a distinction between the action and its factors (kārakas), there would be a destruction of the doctrine of momentary flux; for by means of a factor, the moment of the action must be maintained. (4.20)

It might be the thought of some that the mind, having ceased by its own nature, is apprehended by another mind; thus, the mind—which has perished and is exceedingly fragile—is apprehended by another, immediately succeeding mind. However, this is as useless as the postulation of an eternally abiding person (*puruṣa*). To this it is replied: "If one mind were visible to another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions of cognitions, as well as a confusion of memory."

If a preceding mind, which has ceased by its own nature, were to be grasped by a subsequent mind arising as its immediate successor, then there would be a cognition of cognition: the cognition having a jar as its object is called "cognition," while the cognition having that [first] cognition as its object is called "cognition-of-cognition. By what, then, is this latter grasped? Since there is no established grasper, it too would have to be grasped by another, and that too by another; thus, there would be an infinite regress.

Furthermore, conventional linguistic usage is not possible when cognitions of cognitions have not been apprehended, because the formation of memory-impressions (*saṃskāra*) would be untenable. In that case, there would be an endless, unstable chain (*mālā*) of pot-cognitions of pot-cognitions belonging to the same class, rather than a single pot-cognition. And if the cognitions of pot-cognitions were never brought to completion, how could a cognition of a pot or the like ever arise?

Furthermore, there is this other defect: namely, the confusion of memory (*smṛtisaṃkara*). Because cognitions, subsequent cognitions of those cognitions, and their respective mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) are of a single form, a confusion of memory results. As many as are the experiences of the cognitions and subsequent cognitions, so many confused memories result. Due to that confusion—due to the confusion of memory—there is an inability to determine the memory; not being able to determine, "This is the memory of this particular cognition," how could we engage in linguistic or practical activity? Thus, because they are of similar form, a confusion of memory results.

As long as there is no possibility of conventional usage preceded by the recollection of one's own cognition, all cognitions and their objects would be joined with total confusion. If, out of a desire to avoid an infinite regress, we were to rest upon some final cognition, then the world would be thrown into disorder by the Nihilists (Vaināśikas), who deny even that person—who is more clearly evident than the cognition itself—by means of the inferential mark of the experience of that cognition.

[353,20] But surely, by postulating the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), we may avoid the fault of infinite regress, and likewise, we may refute the postulation of a self (*ātman*). Thus, you who postulate the nature of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) in some form or another do not accord with reason. For that storehouse-consciousness, too, because it is an object of apprehension (*grāhya*) and because it is not established as a permanent entity, all the aforementioned faults necessarily follow.

Certain specific types of nihilists, having conceptualized even "mere existence" under another term as the nature of an experiencer, say: "There exists that being who, casting off and abandoning these five aggregates characterized by form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, links with and grasps other aggregates. It is precisely because of this conceptualization of a single being who links with the aggregates of the past and future that they tremble.

Likewise, they have another contrary conception regarding the aggregates: "Having declared, 'I lead the holy life in the presence of the Teacher for the sake of great disillusionment, dispassion, non-arising, and peace regarding the aggregates,' [they fall away]."

Furthermore, they deny that very being who has arrived—the relationship between the subject and the means of accomplishment—and they negate the self by asserting that there is only momentary consciousness and emptiness. Thus, we shall not enter into those [disputes]. As for doctrines such as Sāṅkhya and Yoga, however, they explicitly accept the *puruṣa* alone as the master, the owner, and the enjoyer of wealth. 4.21.

How do they accept the experiencer by its own term? Because, when the consciousness (*citi*), which does not undergo transition, assumes the form of that [object], there occurs the perception of one's own intellect. "Consciousness" (*citi*) means sentience (*caitanya*), which is the same as the *puruṣa*. And because it is unchanging, that consciousness does not undergo transition. Nevertheless, even though that consciousness does not undergo transition, it assumes the form of that [object]. By the word "that," the mind under discussion is referred back; "assuming the form of that" means assuming the form of that mind.

When that consciousness assumes the form of that [object], there occurs the self-awareness of its own cognition; there arises the apprehension of its own mental state (*bauddha-pratyaya*). For it is for that very purpose that the intellect transforms itself into the form of cognitions such as sound and so forth.

This is demonstrated: for the power of the enjoyer, which is the power of seeing, is indeed immutable, as has been explained in the three preceding aphorisms. And while it is non-transmigrating, it appears as if it were transmigrated into the object—the mental modification—because that modification is its field of perception; thus, though not actually following its movement, it seems to follow it because it perceives through the act of seeing. The mental modification, as soon as it arises, becomes the object of that power. Thus, the power of the enjoyer, perceiving by following the movement of that mental modification, perceives the mental modification itself.

And of that [intellect], which has as its essential nature the apprehension of consciousness (*caitanya*), there is attained a form consisting of the apprehension of consciousness—that is, a form consisting of the apprehension of the *puruṣa*—by means of a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*). This is like a lump of heated iron that has acquired the form of the fire it has grasped; it occurs solely because it is the object of the act of seeing, and thus consists merely of a conformity to the mental modification, being nothing more than a semblance of it. Therefore, it is said: "The modification of the knower is not distinct from the modification of the intellect. The knower is indeed the perception itself, and that is called the "modification. It has been explained that "conformity to the modification" applies to the other [the intellect]. Likewise, it has been proclaimed that "experience is non-distinction from the cognition."

[355,18] And only when there is a distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed does the transformation into the form of the mind become possible. For if there were no distinct enjoyer, it would be groundless to postulate that the mind alone manifests as both the seer and the seen. Therefore, it is rightly said that only the Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and other schools accept the *puruṣa* by its own name; others, however, even while employing different terminology, are nonetheless afraid of that very same [conclusion].

And so it has been said: "The activity of the knower is perceived in the intellect alone, as a mere imitation of the modifications of the intellect, and nowhere else. Neither the netherworld (pātāla), nor the cavities of mountains, nor darkness, nor the bellies of the oceans—none of these are the caves. In which cave, then, is the eternal Brahman deposited? He says: in the intellect alone, as a cave. The discerning ones perceive that which is called the Self and called Brahman as non-different and inseparable from the modification of the intellect, indistinguishable from the intellect's own functioning. (4.22)

For what reason, then, does the person undergo the transformation of the mind's forms, or, when that occurs, is there the experience of one's own intellect? From where does this delusion of the nihilists arise—that the mind alone is both the grasped object and the grasper? He says: "The mind, colored by the seer and the seen, has all things as its object. The seer...

The Puruṣa is the seer; the mind, colored by those two—the objects of sight such as sound and so forth—becomes the knower of all objects for the sake of the Puruṣa’s experience and liberation. The mind is colored by the object of its own conceiving, which acts like a magnet through the presence of the object-field; and because it itself is an object, it becomes connected with the Puruṣa—the subject who is not in physical proximity—by means of its own function, namely, through mental cognition, in the capacity of being an object.

This very mind, through its connection with the Puruṣa by way of the activity of the self, becomes colored by the nature of the Seer; or, it is colored by the objects of thought such as sound and so forth. Thus, the mind alone—colored by both the Seer and the seen—is not the Puruṣa. He provides an explanation of the phrase "colored by the Seer and the seen": it appears as both the object and the subject, and assumes the nature of both the conscious and the unconscious.

[356,19] But how is it that the intellect (*buddhi*), which is itself insentient, attains the nature of sentience? This is not a fault, for due to the constant proximity of the Puruṣa, it appears as if sentient; thus, by those who lack discrimination, it is called "sentient. However, the objects are not so; for they are eternally insentient by nature. Since consciousness (*vitti*) is inherently insentient, it is said to have attained the nature of both sentience and insentience [only through association].

The meaning is that it appears as if having the nature of objects, as if being merely the intrinsic form of sound and so forth. The meaning is that it is insentient yet appears as if sentient, as if having attained the nature of the Puruṣa. It is like a crystal gem; just as a crystal gem assumes the form of lac-dye or other substances when in their proximity, in the very same way, that mind is said to be "all-objected."

Therefore, some are deluded by this similarity between the mind and [the self]. This very similarity of the mind is the cause of great confusion for the Vaiśeṣikas. The Vaiśeṣikas and others, their minds bewildered by the magic show of the mind’s similarity [to the self], claim that the mind itself is conscious. Why? Because they maintain that consciousness is a quality produced by the conjunction of the mind and the person (*puruṣa*), and is something to be manifested. However, their distinction from the Nihilists (*Vaināśika*) is that they accept a single, stable substratum (*dharmin*).

Other Buddhists maintain that all this is indeed consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), and that there is no such thing as a cow or a jar characterized by its own form, which is common to the cognition of everyone in the world; thus they even deny their own experience. Being so deluded, these proponents of nihilism (*vaināśika*), whose intellects are exceedingly tender, are truly pitiable.

Why is this? Because they possess the seed of delusion, namely the mind that manifests in the form of all objective appearances (*sarvarūpākāranirbhāsa*). For their delusion is accompanied by a cause (*sanimitta*), unlike that of those who follow worldly expedients, such as the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyatvādin*) and others, whose delusion is seedless (*nirbīja*). However, because they act solely for the purpose of deceiving the world, no compassion should be shown toward them. Therefore, it is rightly said that those wretched ones, whose deluded minds possess seeds, are objects of pity.

[357,17] Who, then, are those who are non-erroneous? He says: "In concentration and wisdom. The mention of "concentration and wisdom" is for the purpose of including the non-erroneous mind. For those whose minds are distracted are erroneous. When concentration and wisdom are non-erroneous—purified, possessed of discernment, and exceedingly clear and profound—the object to be known appears as a reflection within that concentration and wisdom, which acts as the instrument because it has become the objective support (*ālambana*). It is "other" than the wisdom itself by virtue of its genus, essential nature, activity, and so forth, being distinct from that wisdom.

If that other were merely mind (*cittamātra*), how could the form of wisdom (*prajñārūpa*) be apprehended by wisdom itself? Because of the contradiction of an action operating upon its own self, it could not be apprehended in any way whatsoever. Therefore, that object is other than wisdom; it is that in which the object becomes a reflection, and by which it is apprehended. That which exists as the agent (*kartṛkāraka*) distinct from the object that has become the objective support (*ālambana*) of that wisdom is the Person (*puruṣa*).

Thus, because of the distinction between the nature of the grasper (*grahītṛ*), the grasping (*grahaṇa*), and the graspable (*grāhya*), the distinction between agent (*kartṛ*), instrument (*karaṇa*), and object (*karman*) is established; for a single, partless entity cannot simultaneously be both agent and object in a single moment. Therefore, those who distinguish these three according to their essential natures possess right vision (*samyagdarśana*). The meaning is that the "spiritual" (*pauruṣa*) is attained by them; by implication, however, it is understood that it is known.

And from what [source] does there exist a person (puruṣa) distinct from the mind? Previously, the existence of a distinct person was established by means of the mind's being an object of perception. Now, however, because that very mind acts through association, he says the following for the sake of establishing its master: "Though variegated by innumerable latent impressions (vāsanā), it exists for the sake of another, because it acts through association."

[358,15] Even though that very mind is said to be the cause of delusion because it is variegated by innumerable beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), nevertheless it is asserted that it exists for the sake of another—that is, solely for the enjoyment of another. Because it acts through combination, it depends upon the operation of effects, instruments, objects, and so forth; and because it accomplishes a purpose, it acts through combination. Therefore, due to this acting through combination, like a house and other such things, the mind exists for the sake of another. Indeed, nothing whatsoever in the world is seen to act through combination for its own sake.

Therefore, a mind that acts through combination cannot exist for its own sake; for a mind of pleasure does not exist for the sake of pleasure, nor for the sake of the mind of pleasure. Nor does a mind of knowledge exist for the sake of knowledge, nor for the sake of the mind of knowledge. Rather, both this mind of pleasure and the mind of knowledge exist for the sake of another.

And that person who possesses wealth through enjoyment, a mind of happiness, and a mind of knowledge—through liberation—is indeed the supreme being. It is not merely the body, the senses, or the objects of the senses that constitute the "other. For the nihilist does not accept a mind of happiness as having the body, senses, or objects for its purpose. If he were to accept it so, he would contradict his own tenets; for he maintains that the desire for happiness and liberation belongs to consciousness alone.

Therefore, since it is precisely the body, the senses, and consciousness that are conceived as having a desire for pleasure and liberation, one must accept that the person (puruṣa)—who is distinct from the body, the senses, and their objects—is the one who possesses the purpose of enjoyment and liberation, and is other than consciousness.

If the nihilist (*vaināśika*) were to cite some mere general otherness (*parasāmānyamātra*), or if the nihilist—mistakenly imagining that things acting in combination, such as houses and the like, must have a purpose for another who is a composite of Devadatta and so forth, and thus not desiring any specific "other"—were to think in this way, then he should be asked this: Is the "other" the commonality of the body, the sense organs, and the objects of cognition, or is it all of them together? Is it one among these, or is it something of a different category altogether from these?

First of all, it is not a universal (*sāmānya*). For a nihilist (*vaināśika*) does not accept a universal entity as being the object of the pursuit of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), because that would contradict his own tenets. Nor can he maintain that the body and so forth, taken collectively, are the objects of enjoyment and liberation; for he falsely imagines that only the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantati*) possesses the desire for enjoyment and liberation.

Nor is the continuum of cognition (*jñānasantati*) a single entity—since a continuum is by definition momentary—and since the continuum, being a non-entity like the horn of a hare, cannot possess the desire for enjoyment and liberation. Nor does he accept that any one of the body, the sense-faculties, and so forth, constitutes such an entity; for in his own system, he does not admit that those things distinct from consciousness can possess the desire for enjoyment and liberation.

Furthermore, there exists no entity in reality called a "conglomeration" of body and sense-faculties by means of which you might seek for the mind to have the welfare of another as its purpose. For how can that which is not a real entity possess the capacity for seeking? Nor do you admit any other [self] distinct from the body, sense-faculties, and so forth, which is of a different class from their conglomeration. If you were to postulate an unseen being of a different class who possesses the welfare of enjoyment and liberation, that very one is what we call the "Other."
