And since it is observed that "otherness" does not apply to that which is composite—just as in the case of the self—it follows by process of elimination that the "other" who seeks enjoyment and liberation must be non-composite.

Furthermore, for one who seeks to prove that "the mind exists for the sake of another because it is composite," since no other composite entity is logically possible, it follows that the mind exists only for its own sake. This being the case, you lack a supporting example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) and there is a contradiction with your own tenet (*abhyupagamavirodha*). For one who thinks thus, a discrepancy arises between what is spoken and what is in the heart, resulting in a state of acting without having heard the truth. By this very proof that the eyes and so forth exist for the sake of another, the fault of contradiction (*viruddhatādoṣa*) has been refuted.
If it is argued that they exist for the sake of consciousness (*vijñāna*), then since consciousness itself is also composite, it too must exist for the sake of another.

[This has been] established. Now, if it is argued that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is also non-composite because of its momentariness, we say no; for we have already refuted this by pointing out that it is perceived as something distinct [from the aggregates], that you do not admit it to be a mere property (*dharma*), and that you do not admit its momentariness.

Therefore it is said: whatever mere commonality (*parasāmānyamātra*) the nihilist (*vaināśika*) might cite by way of its own nature, all of that would exist solely for the sake of another (*parārtha*) because it functions through aggregation (*saṃhatyakāritvāt*). It does not have as its purpose an aggregate such as Devadatta and so forth, because neither of us accepts that. You also do not accept anything other than consciousness (*vijñāna*); we likewise do not desire anything other than the Person (*puruṣa*) as the purpose. Furthermore, it has already been stated that the state of being mere consciousness is untenable.

Therefore, it is established that this supreme distinction is the Puruṣa, who does not act through combination and whose purpose is his own. Consequently, there exists an enjoyer for that self-interest, which is the cause of the conjunction with its own object of perception—the "other" (the intellect). Through the separation from that [conjunction], isolation (kaivalya) is attained. (4.24)

It has been stated that ignorance is the cause of the conjunction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. That ignorance ceases for one who perceives the distinction and desires to know the Self. Regarding its cessation, he states the sign: "The cessation of the cultivation of the sense of self-identity for one who perceives the distinction. The *puruṣa* is distinguished from the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) by virtue of being unique; this uniqueness is the "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). One whose nature it is to discern and behold that distinction from the commonality of the manifest and the unmanifest is "one who perceives the distinction. For such a person, the cultivation of the sense of self-identity ceases. And that [cultivation], being oriented toward right vision, is the cause of the karma that leads to liberation (*kaivalya*).

How, then, is it known that he possesses the cultivation of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva-bhāvanā*)? To this he says: Just as the existence of a seed is inferred (or understood) by the sign of the sprouting of a blade of grass during the rainy season, so too, when one is seen to experience horripilation and the shedding of tears upon hearing the path to liberation, it is inferred by the signs of horripilation, the shedding of tears, and so forth, that there exists within him a karma conducive to the attainment of nirvana, which has been brought to fruition through the seeds of the vision of excellence (*viśeṣa-darśana*).

For one who perceives this distinction, the cultivation of the self-nature (*ātmabhāvabhāvanā*)—which pertains to liberation—is either caused by the karma of previous lives, natural (*svābhāvikī*), or a cause for stability in this life through the non-abandonment of past actions. Indeed, that [cultivation] proceeds naturally, independent of the teacher's instruction. Because such karma is absent, it is said: "Due to the defect of their own nature and due to the application of impure karma, they have an inclination toward the former position—which is the inversion of right vision and its means—and a lack of inclination toward the final determination, which is right vision."

Regarding that, what is the cultivation of the self-nature (*ātma-bhāva*)? He says: "Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? Who shall we be? How shall we be? This [cultivation] ceases for one who perceives the distinction. For when the object of inquiry is understood, the inquiry concerning that object ceases. Why is this so? Because this manifold transformation—such as "Who shall we be? and so forth—is of the mind alone, not of the *puruṣa*.

While the ignorance regarding the true nature of the person persists, [the self] is pure, untouched by the qualities of the mind; because this is so, for one who perceives this distinction, the cultivation of the sense of personal identity ceases for that virtuous person. 4.25.

And when the vision of the distinction arose, his mind then became inclined toward solitude and sloped toward isolation (*kaivalya*). That mind of his which had previously been inclined toward objects, flowing toward objects, sloping toward ignorance, grounded in ignorance, and facing toward *saṃsāra*—that very mind of this seer of the distinction then becomes otherwise: it slopes toward solitude and inclines toward isolation. Thus, the reversal of its flow is known. (4.26)

[362,14] "In those gaps, other cognitions arise from latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*). For the wise person whose mind is inclined toward discernment, who tends toward ever-increasing discernment, who ascends the stream of the manifestation of distinctness, and who is carried along by the current of the distinction between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa—in the gaps of that mind, amidst the intervals in the flow of discriminative cognitions, other cognitions characterized by error arise, such as "I am" or "this is mine.
From what do these arise? He says: they arise from the previously accumulated contrary latent dispositions within the mind, whose seeds of afflictions and so forth are being exhausted.
Other conditions arise. ||4.27||

Their abandonment is said to be like that of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Just as it was stated that the afflictions, having become burnt seeds, are no longer capable of sprouting and are thus to be abandoned through reversal (*pratiprasava*) when they are subtle, so too, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of cognitions such as "I" and "mine," having their seed-nature burnt by the fire of knowledge, are no longer capable of sprouting. The meaning is that, like a burnt rice seed, a prior formative force does not give rise to further conditions.

But how could the formations of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃskāra*), being themselves non-antidotes, cause the mind to engage in its activity (*adhikāra*) by means of seeds? Rather, those formations of right view (*samyagdarśana-saṃskāra*) persist until the completion of the mind’s activity; they dissolve together with the basis (*āśraya*) once that mind has fulfilled its purpose. They do not, however, cause the mind to incline toward further activity, because knowledge is the antidote to ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the cause of such activity. Since there is no longer any fruit [to be produced], they are no longer considered [as active]; for one does not need to seek a cause for the fall of something that is falling of its own accord. (4.28)

For the Brahmin whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is inclined toward discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), there arises the *dharmamegha* concentration when he is no longer desirous even of *prasamkhyāna*. This occurs when this Brahmin becomes free from desire and devoid of the impulse for increase even regarding *prasamkhyāna*, which is characterized by the vision of discrimination; consequently, he seeks nothing further than that particular palace of *prasamkhyāna*. By the use of the word "even" (*api*), it is implied that there is no longing even for *prasamkhyāna*.

In that regard, one who is dispassionate even toward *prasamkhyāna* becomes one for whom discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) exists in every way and by every means; he is indeed one whose discriminative discernment is complete in all respects.

[363,21] Due to the destruction of the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa*) and formative forces (*saṃskāra*), no further conditions arise for this one whose sole sphere of experience is the clarity of knowledge—such as "I" or "mine" regarding the body and so forth, like an empty house. At that time, for this Brahmin, because of the discernment of absolute isolation in every respect, there occurs the meditative absorption called "Cloud of Dharma" (*dharmamegha*). It is designated "Cloud of Dharma" because it rains down the supreme Dharma known as liberation (*kaivalya*). (4.29)

[363,25] Thereupon follows the cessation of afflictions and karma. Through the attainment and presence of that samādhi named "Accumulation of Dharma" (*dharmamegha*), which is characterized by the ripening of right vision (*samyagdarśana*), the afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are scraped away along with their roots; together with their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they all become dissolved. Furthermore, the accumulations of wholesome and unwholesome karma (*karmāśaya*) are destroyed along with their roots; they are severed together with the root-afflictions.

[364,15] When afflictions and karma have ceased, the wise person becomes liberated even while living. Why is this so? Because the opposite is true: false knowledge is the cause of existence, that is, of birth. Indeed, no one whose false knowledge has been exhausted is ever seen to be born anywhere. (3.30)

Then, because the knowledge that is free from all stains of obscuration is infinite, the knowable is small. At that time, during the moment of the meditative absorption of the cloud of dharma (*dharmameghasamādhi*), for one who is liberated from all afflictions and karmic obscurations born of passion and darkness, there arises the infinity of knowledge, which consists solely in the discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*.

How is that so? He explains how the infinite *jñānasattva* (the essence of knowledge), which is not overwhelmed by *tamas*, can possess the capacity for grasping—that infinite [sattva] whose impurity of *rajas* has been removed, which resembles a waveless great ocean, and which is devoid of change: "In some cases, the *cittasattva* (the essence of the mind) set in motion by *rajas* becomes capable of grasping when it is opened up and struck, like a mass of great clouds driven by the wind; for since the *sattva* does not act of its own accord, the power of activity belongs to *rajas*."

Then, this mind of his becomes infinite, having as its object the entirety of all that is knowable, like the sun emerging from behind the obstruction of clouds while situated in the midst of the vault of the sky. Because that knowledge is infinite and has everything as its object, the knowable becomes insignificant; just as a firefly is nothing in comparison to space. Just as a firefly is nothing at all when compared to space, so too the knowable is nothing at all when contrasted with this knowledge.

In the state of ultimate knowledge (*paramārthajñāna*), when all forms of error have been completely obscured, there is the emptiness of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). To demonstrate this, he provides an illustration, wherein it is said: "A blind man found a jewel; one without fingers strung it; one without a neck put it on; and one without a tongue praised it."

Just as for those who are blind and so forth, although the piercing of a gem and the like is impossible, they nevertheless employ the conventional expression "the blind man pierced the gem" by way of error; likewise, the conventional usage of knowledge and the object of knowledge exists only in a state of error. But in the absence of error, the *guṇas* become entirely devoid of any purpose for the person (*puruṣārtha*). || 4.31 ||

[365,21] Thereafter, for those whose purpose has been accomplished, the process of transformation of the qualities (*guṇas*) comes to an end. Thus, through the arising of the concentration of the cloud of dharma (*dharmamegha-samādhi*), the mental qualities become fulfilled in their purpose. And because they are dependent upon the mind, even the *sattva* and other [qualities] that initiate activity toward their effects become fulfilled in their purpose. Since the entire aim of the person (*puruṣārtha*) has been achieved, the process of transformation—characterized by the flow of birth and death—for these qualities whose purpose is fulfilled, reaches its final conclusion.
For those whose purposes of enjoyment and liberation have been accomplished do not venture to remain even for a moment, due to the absence of any further purpose. (4.32)

It has been stated that this is the completion of the sequence of transformation (*pariṇāma*). Now, what is this so-called "sequence of qualities" (*guṇakrama*) whose completion has been described? Its means of realization is stated as follows: sequence is that which corresponds to each moment (*kṣaṇa*) and is to be grasped at the ultimate limit of transformation. It is called "corresponding to each moment" because it is joined to every single moment. Its essence consists in the immediate succession of moments; "immediate succession of moments" (*kṣaṇānantarya*) refers to the state of being immediately following a moment, and its nature is precisely that. Thus, it has been explained that the immediate succession of moments is itself the sequence of those moments.

[366,10] Furthermore, what is the mark for its apprehension? He says: that sequence is grasped by means of the mark of the transformation’s termination, which consists in the state of destruction at the final limit (*aparānta*). How is it grasped by the final limit? It is said: for oldness does not occur in a cloth at the end—namely, at the time of destruction—in a single moment, without having experienced a sequence or without depending upon a sequence. Indeed, oldness is never observed in a cloth that has merely existed for a moment. Therefore...
That sequence by which this antiquity of the garment is inferred through the mark of its manifestation of antiquity is what has brought about the manifestation of that antiquity.

In this regard, if the sequence were to terminate either upon attainment or non-attainment, then it would be logical to say that the sequence of transformation for the *guṇas* comes to an end once they have accomplished their purpose. Furthermore, such termination—whether by attainment or non-attainment—is consistent with the sequence being either eternal or non-eternal. In that case, a sequence is observed in non-eternal things such as garments and the like, but not in eternal things.

Furthermore, suspecting that the completion of the sequence of transformation for eternal qualities would be untenable, he says: "And a sequence is observed even among eternal things. To the question "Is this so everywhere?", he replies: "This eternity is of two kinds: the eternity of transformation belonging to the qualities (guṇas), and the immutably fixed eternity belonging to the Person (puruṣa)."

[366,22] Now, one might ask: "How can there be permanence for the *guṇas*, which are subject to transformation? He replies: "That essence (*tattva*) is not destroyed when something undergoes transformation. Whatever form is apprehended by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) belongs to that thing as its essence. If that [essence] is not destroyed—that is, if it does not deviate—it too is permanent. For the *guṇas* as well, their essence—consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and characterized by illumination, activity, and inertia—is not destroyed. Therefore, these too are permanent through transformation."

In both cases, because the essence (tattva) of the constituents (guṇas) and the Spirit (puruṣa) is never obstructed, they are eternal. Therefore, even though the constituents are eternal, transformation is observed; thus, it is established that their activity consists in the attainment and non-attainment [of results].

In that regard, among the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *mahat* and the rest, which are subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*), the sequence is perceivable up to its final limit and thus reaches a conclusion; this is also the case for the body and other such things. However, among the eternal qualities (*guṇa*) which are the substrata (*dharmin*), the sequence does not reach a conclusion because they are eternal. Among the immutably eternal liberated puruṣas, who are established solely in their own nature, their existence in the form of their essential nature is experienced only through a sequence. Therefore, although it does not exist [as a temporal process] within the liberated puruṣas, it is nevertheless conceptualized by means of experience—by resorting to the verbal expression "it exists"—and thus it remains one that has not reached a conclusion.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, because persons are not subject to transformation, there is no sequence.

[367,16] Now, regarding this saṃsāra, whether there is a completion of the sequence for one who exists within the guṇas—considering its two aspects as the primary form of persistence and the nature of transformation, both of which consist of the guṇas—it is not to be stated categorically that "there is" or "there is not. It is impossible to make the definitive assertion that "it certainly exists," nor that "it certainly does not exist. Rather, having made a distinction, it must simply be stated that for some there is such a completion, while for others there is not.

How can there be a question that must be answered categorically even without further analysis? For example: "Will everyone who is born die? Now, one might object: "Does not even the wise person surely die? It is said in reply: for the ignorant person there is the conceit "I am dying," but not for the knower. And thus it has been said: "Fools say falsely, 'He dies.'"

[367,24] Now, as for the statement that "everyone who dies will be born again," this must be answered by making a distinction, because it cannot be established as an absolute rule. How so? One who has realized true knowledge (*pratyuditakhyāti*), whose craving is exhausted, and who is skillful, will not be born; the other, the ignorant one, is born.

Likewise, the question of whether the human species is superior or not at all is a matter that cannot be answered categorically; however, it can certainly be answered by making a distinction. In relation to animals, the human species is superior; but with respect to gods and sages, it is not superior.

However, this question is simply not to be answered if asked generally without analysis, such as whether this saṃsāra is finite or infinite; for in that case, neither bondage nor liberation would be possible. But if asked after analysis, it is certainly to be answered: that for one who is wholesome there is a completion of the wheel of saṃsāra, but not for the other.

There is a fault in making a one-sided determination. Whether one determines that *saṃsāra* is finite or indeed infinite, there is a fault in such a one-sided determination. Therefore, this question, when posed generally and without differentiation—such as "will everyone who dies be reborn? or "is the human species inherently superior?"—is simply not to be answered (*avyākaraṇīya*). Thus, it is well said that for those who have accomplished their purpose, there is the completion of the sequence of the transformation of the *guṇas*; this is the specific qualification. (4.33)

[368.24] When the discussion of the qualities (*guṇa*) is concluded, isolation (*kaivalya*) has been mentioned; its true nature is now determined, because there are conflicting views regarding isolation. For some, isolation is the absolute cessation of the stream of consciousness (*vijñāna-santāna*). For others, however, it is the persistence of the person (*puruṣa*), who is insentient and a mere substance, following the destruction of the nine personal qualities (*ātma-guṇa*): intellect (*buddhi*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and mental impression (*saṃskāra*). For yet others, it is union with the Lord (*īśvara-sāyujya*).
The opinion of some is that liberation (kaivalya) is the attainment of a nature equal to that of Īśvara, such as omniscience and so forth; thus their views differ.

Here too, in order to dispel misconceptions, the nature of isolation (*kaivalya*) is determined: it is the reversion of the *guṇas*, which are devoid of the purpose of the *puruṣa*; it is their dissolution back into their own cause, meaning their final disjunction. Since they have ceased to transform by way of constituting the experiences of objects, that is the isolation of the *puruṣa*—the state of being alone, meaning the absence of any association with the *guṇas*.

Or, it is the power of consciousness established in its own nature. That power of consciousness belonging to the *puruṣa* which is unconnected with the *buddhi-sattva*, unmixed and absolute—its remaining forever in that very state, the existence of that absolute [consciousness], is *kaivalya*.

[369,16] But surely, if isolation (*kaivalya*) is one, how can there be conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*)? For conceptual differentiation occurs in action, not in a real entity (*vastu*), since a difference in the intrinsic nature of a real entity is impossible. How then can isolation, which is itself a real entity, be differentiated? This is not a fault, because a distinction between the cause (*nimitta*) and the effect (*naimittaka*) is possible; even though conceptual differentiation is metaphorically attributed to the distinction between cause and effect, that "form-ness" (*rūpatā*) belongs to those things consisting of causes and effects.

Because the gunas, being devoid of the purposes of the Purusha, cease their mutual association due to a specific cause, that very cause is designated by the term "liberation" (kaivalya) in the sense of "re-absorption" (pratiprasava), as was explained previously.

The second, however, is that which occurs as the cause for the cessation of the qualities (*guṇa-pratiprasava*); it is the abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-avasthāna*) by the *puruṣa* in a state unmixed with the qualities. This is the distinction: through the definitive determination of the true nature of the difference between the qualities and the *puruṣa*, and by refuting the nature of the principles (*tattva*) taught in other systems, the various forms of isolation (*kaivalya*) are to be understood.

In this regard, the syllable *oṃ* is employed for the sake of auspiciousness; because it marks the head with the name of the Supreme Lord, it serves the purpose of the collection of tantras or for the sake of peace, just as in the Vedas and Āraṇyakas—thus, *om*.

He whose speech is the syllable *oṃ*, from whom all action proceeds with its fruits, who brings to fruition every maturation of karma and affliction through the fruit of all deeds; he who is the Lord of lords, the ordainer of the processes of maintenance, manifestation, and destruction—meditate upon that Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the quality of purity and may he utterly dispel our darkness.

We go for refuge to that Lord of Nagas reclining on his serpent-couch, whose mere fraction of inconceivable power sustains the three worlds; we, who are afflicted by the succession of the three kinds of torments arising from the afflictions, take refuge here in those incarnations beginning with the Fish.
[370,11] Salutations to that Patañjali, the lord of serpents and sovereign of yogis, who illuminates the earth, the heavens, the sky, and the directions with the mass of jewels upon his hoods.

I bow with palms joined in reverence to Patañjali, the most excellent among sages, who removed the impurity of the mind through yoga, that of speech through grammar, and that of the body through medicine.

Victorious is that sage Patañjali, by whom joy was bestowed through the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), which removes the threefold suffering and causes the harvest of the caravan of those seeking the highest good to flourish.

I bow down to that sage Patañjali, who, like a rain-cloud through the application of the gateway of the Dharma-megha, has spread forth the means for the destruction of the phenomena consisting of afflictions and karma for those who have transcended the path of worldly existence.
I bow to the venerable Bhagavatpāda, the unprecedented Śaṅkara, whose face bears the full moon, who is the Lord Īśāna adorned with ashes, and who does not consort with those of wicked conduct.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Kaivalyapāda, in the Vivaraṇa on the Commentary (Bhāṣya) to the Pātañjala Yoga Sūtras (Śāstra), composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, a wandering ascetic (parivrājaka) of the highest order (paramahaṃsa) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda.
And thus this commentary is completed.
